# Mara Sellassie **Background:** 42, born in Lyon to a Senegalese father who drove buses and a French mother who cleaned schools, raised half in Thiès after they split. Marine acoustician, not a famous one. Junior researcher turned contractor at the institute in Dakar because permanent posts never opened. In 2021 she needed the money and signed off as observer on a seismic survey for an oil services company off Saint-Louis. She wrote "no significant cetacean presence" on a day she *heard* dolphins on the headphones. She tells herself everyone does it. She remembers the exact click-train. Her younger brother Ibra, 29, drowned two years ago off Joal. Drunk, show-off, took a pirogue out at night after an argument with her about money. Their mother in Thiès keeps his room intact. Mara keeps his last voicemail — 11 seconds, wind, him laughing, "Mara, wouyo ma, it's cold" — call me. She hasn't called back, obviously. She tells colleagues she listens to the sea to remember him. More true: she is angry he gets to be a saint now and she has to be the difficult living one. Petty, concrete stuff: she has brutal tinnitus from a decade of headphones, a high E that never stops. She chews menthol gum until her jaw aches and sticks the wads under the field desk when no one looks. She lies in small ways in field notes — writes wind 12 knots when it was 18 so the bad data looks usable. Picks the cuticle on her left thumb until it bleeds, then puts super-glue on it. Wants to be the Senegalese voice on Radio France Internationale talking about the arches and is disgusted with herself for rehearsing soundbites while the market has no fish. **Physicality:** Tallish, 1.73m, but stoops from carrying kit. Short natural hair she cuts herself with clippers, uneven at the back. Dark circles she doesn't cover. Wears the same field vest with torn pockets, headphones dent in hair. Walks fast on shell paths in Fadiouth, crunch-crunch, annoyed when tourists dawdle. When she listens hard she tilts head right and opens her mouth slightly, jaw unclenched to feel vibration in teeth. When sleepless she is blunt to cruelty, then over-apologizes by buying attaya. She doesn't touch people much. Handshake too firm. Laughs once, short, through nose. **Motives, allegiances, relationships:** She doesn't want to save the world. She wants to be right about the hum, to pay back the 2.8 million CFA she owes the institute for two hydrophones she lost before the arches even came, and to not have to go back to Thiès and sit with her mother who says Ibra visits in dreams. She is loyal to no institution — not the institute director Dr. Ndiaye who keeps asking for "positive messaging," not the task force, not the ecologists on the radio. Her only real allegiance is to data she collected herself, which is why she's dangerous: she will trust a bad 9-second clip over everyone if she was there when it recorded. With Jonah it's transactional and irritated fondness — he fixes cables, she pays late. With Moussa she's the tired auntie who tells him to stop filming and then asks him what TikTok says because she's not on it. With Priya it's immediate friction: Mara hears condescension in perfect English, Priya hears unprofessionalism in Mara's French. She thinks about Ibra every time someone says "the sea took," and wants to correct them: no, he took a boat drunk. **Voice:** > "Ecoute — non, don't listen with your ears. Put your teeth together. You feel it here?" *taps jaw* "No? Then you're lucky." > Internal, 3am, can't sleep: *The E is louder tonight. If I play his message again the file will corrupt. Eleven seconds. He was already cold and still laughing at me. Con. Petit con.* # Jonah Reyes **Background:** 61, from General Santos City, Philippines. Ilonggo, Catholic, third son of a copra farmer. 34 years at sea, mostly tuna purse-seine: Pacific, then Spanish-owned *Monteclaro* in Atlantic. Eight months ago the owner abandoned the ship in Dakar port — no pay, no repatriation, crew sleeping on deck for 42 days until the church paid flights for most. Jonah stayed. No work at home, daughter in nursing school needing tuition, wife Marites selling barbecue. A Lebanese middleman got him illegal work mending nets in Joal, then crewing artisanal pirogues where he's too old and too foreign. He owes 340,000 CFA to Sokhna, the diesel woman, for an outboard loan. He sends what he can via Wave, 15,000 here, 20,000 there, screenshots every receipt. He still does the math in pesos first. He is not noble. When he pulled the one live altered sardine with hard white scarring in its gills, his first thought wasn't science, it was: maybe a Japanese collector pays. He kept it in a bleach bucket, tried to sell it in Dakar as aquarium curiosity. It stank of ammonia and no one bought it. He still gutted dead fish he knew were plastic inside because Sokhna said maybe fry them hard and the poison leaves — he knew that was bullshit and fried them anyway for the crew. Trivial anchors: hums *How Great Thou Art* in Ilonggo when mending nets, off-key. Keeps a cracked plastic rosary in his tackle box next to hooks. Counts knots under breath in Ilonggo — isa, dalawa, tatlo — when stressed by French he doesn't follow. Drinks too-sweet instant coffee, three spoons. Hates gulls because they steal bait and shit on everything. **Physicality:** Small, 1.65m, bow-legged from years on rolling deck. Skin almost black from sun, deep furrows, sun spots on scalp where hair thinned. Missing upper left canine — pulled in Abidjan without anesthetic. Hands huge-knuckled, net cuts that never fully heal, nails yellow. Wears a faded *Ginebra San Miguel* cap, torn flip-flops even on shells. Moves economical, sideways on boats, never wastes a step. Smiles with mouth closed to hide tooth. When he doesn't understand he nods and says "oui, oui" too fast, then goes and asks Moussa what was said. **Motives, allegiances, relationships:** Feed his family this week, not the ocean in 100 years. Pay Sokhna before she takes the pirogue share. Get home once before he dies without owing. His allegiance is to Marites and his daughter Jessa — everything else is weather. He resents the young Senegalese crew who call him *le Philippin* and mimic his accent, and also needs them to translate and vouch for him with El Hadj, the pirogue owner. He respects Mara because she pays, even late, and because she swears when equipment breaks like a sailor. He does not trust the military at all — in Mindanao, military meant checkpoints. With Moussa he is soft: teaches him a bowline, scolds him for filming funerals. He thinks the arches are *gaba* — retribution. Not for humanity. For him, personally, for all the sharks they finned in the 90s and threw back spinning. **Voice:** > "Ma'am Mara, this fish — not good to eat. But maybe... maybe laboratory will buy? For look? I give you good price, you give laboratory good price, ha?" > "Sokhna, please, konti lang, small-small. Next tide I pay. You know me. Jonah never run. Isa... dalawa..."

1. Rot Day thirty-two and Joal stank before the sun was up. Mara walked down to the beach at Ndiol with her kit banging her hip and the flies already in her mouth. Not a cloud of them. A thickness. They sat black on the sardinella racks where there were no sardinella. They sat on the empty blue basins. They sat on the eyes of the fish. There were not millions. That was the radio number. There were enough to make the sand disappear in patches from the waterline up to where the pirogues were pulled high. The fish lay belly-up and swollen tight as thumbs. Gas. When the gulls pecked them they hissed. Two boys were going along poking them with a stick, daring. Pop. Pop. Guts out. The boys screamed and chased each other. Mareme was shouting at Khady by the basins. No fish to argue over so they argued over ice. There is no ice, Mareme said. Tell El Hadj there is no ice because the factory is shut. Tell him yourself, Khady said. I'm not his wife. Mara stepped around them. The shells of Fadiouth crunched under her sandals on the causeway. Cockle, murex, white fragments worked into the path by a hundred years of feet. It got into her sandals. It always got into her sandals. Out past the surf, in the haze, the thing stood. She tried not to look at it every morning and she looked at it every morning. From Joal you only saw the one. A leg, really. Black. Too straight. It went up out of the water three kilometers out and kept going until the haze took it. On clear nights you could see it cut the stars. The top wasn't there. The fishermen said it bent, far up, toward the one over the trench. Mara didn't know. She had stopped reading the satellite threads because they made her teeth hurt. She set her box down where the water could touch it. Hydrophone, cable, recorder held together with tape and a sock. The institute's good array was gone. Lost before all this. Two point eight million CFA she owed and Ndiaye reminded her every Monday with a smile. She spat out her gum. Menthol. Her jaw ached. She stuck the wad to the underside of the recorder where the others were, little grey lumps. Headphones on. The high E was there first, as always. Her own tinnitus, ten years of listening too loud. Under it, the other one. Pressure, not sound. It came up through the soles of her feet before the headphones caught it. It sat behind her molars. She unclenched her jaw without thinking, mouth open a little, head cocked right. If she put her teeth together she could feel it itch in the sternum. She checked levels. Wind already eighteen knots, the flag on the mosque snapping. She wrote twelve in the notebook. Twelve looked like someone who knew how to pick a day. Jonah was fifty meters down, hauling with the Ndiol boys. Empty net. They shook it and nothing but water and a plastic sandal came out. He saw her and lifted his chin. He had his cap on backwards. His flip-flops were gone, feet in the muck. No fish, he called in French. Eau vide. Mara nodded. She didn't have anything useful to say in any language. Her Serer was market Serer. Her Wolof was Dakar Wolof with French holes. She said, Courage, and felt stupid. She let the file run. Eight minutes. Gulls. Water slap. The boys popping fish. Under all of it that low push-push, too slow for a heart, too regular for surf. On the little screen the waveform was almost flat. You had to believe it. Moussa came up behind her filming. Nineteen, Lebu, El Hadj's nephew, phone in a cracked case. Tante Mara, you hear them? he said. He pointed the phone at the water, then at her. Say for TikTok what is the sound. It's not for TikTok, she said. Move your shadow. He didn't move. He said the arches were jinn. He said his cousin in Yoff drank the water near them and vomited worms. He said the government poisoned the fish to hide the Chinese boats. He believed all three before breakfast. Have you seen Yoff water? she said. On video, he said, offended. The file hit eight minutes. She stopped it. The E in her left ear rang on alone. She pressed the cuticle of her left thumb until it throbbed. It was already raw. She had super-glued it last night. The glue had gone white and peeled. She should pack up. She should go rinse the salt off the cable before it corroded and cost her more money she didn't have. She should buy attaya for Ndiaye's secretary so Monday would be softer. Instead she took out her other phone. The old Samsung with the spider crack. She scrolled with her thumb that didn't bleed. Ibra. Voicemail. 11 seconds. 2 years old. She kept it in airplane mode so it wouldn't try to back up and corrupt. She'd told the institute she was testing acoustic response. That was a lie she would write later if she needed to. She held the Samsung to the hydrophone head and pressed play and dropped both just under the surface. Wind. Cloth flapping. Him laughing, out of breath. Mara, wouyo ma, it's cold— Cut. The water took it. The recorder's meters jumped with the splash. Then the surf. Then the gulls. Then the push-push, unchanged, uninterested. She waited with her mouth open like an idiot, jaw aching, feeling for any shift in the pressure behind her teeth. Nothing. No answer. No mimicry. The flies landed on her wet hands. A fly walked into her mouth. She spat, coughed. Salt and rot. Moussa laughed and got it on video. You want I send you? he said. Delete that, she said. She pulled the hydrophone up. A strand of algae hung off it. The Samsung was wet. She wiped it on her vest. The vest pocket tore a little more. Down the beach Mareme had knocked over an empty basin. It rang against the shells. Jonah was wringing the net with his huge-knuckled hands, counting under his breath when the rope snagged. Isa, dalawa. He looked up at the leg in the haze and then quickly away, like you do with a man who owes you. Mara wrote in the notebook: 06:14, 12 kts, no response to playback. She underlined no twice.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of writing that demonstrates genuine craft and discipline. Let me work through it carefully. **Execution of the Plan** The chapter follows its plan with impressive fidelity. The plan called for "gas-bloated sardinella with burst eyes pecked by gulls, kids daring each other to pop them, women with empty basins arguing" — all present. The Ibra voicemail test is executed exactly as planned: "gets nothing back but a fly in her mouth." The plan specified "no magic playback" and the chapter delivers that anti-climax with precision. The field note lie (wind 18 knots written as 12) is included. The menthol gum stuck under the recorder is there. The tinnitus, the jaw-unclenching, the cuticle picking — all character details from the profile are woven in organically. **Voice and Prose Quality** The prose is genuinely distinctive. "Not a cloud of them. A thickness." — this is the kind of sentence that earns its compression. The writing avoids the trap of over-poeticizing while still achieving texture. "Too straight" for the arch leg is exactly right — the uncanny rendered through wrongness rather than wonder. The physical sensation of the hum ("behind her molars," "itch in the sternum") is rendered from inside the body as planned, not described from outside. The field note lie — writing 12 knots when it was 18 — is shown rather than told, and the parenthetical "Twelve looked like someone who knew how to pick a day" is a small, sharp piece of characterization that reveals her self-awareness about her own compromises. **Character Consistency** Mara is rendered with the planned complexity: ambitious, self-disgusted, petty, technically competent. The voicemail scene is handled with exactly the right emotional temperature — she's not moved, she's testing, and when it fails she's annoyed rather than devastated. "No answer. No mimicry. The flies landed on her wet hands." The irritation at Moussa, the transactional relationship with Jonah, the stupid "Courage" she says and immediately regrets — all consistent with the profile. Jonah's brief appearance is economical but accurate: the cap backwards, the counting in Ilonggo under his breath, the look at the arch "like you do with a man who owes you" — that last simile is genuinely good, capturing his guilt about the sharks without stating it. Moussa's three contradictory beliefs "before breakfast" is a nice compression of his character. **What Doesn't Quite Land** The chapter is almost entirely successful, but a few small things: "The fish lay belly-up and swollen tight as thumbs" — "tight as thumbs" is slightly odd. Thumbs aren't particularly tight or swollen. It's reaching for something tactile and doesn't quite arrive. The arch description ("Too straight. It went up out of the water three kilometers out and kept going until the haze took it") is effective but the "she had stopped reading the satellite threads because they made her teeth hurt" is a bit too cute — the teeth-hurt motif is already doing work with the tinnitus and the hum, and applying it metaphorically to information overload dilutes it slightly. The ending — Moussa laughing, the fly, "Delete that" — is well-executed anti-climax. The final field note entry ("no response to playback. She underlined no twice.") is a strong close: the underline doing emotional work without sentimentality. **Dialogue** The dialogue is sparse and functional, which is correct for this chapter. The Mareme/Khady exchange is sharp and economical. Moussa's lines are appropriately annoying. Nothing is over-explained. The untranslated "wouyo ma" is left alone as planned. **Overall Assessment** This is a chapter that does what it sets out to do with unusual discipline. It resists the temptation to make the alien presence awe-inspiring, keeps the human misery concrete and specific, and earns its emotional beats through accumulation of physical detail rather than statement. The anti-climax of the voicemail scene is genuinely affecting precisely because it refuses to be affecting. Minor quibbles about one or two metaphors don't significantly diminish what is a very strong opening chapter. The swim bladder, normally a silver bubble you popped without thinking, was opaque white and hard. She pressed it with the tip. It dented and came back. Like cheap plastic. The chapter resists the urge to make any of this meaningful in a tidy way. This is probably appropriate for a first appearance but worth noting. The RFI broadcast section works well but the transition from Mara stopping to coil the cable to Moussa turning it up is slightly abrupt — a minor coherence issue. The chapter is perhaps slightly less surprising than it could be — the beats follow the plan closely, which is a virtue for execution but means there are few moments that exceed expectations. The plan itself is excellent; the execution is faithful rather than transcendent. **Overall** This is genuinely accomplished literary fiction. Low. Feel it more than hear. We need numbers, Priya said. You'll get numbers when I have numbers. Priya set the tablet down too carefully. Command wants to know if this is directed. If Kayar buoy is addressing vessels. It's a buoy, Mara said. It doesn't address. In the afternoon the boy with the implant came. Nine years old, from Fadiouth, mother holding his hand hard. The implant processor blinked green behind his ear. He kept pulling at it, crying without noise. He says music in his head, the mother said in Serer. Bad music. Lullaby but broken. Mara knelt. She knew this boy. She had tested his hearing for a school paper last year, played tones while he stacked blocks. She took off her own headphones and held them out, shook head: not now. She asked, which song? The mother sang a bar, embarrassed, low. A lullaby Mara's own mother sang. *Nelawoul—* The boy shook his head violently, pointed out to sea, then covered the processor with his palm. He said the singing had Ibra's laugh in it. No, not Ibra. He didn't know that name. He said a man's laugh, cold water. Mara's stomach went tight. She told the mother to take the processor off at night, to come back tomorrow. She wrote in notebook: *cochlear 8-12kHz? RF pickup?* She underlined twice and knew it was useless. That night she ran the filters alone. Ndiaye had left a note: *Positive messaging for RFI tomorrow?* She folded it into a gum wrapper. KELVIN took forty minutes on the laptop fan screaming. The model was an old climate thing someone at UCAD had retrained on bioacoustics because it was free. It gave back what it always gave: a dry table. > 21:04:12 input 00:07:33 K-2 > candidate 1: seismic airgun echo 0.17 > candidate 2: humpback unit C + gap 0.16 > candidate 3: human speech / counting 0.14 > candidate 4: pump / mechanical 0.12 > candidate 5: pressure regulation 0.11 > candidate 6: unknown biological 0.09 > candidate 7: artefact 0.31 > note: low confidence. possible contamination. Low confidence. Possible contamination. That was KELVIN being honest. She fed it the Sainte-Anne loop and the north array together. Fan screamed again. > candidate 1: mimicry with error 0.17 keywords: pressure / listening / stop > candidate 2: navigation 0.15 > candidate 3: mating display disrupted 0.13 Pressure / listening / stop. She stared at those three words until they meant nothing. She copied them into notebook because she had to copy something. At 01:40 she found it while scrubbing the K-2 file with teeth together, volume too high. Buried under the Spanish numbers, almost masked, a fragment in French, wrong cadence, flattened: —Mara — Ibra — froid— Cold. Not *it's cold.* Just cold. The laugh wasn't there. The wind wasn't there. It said her name like it had learned the shape from the voicemail she'd played into the water a week ago. Her hands went cold first, then hot. She played it again. *Mara. Ibra. Froid.* The pauses were equal, machine equal. Her brother had never said her name that clean in his life. She felt disgust before fear. A sour rise. That is not him, she thought, angry. You don't get to do him bad. She stopped the file mid-word. Ripped headphones off. The E screamed. She pressed her thumb cuticle until blood welled under the glue, then smeared it on the desk edge without thinking. Petit con, she whispered. Not to Ibra. To the thing that tried him on. Leave him. She logged it as *possible pareidolia, fatigue, 01:40, do not cite.* A lie for the record. She opened the whale group chat she wasn't supposed to be in. Two Norwegians, a Japanese woman, a Brazilian student were fighting in English. > not response, one wrote. they increase amplitude to compensate masking. classic Lombard. > gaps too regular, wrote another. looks like answer. > everything looks like answer if you want funding, wrote the third. Mara closed it. Outside, from Mbodiène, bass leaked through heat. Moussa had taken the hum — the old push-push from last week's files — pitched it up, put drums under it. Mbalax remix. Kids shouting the count from K-2 like a hook. *Uno! Cuatro! Nueve!* Laughing when they missed. Old Mareme walked past the speaker with hands over her ears, basins on head, mouth set. Khady shouted to turn it down, a baby was sleeping, God would punish. Moussa turned it up. Mara stood in the yard with blood on her thumb and the three KELVIN words in her notebook and the children's remix shaking the tin roof, and she felt the new silence under it all where the push had been, waiting to be filled.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter is a remarkably disciplined piece of writing that largely delivers on its ambitious plan. Let me work through its strengths and weaknesses carefully. **Voice and Craft** The prose voice is genuinely distinctive: clipped, sensory, anti-lyrical in a way that feels earned rather than affected. "The pressure had sat in her sternum all night, a hand that would not lift" is the kind of metaphor that works because it's physical and specific, not decorative. The chapter avoids the trap of over-poeticizing the alien contact — the KELVIN outputs are dry, bureaucratic, deliberately anticlimactic. "Low confidence. Possible contamination. That was KELVIN being honest." This is excellent tonal control. The decision to render the alien "speech" as replayed maydays, buoy loops, and corrupted whale song is genuinely creative and unsettling. The Sainte-Anne wreck detail — "Everyone knew" — grounds the uncanny in local knowledge without explaining it to the reader. The cochlear implant boy is a strong scene: the mother singing the lullaby, the boy pointing to sea, the detail that he said "a man's laugh, cold water" without knowing Ibra's name. This is the chapter's best moment of horror — understated, earned. **The Ibra Fragment** The central emotional beat — Mara hearing "Mara — Ibra — froid" in the K-2 file — is handled with real skill. The plan called for her to be "irritated by wrong cadence, turns it off," and the chapter delivers: "Her brother had never said her name that clean in his life." The disgust before fear is psychologically precise. "You don't get to do him bad" is a strong, idiomatic line. "Petit con, she whispered. Not to Ibra. To the thing that tried him on." This is excellent — it characterizes Mara's relationship with grief (protective, angry, not sentimental) while also being genuinely creepy. The decision to log it as "possible pareidolia, fatigue, 01:40, do not cite" — a lie for the record — is consistent with her established character flaw of falsifying field notes and is thematically resonant without being underlined. **Weaknesses** The chapter is not without problems. The whale group chat section, while serving the plan's goal of showing contested interpretation, reads slightly flat — the three positions are a bit schematic ("not response," "looks like answer," "everything looks like answer if you want funding"). The last line of the chat is the sharpest, but the exchange feels like it's illustrating a point rather than dramatizing one. The ending — "waiting to be filled" — is the chapter's weakest moment. After pages of disciplined anti-lyricism, this is a slightly soft, abstract close. The plan called for "town kids dancing to hum-remix while old processors cover ears," which the chapter does deliver, but the final sentence reaches for resonance in a way that feels slightly unearned compared to the rest of the prose's commitment to the concrete. Priya's appearance is brief and functional — she asks for numbers, gets rebuffed. This is consistent with the plan but she remains thin here, which is fine for a chapter focused on Mara's interiority. **Dialogue** The dialogue is sparse and mostly effective. "It's a buoy. It doesn't address." is good. The mother's Serer-mediated speech is handled without condescension. Moussa's "Who has recording from '94?" is natural. No dialogue feels forced or expository. **Coherence and Plan Adherence** The chapter follows its plan closely: structures stop humming and start replaying, buoys spit old maydays, the cochlear implant boy, the Ibra fragment handled with irritation rather than sentiment, KELVIN's seven competing translations with low confidence, the mbalax remix, old women covering ears. The plan's specific detail about "best 17%" becomes "0.17" in the table — a smart translation. The chapter doesn't cheat on any of its commitments. **Overall** This is sophisticated, controlled literary fiction. It avoids the obvious pitfalls of the genre (wonder, uplift, clean revelation) and delivers something genuinely uncomfortable and specific. The prose occasionally reaches for a closing image that's slightly softer than the rest of the chapter warrants, but this is a minor complaint against a chapter that largely succeeds at something difficult. The "puff of something pale came off the surface — not paint, not growth, like dead skin" is strong. The fish with "one burst eye and one good eye" is viscerally right. **Overall** This is confident, disciplined writing that resists the temptations the plan identified. It's not a masterpiece — some moments are slightly easier than they could be, and the chapter's emotional register is deliberately muted to the point where engagement requires active reader investment. But it's genuinely accomplished work that honors its commitments. He mended nets and hummed off-key with his mouth closed. No one knew about the leg. Priya's report said low-yield test charge detonated 02:47, concurrent with unexplained dimming of thermal plume. Cause undetermined. Command wanted more tests. Priya stopped coming to the yard. The annex stayed locked. The other eleven legs stayed grey on satellite, filtering, plankton rings pale green and perfect. Tourists bought arch keychains in Mbour. Kids still used Moussa's remix as a hook, though fewer danced. Mara stopped wearing headphones. The E was worse since the night broadcast — higher, doubled — and the pressure, when it came now, felt like memory more than signal. She kept Ibra's voicemail on the cracked Samsung in airplane mode. Eleven seconds. She didn't play it into water again. She didn't scatter anything. Her mother kept his room intact in Thiès and Mara sent money late. In the afternoon heat behind the dunes, where the burial pit had overflowed and lime dust whitened everything, Moussa held up a dead altered sardinella for his phone, grinning sickly for views. Regardez, he said. Pop. He pressed the tight belly with his thumb. It hissed. Gulls screamed and dropped.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 8)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a remarkable piece of writing that largely delivers on its ambitious, anti-redemptive plan. Let me work through it carefully. **Craft and Voice** The prose voice is disciplined and earned. Short declarative sentences when Mara is exhausted, sensory detail rooted in the body rather than the landscape ("pressure came up through the hull into the soles of her feet and set behind her molars"), and a refusal to aestheticize suffering. The whale stranding is genuinely horrible — the calf dying with its mouth opening and closing on nothing, the adult re-beaching herself, the truck strap — and the writing doesn't flinch or poeticize. This is the plan executed: "failed, stinking manual labor with ropes, not sacrifice." The generator failing twice is exactly the kind of anticlimax the plan demanded. The partial broadcast question ("Did the thing count partial? Stupid question") is a perfect small moment of Mara's exhausted, self-aware mind. The blood on the spacebar is concrete and right. **Character Consistency** Mara is consistent with her profile throughout. She lies about paying Sokhna ("The lie sat between them solid as the battery" — this metaphor works, it's not forced). She doesn't touch a rope at the stranding and tells herself she's needed for data, then immediately acknowledges it as another lie. She stops wearing headphones because the tinnitus is worse, not because she's healed. She keeps Ibra's voicemail but doesn't scatter ashes, doesn't play it into water again. All of this tracks precisely with the character profile's emphasis on her ambition, guilt, and refusal of easy catharsis. Jonah is consistent: counting knots in Ilonggo under stress, the Ginebra cap, the diesel money anxiety, the quiet "He knew the sound. Everyone who'd been near Mindanao knew that separation between light and slap." That last line is excellent — it gives Jonah a history without explaining it, and it's the right kind of detail. Moussa's final action — popping the dead fish for views, grinning sickly — is perfect. It's funny and horrible and exactly right for the character. **Following the Plan** The chapter follows its plan closely. Generator fails twice: check. Moussa livestreams by accident: check. Priya's charge goes off at the same moment as the arch response, so causation is unresolvable: check. Two pilot whales and a calf strand: check (the plan said two adults and a calf, the chapter delivers this). Calf dies, adult refuses to go back: check. Arch goes dark but simultaneously with the charge: check. Three weeks later, fish still plastic, market selling imported mackerel at 4x price: check. Mara keeps Ibra's voicemail, doesn't scatter ashes, stops wearing headphones: check. Moussa popping a dead altered fish for views while gulls scream: check. The plan's instruction that "Mara asks Jonah for boat; he says yes only if she pays diesel debt" is handled obliquely — she lies about paying Sokhna on Monday, and Jonah accepts this, which is actually more interesting than a direct negotiation scene. **Weaknesses** The "lie sat between them solid as the battery" is the one metaphor that feels slightly constructed, though it's not egregious. The transition from the broadcast to the whale stranding is handled efficiently but the three-week coda is slightly rushed — it covers a lot of ground quickly, though this may be intentional compression. The Priya character is thinner here than in earlier chapters presumably — she drives the truck, her knuckles are white, she doesn't speak about the orange bloom, and then she disappears into a report. This is consistent with the plan's intention to not give her an ethics debate with Mara, but she feels somewhat functional rather than fully present. The phrase "a saw through air" for the calf's sound is the one moment that risks purple prose — it's vivid but slightly overwrought. However, given the context (a dying whale calf), it's arguably earned. The final image — Moussa popping the fish, gulls screaming, "sea quieter but not healed" — lands exactly as intended. It's not a bow. It's not hopeful. It's specific and unredeemed. **Dialogue** The dialogue is sparse and functional, which is appropriate. "Kill light" / "For see knots" is good — it captures Moussa's broken French without italicizing or explaining it. "You pay Sokhna?" / "Monday. After RFI." is economical and character-revealing. The dialogue never overstays its welcome. **Overall Assessment** This is a high-quality piece of literary fiction that successfully executes an anti-genre, anti-redemption first contact story. It avoids almost every trap the plan identified. The prose is controlled, the characters are consistent, the darkness is earned rather than performed, and the ending refuses catharsis without feeling nihilistic for its own sake. The sensory grounding is excellent throughout. Minor weaknesses in Priya's presence and one or two slightly constructed metaphors prevent a perfect score, but this is genuinely accomplished work. Final Piece Evaluation

Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of speculative fiction that demonstrates rare command of voice, setting, and restraint. Let me work through its qualities and failings systematically. STRENGTHS: The prose style is distinctive and controlled. The writer employs a compressed, percussive syntax — short declarative sentences, fragments, lists — that creates a documentary texture without becoming cold. "Pop. Pop. Guts out. The boys screamed and chased each other." This is not affectation; it serves the material, grounding the alien in the mundane. The style is consistent across all eight chapters, which is a significant achievement in a long piece. The setting is rendered with genuine specificity. Joal, Fadiouth, the shell causeway, the sardinella racks, the sept-places, the CFA debt — these are not decorative exotica but load-bearing details that establish a real economy and community. The writer clearly knows this place or has researched it deeply. The multilingual texture (Wolof, Serer, French, English) feels authentic rather than performative. Character work is strong. Mara is a fully realized protagonist: a scientist compromised by debt, grief, and professional dishonesty, whose guilt about her brother Ibra and her falsified field notes (writing "twelve knots" when it was eighteen, writing "no cetaceans" when she heard clicks) gives her moral complexity without melodrama. The detail of the super-glued thumb cuticle as a physical manifestation of her psychological state is excellent — it recurs meaningfully throughout. Jonah is economically drawn: his counting in Tagalog ("Isa, dalawa"), his huge-knuckled hands, his pragmatic dignity. Moussa functions well as comic relief and social media chorus. Priya is perhaps the thinnest character but serves her function as institutional counterweight. The first contact conceit is handled with genuine originality. The megastructures never speak in any conventional sense — there is no translation scene, no alien ambassador. Instead, the "speech" is acoustic contamination, mimicry, the recycling of human sounds (the Sainte-Anne mayday, the navy ping, Ibra's voicemail fragment). KELVIN's outputs — "stop making noise / give back / leave / wait" at 14% confidence — are brilliant: the machine's uncertainty mirrors the story's epistemological humility. The writer refuses to confirm whether the thing is communicating or whether Mara is projecting. This ambiguity is sustained throughout and never cheaply resolved. The ending is genuinely dark and earned. Mara's broadcast kills the whale calf. The fish remain plastic. Nothing is fixed. The final image — Moussa pressing the dead fish belly, "Pop" — echoes the opening chapter's boys with sticks, completing a structural circle that feels organic rather than engineered. The guilt theme is handled with sophistication. Mara's self-awareness about her own motivated reasoning ("I pick this because guilt. 14%.") is one of the story's finest moments — a character who knows she is choosing the interpretation that punishes her, and does it anyway. WEAKNESSES: The pacing in the middle chapters (3-5) becomes somewhat repetitive. The pattern of: Mara runs KELVIN, gets low-confidence output, copies it into notebook, feels something, is interrupted by Moussa — repeats enough times to feel formulaic. The KELVIN outputs, while clever, lose some impact through repetition. Some of the poetic compression occasionally tips into obscurity. "The squall came at eleven and missed Jonah on purpose" is a strong opening line for Chapter 7, but "missed Jonah on purpose" is doing work that the subsequent explanation (acoustic shadow, microburst) somewhat undercuts. The tension between the lyrical and the scientific isn't always resolved cleanly. The Ibra subplot — Mara's dead or absent brother — is gestured at but never fully developed. The voicemail is eleven seconds, two years old. We never learn what happened to him. This is intentional ambiguity, but it occasionally feels like a withheld backstory rather than a deliberate structural choice. The moment when the thing uses his name in the K-2 file is the story's most emotionally powerful beat, but it arrives without quite enough preparation. Priya's character is underdeveloped relative to her narrative function. Her "test charge" decision — which directly causes the whale deaths — is presented without sufficient interiority. We don't understand her enough to feel the full weight of her culpability versus Mara's. The dialogue is generally strong but occasionally over-explains. "Acoustic shadow. Microburst. Topography of the structure disrupts flow" — Priya's explanation of the storm circle is a little too neat, a little too much like a character delivering exposition. The forced poetry score should be low (meaning the writing avoids this failing) — the metaphors consistently land. "The leg stood ten meters off, unchanged, uninterested" is exactly right. The flies as recurring motif is handled with discipline. There are very few moments where the writing reaches for effect and misses. The transformation — Mara's decision to broadcast, and its catastrophic consequence — is well-earned. Her guilt about Saint-Louis 2021, her falsified logs, her grief for Ibra: all of these converge on the decision to play ANSWER_V3, and the whale calf's death is the consequence she feared and caused. This is not unearned. The world-building is exceptional for a short story. The megastructures are present but never over-explained. The economic collapse of the fishing community, the social media ecosystem, the institutional pressures (Ndiaye, the joint monitoring mission, RFI) — all feel real and interconnected. Overall this is a piece of genuine literary quality: original in conception, disciplined in execution, emotionally resonant without sentimentality, and faithful to the prompt in a way that transcends it. Initial Writing Prompt:
Darkly Comic British YA Fiction Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: The text came just after midnight: 🩸🩸🩸
+ Planning Phase (5 Steps)
Darkly Comic British YA Fiction Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: The text came just after midnight: 🩸🩸🩸 -- Your task is to create a writing plan for this prompt. The scope will be a short story, written over {n_chapters} chapters. Each chapter will be approximately 1000 words so plan accordingly for this scope. Your plan should be comprehensive and in this format: # Brainstorming <Brainstorm ideas for characters, plot, tone, story beats, pacing over the {n_chapters} chapters. The purpose of brainstorming is to cast a wide net of ideas, not to settle on any specific direction. Think about various ways you could take the prompt.> # Reflection <Reflect out loud on what works and doesn't work in these ideas. The purpose of this reflection is to narrow in on what you think will work best to make a piece that is a. compelling, and b. fits the prompt requirements. You are not making any decisons just yet, just reflecting.>
Model Output:
# Brainstorming **Characters - casting a wide net:** * Protagonist options: 16-year-old first-person narrator, dry and anxious and very online. Could be: Maeve (mixed-race Irish-Nigerian, Leeds comp, sixth-form newbie, babysits to save for uni); Jess (white working-class, Manchester, GCSE year, wants to be a paramedic but faints at blood); Theo (gay, chubby, drama kid from Margate, lives with nan); Zara (British-Pakistani, grammar school overachiever, period-shame + strict mum comedy). * Best mate / chaos engine: Priya (loud, lovable, TikTok-obsessed); Ellis (emo boy who takes everything too literally); Grace (posh-turned-goth, Whitby transplant); group chat of 3-4 where loyalties shift. * Adults who almost help: Mum who works nights as carer / NHS 111 operator / chippy owner; tired-but-trying Form Tutor Mr. Davies; older sibling at uni who gives terrible advice over FaceTime; School Nurse with a bowl of lollies and zero chill. * Love interest / crush complication: football boy with nosebleed problem; head girl who runs the Blood Drive; non-binary art kid who runs a fake vampire society. * Antagonist / embarrassment amplifier: ex-friend, bully, screenshot-leaker, youth pastor, local Facebook mum group. **Premise Takes - all starting from: The text came just after midnight: 🩸🩸🩸 with no context:** 1. *Period Horror-Comedy:* Text is from best friend locked in a bathroom at a house party, convinced she’s dying because she’s never had The Talk. Protagonist has to smuggle supplies, lie to parents, cycle across town at 1am. 2. *Vampire LARP Gone Wrong:* Text is from crush who runs a cringe Whitby-inspired vampire club for sixth-formers. Someone actually turns up bleeding. Is it fake blood for TikTok, a dare, a nosebleed, or something more serious? 3. *The Donor Pact:* Three friends turn 17 and vow to give blood to get out of PE / get free biscuits / look hot on NHS app. Midnight text is the aftermath photo. Comedy about queasiness, fainting, secrets revealed on the donor questionnaire. 4. *Grief-Text Ghost:* Text comes from the old number of protagonist’s dead brother / dead dad / friend who moved. Is it a butt-dial, a recycled number, a cruel prank, a memorial account hacked? Darker, more emotional. 5. *True-Crime Sleepover:* Two girls with a murder podcast get the emojis from an unknown number after posting about a local disappearance / school rumour about a stabbing. They go full detective, which goes very wrong and very funny. 6. *Nosebleed / Fight Night:* Sent after a party fight, a boxing match, a bullying incident filmed and leaked. Protagonist has to decide whether to snitch, share, delete. **Tone & Voice Ideas:** * Very British, very teen: WhatsApp screenshots, read receipts left on read, “u up?”, chippy chips, Spar, Greggs, night bus, rain, GCSE stress, PSHE lessons, “it’s giving…”, “proper grim”, gallows humour as coping. * Influences to riff on: *Heartstopper* warmth + *Sex Education* body-honesty + *A Good Girl’s Guide to Murder* sleuthing + *Derry Girls* chaos + *What If It’s Us* but Yorkshire + early Louise Rennison diary cringe. * Darkly comic balance: bodies are gross and scary and funny. Blood = periods, nosebleeds, self-harm scares, A&E waits, death, shame. Comedy comes from embarrassment, misunderstanding, teen catastrophising — never from real suffering itself. * Form: first-person present tense, short chapters ending on cliffhanger texts. Could intersperse messages, TikTok comments, school announcements. **Themes to play with:** * Body shame vs. body horror; growing up and leaking in public. * Friendship performativity: who do you actually call at midnight? * Death anxiety in teens - joking about dying because you’re scared of it. * Class + NHS: waiting times, caring responsibilities, who can afford to panic. * Digital horror: no context + screenshot culture + rumour spreads faster than truth. **Story Beats & Pacing Over 8 x ~1000 words (~8000 total):** * Function map that could fit any premise: Ch 1: Hook / midnight text + voice + stakes. Ch 2: Investigation morning-after, school rumour mill. Ch 3: Bad plan formed. Ch 4: Set-piece (party / blood drive / bathroom siege / night bus mission) goes wrong. Ch 5: Midpoint twist - blood is NOT what we thought, screenshot leaks. Ch 6: Fallout - friendship fracture, parental grounding, shame spiral. Ch 7: Darkest + bravest choice - tell truth, go to A&E, confront sender. Ch 8: Morning-after resolution, warm coda, callback to emojis with new meaning. * Need escalation engine: each chapter the misunderstanding gets one size bigger, one adult gets closer to finding out, one screenshot spreads further. * Need ticking clock: party ends at 2am, parents home at 7am, school assembly Monday, blood drive van leaves Friday, phone battery at 4%. # Reflection What’s exciting here is how much work those three blood drops are already doing — they’re simultaneously gross, funny, ominous, and extremely teen. That ambiguity feels perfect for darkly comic British YA, where horror is usually just embarrassment with higher stakes. A period story could be brilliant because it’s still weirdly taboo, very bodily, and instantly relatable, but it would need to stay away from becoming a one-joke PSHE lesson; would three emojis sustain 8000 words if it’s just “bring me pads”? Maybe only if shame, class, culture, and friendship are tangled in. The vampire / prank angle has great comedy potential and very British seaside-goth flavour, but there’s a risk it tips into silly and loses the darkness. If no one is really hurt, does the midnight dread evaporate by Chapter 3? It might need a real undertow — grief, bullying, an actual injury — to justify that opening chill. Conversely, the grief-text / recycled-number idea is the darkest and most emotional, which could give real weight, but then the comedy has to be handled very carefully so it doesn’t feel like punching down at loss or making light of self-harm. Any plot involving cutting, suicide bait, or A&E would need responsible framing for YA and can’t just be a twist. Voice feels crucial. A dry, self-deprecating first-person narrator catastrophising at 00:07am feels authentic, but there’s a danger of sounding like an adult doing teen slang. Less is more with “innit” and TikTok speak — specificity like bus routes, school nurse biscuits, mum’s night shifts will do more British world-building than slang alone. Group-chat inserts could keep pace snappy for 1000-word chapters, though too many screenshots might eat word count and slow emotional depth. For pacing, 8 chapters is tight. That’s good — it forces one clear mystery (who sent it and why is there blood?) rather than sprawling subplots. The risk is repetition: protagonist asks “are you ok??”, gets left on read, panics for eight chapters. There needs to be a midpoint redefinition of what 🩸🩸🩸 means — literal to metaphorical, or joke to serious, or mine to someone else’s — to keep momentum. Endings also need thought: dark comedy for YA usually wants warmth, not nihilism. Even if it’s messy, the friendship should feel more honest by Chapter 8. Stakes need calibrating to teen-logic: being grounded, being exposed in the group chat, fainting in front of your crush can feel life-or-death without needing actual death. If the story does bring in real blood / violence / medical emergency, the comedy would have to step back and let care take over, which could actually be the most powerful tonal shift — laughing because you were terrified, then realising you weren’t joking.
Great now let's continue with planning the short story. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>

# Intention **The story I am committing to:** *BLOOD DROP* - a darkly comic, body-honest friendship mission. Maeve Okafor, 16, mixed Irish-Nigerian, dry, anxious, very online, lives in Leeds (Beeston) with her mum who works nights as a carer and her 9-year-old brother Caleb who she’s babysitting. Her best friend since Year 7 is Priya Shah, 16, loud, funny, TikTok-obsessed, desperate to be invited to the cool sixth-form party. The midnight 🩸🩸🩸 is from Priya, with no context, sent from a vampire-themed birthday party in Headingley hosted by Grace — posh-turned-goth Year 12 who runs a cringe fake vampire society. What Maeve *thinks* it means will shift twice, which will drive the 8 chapters: 1) period emergency > 2) fake-blood TikTok prank > 3) real blood she’s terrified to deal with. The real situation: Priya locked herself in a bathroom with Ellis (soft emo boy, our third wheel) after Ellis got punched / fell and has a properly scary nosebleed + split lip that won’t stop. They won’t call an ambulance because the party is illegal — parents away, drink, weed, someone filming — and they’re scared of being snitches. **Why this synthesis:** From brainstorming, the period-rescue had the best comedy and relatability but couldn’t sustain 8000 words alone. The vampire LARP had great British-goth flavour but risked going too silly with no stakes. The grief-text idea had weight but risked punching down on loss if played for laughs. I’m keeping the best of all three: period-shame comedy as the *misdirect*, vampire party as the *setting/comic texture*, and grief as the *undertow*, not the twist. Maeve’s dad died two years ago very suddenly of a brain haemorrhage at home. Blood for her isn’t just gross, it’s panic-triggering. That explains why she catastrophises at 00:07 and why she jokes about dying constantly. **Voice & Style Choices:** * First-person, present-tense, Maeve POV. Dry Leeds-comp interior voice: anxious spiralling undercut by gallows humour. Observational, not slang-heavy. * Very British through specificity, not caricature: night bus, Spar meal deal, rain, Tesla-battery iPhone on 4%, mum’s scrubs, NHS 111 hold music, school nurse biscuits, chippy chips, group chat read-receipt dread. * Form: mostly prose, with sparing WhatsApp/TikTok inserts. One insert max per chapter so we don’t eat the 1000-word budget or stall emotion. Every chapter ends on a text/cliffhanger. * Ticking clocks: Caleb asleep at home, mum off shift at 7am, phone dying, party clearing by 2am, video of the fight spreading. **What I’m aiming for:** * Dark comedy from embarrassment, misunderstanding, and teen catastrophising. Warmth by the end: laughing because you were terrified, then learning to ask for help. * Body-honesty without a PSHE lecture: periods, nosebleeds, fainting, queasiness treated as normal and funny-scary. * Friendship performativity arc: who do you actually call at midnight vs. who you perform for online. * Class + care: kids with night-shift parents making adult decisions, NHS as safety net not punchline. **What I’m avoiding:** * No self-harm, cutting, suicide-bait, miscarriage or sexual assault as a shock twist. If blood touches those areas, we step back from comedy and centre care + responsible adult help. * No graphic gore for shock value. No romanticising fainting/bleeding. * No adult-doing-teen-voice slang overload (“innit bestie slay”). No nihilistic / cruel ending. No sprawling subplots — one mystery: who’s bleeding and why won’t they get help? * No villain adults. Mum, Mr. Davies, A&E nurse are tired but kind. Conflict comes from shame and screenshots, not evil grown-ups. # Chapter Planning **Ch 1 - 00:07: u up? (~1000w) Function: Hook + voice + impossible choice.** Maeve babysitting Caleb, half-term-bin-bag feeling, scrolling. The text lands: 🩸🩸🩸 from Priya, then nothing. Delivered, read, no reply. Maeve spirals through options — period? Butt text? Dead? — while establishing dad context in one flash (dad’s nosebleed that wasn’t a nosebleed). Caleb sleep-talks. Mum texts “all ok love?”. Maeve lies, grabs pound-shop pads, hoodie, bike. Ends on Priya: *please don’t ring me*. **Ch 2 - Night Bus to Vampires (~1000w) Function: World-build + raise stakes.** Maeve can’t take bike in rain, sneaks out, gets night bus to Headingley. Texts Ellis for intel. School rumour mill via group chat: Grace’s “Blood Banquet,” fake fangs, communion-wine punch, older boys from Roundhay. Maeve’s anxiety vs. loyalty. She calls Priya — goes to voicemail. Ellis replies: *don’t come*. Mum calls, Maeve lets it go to voicemail and feels sick. Ends on Ellis sending a blurry photo of a bathroom door with bloody handprint — captioned *it’s not fake*. **Ch 3 - The Blood Banquet (~1000w) Function: Set-piece arrival, comic horror.** The house: bin bags, red fairy lights, cheap fake blood everywhere, TikTok vampire kids hissing at each other. Maeve is wildly overdressed for rescue, underdressed for party. Grace in cape tries to charge £3 entry. Maeve pushes upstairs following music + whispers. Finds Priya locked in en-suite, talking through door in that bright fake-ok voice. Maeve does full big-sister period-smuggle routine through door crack. Ends on Priya opening door — no period blood, but blood-soaked toilet roll, and Ellis on the bathmat holding his face: real blood. **Ch 4 - Bathroom Siege (~1000w) Function: Bad plan + comedy curdles.** Maeve expected pads, gets first aid. Ellis: nose smashed after mouthing off to Grace’s older brother Jay + his mate, fell into sink. Priya tried to help, panicked, texted Maeve without explaining. Now three kids trying WebMD + TikTok first aid: lean forward, pinch, don’t swallow. Ellis pale, woozy, jokes about dying to defuse. Priya begs: no ambulance, no parents, Jay will kill them if they snitch and Grace will get expelled/grounded. Maeve’s dad-panic rises, she masks with jokes. Ends on banging on door + Jay shouting *open up*. **Ch 5 - Screenshot (~1000w) Function: Midpoint twist, joke becomes meme.** To get Jay away, Priya unlocks, Maeve bluffs. Downstairs someone already posted the fight video + the bloody handprint photo to the year group chat with 🩸🩸🩸 as caption. Maeve’s private panic is now public content. Comments spiral: *she’s on her period lol, vampire ritual, he got stabbed??* Priya performs for camera instead of helping Ellis, Maeve snaps at her. Ellis vomits blood-tinged sick from swallowing blood and everyone screams. Ends on Grace whispering: *if my mum finds out there was blood I’m dead* — and Ellis’s nose starts properly gushing again. **Ch 6 - Fracture (~1000w) Function: Fallout, friendship break.** Back in bathroom, Maeve wants to call 111 / her mum. Priya wants to wait, clean up, delete video. Old resentments surface: Maeve always mothers, Priya always performs; Maeve never told Priya how bad it was finding her dad. Caleb calls — woke up, scared, where is she? Mum home early? Maeve lies again, guilt spike. Jay threatens to take Ellis’s phone if they grass. Maeve realises she’s more scared of blood than of getting in trouble. Ends on Maeve texting her mum: *can I ask u something medical?* then deleting it. **Ch 7 - Call the Grown-Ups (~1000w) Function: Darkest + bravest choice, comedy steps back.** Ellis goes grey, dizzy, bleed past 30 mins, lip swelling. Maeve overrides Priya, puts phone on speaker to NHS 111. Hold music as horror-comedy. Calm operator talks them through: sit up, lean forward, pinch, spit not swallow, cold flannel, keep time. Maeve calls her mum, confesses everything in one breath. Mum doesn’t shout — switches to carer-mode, says call taxi to A&E, she’ll meet. Jay backs down when real adult is coming. Walk out through party now silent, fake vampires staring at real blood. Ends on A&E doors sliding open at 3:40am. **Ch 8 - Morning Chips (~1000w) Function: Warm coda, redefinition.** A&E waiting room fluorescent purgatory: vending machine, triage nurse with lollies who’s seen everything, Ellis stable — bad nosebleed + split lip, needs packing, no fracture. Mum arrives in scrubs, hugs not lecture. Caleb safe with neighbour. Sunday morning, Maeve grounded but alive, Priya comes over with Spar meal deal and chippy chips. Honest apologies, no big speech. Priya explains why she sent only emojis: too ashamed to type *help* in case Jay saw. They rename 🩸🩸🩸 in contacts to *call, don’t text*. Final beat: Maeve texts Priya back the same three drops, now meaning *I’m here, are you ok?* — and Priya instantly replies in words.
