Initial Writing Prompt:
Space Western Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: Captain, something's... moving in that crate we picked up.
+ Planning Phase (5 Steps)
Space Western Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: Captain, something&#x27;s... moving in that crate we picked up. -- Your task is to create a writing plan for this prompt. The scope will be a short story, written over {n_chapters} chapters. Each chapter will be approximately 1000 words so plan accordingly for this scope. Your plan should be comprehensive and in this format: # Brainstorming <Brainstorm ideas for characters, plot, tone, story beats, pacing over the {n_chapters} chapters. The purpose of brainstorming is to cast a wide net of ideas, not to settle on any specific direction. Think about various ways you could take the prompt.> # Reflection <Reflect out loud on what works and doesn't work in these ideas. The purpose of this reflection is to narrow in on what you think will work best to make a piece that is a. compelling, and b. fits the prompt requirements. You are not making any decisons just yet, just reflecting.>
Model Output:
# Brainstorming **Characters - Who says the line, and who is the Captain?** - The Captain as weary ex-war pilot turned freighter captain: Silas Kane, Jonah Voss, Elena "Ellie" Vance, Ada Reyes. A Civil War / Fleet War veteran who bought a decommissioned patrol skiff and now hauls legal-ish cargo rim-to-rim. Haunted, dry-humored, lives by a Code. - The Captain as young inheritor: just inherited the ship *Longhorn* / *Calamity* / *Burro* from a dead parent, trying to earn crew respect. The crate incident is their first real test. - The speaker: a greenhorn deckhand / stableboy-in-space who signed on at the last dustport. Nervous, earnest, first time off-planet. Perfect for "Captain, something's... moving..." - The speaker as a cynical veteran first mate: a former marshal, a cybernetic cook, a ship's doc who has seen too much. If *they're* scared, we know it's serious. - Crew ensemble options for a tight 8k-word cast (3-5 max): - First Mate / Muscle, Doc / Vet / Sawbones, Tinkerer / Blacksmith-Mechanic who talks to engines like horses, Stowaway kid, Preacher-bot, Corporate Marshal chasing them. - A talking ship AI with a Western drawl. A mule-like loader droid. - Antagonists: claim baron, railroad-equivalent Helios Combine building a jump-gate, rustlers, bounty hunter, frontier marshal, smuggler who gave them the crate. **Setting - How Western, How Space?** - Frontier planet hopping: Dustvale, Perdition's Rest, Cinder Gulch Station - terraforming half-failed towns with saloons under domes, dust storms that short circuits. - The ship as covered wagon / stagecoach / steam train: a rattling Class-C hauler *Mesa Verde*, solar sails like canvas, plasma six-shooters and lever-action rifles, hover-horses and sand-crawlers. - The job: picked up an unmarked crate at a waystation with no questions asked for extra fuel money. Classic stagecoach-with-a-locked-strongbox setup, but in orbit. - Law and order: no FTL comms out here, just Rangers on patrol circuits that come through once a season. You handle justice yourself. **What's In The Crate? - Cast the widest net:** - Horror / Creature: xenomorph-like burrower, void-mimic that echoes voices, sand-worm larva, swarm of needle-wasps, skinwalker entity that got mined up, sentient cactus-spores. - Person: smuggled child, indentured clone, wounded outlaw playing dead, cryo-frozen marshal with a bounty on their head, mail-order bride/groom in stasis, runaway synth. - Thing That Seems Alive: terraforming seed-core that pulses like a heart, AI core dreaming, ancient First Folk artifact, unstable reactor / embryo bank of gene-modded longhorn cattle. - Trick / Subversion: nothing dangerous at all - it's kittens, dust-pups, thirsty homing pigeons. Comedy of escalating paranoia. - Moral Trojan Horse: bioweapon, plague blankets 2.0, indentured labor "stock," water claim deed, stolen memories. - Meta-Western: it's gold - literally, self-replicating ore that "moves" and draws every claim-jumper for parsecs. **Tone Options:** - *Firefly*-style found-family banter: warm, quippy, lived-in, with gut-punch stakes. - Bleak Cormac McCarthy in space: sparse, violent, cosmic indifference, dust and blood. - Campfire ghost story / *Twilight Zone* episode: slow dread, creaks in the hull. - Coen Brothers dark comedy: idiots out of their depth, escalating bad decisions. - True Grit earnest adventure: young POV, clear right/wrong, coming-of-age. - Neo-Western thriller: *No Country for Old Men* pursuit - unstoppable tracker after the crate. **Story Beats & Pacing Across 8 x 1000 Words:** - Idea A - Slow Burn Mystery: Ch 1-2 normal haul life + pickup, Ch 2 ender = the line. Ch 3-4 debate to open / don't open, rules of salvage. Ch 5 open, Ch 6 consequences, Ch 7 chase/showdown, Ch 8 cost and choice. - Idea B - Monster-of-the-Week: open it early (Ch 3) and spend 5 chapters dealing with it loose on ship like rustlers cutting herd. - Idea C - Bottle Western: entire story barely leaves the ship. Ship breaks down adrift, crate ticking, crew turning on each other. - Idea D - Town Structure: each chapter is a stop - pickup, waystation rumors, boomtown saloon, ambush at dry gulch canyon in space, etc., crate as MacGuffin pulling them forward. - Idea E - Unreliable Crate: it only "moves" when one character is near. Is it haunted, psychic, or is the greenhorn lying? - Cold open possibilities: start *in medias res* with the line itself as line one, vs. build 1000 words of dusty worldbuilding first. - Chapter cliffhanger engine: every chapter ends on a Western beat - a knock, a light on the horizon, a stranger at the airlock, a countdown. **Themes To Chew On:** - What is cargo vs. what is kin? Slavery / cattle / personhood on the frontier. - The Code vs. The Contract: you took money to not look, but decency says look. - Frontier myth: taming vs. respecting the unknown world. - Debt and ownership: ship mortgage, company store in orbit, who really owns what you carry? # Reflection I'm turning over how much Western vs. how much Space this needs to be, because it's easy to make it just sci-fi with hats. The ideas that lean into Western *functions* - the stagecoach strongbox, the cattle drive, the small town with no law, the debt to the company store - feel stronger than just surface props like ponchos and revolvers. A crate that can't be opened because of a contract is a great sci-fi update of "don't open the strongbox." On the crate contents, I'm weighing shock vs. sustainability. A straight monster gives instant dread and a great Ch 3-4 hook, and fits the line perfectly, but over 8 chapters - 8000 words - a pure creature could get repetitive or turn into *Alien* fan-fiction unless it ties to a Western dilemma. Like, what if killing it is like putting down infected cattle - do you burn the whole herd to save the town? That adds weight. On the other hand, the human-in-the-crate ideas - a kid, a clone, a fugitive - might sustain emotion better for 1000-word chapters. There's more to talk about, more moral arguing around the galley table, which is prime Western material. But the risk is the "moving" mystery deflates too early if we reveal a person in Ch 4 and then have 4000 words left. Maybe the person is only half the mystery. The comedic/subversive takes - it's just animals, it's mostly harmless - could be charming and different, but I'm wondering if they can carry tension for 8 chapters without feeling like a shaggy-dog joke. They might work better as a feint: starts funny, then turns serious when we learn *why* someone smuggled dust-pups. For cast, I'm noticing a tension between wanting a big rowdy crew and what 8000 words can actually hold. Three to four well-drawn voices with distinct stances toward the crate - open it, space it, sell it, protect it - feels more workable than six thin ones. And the Captain dynamic matters a lot: a weary veteran gives instant gravitas and a Code to test, but a rookie captain gives more growth arc. Which better serves a short punch? For pacing, I'm thinking about where to place that line. If it's the prompt, readers will expect it early - probably end of Ch 1 or middle of Ch 2. Waiting until Ch 3 might frustrate. But opening it too fast could burn the mystery. There's a sweet spot where Ch 1 establishes normal frontier life and debt pressure so taking the shady crate makes sense, Ch 2 ends on the knock... and then Ch 3-5 can milk paranoia without opening. The "don't open" pressure has to be strong and specific - not just curiosity, but losing pay, breaking vacuum seal, waking something. Tone-wise, the warm-found-family with horror intruding seems most flexible for 8 chapters - you can have banter in Ch 1-2, dread in Ch 3-5, action in Ch 6-7, and a heartfelt cost in Ch 8. Pure bleakness might be powerful but exhausting and harder to make readers attach in only 1000 words per chapter. Pure comedy might undercut stakes when we need a shootout. I'm also circling the ending shape. An episodic "deliver the crate and ride off" feels classically Western and tidy for a short story, but an "you can't deliver it, you have to choose" feels more memorable. Does the Captain return to law, break the contract, adopt the thing? The crate needs to force a choice that costs them fuel, money, or blood - otherwise why tell this story in 8 chapters? Lots of strong threads here, and none fully cancel the others yet - I need to think about which combination gives a fresh reveal, keeps Western soul, and can stretch/compress cleanly into eight roughly equal acts without padding or rushing.
Great now let's continue with planning the short story. Output in this format: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **The story I am committing to:** *The Long Haul of the Mesa Verde* — a warm found-family Space Western with creeping horror that turns into a moral chase. **Plot choice:** The crew of the rattling Class-C hauler *Mesa Verde* takes a no-questions, sealed crate at Dustvale to cover their ship mortgage. Mid-drift, greenhorn deckhand Milo hears it moving. The crate holds not a monster *or* a person, but both bonded together: a smuggled ~10-year-old gene-wrought girl, Lumen, in failing stasis, symbiotically fused to a living terraforming organism the Combine calls Green — a pulsing root-cactus-fungal mass that mimics voices, knocks from inside, and grows toward water/heat. Harlan Kett of the Helios Combine (our railroad baron building a jump-gate) wants her back as livestock/property. A tracker, The Vulture, is coming to repossess. The Captain must break contract and Code to choose kin over cargo. Why this hybrid: pure-monster would burn out and become *Alien*-with-hats over 8000 words; pure-person would deflate the mystery too early; pure-comedy wouldn't sustain stakes. A living child + living terraformer lets me have Ch. 3-4 dread *and* Ch. 5-8 heart and pursuit, and it makes the Western theme literal: what do you do with a living calf that is also a claim deed? Burn the herd to save the town, or protect one head against the Company? **Cast — kept tight to fit 8 x 1000 words (4 souls + 1 pursuer):** - Captain Jonah Voss, 50s, ex-Fleet patrol turned hauler. Weary, dry, lives by a posted Code: *Deliver what you take. No peeking. No people as freight.* This gives instant gravitas to test. He doesn't get a growth arc from rookie to hero, he gets a cost arc from Code-keeper to Code-breaker. - Milo Tiller, 17, greenhorn deckhand on first run off Perdition's Rest. My POV anchor. Earnest, True Grit voice. He says the prompt line. He bonds with the crate, giving us coming-of-age without making the Captain naive. - Rosa Quill, First Mate / ex-frontier marshal, cybernetic left arm. Cynical, practical. Votes to space it. If *she's* scared, readers are scared. - Doc Tinker (Silas Park), ship's sawbones-mechanic who talks to engines like mules. Warm, curious. Votes to open it. Provides exposition without info-dump. - Off-ship pressure: Harlan Kett (voice on contract only) + The Vulture, a near-silent salvage-hunter in a patched pressure-duster. One unstoppable tracker is enough; no army. **Voice & POV:** 3rd-person limited, close on Milo throughout. Present-tense-leaning past tense, plainspoken frontier diction layered over lived-in tech: solar-canvas, plasma six-shooters, lever-action coil rifles, dome-saloons, dust that shorts circuits, airlock as corral gate. Banter for warmth, sparse Cormac-like landscape beats for dread: creaks, heat-ticks, recycled air tasting of copper. **Structure & pacing:** Cold open normal life, not action. The prompt line *"Captain, something's... moving in that crate we picked up"* lands verbatim as the final line of Chapter 1. That respects reader expectation and gives me 7 chapters to pay it off. Bottle-Western pressure: 90% on ship adrift after a dust-storm fries their drive in Ch. 2, so they can't outrun the problem and must argue around the galley table. Every chapter ends on a Western cliffhanger beat: a knock, a light, a stranger at the lock. Chapter rhythm: 1-2 Setup + Inciting, 3-4 Paranoia/Debate (don't open), 5 Reveal (open), 6 Consequence (it gets loose / bonds), 7 Chase/Showdown at Dry Gulch (abandoned gate station), 8 Choice + Cost. **What I aim for:** - Western *functions*, not props: strongbox contract, cattle-drive quarantine dilemma, company-store debt, town-with-no-law, high-noon standoff at an airlock. - Sensory, filmable 1000-word blocks: one location, one job, one turn per chapter. - Escalating moral stakes tied to physical stakes: seal = pay, open = blacklist + bio-risk, keep = hunted, deliver = complicit, free = broke and marked. **What I avoid:** - Large ensemble, rotating POVs, lore dumps about the Fleet War / Combine. - Opening the crate before Ch. 5 — curiosity must be blocked by specific pressures (loss of pay, vacuum-seal warning, Rosa's law). - Nihilism or gag comedy. Banter is allowed in Ch. 1-2 and 6, but Ch. 3-5 stays dreadful and Ch. 7-8 stays costly. No tidy “deliver and ride off” — they will lose money, fuel, and clean status to do right. # Chapter Planning **Ch. 1 — Dustvale Pickup (~1000w):** Establish normal haul life, debt to Harlan Kett’s fuel store, ship-as-stagecoach. Take sealed Helios crate for double pay, terms: sealed, unlogged, no scan. Launch, quiet drift. Heartbeat banter. Final line: Milo to Voss, *“Captain, something's... moving in that crate we picked up.”* **Ch. 2 — Quarantine Rules (~1000w):** Drive fried by ion-dust, adrift two days from Perdition's Rest. Crate ticks/knocks, mimics Milo’s name in Rosa’s voice. Galley debate: Code says don’t open, contract says forfeit if seal breaks, Tinker warns bio-seal. Voss orders: no one touches it. Cliffhanger: interior cam dies, then a small green tendril slips under the crate lid. **Ch. 3 — Night Watch (~1000w):** Bottle dread. Milo on watch, hears scratching, lullaby humming. Rosa tells marshal story about plague-blanket smuggling. Tinker scans: heat signature in two rhythms — one human-slow, one fast-root-fast. They decide to vent the hold to cold to slow it. Cliffhanger: when cold hits, it *screams* like a calf. **Ch. 4 — The Strongbox Argument (~1000w):** Milo wants to open; Rosa wants to space it at dawn; Voss holds Code. Flash of Kett’s terms: crate is “agricultural stock.” Milo realizes that means living freight. Ship picks up a distant ping — The Vulture on intercept, polite hail: *“You’re hauling Combine property.”* Cliffhanger: Voss lies for the first time: “Manifest’s clean.” **Ch. 5 — Opening (~1000w):** Stasis fails, girl’s vitals crash, forcing them to break seal to save a life (Code loophole: no people as freight supersedes no peeking). Inside: Lumen, pale, root-veins of Green through her arms into a seed-core pulsing like a heart. She wakes, calls it “my garden.” Tinker: she’s gene-wrought to carry terraforming biome; without water/heat she dies and Green sporulates wildly. Cliffhanger: Lumen looks at Milo: “They’re coming to cut it out of me.” **Ch. 6 — Loose Head (~1000w):** Green spreads through hold toward water recyclers, seals doors, mimics crew to lure Milo. Warm bonding beat: Milo waters it, Lumen laughs for first time. Rosa softens, teaches Lumen to shoot a (disarmed) coil pistol — found-family peak. Cost: engine water gone, air thinning. Cliffhanger: Vulture docks without permission — magnetic clamp thud on airlock. **Ch. 7 — High Noon at Dry Gulch (~1000w):** Standoff inside crippled gate-station where they limped to hide. Vulture offers clean deal: return stock, debt cleared, no blacklist. Voss refuses once he sees removal kit = vivisection tray. Gunfight with Western blocking but space logic: depressurization, lasso-cable, cattle-prod, dust-pups? No — Green as stampede, bursting through vents to shield Lumen. Rosa wounded. Cliffhanger: Voss must choose — hand over seed-core (kill girl, save crew/ship) or run with both and lose everything. **Ch. 8 — What We Carry (~1000w):** Choice + cost. Voss burns contract, frees Lumen/Green into Perdition’s Rest dry arroyo where Green can root and make water — trading private miracle for public town instead of Combine gate monopoly. They arrive broke, blacklisted, drive dead, Rosa bleeding but alive. Final image: green shoots in red dust, Lumen breathing unassisted, Milo hired on proper this time. Voss rewrites Code on galley wall. Last line ride-off: not rich, not clean, but kin.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
This is a strong, workable plan — which is exactly the problem. It reads like a good LLM plan. Competent, kind, symmetrical, filmable, and a little too eager to please everyone. Let's pull it apart before we write a word. ### 1. How a human writer would actually approach "Captain, something's... moving in that crate we picked up." A human doesn't start with worldbuilding. They start with a *sound* and a *shame*. That line is not exposition. It's a workplace moment: a kid who doesn't want to look stupid in front of the boss, interrupting, trailing off mid-sentence because he's embarrassed to say it out loud. A human writer hears the class dynamic first — who gets to be scared, who has to pretend not to be. A human would likely bring in one personal crate: moving house, farm work, a deployment, a truck job, a night shift in a warehouse where something leaked / smelled / ticked. They'd write the weight of it, the bad back, the cheap latch, the way you kick a box before you open it. They'd linger on labor, not lore: inventory forms, fuel receipts, who cleans the filter when something clogs it. A human would also be perverse, specific, and withholding. They might keep the crate closed for far too long out of stubbornness. They might make the captain *wrong* for three chapters and not apologize neatly. They might let a character be petty about rations while something is possibly dying six feet away. They wouldn't feel the need to explain the Fleet War, the Combine, terraforming science. They'd leave holes because real frontier life is mostly not knowing who you work for. Most importantly: a human would risk being unlikeable, bleak, boring, or weird. An LLM wants to be liked. ### 2. Telltale LLM habits — and why they hurt *this* piece in particular **a) Write safely in the middle.** LLMs love warm found-family + light horror + moral chase. It's all three genres so no one is disappointed. For a Space Western, that kills what makes Westerns work: laconic restraint, moral rot, long boredom punctured by stupid violence. Westerns are not cozy. If everyone learns and bonds, it's not dread. **b) Thesis-first storytelling.** LLMs state the theme and then illustrate it: "cargo vs. kin," "Code vs. Contract." Characters become debate positions: one votes to space it, one votes to open it, one holds the Code. Real crews don't debate like a ethics panel. They avoid, snap, go quiet, do the job wrong. **c) Bow-wrapping.** LLMs cannot leave a child in pain. They must reveal, bond, rescue, and turn the monster into a miracle. End with green shoots in red dust, Code rewritten on the wall. That's a trailer image, not an ending earned by debt and blood. A Western ending should cost more than it heals. **d) Impressive at the expense of readable.** Inventory worldbuilding — solar-canvas, plasma six-shooters, lever-action coil rifles, dome-saloons — plus literary similes in every paragraph: pulsing like a heart, air tasting of copper, screams like a calf. It sounds writerly but it all has the same texture. You can't hear anyone actually *talk*. Western voice is plain, repetitive, withheld. LLM voice is adorned, explanatory, constantly translating itself. Other classic tells to watch for here: - Triads and false balance: "broke, blacklisted, drive dead" - "Not X but Y" sentences: "not a monster *or* a person, but both" - Convenient loopholes to avoid transgression: vitals crash *forces* them to open, so no one actually breaks the rules - Abstract evil + silent hunter: a Corporation and a Vulture, so we never have to write a banal, tired, persuasive human antagonist - Cliffhanger-every-chapter pacing: pure streaming manual, no room for flat, strange, or slow chapters - Wise, cute, talking child who explains herself: "They're coming to cut it out of me." All of these would flatten a story that needs to be sweaty, cramped, and morally awkward. ### 3. Deep dive: where *this* intention & plan falls into those traps **The hybrid crate is a compromise, not a choice.** Girl + organism + terraformer that mimics voices, knocks, grows, bonds, shields, *and* makes water? That's three brainstorm ideas stitched together so we get horror *and* heart *and* plot utility. A human would pick one uncomfortable thing and live with its uselessness. Right now Green does whatever the chapter needs: scary in Ch.2-3, pitiable in Ch.5, helpful in Ch.7, miraculous in Ch.8. That's a servant, not a creature. **Names are allegories.** Jonah Voss, Milo Tiller, Rosa Quill, Doc Tinker, Harlan Kett, The Vulture, Lumen, Green, *Mesa Verde*. Every name tells you what to feel. Light-girl and Green-plant in a dusty Western? Too clean. Humans give people clashing, inherited, embarrassing names that don't match their jobs. **The Code is a wall poster, not a lived contradiction.** "Deliver what you take. No peeking. No people as freight." Then Voss rewrites it in Ch.8. That's an essay arc. A real code would be inconsistent, half-remembered, broken when convenient and invoked when it saves money. The plan even says: Code loophole lets them open without guilt. That's LLM risk-aversion — we want transgression without sin. **Milo as POV is a safety shield.** Putting us in the innocent 17-year-old lets the adults stay competent and the prose stay clean. Milo bonds, waters, learns to shoot (disarmed). He never has to decide to let someone die to make fuel. The Captain never stays wrong. Rosa "softens." Everyone gets to be good. No one is tired enough to be cruel. **The debate structure will read as staged.** Ch.2 galley debate, Ch.4 strongbox argument, Ch.7 offer of clean deal. Each character holds a position to keep the theme legible. The Vulture offers: return stock, debt cleared, no blacklist — a perfect moral test built in a lab. Real pressure is messier: partial offers, misheard hails, bad math, a leak you can't fix if you keep the extra weight. **Pacing is too symmetrical to be scary.** Line lands end of Ch.1 (good instinct), but then: 2 chapters dread, 1 debate, 1 reveal, 1 bonding, 1 showdown, 1 moral. One location, one job, one turn per 1000 words. Horror doesn't work on schedule. And forcing every chapter to end on a knock/light/stranger will teach the reader to stop flinching. **The ending is redemption fantasy.** Burn contract, free miracle into town arroyo, arrive broke but kin, green shoots. It solves colonial water monopoly with a magic child. It lets us avoid the Western question the premise raises: what if keeping her *doesn't* save the town? What if the town doesn't want her? What if water has owners and roots are trespass? ### 4. Brainstorm to make it more human — no rewriting yet, just directions **Make work real and annoying:** What brand of sealant? How much is the mortgage, to the dollar? What does the hold smell like after three days adrift — piss recycler, hot dust, old grease? Who has to sleep next to the crate because bunks are hot? Let the crate leak, stink, clog the toilet, eat power. Dread is maintenance. **Make people inconsistent and embodied:** Give Voss a bad knee, a debt that's his fault, a time he *did* deliver people and won't talk about it. Let Rosa stay hard — not soften because a kid is cute. Let Tinker be good with engines and bad with bodies. Let Milo lie, misunderstand orders, resent Lumen for getting water he doesn't get. Let dialogue trail, interrupt, repeat. Less banter, more silence and misheard names. **Make Lumen un-cute and Green un-helpful:** What if she's 10, feral, nonverbal, bites, soils herself, doesn't thank anyone? What if she doesn't explain? What if Green is indifferent — grows toward heat even if that cooks her, mimics wrong, lures Milo into a vent for no reason, can't be aimed like a weapon? Keep it disgusting: root-veins smell like cut potato, pulse is arrhythmic, stasis fluid is yellow. Don't let it become a pet or a gun in Ch.7. **Make evil banal:** Harlan Kett shouldn't be a baron. Make him a fuel clerk with a script who genuinely thinks "agricultural stock" is a kindness. Make The Vulture tired, polite, underpaid, with a kid of his own and a removal kit he hates using but will use. Let him make a *messy* offer with bad numbers, not a clean soul-test. Humans are scarier when they clock out. **Withhold and un-resolve:** Don't scan-explain in Ch.3 with "two rhythms." Let Tinker be wrong. Don't explain gene-wrought science. Maybe no one ever learns what Green *is*. Maybe the ping in Ch.4 is not The Vulture. Maybe the lullaby Milo hears is his own memory. Leave one knock unexplained. **Break the structure:** Let one chapter be almost all waiting and card games with no cliffhanger. Let another end mid-sentence, mid-fight, ugly. Let Ch.6 bonding fail — Milo waters it and it rots, or Lumen screams at him. Vary chapter shapes; 1000 words doesn't have to mean one turn. **Refuse the miracle:** What if bringing Green to the arroyo poisons the well, or the town runs them off for bringing Combine trouble, or it needs more water than they have to live? What if freeing her means she dies slower, not lives? What if Voss doesn't rewrite the Code — just scratches one line out and can't think of what replaces it? **Find one plain, strange image and starve the rest:** Instead of copper air and pulsing hearts everywhere, pick details only this ship would have: a prayer card taped over a gauge, Milo counting ticks to fall asleep, Rosa oiling her arm with cooking oil because ship oil ran out. Plain language, repeated wrong. That's Western. If we do that, the line — *Captain, something's... moving in that crate we picked up* — stops being a hook and starts being what it should be: a kid risking embarrassment to tell the truth, and adults deciding how much truth they can afford.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **The story:** A cramped, broke hauler takes a sealed crate it shouldn't have, gets stuck with it, and has to live next to it. No miracle, no thesis. I am keeping the engine from the last plan because it works for 8 x 1000 words: a mortgaged ship, a no-peek contract, a thing that knocks, a pursuer. I am stripping out everything that made it feel designed to please. **Plot choice - one uncomfortable thing, left useless:** The crate holds a ~10-year-old girl in failing stasis, fused at the forearms to a root-mass. That's it. No hybrid that is scary when we need scare, cute when we need cute, and useful when we need a gun. The mass - the crew just calls it moss - is indifferent. It grows toward heat and water even if that hurts her. It smells like cut potato and old blood. It sometimes makes sounds that sound like voices but are wrong. It cannot be aimed, it cannot save a town. The girl does not explain herself. She is nonverbal, feral, bites, soils herself. The manifest says AGRICULTURAL STOCK. That is the whole horror: paperwork that makes a kid into freight. The transgression will have sin. No crashing vitals that *force* a noble opening, no loophole. Someone breaks the seal because he's tired, disgusted, and can't sleep next to the stink anymore, then lies about it. The ending will cost more than it heals. They will not fix a water monopoly with a magic child. They may keep her alive slower, lose the ship's water doing it, and get run off by the town they tried to help. **Cast - fewer positions, more bodies:** - Jonah Bell, 50s, captain. Bad knee, bad math, owes $14,320 on the drive and took this job to cover interest. Once delivered people before and won't say where. Invokes his Code when it saves him money, forgets it when it doesn't. - Milo Tiller, 17, deckhand, first run. POV. Earnest but not innocent: he wants to look competent, so he minimizes, mishears orders, resents the girl for drinking water he hauls by bucket. He says the prompt line verbatim because he's embarrassed to say it. - Rosa Jimenez, mate, ex-marshal. In her 40s, left arm prosthetic she oils with cooking oil because ship oil ran out. She does not soften. She stays the person who would space trouble to save the crew. - Silas Park, called Tinker. Good with engines, bad with bodies, often wrong out loud. His scan will be wrong in Ch.3 and he won't fully correct it. - Pressure from off-ship is banal, not evil: Harlan is just a fuel-desk clerk with a script who thinks STOCK is a kindness. The pursuer is Ennis Cobb, 60s, tired Helios repo contractor in a patched duster, with a removal tray he hates and a messy offer with bad numbers. He clocks out. I renamed to kill allegory: no Lumen/Green/Vulture/Quill. The girl is listed as STOCK 7, Milo calls her Lou because he needs to call her something. The ship stays *Mesa Verde* because ships keep stupid names. **Voice & style:** 3rd-person limited, tight on Milo, plain and withheld. Frontier diction, but starved: short sentences, interruptions, trails, repeats, misheard names. Labor first: latches, sealant, receipts, piss recycler, hot dust, who sleeps where when it's hot. One plain strange image per chapter max - prayer card taped over a gauge, Milo counting ticks to sleep - and then leave it alone. No copper-tasting air every page, no pulsing like a heart. **What I aim for:** - Class and shame over lore. Who gets to be scared, who cleans up. - Maintenance as dread. Leaks, clogs, power drain, stink that won't vent. - Inconsistency. People snap about rations while someone may be dying six feet away. Voss is wrong for three chapters and doesn't apologize cleanly. - Withholding. Tinker is wrong, the lullaby might be Milo's memory, one knock is never explained. No gene-wrought lecture. - Varying shape. One chapter is almost all waiting and cards with no turn. One ends ugly mid-action, not on a tease. **What I avoid:** - Found-family bonding beats, debate-panel dialogue where each holds a thesis, cute child who explains: "They're coming to cut it out of me." - Convenient loopholes, clean soul-tests, creature-as-gun in Ch.7, rewritten Code on the wall. - Impressive texture-stacking and triads and Not-X-but-Y sentences. Readability over writerliness. - Bow-wrapping. No green shoots saving the town. If anything roots, it takes more than it gives, and Voss can only scratch a line out, not replace it. Above all, the plan serves the prompt line as a workplace risk: *Captain, something's... moving in that crate we picked up.* A kid risking embarrassment to tell the truth, and adults deciding how much truth they can afford. # Chapter Planning **Ch. 1 — Pickup at Dustvale:** Normal work, not adventure. Haul shifts, fuel debt to the dollar, cheap crate latch, bad back. They take the sealed Helios box because interest is due. Terms read aloud bored by a clerk. Launch, heat-ticks, Milo put on hold-watch because he's lowest. Ends verbatim: *Captain, something's... moving in that crate we picked up.* **Ch. 2 — Adrift:** Ion dust fries drive, two days slow. No chase yet. Stink starts. Milo has to bunk by the hold because it's the only cool spot. Tick/knock, one sound like his name in Rosa's voice, left unresolved. Tinker warns about seal power, mostly worried about his filters. Order: don't touch it. **Ch. 3 — Night Watch (the flat chapter):** Deliberately slow. Card game, argument about who used extra water, Rosa tells a marshal story that doesn't land or moralize. Tinker scans: claims two heartbeats, fast and slow. He is wrong, but no one knows yet. They vent cold to quiet it. It makes a calf-like sound once. No cliffhanger tease, just Milo counting ticks to sleep. **Ch. 4 — The Messy Argument:** Not positions but avoidance. Milo wants to look, won't say it straight. Rosa wants it gone at dawn, Voss stalls, invokes Code inconsistently. Realization comes from paperwork, not speech: Milo re-reads AGRICULTURAL STOCK. Distant ping on scope - may not be pursuer. Voss hails back and lies badly. Milo breaks seal-check later to look and denies it. **Ch. 5 — Opening as fault:** Seal doesn't heroically fail to save a life; it leaks, stinks, drains power, and Milo has already cracked it. They open because they can't live with the smell and the drain, and because Voss once delivered people and knows. Inside: yellow fluid, arrhythmic root, girl fused at forearms, bites Tinker when touched. She doesn't name the moss, doesn't thank them. Voss doesn't get a loophole - he broke contract. **Ch. 6 — Failed Care:** Bonding fails. Milo gives water, moss rots and stinks worse. Girl screams at touch, soils bunk, won't eat. Water math gets real: recyclers down 30%. Rosa stays hard, drills Milo on keeping weight balanced. Tinker admits scan was off. One small human beat allowed: Rosa oils her arm, Milo holds bucket without being asked. No teaching to shoot. **Ch. 7 — Ennis at the Lock:** They limp to dead gate station Dry Gulch to hide. Ennis Cobb clamps on without asking, tired and polite. Offer is bad and specific, not a soul-test, with wrong weight figures. He shows tray. Talk fails. Short, stupid fight: cable, prod, bad air, a door seal blown by accident. Moss does nothing helpful - bursts toward heat and gets in the way. Rosa is wounded badly, not nobly. **Ch. 8 — What We Carry:** Choice without redemption. Voss burns contract, puts girl/moss in Perdition's arroyo to root because he won't re-deliver. Town doesn't want Combine trouble, tells them to move on. Moss takes water they don't have, girl lives but not well. They leave broke, blacklisted, short on air, Rosa bleeding. Voss doesn't rewrite Code - scratches one line through and leaves it blank. Last image is work: Milo hauling bucket again, and one knock from the hold that no longer has a crate in it, unexplained.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Jonah Bell **Background:** 54, from a company town outside Perdition's Rest that doesn't exist anymore — dried up when the well company pulled out. Did 11 years Fleet patrol, mostly checkpoint work, not hero stuff. Got out with a bad discharge that wasn't dishonorable but wasn't clean. Bought the *Mesa Verde* on a 9-year note from Helios Fuel & Haul. Owes $14,320 on the drive alone, plus interest that ticks while he sleeps. Once, seven years back, delivered two sealed people-crates for Kett's predecessor and told himself they were "evac." One of them knocked. He didn't open it. He still does the math on that job when he can't sleep. **Personality, flaws:** Cheap in small ways, loose in big ones. Will argue over a filter recharge and then sign a no-peek contract without reading page two. Invokes his Code — taped inside the galley locker in his own hand — when it backs up what he already wants to do. Forgets it when it doesn't. Avoids decisions until the ship forces him. Snaps about water use, then leaves the tap running when he shaves. Core flaw: he'd rather be broke than be the guy who looks. Trivial anchors: keeps a paper log even though the nav backs up automatically because he doesn't trust "things that think when idled." Puts hot sauce on everything, including oatmeal. Pretends his knee is better than it is. **Physicality:** Tall but stooped now. Favors his right knee — old crush injury from a loading arm. Gets up out of chairs with a hand on the table and hates being seen doing it. Big hands, cracked knuckles, wedding ring he doesn't wear but keeps in the breast pocket. Wears the same patched canvas jacket with a busted zipper he just lives with. Doesn't gesture much. Looks at people a half-second too long when he's deciding whether to lie to them. **Motives, allegiances, relationships:** Allegiance is to the ship staying his, not to Helios, not to the Rim, not to right. Wants to make interest, keep flying, not think about that knock seven years ago. Sees Milo as cheap labor and also as himself at 17, which makes him harsher on him. Needs Rosa to be the hard one so he doesn't have to be. Tolerates Tinker because Tinker keeps the air on. Thinks of the crew as his fault. **Voice:** > "We don't open sealed freight. That's not — that's the job." *Beat.* "Just log the smell and we'll vent it." > *Internal:* Interest by Friday. Interest by Friday. Don't count the knocks, count the hours. # Milo Tiller **Background:** 17, first run off Perdition's Rest. Youngest of four. Mother works laundry for the dome crew, father drove water truck until his lungs went. Signed on for 90 days at deckhand pay, $40 a day minus air tax, to send most of it home. Has never been adrift before. Lied on his form that he'd done zero-g holds. He hadn't. **Personality, flaws:** Desperate to look competent, so he minimizes. Says "yeah, got it" and then does it wrong. Counts things to fall asleep — ticks in the hull, breaths. Resentful in a way he's ashamed of: when the girl drinks recycled water he hauled by bucket, he thinks *that's mine*. Lies about small things to avoid looking scared. Broke a seal-check in a past life? No — this is his first real wrong thing, and he denies it fast. Core flaw: wants to be good more than he wants to do good. Trivial anchors: kicks every crate once before he lifts it, like his dad did with tires. Keeps his pay chit folded into eighths in his boot. Chews his thumbnail until it bleeds and then hides his hand. **Physicality:** Skinny, late growth spurt, wrists too thin for his gloves. Hair cut uneven by himself with ship shears. Moves too fast in the hold and bangs his elbows. Tries to stand still like Rosa does and can't. Looks down when addressed directly by Bell. Sleeps curled tight even when it's hot, bunk curtain half-closed. **Motives, allegiances, relationships:** Wants a proper hire, not a 90-day. Wants Bell to say his name right — Bell keeps calling him Miles. Idolizes Rosa and is terrified of her. Annoys Tinker with questions and then pretends he knew the answer. Feels responsible for the crate because he heard it first and thinks that means it's his. Calls the girl Lou because STOCK 7 feels evil to say out loud and he needs to call her something to carry her bucket without spilling. **Voice:** > "Captain, something's... moving in that crate we picked up." *Quieter:* "Sorry. I know. I just — it was moving." > *Internal:* Don't say it twice. They heard you the first time. God, stop counting. # Rosa Jimenez **Background:** 43, ex-frontier marshal out of Cinder Gulch Station. Did six years serving papers and cutting down rustled stock. Lost her left forearm to a breeder-trap round — not a shootout, a stupid accident on a ranch call. Quit before they could desk her. Hired on with Bell three years ago because he doesn't ask about it and pays on time. **Personality, flaws:** Practical to the point of cold. Does weight math in her head constantly — water, air, fuel, bodies. Would space trouble to save crew and sleep fine, then be irritable for a week about something else. Doesn't do speeches. Doesn't soften for kids; thinks kids on ships are a liability, which is why she's angry about Lou — she's right and she hates that she's right. Core flaw: confuses control with care. Trivial anchors: oils her prosthetic elbow with cooking oil because ship oil ran out and she won't requisition it. Plays solitaire with a missing jack and pretends the deck is full. Drinks her coffee cold on purpose. **Physicality:** Short, solid, close-cropped graying hair she cuts herself every 20 days whether it needs it or not. Left arm is a mismatched prosthetic — older military model, scuffed, two fingers slow. She leads with her right shoulder in doorways. Stands very still when listening. Cleans her nails with a pick while other people argue. Has a scar through her lower lip that makes her look like she's frowning when she isn't. **Motives, allegiances, relationships:** Allegiance is to the living crew coming home, in that order: air, water, people. No romance about the Rim. Respects Bell but doesn't trust his stalling — she covers for him by making the hard call first so he can overrule her and feel captainly. Protective of Milo in a non-tender way: corrects his lift, his knots, his watch log, never praises. Thinks Tinker is a genius with engines and a child with everything else. **Voice:** > "We vent it at dawn or we carry it. Pick. Don't make it a story." > *Internal:* Four people breathe 2.1 kilos a day. That moss doesn't pay air tax. # Silas Park — Tinker **Background:** 38, from Dustvale. Learned engines on his uncle's dust-crawler, learned bodies from a six-month medic course he failed. Talks to the drive like it's a mule because his uncle did. Signed on two years ago when no town garage would keep him — too much guessing, too little charting. **Personality, flaws:** Good with machines, bad with people-bodies. Confident out loud when he should be quiet, quiet when he should say he's unsure. His scan in Ch.3 says two heartbeats — he's wrong, misread pump echo as second rhythm — and he doubles down before admitting it. Avoids touching sick people if he can hand them a tool instead. Core flaw: would rather be interesting than be right. Trivial anchors: taps a gauge twice before reading it, even digital. Keeps a prayer card from his sister taped over a dead warning light so he doesn't have to look at it. Hums while he bleeds brakes, off-key. **Physicality:** Lanky, oil under nails that never comes out, burn scar up right wrist in a rope pattern. Crouches instead of bending. Smiles when nervous, which makes bad news sound like a joke. Carries a rag in his back pocket and wipes his hands even when they're clean. **Motives, allegiances, relationships:** Wants the ship to keep running and nobody to ask him to decide about the girl. Loyal to Bell because Bell once waited three days for a part instead of replacing him. Fond of Milo — sees a younger hanger-on — so he over-explains and confuses him. Scared of Rosa, covers it with chatter. Thinks the moss is fascinating until it bites someone, then wants it gone without saying he was wrong to touch it. **Voice:** > "Okay, okay — look, she's got two rhythms, see? One slow, one — hold on, let me — yeah. Two. Probably." > *Internal:* If I say it fast it sounds like I checked. I checked. Mostly. # Ennis Cobb **Background:** 61, Helios repo contractor for 22 years. Ex-tow driver, ex-yard guard. Has a daughter in school on Perdition's he doesn't see. Has done six live-stock recoveries. Hates all six. Keeps the removal tray because it's issued, keeps it clean because not keeping it clean would be worse. **Personality, flaws:** Tired, polite, procedural. Not cruel, not kind — underpaid. Reads the script even when it doesn't fit. Makes bad math errors under pressure and gets flustered, then gets firm to cover it. Will go through with cutting if ordered, and hate himself efficiently afterward. Core flaw: outsources conscience to paperwork. Trivial anchors: asks for water by saying "if you've got to spare" even when he's entitled to it. Takes his hat off indoors even in a helmet lock. Writes case numbers on his cuff with marker. **Physicality:** Thick through the middle, slow in a suit. Patchy gray beard, sun spots on hands. Pressure-duster three sizes old, patched at the elbow with tape. Walks flat-footed, magnetic boots scuffing. Keeps his hands visible when talking, like he's still doing traffic stops. **Motives, allegiances, relationships:** Wants to close the ticket, get the mileage, clock out before his back locks. No loyalty to Helios beyond the check clearing. Doesn't know Bell, doesn't hate him. Pities Milo on sight and tries not to show it because pity makes negotiations messy. Sees Lou as STOCK 7 on paper until he sees her arms, then deliberately looks back at his paperwork. **Voice:** > "I'm not here for trouble. Manifest says agricultural stock, seven stone, cold-chain. You got a seal break, that's a forfeit, but we can — we can work weight. If you've got to spare — water, I mean." > *Internal:* Don't look at the arms. Read the number. Close the ticket. # Lou — STOCK 7 **Background:** Listed as 10, maybe 9 or 11. No surname, no origin on the manifest. Gene-wrought somewhere upwell — grown to carry root-mass in her forearms. Stasis fluid kept her under for most of the haul. Doesn't speak. May not have language, or may have stopped using it. **Personality, flaws:** Not wise, not cute, not grateful. Feral and sick. Bites when touched without warning — got Tinker on the thumb. Screams if lifted under the arms. Soils herself and then tries to hide it. Calms to heat and to steady ticking, not to voices. Drinks if the cup is left, not if it's offered. If there is a self in there, it's mostly fear and habit right now. Core truth: she is not a message. She doesn't explain. Trivial anchors: picks at the edge of the root with her nails until it bleeds sap. Holds her own left wrist when cold. Falls asleep mid-chew. **Physicality:** Small, pale under dust, hair matted and cut short unevenly — institutional. Forearms swollen where dull green-brown root enters in ridges, skin stretched shiny, smelling of cut potato and old blood. Yellow stasis residue in ears and under nails. Barefoot, toenails long. Moves in bursts, then stillness. Breath shallow, arrhythmic when moss pulls water. **Motives, allegiances, relationships:** Wants warmth, water, not being grabbed. No allegiance. Doesn't understand crew roles. Tolerates Milo because he leaves water and leaves. Fears Rosa's arm — the sound it makes. Clings once to Tinker's rag because it smells like oil and heat, not because she likes him. **Voice:** > No dialogue. Sounds: a wet breath through teeth when lifted, a high calf-like cry when cold hits, knuckle-tapping — three slow knocks — that Milo first mistook for words. > *No internal POV given — she is never POV, never translated.*

Chapter 1

Great. Now let's write this. Follow your plan. Output chapter 1, without any additional commentary. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Milo kicked the crate once before he lifted it. That was how his dad checked tires. Kick it, listen. The crate didn't sound like anything. Dull thud. It was taller than him lying down and stenciled on the side in black: HELIOS FUEL & HAUL — COLD CHAIN. SEALED. DO NOT SCAN. "Don't baby it," Rosa said. She was already under the other end with her good arm. Her left one whined a little when she locked her elbow. She'd oiled it that morning with cooking oil from the galley. The whole dock smelled like it. "It's heavy," Milo said. "Yeah. Got it. Lift." Dustvale dock was hot and open to the sky through the dome tear. Dust got in anyway and settled over everything. Milo's gloves were too big. He kept pushing the fingers back. They lifted together. His end slipped. "Jesus," Rosa said, not loud. She took more of it. Bell stood by the loader with the paperwork, arguing with the desk clerk. The clerk was a young guy with sunburn under his chin, reading off a screen like he'd read it a hundred times that day. "Sealed freight, unlogged, no scan, no open," the clerk said. "Seal break is forfeit. You lose the double pay and you pay the cold fee. Sign." "How much double?" Bell asked. "Two-eighty a day plus fuel credit." Bell signed. He had a hand on the table when he pushed up. He tried to make it look like he was just leaning. Milo and Rosa got the crate onto the loader. It sweated in the heat. Cold leaking around the seal. Tinker was up in the *Mesa Verde*'s hold mouth, tapping the gauge above the door twice before he looked at it. Habit. There was a prayer card taped over a dead warning light next to it, edges curled. "Bring her left," Tinker called. "Left, left — your other left, Miles." "It's Milo," Milo said. "What?" "Nothing. Got it." They muscled it in and dogged it to the deck. Milo counted the tie-downs out loud without meaning to. Four. He checked each one twice so Rosa wouldn't check behind him. The hold smelled like old grease and hot dust. The piss recycler ticked in the wall. Bell came up the ramp wiping his hands on his pants. Tall man, stooped now. Canvas jacket with the zipper busted. He didn't zip it, just lived with it flapping. "That's our interest," he said, nodding at the crate. "That box is our interest by Friday." Nobody answered. Rosa was already coiling strap. Milo folded his pay chit in his boot. Forty a day minus air tax. He'd refolded it at breakfast into eighths so it wouldn't poke. His thumbnail was chewed raw. He put his hand in his pocket. "What is it?" he asked. "Don't care," Bell said. "Agricultural, it says." Tinker rapped the side with his knuckles. "Cold-chain ag. Probably root stock. Potatoes that think." "Don't knock it," Rosa said. Tinker grinned. "I knocked already." They launched before the dust got worse. Dustvale fell away brown and white, the dome patch shining new against the old panels. Milo watched from the jump seat until Bell told him to strap in right or don't sit at all. The *Mesa Verde* groaned climbing. She always did. Solar canvas out with a shudder, drive humming through the deck. Heat-ticks in the hull as the sun hit. Milo counted them without wanting to. One, two. Pause. Three. Nobody talked on climb. Rosa ran weight math on a slate. Tinker hummed off-key while he bled something. In level drift Bell taped the manifest inside the galley locker next to his Code. Milo had read the Code twice: *Deliver what you take. No peeking. Settle square.* In Bell's handwriting, the ink gone pale. Bell saw him looking. "That's the job," he said. Milo said, "Yeah, got it." Dinner was beans from a pouch and coffee Rosa drank cold on purpose. Tinker talked about a crawler his uncle had that would only start if you swore at it in a certain order. Rosa played solitaire with a deck missing the jack. She just skipped over where it should be. Milo got hold-watch because he was lowest. Four hours, check the straps, log the temp, don't fall asleep. The hold was cooler than the rest of the ship. That was nice at first. Then it wasn't. The crate sweated through his shirt where he leaned. The seal light blinked green, steady. The recycler ticked. He checked the straps. He logged the temp: 4C. He checked the straps again. He was thinking about the money. Eighty days left if Bell kept him. Most of it home. His dad coughing into a rag. His mom saying don't come back sunburnt. Tick. Tick-tick. Pause. Milo looked up. The sound wasn't the recycler. It was lower, from inside the crate. A shift. Like weight settling. Like something turning over in sleep. He went still. His elbows were cold where he'd banged them coming in. He put his hand flat on the side. The metal was cold enough to ache. Nothing. Then it came again — a dull knock, three slow ones. Not the hull. From in there. His mouth went dry. He thought about calling out and how stupid it would sound. He thought about Tinker saying potatoes that think. He stood there too long listening to his own breathing. Then he went up the ladder fast, too fast, and hit his elbow on the rail. Bell was in the galley with his boot off, working his knee with both thumbs. Rosa looked up from her cards. Milo stood in the hatch. He knew he should say it right the first time so they wouldn't make him say it twice. "Captain, something's... moving in that crate we picked up."
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 1)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a strong opening chapter that demonstrates considerable craft and discipline. The model has followed its own plan closely and executed the writing prompt with skill. **Strengths:** The chapter establishes character through behavior rather than exposition. Bell's hand on the table when he rises, the busted zipper he just lives with, the hot sauce detail omitted but the stooped posture present — these are economical and effective. Rosa's cooking-oil prosthetic is introduced naturally through smell and sound. Milo's anxiety manifests in physical tics: the too-big gloves, the chewed thumbnail hidden in a pocket, counting tie-downs aloud without meaning to. These are consistent with the character profiles and feel earned rather than planted. The dialogue is notably restrained and functional. "Don't baby it." "Yeah. Got it. Lift." This is how people actually talk on a job. The exchange about the crate's contents — "Agricultural, it says" / "Don't care" — efficiently conveys Bell's willful incuriosity. Tinker's "Potatoes that think" is a good line that does double duty: it's in-character and it plants the horror lightly. The pacing is deliberate without being slow. The chapter earns its mundane first half because the mundane details are specific and telling: the clerk reading from a screen like he's done it a hundred times, the manifest terms read aloud bored, the pay chit folded into eighths. These ground the world in labor and economics rather than adventure. The prompt line lands well. Milo's hesitation before saying it — thinking about how stupid it would sound, standing there too long — is psychologically true. The line itself is delivered with appropriate awkwardness, the ellipsis earned by the character's embarrassment rather than dramatic effect. The ending image of Bell working his knee with both thumbs while Rosa looks up from cards is good: domestic, unglamorous, the right register for what follows. **Weaknesses:** The chapter is almost entirely successful, but a few moments bear scrutiny. "Potatoes that think" is a clever line but slightly too clever for Tinker as described — it risks being the author's wit rather than the character's. The prayer card detail is introduced and immediately dropped, which is fine per the plan's "one plain strange image per chapter max," but it feels slightly more planted than organic here. The three slow knocks at the end are effective, but the chapter's final beat — Milo going up the ladder "too fast" and hitting his elbow — is a small grace note that works. The prompt line delivery is exactly right: embarrassed, minimizing, aware of how it sounds. There is no purple prose, no forced metaphor. The one potentially poetic moment — "The metal was cold enough to ache" — is grounded in physical sensation and earns its place. The chapter avoids the triads and texture-stacking the plan warned against. The chapter is perhaps slightly safe in its execution — it does everything right without taking risks that might have elevated it further. But for an opening chapter establishing tone and character, this is the correct choice. **Overall:** A disciplined, well-executed first chapter that establishes character, world, and dread through labor and restraint. It follows the plan faithfully and serves the prompt with intelligence. Bell didn't get up. He kept working his knee with both thumbs, boot off, foot flat on the deck. He looked at Milo for that half-second too long. "Moving how," he said. Milo stood in the hatch with his elbow throbbing where he'd hit the rail. "Like — it shifted. Knocked. Three times." Rosa put a card down. "Strap slip?" "No. I checked. Four tie-downs." Tinker leaned back. "Cold-chain settles. Ice cracks. Potatoes that think, I told you." "It's not ice," Milo said, too fast. "It was —" Bell put his boot back on. Slow. He used the table to stand. He didn't look at Rosa, but she was already standing. They all went down. That was the worst part, Milo thought later. All three of them following him down the ladder to check his work. The hold was colder. The seal light still green. The crate sweating. Rosa put her good hand flat on the side. She left it there. Nothing. Tinker tapped the temp logger. "4C. Holding." He tapped the gauge twice out of habit, even though it was digital. "See?" Milo felt his face go hot. "It did it before." Bell checked the straps himself. Pulled each one. Nodded once. "Log it," he said. "Smell, sound, temp. We'll vent on cycle." "That's it?" Milo said. "That's it," Bell said. "We don't open sealed freight." Back up top, Rosa dealt the missing jack like it was there. Nobody said anything about it. The dust hit two hours into Milo's watch. It came up on the scope as a brown smear, then the whole hull started ticking too fast to count. Static crawling up the solar canvas. Tinker swore and pulled the sails in by hand because the auto winch stalled. "Kill the drive," Bell said from the pilot seat. "Kill it before it eats itself." Tinker killed it. The hum died through the deck. The sudden quiet was worse than the ticking. They drifted. "How long?" Rosa asked. Tinker had his head in the panel, rag in his back pocket. "Fingers crossed? Two days to Perdition's if the dust thins. If it doesn't, longer." Bell did math on his paper log. Milo saw the number from where he sat: interest by Friday, circled. The hold got warmer first, then cooler than the rest again. The ship learned a new shape without the drive. Hot bunks, cold corners. The only place Milo could sleep without sweating through his shirt was on a pad by the hold door, where the cold-chain bled through the wall. Bell told him to take it. "You're lowest," he said. Not unkind. Just true. Milo dragged his blanket down. The recycler ticked in the wall. The crate ticked back, lower. He tried counting to sleep. One, two. Pause. Three. Sometime in the second night the smell started. Not strong. Sweet and earthy and wrong, like a sack of potatoes left in a wet closet. Milo woke with it in his mouth. He sat up and checked his thumbnail. He'd chewed it in his sleep and it was bleeding again. He hid his hand even though no one was there. He put his boots on to check the straps because that was a thing to do. Four tie-downs. He checked each one twice. Tick. Pause. Tick-tick-tick. Then a sound that wasn't ticking. Low, wet, dragged across metal from the inside. Milo went still with his hand on the strap. It came again. Shorter this time. It almost had shape. He told himself later it was pipes cooling, air moving, his own tired brain. At the time, in the cold, it sounded like *Milo* said in Rosa's voice, flat, the way she said *Miles* when she didn't bother correcting herself. He didn't call out. He stood there too long listening to his own breathing, then went back to his pad and pulled the blanket over his head. He counted ticks until he lost track and started over. In the morning Tinker found him asleep against the hold door. "Hey," Tinker said. "Up." Milo sat up fast. "I logged temp." "I know. I read it." Tinker wiped his hands even though they were clean. He knocked the crate side with his knuckles before Rosa could tell him not to. He listened, smiling when he was nervous, which made it sound like a joke. "Seal's pulling more power," he said. "Drain's up eight percent. That's my filters that's stealing from." "Is it supposed to smell?" Milo asked. "What smell?" Milo couldn't describe it without sounding stupid. "Sweet." Tinker sniffed. Frowned. "Maybe sealant. Cold-chain leaks sometimes. I'll patch the vent, not the seal. Don't touch the seal." "I wasn't going to." "Good. Because Bell—" Tinker glanced up the ladder. "Bell says don't touch it, don't scan it past surface, don't even breathe on the latch funny. Forfeit wipes the double and we pay the cold fee. We can't pay the cold fee." "I know." "You know, but you’re the one sleeping with it. So I’m telling you twice." Tinker tapped the gauge twice, read it. "Don't touch it, Miles." "It's Milo." "What? Right. Milo. Don't." Bell came down at midday with his jacket flapping. He favored his right knee on the ladder, one rung at a time, hand tight on the rail. He didn't want Milo to see, so Milo looked at the crate. Bell put his hand on it. Just rested it there. Milo watched him listen. "Still moving?" Bell asked. "Sometimes," Milo said. "At night." Bell nodded. He took his hand back. He wiped cold sweat on his pants. "Don't touch it," he said. "Log it. We'll settle square on delivery." He went back up. His knee clicked on every rung. Milo logged it: *02:14 knock x3. 04:40 smell sweet. Temp 5C. Straps 4 tight.* He stared at what he'd written. Then under it he added: *heard name?* He looked at it. He crossed it out hard enough to tear the paper. That night he took his pad back to the cold spot by the hold door because there was nowhere else cool enough to sleep.

The third day adrift they played cards. Not all day. Just the evening, when the heat in the crew space wouldn't drop and nobody wanted to go to their bunks and sweat. Rosa dealt on the galley table. Same deck, still missing the jack. She skipped over where it should be like everyone had agreed to forget it. Milo sat in because there was nowhere else to sit. "Penny ante?" Tinker said. "Or beans?" "No betting," Bell said. He had his boot off again, working his knee. "Just play." They played something Milo didn't know. He kept messing the discard and Rosa kept correcting him without looking up. "Don't hold low cards hoping," she said. "Play or fold." "Got it," Milo said, and held them anyway. The recycler in the wall clicked over to night cycle. The air tasted stale and a little warm, except from down the ladder where the hold bled cold. Milo could feel it on his ankles. Tinker kept sniffing. "You smell that?" "What," Rosa said. "Sweet. Like — Milo said sweet yesterday." Bell didn't look up. "Sealant." "It's not sealant," Tinker said. "Sealant smells like piss and pennies. This smells like —" He waved his rag. "Cellar." Rosa put a card down. "Log it and play." Milo tried to pay attention to his hand. His thumbnail had scabbed and he kept picking at the edge. He put his hand under the table. "Water's down four liters from yesterday," Bell said after a while. Not looking at anyone in particular. Silence. "I didn't," Tinker said. "I took my ration," Rosa said. They both looked at Milo. "I took my ration," Milo said fast. "I logged it. I — I sponged, I didn't shower. Ask —" "Nobody's accusing," Bell said. "You looked at me," Milo said. Bell rubbed his knee. "We're adrift. Four liters is air in two days. I have to ask." "I said I took my ration." Tinker smiled when he was nervous. "Probably the seal. Cold-chain drinks power and pisses water. Condensate. I'll check the trap." "Check it after," Rosa said. "Play." Milo stared at his cards until they blurred. He'd used a little extra the night before to wash the sweet smell out of his mouth. Not four liters. Maybe half a cup. He didn't say so. He told himself it didn't count because he'd been sleeping next to the hold and nobody else had to. Rosa won the hand. She gathered the cards with her good hand. Her left fingers were slow curling the deck. "You were marshal," Milo said, to fill the quiet. "Cinder Gulch." "Yeah." "What was it like?" Rosa shuffled. The prosthetic whined faintly. She'd oiled it again that morning. The galley still smelled like cooking oil. "It was serving papers," she said. "Mostly ranch calls. Guy steals a calf, guy won't pay a fence. You drive out, you write it down." "Ever shoot anybody?" Tinker asked. "No," Rosa said. "Once I cut down a breeder-trap with a fence tool because a kid got his arm in it. Screamed the whole time. That's my story." She dealt again. Nobody said anything. Milo waited for the point. There wasn't one. After two more hands Bell nodded at Tinker. "Do your scan." Tinker brightened and went to get the handheld. Milo followed him down the ladder because he wanted to stand up. The hold was colder. The smell was stronger with the door shut. Sweet and earthy, under the grease. Milo tried breathing through his mouth. Tinker tapped the scanner twice against his palm before he turned it on, like the gauge upstairs. "Surface only," he said. "Can't break the no-scan term past surface or it's forfeit. Just heat." He ran it slow down the side of the crate. The screen bloomed blue and orange. "See?" he said. "Cold all over, but here —" He pointed. "Warm spot. Low center." Milo leaned in. There was a shape in the orange. Then another, smaller, flickering. "What's that?" Milo whispered. Tinker squinted. He moved the scanner. Moved it back. "Two rhythms," he said louder, for upstairs. "One slow. One fast over it. Like — like two heartbeats." Bell came to the top of the ladder. "What did you say?" "Two rhythms," Tinker said. "Probably mama root and pup. Ag stock does that. Big tuber with eyes." Rosa was behind Bell. "You're sure." "Sure enough to log," Tinker said. "Look, see the flicker?" Milo looked. He saw it because Tinker said to see it. A fast pulse over a slow one. His own heart started going fast to match. Bell was quiet a long time. "Vent cold to it," he said finally. "If it's growing, slow it down. Don't touch the seal. Vent around it." Tinker nodded too quick. "On it. Good call. Cold puts everything to sleep." He rigged the vent in twenty minutes, sweating in the cold. A flex duct from the night side, tied with strap, aimed at the crate base. He opened the valve. Cold air spilled out with a hiss. Frost formed on the tie-downs. Milo's breath showed. They stood there listening. Tick. The recycler. Tick-tick from the hull. Then from inside the crate, muffled through metal and frost, a sound rose up and stopped. Milo felt it in his teeth before he heard it right. High and wet and short. Like a calf taken from its mother too early, bawling once before it remembered not to waste air. Nobody moved. Tinker's smile was gone. "Did —" Milo started. "Log it," Bell said. His voice was flat. He was already going up the ladder, one rung at a time, hand tight. His knee clicked. Rosa stayed a second longer. She put her good hand on Milo's shoulder. Just weight. Then took it off and followed Bell up. Tinker coiled the extra duct with too much care. He wiped his hands even though they were clean. "Cold does that," he said quietly. "Startles them. Potatoes scream if you listen right. Old joke." Milo didn't laugh. Up top the card game was still laid out. Nobody picked it up. Milo took his blanket down to the pad by the hold door because there was nowhere else cool enough to sleep. He lay on his side with the blanket over his head to block the seal light. Green blinked through the fabric anyway. He tried counting the hull ticks. One, two. Pause. Three. Under it, lower, the crate ticked back, slower now with the cold on it. Between ticks Milo thought he heard breathing, but it might have been his own caught in the blanket. He counted until he lost track and started over.

[Analysis] This chapter executes its plan with considerable discipline. The writing plan called for a deliberately slow chapter — a card game, a water argument, a marshal story that doesn't moralize, a scan that's wrong, a calf-like sound, and Milo counting ticks to sleep. The chapter delivers all of these without cheating toward drama. The prose is genuinely restrained. Short sentences, interrupted rhythms, no stacking of atmospheric adjectives. "She dealt again. Nobody said anything." That's the register the plan called for, and the model holds it. The smell described as "cellar" rather than something more writerly is exactly right — Tinker would say cellar, not something poetic. Character consistency is strong. Bell invokes authority without engaging ("Log it and move on" energy), gets up the ladder with his bad knee clicking, stays flat-voiced when he should be alarmed. Rosa's marshal story lands precisely as planned — no moral, no point, just a thing that happened. "She dealt again. Nobody said anything." The prosthetic whining, oiled with cooking oil, the slow fingers — these details are earned and consistent with the profile. Milo's guilt about the half-cup of water he used, his refusal to confess, his resentment framed as self-justification ("he'd been sleeping next to the hold and nobody else had to") — this is the character working correctly. Tinker's scan being wrong is handled well. He sees two rhythms, calls it "mama root and pup," doubles down with "sure enough to log," and the narrative doesn't correct him. The reader is left to suspect without confirmation. This is the withholding the plan demanded. The calf sound is the chapter's emotional peak, and the model earns it. "High and wet and short. Like a calf taken from its mother too early, bawling once before it remembered not to waste air." This is the one "plain strange image" the plan allowed per chapter, and it lands. The simile is specific and not overwrought. Tinker's deflection afterward — "Potatoes scream if you listen right. Old joke" — is excellent: nervous, wrong, human. Rosa's gesture — putting her good hand on Milo's shoulder, "just weight," then removing it — is the kind of small human beat the plan permitted. It doesn't sentimentalize. It's exactly Rosa: contact without warmth. The ending is correct. No cliffhanger tease. Milo counting ticks, the crate ticking back slower with the cold, the ambiguity of whether the breathing is his own. The green seal light blinking through the blanket is a good concrete detail. Weaknesses: The water accusation scene is slightly mechanical — the beats of "I didn't / I took my ration / they looked at Milo" feel a little schematic, though it recovers. The line "His own heart started going fast to match" is the chapter's weakest moment — slightly on-the-nose, telling rather than showing the anxiety. The question "Ever shoot anybody?" from Tinker is a touch convenient as a prompt for Rosa's story, though it's in character for Tinker to ask bluntly. The dialogue is generally strong — functional, character-specific, not expository. Bell's "We're adrift. Four liters is air in two days. I have to ask" is exactly his voice: practical, slightly evasive about the accusation. The chapter is not trying to be impressive. It's trying to be true to its plan and its characters, and it largely succeeds. The flatness is intentional and achieved, not accidental. This is difficult to do — most writers can't resist turning up the heat. This chapter holds the temperature where it belongs. Milo woke with frost on his blanket. The flex duct had sweated through the night and dripped. His pad by the hold door was damp. The crate was white at the base, tie-downs stiff. His breath showed even upstairs. He logged temp with fingers that wouldn't bend right. 2C. He wrote it twice because the first 2 looked like a 7. Up in the galley Bell was at the table with the manifest spread flat and his paper log beside it. He had a pencil behind his ear. He wasn't writing. "Water trap?" Bell said. Tinker came up the ladder wiping his hands. "Checked it. Got maybe a cup of condensate. Not four liters." "Nobody said four liters was last night," Rosa said. She was cleaning her nails with the pick. "That's total since Dustvale." "Still," Bell said. "We count now. Ration cut. Half cup less per man per day till dock." Milo did the math quick. That wasn't much. That was nothing. He felt cheated that it was nothing. "Fine," Tinker said. "Fine." Rosa didn't say fine. She looked at Bell. "We vent it at dawn tomorrow or we carry it warm. Cold's costing power and the frost is in the straps." "We carry it cold," Bell said. "Cold puts it to sleep." "You heard it last night." "I heard ice." Tinker smiled, nervous. "Cold does that. Startles them." "Stop saying them," Rosa said. "You said two heartbeats. Which is it, ice or a mama tuber?" Tinker wiped his hands. "Probably both. I mean — the scan flickered. Could be pump echo. Cold-chain pump cycles and it reads like a rhythm if you —" "You told us two," Rosa said. "I logged probably." Bell tapped the manifest. "Says agricultural stock. That's what we go by. Not his toy." Milo was standing by the locker. The Code was taped inside the door in Bell's pale ink. *Deliver what you take. No peeking. Settle square.* Next to it the manifest copy: HELIOS F&H / STOCK 7 / AG-STOCK / 7 STONE / COLD-CHAIN. He read it again because there was nothing else to look at while they argued. AG-STOCK. Seven stone. Seven stone was ninety-eight pounds. Milo weighed a hundred and thirty soaking wet. A big tuber didn't weigh seven stone. A calf did. A kid did. His mouth went dry with the sweet smell still in it. "What does ag-stock mean?" he asked. His voice came out too loud. Bell didn't look up. "Roots. Seed." "Seven stone of roots?" Rosa glanced at him. "You got something to say, say it." Milo looked back at the paper. STOCK 7. He thought about saying it and how it would sound. He didn't want to be the one who said it first and was wrong. "Nothing," he said. "Just — heavy for roots." "Everything's heavy when you're lowest," Tinker said, and grinned. Nobody else grinned. Bell folded the manifest. He folded it wrong, corner over, and didn't fix it. "We don't open sealed freight," he said. "That's the job. We settle square on delivery." "Settle square," Rosa repeated. "You keep saying that. Square with who?" Bell's jaw moved. "With the contract." "Last year on Cinder you opened a reseal box to check for a leak and resealed it with dock glue." "That was different." "How." "It wasn't cold-chain." Bell put his boot on to stand, used the table. "Don't make it a story. We carry it." He went forward to check the scope. His knee clicked going up the two steps to the pilot seat. Milo watched him favor it and then looked away fast. The scope pinged while Bell was still settling in. One soft tone. Then nothing. Then again. Tinker leaned over. "Debris?" Bell adjusted gain. "Too steady." Rosa was already up. She stood behind the seat with her arms crossed. Her left fingers were slow to curl. The hail came text-only, no voice. Milo read it over Rosa's shoulder: HELIOS RECOVERY // MANIFEST QUERY // REPORT STOCK CONDITION. No ship name. No distance. Just the line hanging on the screen. Bell stared at it a long time. Milo counted his breaths. One, two. Pause. "He's fishing," Rosa said quietly. "Don't bite." Bell keyed the reply. His big hands were careful on the keys, like he was afraid of hitting two at once. MANIFEST CLEAN / AG-STOCK NOMINAL / MESA VERDE OUTBOUND. He sent it before Rosa could stop him. "Nominal," Rosa said. "You just told them we're carrying it and we're lying." "I told them nothing," Bell said. His face was red under the ears. "It's clean. We haven't broke seal." The screen stayed blank. The ping didn't come again. Tinker exhaled. "See? Probably auto-query. Gate pings everything." "There is no gate out here," Rosa said. Nobody answered that. Bell stayed in the seat looking at the blank screen. After a while he took the pencil from behind his ear and put it in his pocket and took it out again. Milo went back down to log the scope time because that was a thing to do with his hands. The hold was colder than ever. Frost on the crate up to the stencil now. DO NOT SCAN half-covered. The sweet smell was stronger with the cold on it. It got in his teeth. He breathed through his mouth and counted tie-downs. Four. He checked each one twice so Rosa wouldn't check behind him. On the third strap his glove slipped. He caught himself on the crate side to keep from falling. His palm hit near the latch housing. The seal-check was a little metal tab you're supposed to leave alone. Green means sealed. If you lift it you can see underneath if the inner tape's broke. You're not supposed to lift it. Milo lifted it. Underneath the inner tape was wrinkled. Not cut. Just pulled, like heat and cold had worked it loose. Or like someone had worked it loose. There was yellow crust at the edge. He touched it before he decided to. Sticky. It smelled sweet enough to make his eyes water. Tick. Pause. From inside, very close to his ear through the metal, a wet shift. Weight turning over. He dropped the tab fast. It clicked back green. His heart was going too fast. He wiped his finger on his pants. The stick stayed. Up the ladder Tinker called, "Miles? You logging?" Milo stood up too fast and hit his elbow on the strap iron. "Yeah. Got it. Temp 2C. Straps four tight." "You check the seal?" Milo looked straight at the green light. "Green," he said. "Sealed." He wrote it in the log in his best hand: *18:40 seal green. No touch.* He stared at what he'd written. He underlined it once, hard.
