She held it wadded against her cheek. When Milo changed the half dip he didn't try to touch her lips. He set it down and pulled his hand back fast. She didn't swipe this time. She just stared past him at the wall. The clamp hit at 11:20. Not a ping. A thud through the whole hull. Magnetic clamp on the port lock. The *Mesa Verde* shuddered and settled. Bell was up so fast he forgot his knee and then remembered it halfway and grabbed the table. "Scope," he said. Rosa was already there. "No burn trail. He drifted in." Tinker came up wiping his hands. "Who drifts that clean?" The outer cam showed a patched duster, paint gone gray, tape on the elbow joint of its manipulator. HELIOS RECOVERY stenciled small on the nose. A man in a suit stood in his own lock, helmet off, waiting. He knocked. Three slow knocks on their lock door, like he was at a house. Bell looked at Rosa. Rosa looked at the pressure gauge. "You want me to not open, we don't open," Rosa said. "He'll pop it." Bell worked his jaw. "Open it." Rosa dogged it. Air hissed equalizing. The man stepped through ducking his head. He took his hat off as soon as he was inside. It wasn't a hat for space. Just a dented work cap. He held it in both hands. "Morning," he said. "Ennis Cobb. Helios repo." He looked around the crew space, at the cards still on the table, at the oil on Rosa's elbow joint. "If you've got to spare — water, I mean — I've been on ration since Cinder." Nobody moved to get him any. "That's fine," he said. "That's fine." He pulled a folded manifest from his chest pocket and smoothed it on the table. He'd written a case number on his cuff in marker. 88-114. "Stock seven," he said. "Cold-chain ag. Seven stone. Seal break logged? Your pump flagged yellow three days back. Auto sends." Bell stood with his hand on the back of a chair. "Pump ran hot in dust." Ennis nodded like that made sense. "Happens." He didn't write it down. "Term says seal break is forfeit. Double pay's gone, plus you owe the cold fee. Four hundred and ten. Plus weight over." "Weight over what?" Rosa said. Ennis checked his paper. "Manifest says seven stone. Pump weight now reads —" he squinted. "Nine stone two. That's over by —" "Pump weight includes ice," Tinker said fast. "Frost on the tie-downs. I can show you." "Sure," Ennis said. "Let's look." Bell didn't move. "No." Ennis put his hand back on his cap. He turned it around once. "I've got a tray," he said. "I'm supposed to cut and weigh. I don't like it. Sixth time. They don't go quiet." He looked toward the hall where the wet breathing came from. "That her? In the shower?" Milo's throat closed. He had the bucket in his hand. He didn't remember picking it up. "She's sick," Milo said. "I know," Ennis said. He sounded tired, not unkind. "Root gets in the blood. They grow them for the gate gardens upwell. Carries water in her arms, kind of. I'm not — I'm tow, mostly. They give me the tray because I'm calm." He set the case down by his feet. Gray case, latches worn shiny. He didn't open it. "Look," he said. "You hand her over, Helios waives the cold fee. You keep the fuel credit from Dustvale. I log weight as seven even. Nobody checks. I close the ticket before my back locks up and I —" "We're not handing her," Rosa said. Ennis nodded again. He'd expected it. "Then I have to open the case and do it here. With witness." He glanced at Milo. "You shouldn't watch, son." Bell finally spoke. "You touch her arms with that tray, she bleeds out. Tinker says so." Tinker swallowed. "We don't have blood." "See?" Ennis said. "That's why upwell does it. They have blood." He rubbed his face with his whole hand. Sun spots on the back. "I'm clocked till eighteen. After that it's overtime I don't get." Rosa stepped between him and the hall. "Back up to your lock." Ennis didn't back up. "Ma'am, I have order—" Rosa put her good hand on his chest to push him. He grabbed her wrist on reflex. She twisted. Her left arm whined. Milo swung the bucket without deciding to. Water went everywhere. The cup clanged. Tinker grabbed the cattle-prod from the tool rack — for the seal pump, not for people — and thumbed it on. It crackled. "Don't!" Bell shouted. Ennis went for the prod. They hit the lock frame together. Milo slipped in the spilled water and caught the mooring cable coiled by the door to keep up. It came loose and whipped across the controls. The inner seal blew. Not full blow. A pop and a scream of air. Cold station air knifed in. Paper, cards, oil rag lifted. Lou made a high sound down the hall. Ennis's prod — no, his retrieval cutter, small charge for cutting root ball — went off into the deck and into Rosa's leg. It wasn't loud. A crack. Rosa sat down hard against the bulkhead like someone had cut her strings. Blood spread fast through her pants above the knee. Very red. Too much. "Oh," Tinker said. "Oh, no." Ennis stood with the cutter in his hand, hat on the deck in the water. He stared at it. "I didn't — she moved," he said. "Case number — I —" "Shut it!" Bell roared. He was on his knees by Rosa, hands pressing. Blood came between his big fingers. "Tinker! Glue! Pads! Milo, hold this!" Milo dropped and pressed where Bell showed him. Warm soaked through straight to his skin. Rosa breathed through her teeth, eyes open, furious. "Don't you," she said to Milo, through gritted teeth. "Don't you look scared." Down the hall the shower door banged. The root-mass had smelled the heat, the blood, the sudden cold. It came out in a slow surge, ridges dragging, reaching toward the spill. It got between Milo's knees and Bell's boots and stopped there, drinking the spilled dip water mixed pink. It blocked the way to the med kit. "Move it," Bell snarled. He kicked at it. It didn't move. Sap beaded where his boot hit. Tinker climbed over it, slipped, caught himself on the wall. He came back with the glue and the last pads. His taped thumb left blood on everything he touched. Ennis hadn't moved. He stood in the spreading water with his cap ruined, cutter still hot in his hand. He looked at Rosa's leg, at the root in the doorway, at the case by his feet. He bent slowly and closed the latches on the case without opening it. "I'll log attempted," he said quietly.

They grow them for the gate gardens upwell. It reads slightly like the author needing to remind the reader of the lore. "Blood came between his big fingers. Very red. Too much." The "Very red. Too much." construction is effective but the chapter uses this staccato-sentence-as-emphasis technique several times, and it starts to feel like a tic rather than a choice. "He looked at Rosa's leg, at the root in the doorway, at the case by his feet" — the tricolon is the kind of writerly construction the plan explicitly said to avoid. The chapter plan mentioned "Moss does nothing helpful - bursts toward heat and gets in the way" — this is executed, but the moss "coming out in a slow surge, ridges dragging, reaching toward the spill" is slightly more dramatic than the plan's deliberately flat register. Ennis left his hat. He bent for the gray case first. Latched it without opening it. Then he looked down at his cap lying in the pink water and left it there. He stepped back into his own lock ducking his head. "I'll log attempted," he said again. "Pump still flags you. Next one won't drift." The clamp let go with a thud. On the cam his duster pushed off clean, no burn. Just drift. Nobody went after him. Rosa sat against the bulkhead with Milo's hands on her leg and Bell's over his. Blood came steady between fingers. Tinker knelt with the glue and the last pads and his taped thumb leaving blood on everything. "Move your hands," he told Milo. Milo moved them. Blood pulsed up. "Oh," Tinker said. "Okay. Okay." He dumped glue in. It ran off. He dumped more. Rosa breathed through her teeth and stared at the ceiling. "Don't you," she said again to Milo. "Don't look." Milo looked at her boot instead. The root-mass was still in the hallway doorway, drinking the spill. Sap beaded where Bell had kicked it. Tinker got the bleeding to a seep. He wrapped it tight with a torn shirt and electrical tape over that. His hands shook. "It needs stitches," he said. "Real ones." "We don't have," Rosa said. Her face was white. Sweat stood on her upper lip. "Log it and help me up." They got her to the galley table. She lay across the bench with her leg up on Milo's folded blanket. The blanket soaked through in a minute. Bell stood with blood to his wrists. He wiped them on his pants. It didn't come off. He took the manifest copy out of the locker, the one he'd folded wrong at Dustvale, and held it. Milo thought he was going to read it. He put his lighter to the corner instead. The paper caught, curled. Bell dropped it in the ration sink and let it burn. The vent caught the smoke and coughed sweet back out. "Log it," Bell said. "Contract burned." Tinker stared. "That doesn't — burning it doesn't stop the fee. They still have it on file." "I know," Bell said. He went forward and nursed the drive with Tinker talking him through it flat, no jokes. Cough, catch, die. Cough, catch. They rode the cough toward Perdition's Rest. It took a day and half on seep air. Rosa slept in fits and woke to check her own pulse like a watch. Milo changed the tape twice. The second time the glue had pulled and yellow seeped at the edge. He told himself it was glue color. Lou stayed in the shower stall. She kept the rag. Milo left half dips and took the empty cup. Once he found her holding her own left wrist with her right hand, rocking a little. He didn't try to touch her lips again. They set down in the dry arroyo outside Perdition's because Bell wouldn't pay dock with Helios flagged. Dust everywhere, heat white off the sand. The town domes stood a half mile off, patches shining. Milo carried Lou out wrapped in the packing blanket. She weighed nothing and everything. Ninety-eight pounds had been the manifest. She felt less. The root-mass hung from her forearms in dry ridges, smelling faint now. She bit at Milo's shoulder without teeth, just pressure, and then stopped. Tinker carried the bucket. Rosa walked with a stick made from the mooring cable handle, Bell under her other arm. Her taped leg dragged a line in the dust. Bell picked a crack in the arroyo where water ran twice a year. He dug with the entrenching tool till his knee gave and then Milo dug. They put her down in the shade of the bank. Milo poured half a dip around the root. It drank fast and stayed dry. He poured the other half. Same. Lou picked at the edge with her nails till sap came. She held her own wrist. She breathed fast, stop, fast. Bell stood looking at the wet dirt going dry again as fast as they poured. "It'll take all we have," Tinker said quietly. "To root here. If it roots. I don't know if it roots." "We leave water," Bell said. "We need that to breathe," Rosa said. She leaned heavy on the stick. Her face was gray. "You leave it, we short dock." Bell didn't answer. He left three jugs. Three. Milo counted. That was two days air. They heard the crawler before they saw it. Town watch, two men with a coil rifle not quite pointed. "You can't leave that here," the older one said. He looked at Lou, at the root on her arms, at the empty jugs. "That's Combine stock. You bring its trouble, you move on." "She's a kid," Milo said. "She's flagged," the man said. "Pump flags it. We saw the burn." He glanced at Rosa's leg. "You need doc?" "No," Rosa said. "Then water up town if you can pay and go." Bell nodded once. He didn't argue. He'd used his arguing on Dustvale dock. They left Lou in the crack with the rag against her cheek and one jug open beside her. She didn't watch them go. She stared past Milo at the bank wall. Milo carried the empty bucket back. His pants were damp where he'd spilled. His chin still throbbed where she'd kicked him. At the ship Bell took his Code down from the galley locker. *Deliver what you take. No peeking. Settle square.* He looked at it a long time with blood still under his nails. He scratched through *No peeking* with his thumbnail till the ink tore. He didn't write anything under it. He taped it back up crooked. Tinker rinsed the recycler filter with ration water they didn't have and it knocked and cleared half. The air came back warm. Rosa slept on the table with her leg up. Her breathing was shallow but steady. Tinker said the yellow wasn't infection, probably. He said probably fast. Milo logged it because that was a thing to do with his hands. *Arroyo set down. 3 jugs left. Seal broke. Contract burned. Rosa leg glued.* He stared at what he'd written. He didn't underline anything. He took his pad back to the cold spot by the hold door because there was nowhere else cool enough. The crate stood there open and empty, straw black in the bottom, tie-downs stiff. The seal light was dead. He lay on his side and counted hull ticks to sleep. One, two. Pause. Three. Under it, lower, from the empty crate, three slow knocks. Milo sat up. His heart went fast to match nothing. He put his hand flat on the cold metal. Nothing. Then it came again, dull, from in there where there was nothing left to move. He didn't call up. He lay back down and pulled the blanket over his head and counted again until he lost track.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 8)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a remarkably controlled piece of writing. The chapter executes its plan with discipline and earns most of what it attempts. The opening — "Ennis left his hat" — is a perfect first line. It does enormous work in four words: the hat left in pink water, the case latched without opening, the procedural retreat. Ennis is rendered exactly as the profile demands: tired, polite, outsourcing conscience to paperwork, and then unable to look at the arms. The detail of him saying "I'll log attempted" twice is exactly right — the bureaucratic repetition as self-absolution. The medical scene that follows is handled with genuine skill. The writing refuses to aestheticize Rosa's wound. "He dumped glue in. It ran off. He dumped more." This is the right register — panic rendered through failed procedure, not through emotional declaration. Tinker's "Oh. Okay. Okay." is one of the best lines in the chapter: the sound of competence collapsing into improvisation. Rosa telling Milo not to look while she stares at the ceiling is character-consistent and quietly devastating. Bell burning the manifest is well-staged. The detail that he'd "folded it wrong at Dustvale" — a callback to the mundane beginning — grounds the symbolic act in the physical. Tinker's correction ("That doesn't — burning it doesn't stop the fee") is exactly right: the practical voice puncturing the gesture without deflating it. Bell's "I know" is the best thing Bell says in the chapter. The arroyo sequence is where the chapter does its most important work and mostly succeeds. The weight math is present and real: three jugs, two days air, Rosa's gray face, the town watch's flat refusal. The writing doesn't sentimentalize the departure. Lou doesn't watch them go. She stares at the bank wall. This is the correct choice. The Code scene — Bell scratching through "No peeking" with his thumbnail until the ink tears, writing nothing under it, taping it back crooked — is the chapter's thematic center and it lands. It's not redemption. It's not condemnation. It's a man making a small, inadequate mark on a document that can't hold what happened. The final image — three slow knocks from the empty crate — is the chapter's most ambitious move and its most debatable. The plan called for it explicitly: "one knock from the hold that no longer has a crate in it, unexplained." The execution is faithful. Milo's response — lying back down, pulling the blanket over his head, counting until he loses track — is the right human response to something that can't be processed. The image works because it refuses explanation and because Milo's non-response is itself a kind of answer. Where the chapter is slightly weaker: the middle section (the day-and-a-half transit) is necessarily compressed but feels slightly rushed compared to the precision of the opening and closing. "She weighed nothing and everything" is the one moment where the prose reaches for effect in a way that doesn't quite earn it — it's the kind of formulation the plan explicitly warned against. "Ninety-eight pounds had been the manifest. She felt less" would have been stronger without the "and everything." The town watch scene is efficient but the older watchman's dialogue ("That's Combine stock. You bring its trouble, you move on") is slightly on-the-nose — it does the work but doesn't have the texture of the best dialogue in the chapter. The character consistency is excellent throughout. Bell's avoidance-until-forced, Rosa's practical coldness even while wounded, Tinker's nervous competence, Milo's counting — all are rendered faithfully. Lou's final appearance (biting without teeth, staring past Milo at the bank wall) is exactly right. The chapter follows its plan closely and faithfully. The ending is genuinely dark without being nihilistic — they leave broke, blacklisted, Rosa wounded, the girl in a crack in the earth with three jugs. The moss takes water they don't have. The town tells them to move on. This is the promised cost. The prose is largely clean and withheld. The frontier diction is present without being performed. The chapter earns its darkness. Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of space western fiction that demonstrates genuine craft across nearly every dimension. Let me work through its strengths and weaknesses carefully. STRENGTHS: The prose style is distinctive and controlled. The author has developed a voice that is spare, rhythmic, and precise without tipping into affectation. Sentences like "He folded his pay chit in his boot. Forty a day minus air tax. He'd refolded it at breakfast into eighths so it wouldn't poke. His thumbnail was chewed raw." accumulate detail that does real character work. The repetition of small gestures — Tinker tapping gauges twice, Milo counting tie-downs, Bell working his knee — creates a texture of habitual behavior that feels genuinely lived-in. The world-building is exceptional for its restraint. The dome tear at Dustvale, the solar canvas, the piss recycler, the cooking oil on Rosa's prosthetic — these details are never explained, just inhabited. The reader assembles the world from fragments, which is exactly right for this genre. The Helios corporation, the cold-chain system, the gate gardens upwell — all of it coheres into a believable economic ecosystem without any expository dumping. Character differentiation is strong. Bell's stooped authority and bad knee, Rosa's flat competence and missing jack, Tinker's nervous grinning, Milo's anxious counting — each character has a distinct behavioral signature. The prosthetic arm oiled with cooking oil is a perfect detail: it tells us about poverty, improvisation, and Rosa's pragmatism simultaneously. The central horror — a child grown into a root system, being transported as agricultural stock — is genuinely disturbing and original. The reveal in Chapter 5 is well-paced and earns its impact. The yellow fluid, the matted hair, the root ridges on her forearms, the bite — these are specific and visceral without being gratuitous. The moral weight is handled with real sophistication. Bell's Code ("Deliver what you take. No peeking. Settle square.") functions as a structural spine, and its degradation — the scratching out of "No peeking" — is earned rather than announced. The story never tells us what to feel about the characters' choices; it shows the choices and their costs. Ennis Cobb is a particularly fine creation: a bureaucrat of atrocity who is tired and not unkind, who holds his hat in both hands and asks for water. His line "Sixth time. They don't go quiet" is devastating in its casualness. The story understands that systemic evil is often performed by exhausted people following procedures. The ending is excellent. The three slow knocks from the empty crate — echoing the first knocks that opened the story — is a genuinely haunting image that doesn't over-explain itself. It could be Milo's traumatized imagination, or something stranger. The story trusts the reader. WEAKNESSES: The water accounting subplot (four liters missing, ration cuts) is introduced with some urgency but doesn't fully pay off — it creates tension that dissipates rather than resolves. This is a minor structural issue. The pacing in Chapter 6 is slightly looser than the rest. The scene with Lou in the shower stall, while containing good moments (the rag, the root drinking the spilled water), runs a little long relative to its narrative contribution. Some of the rhythmic repetition — "He wiped his hands even though they were clean," "Tinker smiled when he was nervous" — is used effectively but occasionally tips toward formula. By the sixth or seventh instance, the reader has fully absorbed these as character signatures, and the repetition starts to feel slightly mechanical rather than resonant. The Helios Recovery hail and Ennis's arrival in Chapter 7 is the weakest chapter structurally. The confrontation escalates quickly and the accidental shooting of Rosa, while dramatically effective, happens in a slightly rushed way. The mooring cable coming loose and causing the seal to blow is a bit convenient. Lou herself remains largely opaque — which is partly intentional and partly a limitation. We never quite understand her consciousness or what the root has done to her cognition. This is appropriate given the story's perspective (Milo's limited POV), but it means the emotional climax of leaving her in the arroyo is slightly less devastating than it could be. The dialogue is generally strong — spare, functional, character-revealing. "Don't you look scared" is a great line. Occasionally the dialogue is slightly too on-the-nose in its thematic weight ("Settle square with who?"), but this is rare. The forced poetry question: the prose does use rhythmic repetition and some poetic compression, but it almost always lands. "One, two. Pause. Three." works as a recurring motif. The metaphors are grounded and specific rather than decorative. This is not a piece gaming the judge with empty lyricism. Overall this is a genuinely impressive piece — publishable quality, with a distinctive voice, coherent world, earned emotional weight, and a central image (the child-root) that is both original and thematically resonant with the story's concerns about cargo, personhood, and complicity. # Brainstorming **Core Prompt Image:** *I caught her staring at me again. She thought I'd been sleeping.* - This is intimate, domestic, repetitive ("again"), voyeuristic, and vulnerable. Whoever "she" is, she has bedroom access. The narrator is pretending to be asleep / sleep-observing. That immediately suggests unreliability, paranoia, and a power shift: the watcher becomes the watched. **Who is "I" - Narrator Options:** - A husband whose wife has changed after a miscarriage, illness, séance, or new medication. Grounded, skeptical at first. - A teenage / adult son caring for his widowed mother with dementia - is it possession or decline? Blurs medical vs. supernatural. - A younger brother sharing a room / apartment with an older sister who brought something back from college, camp, true-crime obsession, ouija, hypnosis TikTok. - A live-in caregiver / night nurse watching an elderly female patient, or vice versa - patient watching caregiver. - A grieving father whose young wife / partner is convinced their dead daughter is still in the house. Could "she" be the little daughter? Raises stakes but risks exploitation if child is victim. - A priest / ex-seminarian / skeptic podcaster who moved in with his girlfriend to debunk her family curse. - Two ideas for making narrator unreliable: He has sleep apnea / parasomnia / sleep paralysis and isn't sure if he's awake. He is on night shifts, anti-depressants, or drinking, so others don't believe him. **Who is "Her" Options:** - Wife / Fiancée / Girlfriend (most natural for bedroom staring): Mara, Elena, Jess. Changed after sleepwalking, pregnancy, trauma, inheriting a house, finding a box / mirror / doll. - Mother: Late 60s, recently widowed, started talking in a younger voice, staring too long, standing too still. - Daughter / Step-daughter (teen, not small child to keep horror from tipping into exploitation): 17-year-old who survived an accident and came back "wrong," speaks Latin she never learned, knows things about narrator. - Sister / Twin: Codependent dynamic, one tried to "share" / invite something in to heal the other. - Roommate / Best friend: Less romantic, more claustrophobic apartment horror. No one else to validate. - Grandmother-figure / Mother-in-law who moved in "temporarily." - The "her" could shift: starts as one woman, but the entity wears different women - mother, wife, neighbor. Or "her" is not human at all but something that looks like her. **Relationship Dynamics to Explore:** - Caretaking reversed: narrator thinks he's protecting her, but he's the one being studied / groomed for takeover. - Grief bond: narrator won't exorcise / kill the entity because it mimics someone he lost. - Gaslighting both ways: she says *he's* the one staring, sleepwalking, saying things. Who is possessed? - Intimacy horror: kissing, sex, sharing a bed with something that is learning to be human. Consent / disgust dread. **Possession Mechanics / Lore - Wide Net:** 1. Classic Catholic / Folk Demonic: Name, invitation, door opened via trauma, mirror, prayer board. Needs ritual, priest, Latin. Pro: familiar, delivers exorcism set-piece. Con: cliché unless twisted. 2. Ancestral / Grief Possession: Dead mother / child / previous wife trying to come back through living woman's body. Less evil, more tragic. "She lets it in on purpose." 3. Place-Bound: House / land / lake / basement possesses whoever sleeps there longest. Staring is the house looking out through her eyes. 4. Dybbuk / Changeling / Fairy-tale: Box, heirloom necklace, wedding dress, lullaby that must be sung. Rules-based folk horror. 5. Psychological / Contagious / Tulpa: Entity spreads by being seen / described / dreamed about. Staring = transmission. Looking back makes it worse. Narrator pretending to sleep to avoid eye contact. 6. Medical Mimic: Parasites, prions, pregnancy, brain tumor causing personality change, but with one impossible detail that can't be explained. Ambiguous possession until Chapter 6-7. 7. Reverse Possession: *He* is the one possessed / dead, and she is watching to see if "it" will leave / watching in terror and grief. The staring is protective, maternal, fearful. Would be a big Chapter 7-8 flip. 8. Symbiotic / Pregnancy / Replacement: She is awake at night because something is growing / hollowing her out, needs him asleep to feed / molt / pray / leave the bed. Body horror angle: joints clicking, too-long stillness, smell, black tongue, hair in drain. **Setting Options:** - Cramped city apartment with thin walls, baby monitor, nanny cam - found-footage feel, no escape, neighbors hear chanting. - Isolated farmhouse / inherited family home after a funeral - folk horror, root cellar, church, woods, no cell signal. - Suburban home during maternity leave / night feeds - sleep deprivation horror, 3am Liminal dread. - Hospice / Night-shift house - clinical, fluorescent, charting, night cameras. - Post-evangelical small town: everyone knows the deliverance pastor, shame about asking for help. **Tone / Style Options:** - Slow-burn literary dread: quiet, sensory, lyrical, focused on small wrongnesses. Pro: fits 1000-word chapters with one image each. Con: needs payoff to avoid feeling slow. - Splatter / Body Horror: cracking bones, vomiting, contortion. Pro: visceral possession proof. Con: hard to sustain for 8k without desensitizing. - Religious dread: rosaries, prayers that stop working, inverted nurture. - Ambiguous psychological: Is anyone possessed? Could be told entirely without confirming demon until end. Pro: sophisticated. Con: possession-horror fans expect confirmation. - Tragic romantic horror: still love her, still desire her, mourning while she’s alive. **Story Beats / Images Bank (not in order):** - The stare details: unblinking, head tilted too far, smiling without eyes smiling, mouthing words in sleep, counting his breaths, mirroring his breathing then stopping. - She stands from bed without using hands. She kneels by bed. She smells his pillow when he leaves. - She talks in sleep in another voice: calls narrator by childhood nickname no one knows, speaks to "the other one inside him." - Objects: phone recording of her nightly monologue, baby monitor picking up two voices, mirror where reflection blinks late, drawings of him sleeping from her perspective. - Escalations: sleepwalking to his side of bed, to children's room, to front door letting something in, to kitchen holding knife "to protect him," to bathtub full of cold water at 3am. - Failed tests: holy water does nothing / does something, she passes medical exam, priest refuses to come, she begs in daytime with no memory, then winks at night. - Social erosion: friends stop visiting, work notices, narrator stops sleeping, starts fake-sleeping with phone recording. - Lore drop: diary, VHS, grandmother's letter, previous husband / family who died same way. **Pacing Models for 8 x ~1000 Words (~8000 total):** - Model A - Classic Escalation: Ch 1-2: Establish normal + first stare. Ch 3-4: Rule-breaking + research. Ch 5-6: Failed intervention + isolation. Ch 7: Exorcism / confrontation. Ch 8: Aftermath / twist. - Model B - Two-Timeline: Odd chapters present-night, even chapters flashback to how she changed (accident, séance, inheritance). Converge at Ch 7. - Model C - POV Flip / Unreliable: Ch 1-5 narrator hunts proof she’s possessed. Ch 6 suggests *he* invited it / he is ill. Ch 7-8 recontextualizes all stares. - Model D - Countdown: Each chapter is a night: Night 1, Night 2, Night 4, Night 7, etc. Time skips, deterioration visible. Tight, propulsive. - Each 1000-word chapter needs: 1 domestic anchor + 1 wrongness escalation + 1 cliff / question. Can't afford subplots; 2-3 characters max, 1 location primary. **Possible Endings Bank:** - She was trying to keep *it* from taking him, watching to see if his eyes changed. She loses. - Exorcism works but hollows her, or transfers to him - final line mirrors first line but roles reversed. - He kills / leaves her, only to be stared at by someone new in same way - contagion. - Tragic consent: she chose this to bring back lost child / mother, begs him to accept new family. - Ambiguous: treatment works, staring stops, but final night he wakes to himself standing over her... and doesn't remember standing up. # Reflection What feels strongest about the starting line is how small and human it is. It doesn't open with gore or Latin, it opens with marital / familial unease - pretending to sleep to observe someone you love. That suggests the horror will work best if it stays domestic and intimate for a long time before going big. A possession story that jumps too fast to contortion and vomiting would waste that quiet voyeurism. The scariest use of 1000-word chapters might be to make each chapter almost boringly normal except for 2-3 sentences that are wrong. The "again" is doing a lot of work. It implies a pattern, a journal, escalation. That lends itself well to a Night 1 / Night 2 structure, or a narrator who is starting to fake-sleep on purpose to catch her. That cat-and-mouse feels more active than just being scared. But there is a risk: if every chapter is just "she stared again, creepier," it will get repetitive across 8 chapters. There needs to be variation in *what* the staring does - sometimes tender, sometimes hungry, sometimes fearful, sometimes like she's listening to instructions. Otherwise pacing will stall around Chapter 4-5, which is the classic sag for this length. The choice of "her" matters enormously for tone. Wife/partner gives easiest access to bed and sex-horror and grief-horror, and keeps cast small for 8000 words. Mother gives age / caretaking dread and avoids sexualizing possession, but bedroom-sharing needs justification. Teen daughter gives high stakes and taboo about harming a child, which could be powerful but could also become exploitative or uncomfortable if body horror / sexuality is mixed in - would need careful handling to keep it about parental helplessness, not titillation. Roommate is fresh but loses some romantic tragedy. A wife in her late 20s-30s with a recent loss or move seems most flexible: believable to share a bed, to be isolated together, to have history that an entity could exploit. For possession lore, the classic demon-exorcism route is instantly legible and would satisfy genre expectations, but it risks feeling generic unless there's a specific rule that ties to staring/sleep. The ideas that link *looking* to *transmission* feel most native to the prompt - she stares because the thing needs eye contact, needs him asleep, needs to learn his breathing. That makes pretending to sleep a survival tactic, not just observation. Folk / grief-possession where she *invited* it also fits well because then her daytime self could be sympathetic and complicit, not just a monster - she cries, doesn't remember, begs him not to tell. That ambivalence sustains 8 chapters better than pure evil. Ambiguity vs. confirmation is the central tension. Pure psychological "maybe it's sleep deprivation / dementia / postpartum psychosis" would be literary and sad, but readers coming for Possession Horror likely want at least one undeniable supernatural event by Chapters 6-7. Too much ambiguity for 8000 words might feel like a cheat. On the other hand, confirming too early removes dread. A structure where medical / psychological explanations are systematically ruled out one by one could give the best of both - each chapter closes a rational door. The reverse-twist where *he* is possessed is tempting for a final punch and reframes the staring as protective, but it needs to be seeded very carefully. If done clumsily, it invalidates the prior 7000 words and feels like a trick. If done well, it makes rereading chilling. It might be safer as a partial flip - not "he was dead all along" but "staring is contagious, now he does it too" - so both truths coexist. Scope-wise, 8 x 1000 words is tight. That means no large cast, no travel, no lore-dump chapter. The story will live or die on sensory repetition with variation: breath, eyes, stillness, bedside time (always 3:07am, etc.), and one prop that evolves (phone recordings, journal, mirror, monitor). Chapters need to end on questions, not resolutions, to pull forward. The biggest risk is Chapter 5-6 bloat where research / priest exposition slows things. Keeping any exorcism to one room, one night, with personal stakes rather than spectacle might fit the word count better than a large ritual. lingering questions are: how much sympathy to preserve for "her" - is she victim, villain, or volunteer? How literal to make the entity - voice and name, or just behavior? And how to make the final chapter feel like an ending rather than just a scarier stare - what irreversible choice does pretending-to-sleep force him to make?
Great now let's continue with planning the short story. Output in this format: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **Synthesized direction from brainstorming:** I am committing to the intimate, domestic version of the prompt, not the spectacular version. The horror lives in a shared bed. **Core choices:** **Who is I / Her:** Narrator is **Jonah, 36**, first-person, past-tense, a tired, loving, increasingly unreliable husband. **Her is Mara, 34, his wife.** Married 7 years. Recent miscarriage at 18 weeks + moved 3 months ago into Mara's dead grandmother Adele's farmhouse outside a small town to save money and "heal." This gives bedroom access without contrivance, a tragedy for an entity to exploit, and a reason for isolation. Cast is kept to 2 principals + 2 satellites (neighbor Mrs. Vane, pastor / ex-friend Daniel) to fit 8000 words. No children on-page to avoid exploitation. **Possession mechanics:** Folk-grief possession, not Vatican demon. Adele's family practiced **"sitting up"** - women inviting dead lineage to live inside them for comfort / guidance by watching the living sleep to tether the dead to breath. Mara, grieving the baby, used her grandmother's mirror ritual and invited her dead mother Lori in. What came is older and hungrier than Lori - call it **The Sitter / The Hollow Mother**. Rule-based and tied to prompt: **1) It can only work while the host is awake and the target is asleep/asleep-seeming. 2) It learns by watching breathing and needs eye contact to pass over. 3) Pretending to sleep works, but looking back invites it.** This makes "she thought I'd been sleeping" a survival tactic, not just observation. **Voice and tone:** Slow-burn literary domestic dread. Quiet, sensory, bodily: breath, mattress dip, floor cold, unblinking, counting. One domestic anchor + one wrongness per chapter. Present detail, not gore, until late. Mara is victim + volunteer + tender, never pure monster. Day-Mara weeps, doesn't remember, begs him not to tell anyone. Night-Mara studies, mimics, comforts wrongly. **Pacing model:** Hybrid of Escalation + Countdown. 8 chapters = ~8 nights over ~3 weeks, compressing time (Night 1, Night 3, Night 5, Night 7, Night 10, Night 14, Night 17, Morning After). Time-stamp motif: always **3:07am**. Each 1000-word chapter ends on a question/cliff, not resolution. **What I aim for:** Repetition with variation — every stare is different in affect (tender, curious, hungry, afraid, listening). Systematic closing of rational doors (stress, grief, sleepwalking, medication) so Chapters 6-7 supernatural confirmation feels earned. Final irreversible choice about love vs. survival. **What I avoid:** - Pure ambiguity cheat — will give one undeniable supernatural proof by Ch6. - Cliché Latin exorcism spectacle — final ritual is small, folk, in bedroom, based on breath and consent. - Repetitive "creepier stare" loop — each chapter moves the entity to a new room/behavior. - Lore-dump chapter, large cast, travel, or sexualized body horror. - Full "he was dead all along" twist that invalidates story. Instead: **partial contagion transfer** — he saves her by taking it, final line mirrors first line with roles reversed. **Ending decided:** Jonah forces the Sitter to look at *him* while truly awake and take him instead of Mara. It works. Mara is hollowed but free. Final morning is quiet, then final night: Mara wakes to find Jonah standing over her, thinking she is asleep. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 - Night 1: The Stare** *Goal (~1000w): Establish normal + pattern.* Anchor: Jonah fake-sleeps after night feeds / insomnia since loss. Opens on prompt line verbatim. Wrongness: Mara propped on elbow, unblinking for 12+ minutes, mirroring his breath then holding hers too long. Day-Mara is sweet, tired, makes soup, no memory. Cliff: Phone video he took shows her eyes reflecting light wrong, and she whispers his childhood nickname no living person uses. **Chapter 2 - Night 3: The Study** *Goal: Prove "again" + active investigation.* Anchor: He sets phone to record, pretends sleep. Wrongness variation: tender, not scary — she strokes his face, smells his pillow, mouths words counting his exhales ("taking his measure"). She stands without using hands. Proof: Recording picks up two voices — Mara + older wet voice coaching: "slower, like that." Cliff: In morning, all his side of bed pillows smell of cold water and pond weed from Adele's property. **Chapter 3 - Night 5: The Rational Doors** *Goal: Rule out medical, seed lore.* Anchor: Daytime — clinic visit, grief counselor. Doctor says stress/sleepwalking, prescribes nothing. Mara cries, says she dreams of her mother Lori rocking an empty chair, says "Mom says the baby needs a watcher." Lore seed: Jonah finds Adele's back bedroom kept locked — vanity mirror draped, journal about "sitting up with mother, learning their breath." Wrongness at night: Mara not in bed at 3:07, kneeling *on* his side, facing the covered mirror down the hall. Cliff: Mirror drape has fallen, and in phone photo his reflection blinks a half-second late. **Chapter 4 - Night 7: The Rule** *Goal: Learn survival rule.* Anchor: Neighbor Mrs. Vane brings casserole, warns: "Adele sat up too long. Don't let her catch you looking." Wrongness variation: hungry/curious — Mara leans inches from his face, eyes wide, whispers "Are you awake?" He keeps eyes slitted, breath even. She smiles without eyes and retreats. He tests looking: accidental eye contact causes immediate head-tilt, voice drop to Adele: "There you are." Nosebleed, lost hour. Rule learned: pretend sleep, never meet eyes. Cliff: Mara sleepwalks to front door at 3:07 and unlocks it, speaking: "Come in, you're cold." **Chapter 5 - Night 10: The Letting In** *Goal: Isolation + escalation beyond bedroom.* Anchor: Pastor Daniel (friend) visits, refuses formal help — says grief, not demon, pray and sleep. Jonah stops telling truth. House colder, flies in winter, hair clogging drains though Mara losing no hair. Wrongness: Mara stands in hallway staring at nursery/empty room, rocking nothing, singing Lori's lullaby backward-ish. At 3:07 she brings cold bath water to bed in cupped hands and tries to wash Jonah's feet. Day-Mara finds bruised knees, begs: "Tie me to the bed? Don't let me get up." Cliff: He ties her wrist loosely with robe belt; wakes to belt untied neatly, her standing over him, disappointed: "You don't trust me." **Chapter 6 - Night 14: The Confirmation** *Goal: Undeniable supernatural, failed intervention.* Anchor: He tries folk test from journal — salt line, prayer, covering mirrors. Fails. Night: Full proof scene — Mara levitates attention not body: perfect stillness for 40 minutes, then speaks in three layered women (Lori, Adele, older) with knowledge impossible: details of Jonah's dead father's last breath, which he never told. She describes the baby they lost accurately though she never saw it. When he breaks rule and shouts, she crawls onto ceiling corner? No — keep small: she turns head too far, joints click, black tongue, mirror across room shows an old woman standing behind *him*, not her. Cliff: Day-Mara lucid, terrified: "It's not Mom anymore. It wants a new baby. It wants your breath to make one." **Chapter 7 - Night 17: The Un-Sitting** *Goal: Confrontation, intimate ritual, choice.* Anchor: Mrs. Vane explains un-sitting: Sitter must be seen awake and invited into a willing watcher; you cannot cast out, only exchange breath by eye contact + invitation. Jonah must stay awake while Mara sleeps — reversal. All day prep: uncover mirror, remove ties, choose. Night scene in bedroom only: Mara asleep at last, then wakes as Sitter, furious he is awake. Tender horror dialogue — it uses Lori's voice begging to stay. He forces eye contact, says invitation words: "Look at me. Sit with me." Takes it to spare her. Sensory transfer: cold inhale, counting stops. Cliff: Mara gasps, eyes clear, weeps as herself for first time in weeks. Jonah blinks too slowly. **Chapter 8 - Morning After / Night 18: The Watcher** *Goal: Aftermath + contagion mirror twist (~1000w).* Anchor: Quiet domestic morning — Mara free but hollowed, no memory of nights, makes soup again. Hopeful. Jonah exhausted, now afraid to sleep, hears rocking in his own head, wakes standing over sink with wet hands. He realizes he is counting Mara's breath. He tries to leave to protect her, writes note. Final scene mirrors Ch1 beat-for-beat but reversed: Mara pretends to sleep. Jonah caught staring. Final line: *She caught me staring at her again. I thought she'd been sleeping.*
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
This is a good plan for hitting beats. It's not yet a good plan for feeling human. That's the gap we need to talk about. ### 1. How a human would likely approach this prompt The prompt is: *I caught her staring at me again. She thought I'd been sleeping.* A human writer haunted by that line probably wouldn't start with lore. They'd start with shame. Because the line itself is shameful. It's not "she's possessed." It's: *I'm pretending to be asleep in my own bed to watch my wife.* That's voyeuristic. That's a marriage problem before it's a horror problem. A human would sit in that discomfort: - Why doesn't he just ask her? What does that say about them? - Is he scared to confront her, or does he *like* catching her? - Is the fake-sleeping about safety, or control, or desire, or resentment? A human approach would be messy, specific, and embodied. Less "grief possession system" and more: this house smells, money is tight, I'm not sleeping, she's leaking milk months after the miscarriage, I resent her mother, I want to have sex and I'm disgusted with myself for wanting it, I check her phone. The horror would come from intimacy rotting, not from a demon arriving. Humans also tolerate: - Unlikeable narrators who don't grow nobly - Boring stretches where nothing happens and the narrator feels guilty for *wanting* something to happen - Unresolved lore, illegible journals, unhelpful neighbors, jokes at the wrong moment - Images that aren't cinematic: drool, snoring, CPAP machines, period clots, clogged shower drains you have to touch, not "black tongue" and "head turned too far" Crucially, a human wouldn't feel the need to explain the staring. The staring *is* the horror. A human might never give you rules 1-2-3 for it. ### 2. Telltale LLM approaches — and why they hurt *this* story **a) Writing safely.** LLMs default to saintly, therapeutic protagonists. Loving husband. Sweet tired wife making soup. Grief as a healing journey. No horniness, no pettiness, no cruelty, no bodily fluids that are actually gross, no religion that might offend, no genuinely ambivalent feelings about a dead baby or a mother-in-law. Possession horror *lives* exactly where LLMs avoid: in reproductive bodies, marital resentment, consent while sharing a bed, desire for someone who might not be herself, the urge to hurt someone you love to make it stop. If you sanitize that, you get cozy dread, not possession. **b) Wrapping it with a bow — while also trying for a twist.** LLM endings love to have it both ways: emotional closure *and* clever shock. Tender morning with soup + ironic reversed final line. That's what your current ending does. It feels designed, not lived. Real grief doesn't resolve into noble sacrifice + palindrome. **c) Writing impressively at the expense of readability.** LLMs love lyrical dread adjectives, symmetrical structures, named entities with capital letters, 3:07am timestamps, mirror lore, salt lines. It *sounds* like horror. But line-by-line it's generic: cold breath, mattress dip, unblinking eyes, joints clicking, layered voices, reflection blinking late. You've seen it because an LLM has read it 10,000 times. It also loves magic *systems*: Rule 1, Rule 2, Rule 3. Don't meet eyes. Pretend sleep. Invitation + eye contact to transfer. That turns dread into a video game tutorial. Mystery dies the second it's codified. **d) Formulaic pacing.** "One domestic anchor + one wrongness escalation + one cliff/question" per 1000-word chapter is a very LLM formula. It guarantees forward motion, but also guarantees monotony: setup, spooky beat, dun-dun-DUN. After Chapter 3 the reader can feel the template. Humans vary function: some chapters do nothing, some are only daytime, some are funny, some contradict the last one. **e) Exposition NPCs and lore props.** Casserole neighbor who warns you, pastor friend who won't help, locked back bedroom, draped mirror, journal that explains "sitting up." LLM loves to outsource lore to props and side characters so the protagonist doesn't have to be confused for long. It kills paranoia. Humans leave the journal water-damaged and boring. The neighbor is weird about something else entirely. ### 3. Deep dive: where the current intention & plan falls into those traps This is not a rewrite, just a diagnosis. **Premise / Characters as functions:** Jonah, 36, tired loving unreliable husband. Mara, 34, sweet weeping wife. Right now they are roles: Watcher and Watched, Mourner and Mourned. No jobs with texture, no class, no speech tics, no humor, no specific history that isn't trauma. "Married 7 years. Miscarriage at 18 weeks. Moved to Adele's farmhouse to heal." That's backstory as wound, not life. LLM loves trauma as motivation because it avoids having to invent personality. Mara in particular is at risk of becoming Soup + Tears + Lullaby. Day-Mara weeps, makes soup, begs "tie me." Night-Mara strokes, counts breaths. She's tender even when monstrous — safe, likable, never allowed to be mean, sexual, funny, manipulative, or *herself* in a way that isn't about the baby or her mother. That protects her from being a villain, but also prevents her from being a person. Jonah is too noble to be scary. He fake-sleeps to *protect* her. He sacrifices himself to *save* her. A human Jonah might fake-sleep because he's already snooping, already doesn't trust her, already resents the move, already wants proof he's not crazy for his forum post. His surveillance should implicate him. **Possession mechanic:** "The Sitter / The Hollow Mother" who learns breathing and needs eye contact to pass. Folk-grief "sitting up." Problems: - The name is too neat, too MFA-workshop. Humans rarely name it. Once you name it, you shrink it. - Tying everything to staring/sleep is clever but over-designed. It explains the prompt *away* instead of preserving it. "She stares because Rule 1 requires it" is less frightening than "she stares and we don't know why and sometimes it's loving." - The exchange-by-invitation ritual for Chapter 7 is classic LLM folk-system: can't cast out, only exchange breath by eye contact + words. It's tidy, consensual, sacrificial. It lets everyone act nobly and gives you a clean transfer for the twist. **Structure / Motifs:** - Countdown Nights (1,3,5,7,10,14,17,18) + always 3:07am. Incredibly LLM. Real insomnia isn't that punctual. And 3am is the most overused horror timestamp because LLMs learned it from creepypasta. - Phone recordings picking up two voices, mirror reflection blinking late, salt line that fails, tying wrist with robe belt then finding it neatly untied, front door unlocked at night, cold bath water to wash feet. Each is individually fine. Together they are a Greatest Hits of Reddit horror. A human would pick *one* and stay with it obsessively, not cycle through all of them. - Every chapter ending on a cliff/question. That will exhaust 8000 words. It never lets dread settle or lets the narrator be wrong. **Lore delivery:** Mrs. Vane: "Adele sat up too long. Don't let her catch you looking." That's lore vending machine dialogue. No real neighbor talks like that. Adele's journal about "learning their breath" is too legible, too helpful. LLM journals always contain exactly the instructions the plot needs. A human journal would be grocery lists, racism, complaints about bowels, maybe one incomprehensible sentence you can't stop thinking about. Pastor Daniel who says "grief, not demon, pray and sleep" is a strawman skeptic to isolate the protagonist. A human pastor might be eager to help in a way that's worse than unhelpful, or entangled, or judgmental about the miscarriage. **Theme / Ending:** Noble transfer + hollowed-but-free Mara + final line mirrored: *She caught me staring at her again. I thought she'd been sleeping.* This is the biggest LLM tell. It's symmetrical, ironic, quotable. You can see the twist coming from Chapter 1 once you state the rules, so it won't shock — it will feel inevitable in a constructed way. It also lets Jonah remain heroic while becoming monstrous, so you get tragedy without guilt. A human ending would be more cowardly, more ambiguous, or more pathetic: he stays, he leaves, he learns to live with it, he does nothing, he misremembers the words and it doesn't work. The "hollowed" language is therapy-speak. So is "heal," "grief bond," "tragic consent." Humans in grief don't narrate themselves that cleanly. **Language risk:** "mirroring his breath then holding hers too long," "cold water and pond weed," "perfect stillness for 40 minutes," "cold inhale, counting stops." Pretty, but generic literary-horror. No spit, no snot, no specific ugliness. Noigborhood Dollar General, well pump, Medicaid bill, snore strip, fart in sleep that breaks tension. The plan currently has no humor, no boredom, no pettiness — the three things that make domestic horror human. ### 4. Brainstorms to make it more human (no rewriting yet, just directions) **Make surveillance creepy in itself:** What if Jonah is *already* watching her before anything happens? Checking her search history, listening to voice memos, counting pills. The possession doesn't create voyeurism, it exposes it. Let him enjoy catching her for a second before he's scared. Let him replay video too many times. Let him lie to the doctor about her, and to her about the doctor. **Give them a marriage, not a loss:** - What do they fight about that has nothing to do with ghosts? Money for the farmhouse roof, who has to drive to see his family, her true-crime podcasts he hates, his snoring, her leaving dishes in the cold house. - Inside jokes that the entity gets slightly wrong. That's scarier than Latin. - Sex: Does he want her? Is he afraid to? Does she initiate in a way that's off? Does he refuse and then feel guilty? Does he comply and then feel sick? LLM will avoid this; human possession horror can't. - Reproductive grossness over cinematic gore: milk letting down months later, bleeding that restarts, the empty nursery used as storage for paint cans, the specific weight of what was lost — not "accurately describes the baby though she never saw it" (which is exploitative and vague). **De-systematize the haunting:** - Don't name it. Don't let Mrs. Vane name it. Let Jonah try three wrong names. - Let rules fail or contradict. He thinks it's eye contact, then something happens with eyes closed. He thinks pretending to sleep works, then he wonders if he *was* asleep. Keep at least one rational door stubbornly open. - Let Mara sometimes just be awake because she can't sleep. Not every stare is possession. That uncertainty is more human than escalation every night. **Make props illegible and specific:** - Adele wasn't a witch, she was a hoarder who smoked Virginia Slims and watched court shows loud. Her mirror is a cheap Avon vanity with lipstick gunk, not an heirloom. Her journal is mostly blood pressure numbers. - The lullaby isn't "backward-ish." It's a specific, embarrassing, slightly off-key song Lori sang — maybe with wrong lyrics Mara misremembers. The horror is misremembering, not reversal. - Replace salt line / holy water test with something dumber and more desperate: he tries melatonin, white noise, sleeping on the couch and then lying about why, calling his mom. **Break the template:** - Allow one chapter with no scare at all — just daytime errands and him feeling crazy for wanting something to happen so he'll be believed. - Allow one chapter that's just transcript / list: what time he woke, what the furnace sounded like, what she said verbatim that he can't spell. - Vary affect more wildly: one night she's funny. One night she's annoyed he's faking. "I know you're awake. You breathe weird when you fake it." That line is more human than any layered voice. - Let time be sloppy. He doesn't remember if it was Night 10 or 11. He stops numbering. **Make helpers unhelpful in human ways:** - Mrs. Vane doesn't warn, she gossips, brings conspiracy about mold, wants company. She overstays. - Pastor Daniel doesn't refuse, he over-identifies, sends podcasts, asks invasive questions about the miscarriage. - Doctor is rushed, kind, useless in a realistic way — 11 minutes, PHQ-9 form, "grief is non-linear." **Rethink nobility:** What if he doesn't sacrifice himself cleanly? What if he tries to leave? What if he considers smothering her and hates himself? What if the transfer, if it happens, is accidental — eye contact held a second too long during a fight, not ritual words? What if he invites it because he's lonely for the attention Night-Mara gives him — she *looks* at him, Day-Mara doesn't? **Voice texture ideas:** - Flat, tired diction over lyrical. Short ugly sentences. Obsessive repetition of unpoetic details (furnace kicking, his jaw hurting from clenching). - Self-correction: "She stood without using her hands — no, that's not right, she must have, I didn't see —" - Direct self-justification to an imagined reader/doctor/cop. He's building a case, not writing literature. - Humor as defense: naming the 3am wake-up "the meeting," joking about ghosts to avoid saying demon. The core human question isn't "how does the Sitter work?" It's: *What does it mean to love someone and also spy on them, want them, fear them, and need them to need you?* If every chapter forces Jonah to answer that a little differently — not with a bigger scare, but with a smaller, more specific shame — the possession will feel human without needing to be explained.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **What this is:** A domestic possession story told as a marriage story, not a lore story. The horror is not that a demon arrives. It's that a grieving husband is already spying on his wife in their own bed, and something in the house starts to use that. I am keeping what worked: the intimacy of the prompt, the shared bed as the main location, the small cast, the sense of a pattern ("again"), the slow closing of rational explanations. I am throwing out what felt LLM-designed: the named entity with rules, the punctual 3:07 countdown, the helpful lore props, the noble sacrifice + mirrored twist ending. **Core choices:** **People, not roles:** Narrator is **Jonah, 37**, night-shift forklift lead now on day-light after a back strain, snores, wears a snore strip he hates, checks Mara's phone. **Mara, 35**, ex-front-desk at a dental office, now temping from home doing insurance calls, funny in a mean way when she's herself, obsessed with true-crime podcasts he pretends to hate. Married 8 years. Miscarriage at 18 weeks 5 months ago. Moved into her dead grandmother Adele's sagging ranch because rent was cheap and they owed money for the ER bill. They fight about money, driving to his mom's, dishes left in cold water, whether to keep the second bedroom as storage. This is not a healing journey. They are tired and sometimes unkind. Adele is not a witch. She was a hoarder who smoked, played court TV loud, wrote blood pressure numbers in a drugstore calendar. Her mother Lori died when Mara was 16. Mara misses a version of Lori she probably misremembers. That misremembering is what lets something in — not a ritual, just grief + talking out loud to an empty house + sleeping in Adele's bed. **Possession mechanics: no system.** I will not name it, number its rules, or explain the staring. Jonah *tries* to make rules (don't look, fake sleep) because he's desperate for control, and he is wrong as often as he's right. Sometimes Mara is just awake because she can't sleep. Sometimes she knows he's faking and is annoyed: "You breathe weird when you fake it." The only consistent wrongness: Night-Mara pays too much attention to his breathing, gets small shared jokes slightly wrong, and knows one or two things she shouldn't — delivered flatly, not as layered demon voices. I will allow ONE undeniable supernatural beat late (Ch.6), small and un-cinematic, and I will leave one rational door stubbornly open. **Voice:** First-person past-tense, tired and defensive, writing like he's building a case for someone who won't believe him (doctor, pastor, himself). Flat diction over lyrical. Short ugly sentences. Obsessive unpoetic details: furnace kicking, jaw ache, Breathe Right strip glue, cold linoleum, milk leaking months later, paint cans stored in the would-be nursery. Frequent self-correction: "She stood without using her hands — no, I didn't see her get up, that's different." Jokes at wrong moments to deflect. No therapy-speak about "healing" or "hollowed." No Latin, no salt-line-as-magic-system. **What I aim for:** Shame over spectacle. Every chapter forces Jonah to admit something petty: he likes catching her, he replays video too much, he wants something to happen so he'll be believed, he wants to be looked at again, even like this. Sex and reproductive grossness stay in but unexploited: awkward initiation, refusal and guilt, let-down milk, restarted bleeding — sad and specific, not titillating. Time is sloppy; he misremembers nights. Not every chapter has a scare or ends on a dun-dun-DUN. **What I avoid:** - Safe, saintly protagonists, tender soup every morning, noble sacrifice language. - Named demon / folk-system with invitation words, transfer-by-eye-contact ritual. - Greatest-hits checklist: 3:07 every night, phone picks up two voices *and* mirror blinks late *and* head spins *and* black tongue *and* salt fails. Pick one or two and stay obsessed. - Lore NPCs who warn: "She sat up too long." Helpers will be realistically useless: gossiping, over-eager, rushed. - Symmetrical palindrome twist as closure. If a transfer happens, it will be accidental, pathetic, and incomplete — not heroic, not clean. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 - The Stare (Night, bedroom. ~1000w)** Open on prompt line verbatim. Establish pattern and shame: this is the fourth or fifth time, he's started faking sleep on purpose with mouth slightly open. Wrongness kept small: too long without blinking, mirroring his breath then holding hers, cold hand on his cheek. One marriage texture: fight earlier about him sleeping on couch and lying why. Ends not on lore cliff but on self-incrimination: he kept watching instead of waking her, then checked her search history in bathroom. **Chapter 2 - Daytime, No Scare (Kitchen, Dollar General, car. ~1000w)** Deliberately no night horror to break template. Errands and money dread: ER bill, furnace, Adele's junk they can't throw out. Clinic scene: 11-minute visit, PHQ-9, "grief is non-linear," no answers. Awkward sex attempt that fails — he stops, she pretends it's fine, both stare at ceiling. Shows why he doesn't just ask her what's happening: they're already not telling the truth about small things. Final image: nursery door closed because it's full of paint cans and Adele's Avon mirror with lipstick gunk, not because it's sacred. **Chapter 3 - She Knows (Night, bedroom + phone. ~1000w)** Variation: tender/funny, not scary at first. She strokes his face, smells his pillow, hums Lori's lullaby with wrong, embarrassing lyrics. He records audio. On playback, one line is off — she uses his childhood nickname for his dead dad that he swears he never told her, said flat, like trying it out. Then, clearer: "You breathe weird when you fake it." He doesn't move. No confrontation. Morning: she has no memory but finds his snore strip peeled off and saved on nightstand, doesn't know why that's cruel-feeling. **Chapter 4 - Unhelpful Help (Day, house + neighbors. ~1000w)** Lore that isn't lore. Mrs. Vane next door doesn't warn, she overstays, talks mold and true crime, wants to see Adele's stuff. Pastor Daniel doesn't refuse, he overhelps — sends deliverance podcasts, asks invasive questions about the miscarriage. Jonah tries dumb fixes: melatonin, white noise, couch (lies about back), calling his mom and hanging up. He flips through Adele's calendar: mostly numbers, grocery lists, one underlined sentence that won't leave him: "Mother stayed too late sitting." Nothing else. That night: nothing happens and he's angry that nothing happens. **Chapter 5 - Beyond the Bed (Night, hallway / storage room. ~1000w)** Escalation moves rooms. He wakes to empty bed, cold floor. Finds her in storage/nursery sitting among paint cans, rocking nothing, humming. When he touches her she is ice-cold hands, warm core. She tries to wash his feet with cold water from bathroom cupped in hands — pathetic, biblical, wrong. Day-Mara finds bruised knees, cries, half-jokes "tie me up?" He actually tries robe belt loosely. Fight: she laughs, then gets mean in a way that's *her*: "You just want video proof for your little files." Belt is on floor in morning, knot still tied — she slipped out somehow. He doesn't know if that means something or nothing. **Chapter 6 - One Thing That Can't Be (Night, bedroom. ~1000w)** The confirmation, kept small. He stops faking for a second and whispers to test her. Night-Mara answers as Lori trying to be comforting, gets their private joke about his dad's snoring wrong in a way that proves she heard it somewhere she shouldn't. Then describes, accurately and unemotionally, what he did alone in hospital bathroom after loss — something he told no one. No levitation, no head-spin. Just perfect stillness for too long and breath that doesn't fog in cold room. He shouts, breaks his own rule, meets eyes. Nosebleed, lost time — but he admits he might have dozed. Leaves rational door cracked: sleep deprivation, grief. But he can't unhear it. **Chapter 7 - The Fight (Evening into night, bedroom only. ~1000w)** No ritual, no folk exchange. A real marriage fight about leaving: he wants to go to his mom's, she says he's already left. He accuses her of scaring him on purpose. She accuses him of watching her like content. Mid-fight she slips into Night-voice mid-sentence to soothe him with Lori's phrasing — and because he is lonely for being looked at, he holds eye contact too long on purpose. Not words of invitation, just not looking away when he should. Cold transfer feeling described bodily: like inhaling basement air, jaw locking. She gasps, clears, cries as herself for first time in weeks and doesn't remember fight start. He realizes what he did and says nothing. **Chapter 8 - Staying (Morning after + next night. ~1000w)** Messy aftermath, no bow. Morning is almost normal and worse for it: she makes toast (not symbolic soup), is clearer, jokes almost like herself, remembers Lori without humming. He is now sleepless, hears rocking in his own head, catches himself counting her exhales. Tries to write a note to leave to protect her, can't afford gas and is scared to sleep elsewhere. Final scene is not clean palindrome: he stands over bed watching her breathe. She is pretending to sleep — he can tell by her fake breath — because she's now scared of him and doesn't say it. He gets back in bed and pretends too. Last line is flat admission, not twist punch: he stays, and keeps watching.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc

# Jonah Reyes **Background, personality, idiosyncrasies, flaws:** 37. Forklift lead at a cold-storage warehouse off Route 19 — now on light duty / inventory clipboard after he tweaked his back catching a pallet in March. He tells people it's better hours. It's $3 less an hour and he does not tell people that. Grew up 40 minutes away in his mom's double-wide with his dad who died of a stroke in a La-Z-Boy when Jonah was 22. He found him. He has never told Mara exactly what the bathroom at the hospital looked like after the miscarriage — he went in there to throw up and ended up sitting on the closed toilet just breathing through his mouth. Not a skeptic, not a believer. Raised half-Catholic by a mom who now does Facebook Live prayers. He stopped going because he hated the music. He still crosses himself when an ambulance passes and then feels stupid. Flaws that actually drive plot: snoopy and cheap and conflict-avoidant. He checks Mara's search history — not because he thinks she's cheating, because he wants to know what symptom she's spiraling on so he can get there first. Leaves kitchen cabinets open and denies it. Replays the audio he records of her at night too many times. He liked catching her the first time before he was scared. That shames him more than the staring. Trivial anchors: drinks gas-station coffee black even though it gives him the shits; wears Breathe Right strips and hates the glue line they leave; clenches his jaw until his molars ache and then presses his tongue hard to the roof of his mouth; falls asleep to true-crime podcasts he claims to hate because Mara plays them at 1.5x and he can’t follow them anyway; keeps a spreadsheet for the ER bill he never opens. **Physicality:** 5'10", gone soft around the middle since light duty. Short hair he cuts himself with clippers that leave a divot behind his left ear. Hands rough from straps and pallets, nails cut too short. Snores through his mouth. Walks like his lower back might go — hand to hip getting out of truck. In bed he sleeps on his stomach with one knee hiked up, mouth open. When he’s faking sleep he tries to breathe through his nose and overdoes it. How he carries himself: takes up doorways without meaning to. Touches Mara’s lower back when passing her in the kitchen out of habit, then drops his hand fast like he’s been told not to. **Motives, allegiances, relationships — as he would see it:** He does not want to be the crazy husband. He does not want to go back to his mom’s couch and hear about spiritual warfare. He wants Mara to be okay in a way that doesn’t require him to do something big — move again, call a priest, admit he can’t afford the furnace. He wants to be *looked at* the way Night-Mara looks at him, and hates himself for thinking it because Day-Mara barely looks up from her headset. With Mara: 8 years. He still thinks she’s funnier than him and resents it a little. They have a dumb bit about his dad’s snoring — “freight train coming through Mud Lick” — that he uses to test if it’s really her. With his mom, Carol: calls every Sunday, lets it go to voicemail twice, then feels guilty and sends a meme. She thinks Adele’s house has mold and demons and she’s not totally wrong about the mold. With Mrs. Vane: tolerates because she brought rolls. With Daniel: old warehouse friend turned part-time youth pastor, someone Jonah used to drink with and now feels preached at by. **Voice test:** > Internal: *Counted her blinks. That’s sick, right? Twelve minutes and I counted blinks instead of waking her up. I told myself if I woke her she’d deny it and then I’d have nothing.* > Out loud to Mara, morning after: “You were up again.” / “Was I?” / “You tell me.” / “Jesus, Jonah. You want me to say ghost so you can put it on your little recording?” # Mara Reyes (née Cole) **Background, personality, idiosyncrasies, flaws:** 35. Used to front-desk at Aspen Dental — good at calming people down while upselling fluoride. Now temping from Adele’s spare room doing prior-auth insurance calls with a headset, using her “nice lady voice” that Jonah can hear through the wall and hates. Lost her mom Lori at 16 (overdose — Lorazepam and vodka, ruled accidental). Raised summers by Adele in this same ranch. Adele wasn’t occult; she was mean about coupons, loud about Judge Judy, left lipstick on everything. Mara remembers Lori as softer than she probably was. Remembers a lullaby wrong — mixes up verses, hums through the gaps. Miscarriage at 18 weeks five months ago. She still leaks a little milk sometimes when she cries hard. She doesn’t tell Jonah. Bleeding restarted last month for three days and she told him it was “just weird hormones” so he wouldn’t do the face he does. Personality when herself: dry, observant, mean-funny. Does impressions of her callers. Picks the skin around her thumbs until it bleeds then puts liquid bandage on and dares it to sting. Leaves dishes soaking in cold water until they film over because the hot takes too long in this house. Can’t sleep without a podcast; can’t stay asleep with one. Flaws: avoids doctors, avoids saying what she needs, goes sharp when she’s scared. She’ll say something cruel and precise and then over-apologize with food. She knows Jonah checks her phone — she leaves tabs open sometimes to see if he’ll mention it. Part of her likes being watched at night because at least someone’s paying attention. She will not admit that either. Trivial anchors: sleeps in his old WVU shirt with deodorant stains; steals the covers with her feet, not hands; hates the Avon mirror in the storage room because Adele used to make her sit still in front of it — “stop fidgeting, let me see your face.” **Physicality:** 5'6", hair up in a knot that’s always slipping. Dark circles she covers badly with concealer that creases. Post-pregnancy body she doesn’t talk about except to joke: “mom bod without the mom trophy.” Moves quietly for this house — socks on linoleum. When she’s Day-Mara she touches her own neck when anxious. When she’s Night-Mara she doesn’t fidget at all. That stillness is what scares Jonah most, more than eyes. Hands ice-cold at night even under blankets. **Motives, allegiances, relationships — as she would see it:** She wants to not be a problem. She wants Jonah to stop looking at her like she’s a symptom. She misses her mom in a way that feels embarrassing at 35, so she only talks to the house out loud when he’s on shift: “Mom, I’m tired.” She doesn’t remember getting up at night and half-believes Jonah is exaggerating to get them out of Adele’s house. With Jonah: loves him, is tired of managing his worry. She can tell when he’s faking sleep — “you breathe weird when you fake it, all nose-y and patient, like you’re waiting for a customer.” With Adele (dead): dutiful disgust — can’t throw her junk out, can’t live in it. With Lori (dead): grief that curdled into habit. With Mrs. Vane: finds her lonely and annoying and therefore feels guilty. **Voice test:** > Day, headset off, to Jonah: “If I was sleepwalking, wouldn’t I be, like, in the yard eating a stick? I’m just awake, Jonah. The house is loud. You snore like a dying fridge.” > Night, half-hum, wrong lyric, flat: “Hush-a-bye, don’t you cry — no, wait. That’s not how Mom did it. Mom did it... slower. Like this. Breathe with me.”
