End cliffhanger: headlights slowly circle the cul-de-sac twice after parents leave. **Ch 2 - “Don’t Go In The Basement” (~1000w, ACT I Lock-In)** Goal: Turn isolation up, plant tools. Storm knocks power/flicker. Maya gets kids to bed upstairs, baby monitor on. Texts from Jenna: “btw don’t go in basement lol” + “Kyle might stop by, don’t let him in.” Back slider found UNLOCKED though Maya locked it. Discovers indoor nanny cam blinking, duffel in garage she’s told not to touch. She barricades what she can, keeps knife in pocket but puts it back — trying to be professional. End cliffhanger: back door beep — someone punches the code in correctly. **Ch 3 - “We Thought You’d Be Gone” (~1000w, ACT IIa Intrusion)** Goal: Threat arrives, Maya tries smart first. Kyle + Drez enter loud, then freeze seeing her. Patter-heavy: they lie (“Brad said we could crash”), probe if she’s alone, spot monitor. Maya tries de-escalation: offers to leave kids sleeping, let them take duffel and go, no cops. They laugh, take her phone, shove her into kitchen counter — first injury. Drez heads upstairs toward kid noise. Line crossed. End cliffhanger: upstairs floorboard creak over the monitor + Lila whispering “Maya?” **Ch 4 - “Upstairs Is Mine” (~1000w, ACT IIa Protect)** Goal: Protective violence, Maya gets hurt earning the turn. Maya bluffs to pull Drez back downstairs, locks kids in master bath with tablet + instructions: “No matter what you hear, don’t come out.” Fight in hallway/stairs — ugly, clumsy, real. She gets punched, zip-tied with a phone charger, mocked as “the help.” Uses medic calm to slow bleeding, pick tie with bobby pin while they crack the office safe. End cliffhanger: free-handed in the dark laundry room, listening to them argue on the baby monitor, she whispers: “Okay. My turn.” **Ch 5 - “Home Field Disadvantage” (~1000w, ACT IIb Hunter I)** Goal: First tailored payback using the house. Maya goes predator with kitchen/garage/kid clutter. Lures Drez alone: LEGO ambush on stairs, boiling pasta water threat (not gratuitous), scalp-stapler? No — uses first-aid + cleaning chemicals to blind/disorient, then slams his hand in the safe drawer he was robbing — the thief’s hand punished. Zip-ties him to water heater in basement he told her not to enter, takes his phone. Leaves him live-streamed to Lila’s tablet as receipt. End cliffhanger: Kyle racking a stolen pistol upstairs shouting “I know you’re up here with my niece!” **Ch 6 - “Say It For The Camera” (~1000w, ACT IIb Hunter II)** Goal: Finish intruders + get confession that implicates parents. Cat-and-mouse with Kyle using baby monitors as walkie-talkies, toy walkie static, breaker box kill to darken house. Maya knows layout now; he doesn’t. She traps him in garage with her car blocking his exit, pepper-sprays with DIY, drops him with iron skillet — humiliating, not lethal. Forces both men at gun-distance (unloaded / safe held by her) to confess on nanny cam + tablet: whose safe, whose Oxy, whose code, Brad owes them money. End cliffhanger: garage door opens — Jenna and Brad are home early, drunk, staring at bloody Maya holding a bat. **Ch 7 - “Triple Rate After Midnight” (~1000w, ACT III Employers)** Goal: Social revenge. Parents instantly flip: Brad grabs Maya, Jenna screams she’ll call cops on *Maya* for assault, breaking, “scaring kids.” They offer $60 to “forget this.” Maya snaps — not into murder, into accountability. Plays back confession videos, shows Venmo short, shows nanny cam footage of them hitting her. Locks front door, makes them count out cash + transfer triple pay + “hazard fee” while Kyle/Drez groan tied up. Makes Brad walk barefoot in rain to move her car, makes Jenna apologize to kids’ door. End cliffhanger: red-and-blue lights wash the windows — cops, and Jenna smiles: “Watch this.” **Ch 8 - “Morning Person” (~1000w, ACT III Fallout)** Goal: Payoff + cost. Cops separate everyone. Bodycam + tablet + nanny cam + Maya’s calm medic report win over Jenna’s lies. EMTs treat Maya’s split lip, sprained wrist — she’s shaky now that adrenaline drops. Kids burst out, Noah gives her crayon drawing: her with a skillet cape. Kyle/Drez arrested; Brad detained about pills/cash. Jenna tries last guilt-trip; Maya just holds up phone showing payment received. Final image at dawn: Maya limping to her unblocked car, kids safe in doorway in blankets, Lila still filming. Last line about new rule: she doesn’t babysit for people who don’t respect the sitter — ever again.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
# How A Human Would Actually Approach This A human writer handed "They fucked with the wrong babysitter" wouldn't start with structure. They'd start with a grudge. Anyone who's actually babysat, waited tables, cleaned houses, done care work — they have one specific night they still think about. Not "entitled parents" in general, but *that* mom who counted the chicken nuggets, *that* dad who stood too close in the hallway and said "we pay extra for cool girls," *that* Venmo that never came and you were too embarrassed to chase twice. The story would come out lopsided, petty, sensory, and a little ashamed — not righteous. A human would also bring: **1. A body, not a backstory.** Tired feet, period leaking onto a borrowed towel, contact going dry, breast pump in the car, back aching from a cheap couch, smelling like someone else's lasagna. Fear as nausea, shaking hands, needing to pee during a break-in and being angry about it. **2. Moral mess.** A human Maya might seriously consider leaving. Might consider stealing from that safe herself. Might hate the kids for an hour. Might hit someone harder than she needed to and *like it* for three seconds and then feel sick. Humans let protagonists be embarrassing. **3. Unfairness that doesn't resolve.** Humans know you don't always get paid triple. Sometimes you get $40 short and a bad reference and you still need the job next week. Pulp, at its best, is not about justice working — it's about someone taking a piece back anyway and paying for it. **4. People talking like people, not like dialogue.** Repeating themselves, talking over each other, not having a comeback. Especially when drunk, scared, high, young. Drunk parents don't monologue villainy, they loop: "you're being crazy, you're being crazy, why are you being crazy?" That's the opposite of how LLMs usually handle this. # Telltale LLM Moves — And Why They Kill Pulp **1. Safe revenge.** LLMs want revenge to be proportional, defensible, and legally exonerated. De-escalate first, try to call cops first, get hurt first, only injure to stop, threaten with an *unloaded* gun, record a confession, let the cops sort it out. That's HR-approved revenge. Pulp needs transgression. It needs the reader to think "oh no, don't —" and then feel complicit when she does. **2. The bow ending.** LLMs love to wrap up with bodycam + nanny cam + tablet video all aligning to prove the heroine was perfect, plus cash received, villains arrested, kids safe with a cute crayon drawing. Everything witnessed, everything paid. Real pulp ends with a cost and a stain. Someone limps. Someone lies and gets away with it. Money feels dirty. **3. Writing impressively instead of plainly.** LLMs reach for lyrical similes, thesaurus verbs, rule-of-three descriptions, epigrammatic last lines: "Okay. My turn." / "Upstairs Is Mine." Every chapter title a punchline. In 1000-word chapters that kills momentum. Pulp lives on short, ugly, Anglo-Saxon words: tired, sticky, broke, locked, blood in the mouth. Readability *is* style. **4. Theme-explaining and therapy language.** Words like accountability, boundaries, dignity of labor, trauma, emotional labor, hazard fee. Characters announcing the theme. An LLM narrator will name the feeling: "she felt the familiar rage of undervalued care workers." A human would just think: *Pay me, you fuck.* **5. Backstory as badge.** Ex-Army medic turned nursing student is a classic LLM competence shortcut: diverse enough, sympathetic enough, skilled enough to justify cool moves, damaged enough to be interesting but not difficult. It's plausible on paper and generic in practice. Same with "retired dispatcher" or "ex-con trying to go straight" — it's a skill kit, not a person. **6. Plot-device kids.** Precocious 9-year-old who films everything is incredibly LLM-convenient. It's a camera with pigtails. It solves the third-act proof problem without having to write a messy he-said/she-said. Real kids are inconvenient: they cry at the wrong time, they like the bad uncle, they repeat something racist they heard at home, they wet the bed mid-crisis. **7. Stereotype villains + perfect victim.** Crypto-bro dad + realtor mom + idiot brother + twitchy friend reads like it was assembled from Reddit threads. Everyone stays in their lane. The sitter is always reasonable, always professional until forced. That moral licensing — she must be PERFECT before she's allowed to be violent — is very LLM. Humans will let the sitter be late, steal a snack, snap at a kid, and still deserve not to be assaulted. **8. Rube Goldberg set-pieces and cliffhanger symmetry.** LLMs love Home Alone traps, house-as-maze, DIY pepper spray, breaker-box kills, and ending *every* chapter on a gasp. When everything is clever and everything cliffhangs, nothing lands. Humans do boredom, waiting, anticlimax, chapters that end flat because she's just sitting on the laundry floor listening. # Deep Dive: Where The Current Intention & Plan Falls Into Those Traps This isn't that the plan is bad — the engine is right. It's that it's currently too clean to be pulp. **Maya:** “Dry, tired, funny, calm under pressure” is a description of a voice, not a voice. And ex-medic is doing too much work. It lets her pick a zip-tie with a bobby pin while bleeding calmly, triage herself, set traps — competence porn. Where is she incompetent? Where does she freeze, misread the house, drop the knife, text the wrong person? Right now she de-escalates, sacrifices, then becomes flawless hunter. That's a superhero arc in scrubs. **The kids as receipts:** Lila with a tablet + nanny cam + bodycam is triple redundancy to ensure Maya will be believed. That's the LLM fear of ambiguity. It guarantees a tidy legal win in Ch.8 and removes the most human horror: what if you do everything right and the drunk homeowners with the nice house are still believed over you? **The villains as functions:** Kyle and Drez exist to be humiliated one by one. Jenna and Brad exist to be billed. No one gets a moment where you understand why they thought they could do this — which makes the revenge less satisfying, not more. Kyle loving his niece and still scaring her would be more disturbing than Kyle shouting "I know you're up here!" **Specific beats that feel LLM-assembled:** * Ch1 checklist of disrespect — cold pizza, short Venmo, thermostat locked, pantry off limits, blocked car — is every babysitter horror story at once. A human would pick *one* humiliation and let it fester all night. The $40 short is enough. Don't need five. * Ch2 storm + power flicker + "don't go in basement lol" text + unlocked slider + blinking cam + duffel you're told not to touch. That's five isolation devices stacked. Pick one and make it dumb and human — like she *thought* she locked it but she was carrying laundry and a kid and didn't. * Ch3 "offers to let them take duffel and go, no cops" — impossibly noble. A human might offer them anything to not go upstairs because she is terrified of being blamed for a noise complaint, not because she's heroic. * Ch5 LEGO ambush, pasta water, hand slammed in safe drawer. Clever-punishment violence. The symbolism — thief's hand punished — is very LLM neat. Real violence is clumsier, less poetic, and leaves you shaking. * Ch6 forced confession on camera at gun-distance but unloaded. Classic LLM loophole: get the power fantasy of a gun without the moral stain of using it. Pulp would make her decide whether to bluff, and make the bluff go wrong. * Ch7 "makes them count out cash + transfer triple pay + hazard fee while men groan tied up" and "makes Brad walk barefoot in rain" and "makes Jenna apologize to kids' door." This is revenge as itemized invoice + public apology ritual. Very satisfying to outline, very safe to read. It's Etsy, not pulp. * Ch8 cops separate everyone, calm medic report wins, EMTs, crayon drawing of her with skillet cape, payment received, dawn walkaway with new rule. That's three bows: legal, financial, sentimental. And that last line rule — "she doesn't babysit for people who don't respect the sitter" — is a fortune cookie, not a scar. **Voice problem:** "Elmore Leonard / Tarantino-light" + first-person past tense + short punchy sentences + great asshole dialogue is what every LLM says when asked for pulp. But Leonard's people are losers who think they're smart. Tarantino's people talk too much because they're scared. What does *Maya* sound like when she's not being badass? How does she talk to herself when no one can hear? The plan has no idiolect, no code-switch, no region, no age in the syntax. # Brainstorms To Make It More Human (No Rewriting Yet, Just Directions) **Make Maya specific and slightly unlikeable:** * Give her money shame in particulars: $162 for rent, phone at 7%, period starting without a pad so she's stuffing toilet paper, stealing cheese sticks from their fridge and hating herself for it. * Let her resent the kids. Lila corrects her pronunciation. Noah kicks her in the shin and she thinks something mean. She doesn't go maternal instantly; she stays because leaving would be worse for *her* — she'd never forgive herself, she'd lose the reference. * Let her be bad at parts: she freezes on the stairs. She drops her own phone in the toilet earlier so the "they take her phone" beat actually hurts. She misremembers the code. Her wrist swells in Ch4 and *stays* swollen, fucking up everything she tries in Ch5-6. * Give her a mouth: not quips, but muttered Spanish when angry, nurse-gallows humor that's inappropriate, intrusive thoughts she doesn't say out loud. Let her be sexual — noticing Drez is hot and hating that she noticed when she's scared. **Make the kids inconvenient:** * What if Lila *likes* Uncle Kyle and runs to him, ruining Maya's plan? What if Noah sleepwalks downstairs at the worst moment because that's what he does, not to help the plot but because he's six and overtired? What if Lila filmed Maya yelling, not just the men, and that video could hurt Maya too? * Cut one recording device. Better: footage is shaky, dark, ambiguous. Or Lila stops filming because she's scared and Maya is furious about it and then ashamed for being furious at a child. **Make the villains pathetic-human, not evil-smart:** * Kyle owes back child support, genuinely thinks Brad owes him and this is how brothers do. He brought dinosaur gummies for Noah. He's still willing to scare a woman to get it. Both can be true. * Drez isn't twitchy-evil, he's dopesick and embarrassed and keeps apologizing while doing terrible things. Apologetic violence is scarier and sadder. * Jenna and Brad: don't make them sober villains. Make them drunk-looping, condescending in that specific realtor way: touching Maya's arm while talking over her, calling her "sweetie," saying "we've all had hard months." Brad moving her car barefoot shouldn't feel triumphant — it should feel grubby and small while the kids listen through a door. **Make the house gross and real:** * Not a maze, a lived-in rental with a sticky island, a dead Roomba, a safe with the factory code still on a Post-it because Brad is lazy, a basement that smells like cat piss, toys that hurt *her* more than him because she steps on them while carrying Noah. * Continuity of hurt: split lip that keeps reopening when she talks, blood on someone else's white towel she knows she'll be blamed for. **Make violence ugly, brief, and costly:** * No multi-trap gauntlet. Maybe she only gets *one* good hit in, and it's desperate and too hard, and she vomits. Maybe she enjoys it for a second. Maybe she uses a tool wrong. * Let her lie. To the kids ("everything's fine"), to the cops (leaves out that she considered taking the pills, leaves out that she hit Drez after he was down). Let the reader sit with that lie instead of bodycam absolution. **Make money and ending unresolved:** * What if the transfer doesn't go through? What if she takes cash from the safe and that's theft and she knows it? What if she gets paid but loses the family as clients and the agency drops her because Jenna leaves a 2-star review that says "unstable"? * Kill the cape drawing. Or keep a drawing but make it upsetting — Noah draws what he *heard*, not a superhero. Or Lila doesn't thank her, just asks "are you coming back tomorrow?" and Maya has to say no. * Don't end at dawn walking away with a rule. End mid-exhaustion: in the ER waiting room, in her car that won't start, falling asleep with the doors locked while it's light out. No lesson, just aftermath. **Voice exercises to try:** * Ban words for a draft: accountability, trauma, boundaries, dignity, hazard fee, empowered, processing. Replace with pulp plain-speak: stiffed, owed, pay me, get out, don't touch them. * Write one chapter where nothing clever happens — just waiting, listening to the monitor, trying not to cry because crying will scare the kids. Let boredom + dread do the work traps were doing. * Give Maya one repeated tic, not a catchphrase: checking the time, doing math in her head ($160 divided by...), narrating injuries to herself like triage notes because that's how she stays calm.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **This is a grubby, working-class pulp revenge story, not a competence fantasy.** The engine is still underestimation — broke babysitter mistaken for pushover — but the payoff will be transgressive and stained, not HR-approved. * **Protagonist locked:** Maya Reyes, 32, ex-Army medic turned nursing student. I am keeping the backstory because it explains *how she stays calm*, but stripping it of superhero use. She does triage self-talk in her head to keep from panicking. She is also bad at a lot: she freezes on stairs, she drops things, she misreads people, her left wrist swells in Ch4 and stays fucked for the rest of the night. She is specific and sometimes unlikeable. Money shame in numbers: $162 rent short, phone at 7% after she dropped it in the toilet earlier, period starting with no pad so she's wadded with toilet paper, stealing cheese sticks from the fridge and hating herself. She resents Lila for correcting her English and thinks something mean when Noah kicks her. She notices Drez is hot and is disgusted with herself for noticing while scared. She considers stealing from the safe herself. She considers leaving. * **Voice locked:** First-person past tense, Maya. Plain, tired, bodily pulp. Short Anglo-Saxon words: sticky, broke, locked, tired, blood. No lyrical similes, no epigrams. Her tics, not catchphrases: checking the time and doing math in her head ($120 divided by 5 hours...), narrating her own injuries like chart notes (split lip, 1cm, keeps reopening when I talk), muttering in Spanish when angry, inappropriate nurse humor she doesn't say out loud. Drunk/scared people loop and interrupt, they don't deliver villain monologues. * **Banned language for the draft:** accountability, boundaries, dignity, trauma, emotional labor, empowered, processing, hazard fee, justice. Replace with: stiffed, owed, pay me, get out, don't touch them. * **The kids as inconveniences, not cameras:** Lila, 9, anxious and ingratiating — she *likes* Uncle Kyle and runs to him, wrecking Maya's plan. She starts filming on her tablet then stops because she's scared, and Maya is furious at her for stopping then ashamed. She also filmed Maya screaming, which can hurt Maya later. Noah, 6, sleepwalker who comes downstairs at the worst time because he's overtired, not to advance plot. They stay mostly upstairs behind a door, heard muffled via one baby monitor. No graphic peril, no sexualization. What they hear leaves a mark. * **Villains as pathetic, not functions:** Kyle, dad's younger brother, 30, owes back child support, truly thinks Brad owes him and this is how brothers settle it. He brought dinosaur gummies for Noah. He will still scare a woman to get what he wants. Drez, 26, dopesick and embarrassed, keeps apologizing while doing terrible things. Apologetic violence. Jenna (realtor) and Brad (crypto) aren't sober evil — they come home drunk, touch Maya's arm while talking over her, call her sweetie, loop "you're being crazy, why are you being crazy." * **House as gross and real, not a maze:** Lived-in suburban rental: sticky island, dead Roomba, white towels Maya bleeds on and knows she'll be blamed for, basement that smells like cat piss, office safe with factory code on a Post-it because Brad is lazy. One layout learned early and reused badly — Maya steps on toys while carrying Noah and hurts *herself* more. * **Violence: brief, ugly, costly.** No Home Alone gauntlet. She gets *one* good desperate hit and it's too hard, after he's down, and she enjoys it for two seconds then vomits. Tools used wrong. Split lip keeps reopening. She lies afterward — to kids (everything's fine), to cops (leaves out the extra hit, leaves out that she took cash). Reader sits with the lie. * **Money and ending unresolved.** No triple-pay + bodycam + cape-drawing triple bow. Transfer pends / doesn't clear. Cash she takes from safe is theft and she knows it. Agency drops her after Jenna's 2-star "unstable" review. End in exhaustion, not dawn triumph with a rule. * **Structure for 8 x 1000 words:** Real-time night ~9:47pm to ~5:15am. Small cast only: Maya + 2 kids + 2 intruders + 2 parents. One humiliation that festers (stiffed + blocked in so she can't leave), one isolation failure that is *her* fault, not five stacked devices. Not every chapter ends on a gasp — some end flat on waiting/listening because dread does more work than traps. **Aim for:** body, pettiness, moral mess, complicity, pulp plain-speak. **Avoid:** safe proportional revenge, legal absolution, clever-punishment symbolism, itemized invoice revenge, perfect victim licensing, stereotype dialogue, flawless hunter turn. # Chapter Planning **Ch 1 - 9:47 PM - The Stiff** Maya arrives already late into leaving parents. Establish in 1000 words: body tired, cheese stick theft, Lila correcting her, Noah kick. *One* festering disrespect: Jenna Venmos $80 not $120 — "we'll fix later lol" — and Brad has blocked her Corolla in with the Tesla so she literally cannot leave without asking. Map house in passing: stairs, office, kitchen island, back slider, garage. Lila: Uncle Kyle gives good hugs but Mom says don't open for him. End flat, not clever: Maya doing math in head, hearing a car circle twice. **Ch 2 - 10:40 PM - My Fault** Kids to bed upstairs, monitor on. Maya drops phone in toilet earlier = cracked, 7%. No storm damnation, just rain. Jenna texts: Kyle might stop by don't let him in lol + btw don't go in basement. Maya carrying laundry + Noah half-asleep leaves back slider thinking she locked it — she didn't. Finds blinking nanny cam, cat-piss basement, duffel in garage she's told not to touch. Puts kitchen knife in pocket, then puts it back to stay professional. End: back door beep — code punched right. **Ch 3 - 11:30 PM - Uncle Kyle** Kyle + Drez walk in like they live there, freeze. Talky, losery patter: Brad said we could crash, you must be the sitter, kids asleep? Maya doesn't play hero — she begs them to take duffel and go because she'll get blamed for noise, for mess. Lila hears Kyle, runs down happy, ruins containment. They take Maya's dying phone, shove her into counter — split lip on island edge. Drez, sweating and sorry, keeps saying sorry while blocking stairs. Noah sleepwalks out at monitor creak. End with Lila whispering "Maya?" over monitor while Drez turns toward stairs. **Ch 4 - 12:15 AM - Upstairs Is Off** Ugly protective scramble. Maya gets Noah back up, shoves both kids in master bath with tablet + gummies + lie: don't come out no matter what. Hallway fight: she freezes, drops knife, gets punched, wrist twisted, hog-tied with phone charger cord. Mocked as "the help." While they work the office safe, she picks/breaks free clumsily with a bobby pin, wrist swelling fast. Hides in dark laundry room bleeding on white towel, listening on monitor. No badass line. End flat: sitting on floor trying not to cry because crying will scare kids through monitor. **Ch 5 - 1:20 AM - Too Hard** One desperate turn, not a gauntlet. Lure Drez alone with monitor static. Steps on Lego herself, blinds him with bleach spray wrong, hits him once with iron skillet after he's already down — too hard — and likes it for a second then vomits on basement stairs. Drags/ties him to water heater in the basement she was told not to enter. Takes his phone. Lila started filming then stopped; footage dark/shaky, also has Maya screaming. End: Kyle upstairs racking Brad's pistol shouting for his niece, Maya with shaking hands and a swollen wrist that won't grip. **Ch 6 - 2:40 AM - Bluff Called** Cat-and-mouse without cleverness. Breaker kill fails — she flips wrong switch, kills baby monitor instead. Hides, breathes, cat-piss smell. Gets Kyle into garage where her blocked Corolla still traps his exit. DIY spray + skillet, clumsy drop. Gets pistol, tries to bluff a confession for Drez's phone — Kyle calls it, unloaded/mis-handled, struggle. She gets audio confession anyway: whose Oxy, whose cash, Brad owes Kyle, code on Post-it — but audio is garbled, half-usable. Both men tied, groaning. End: garage door opens — Jenna and Brad home early, drunk, staring at bloody Maya holding a bat. **Ch 7 - 3:30 AM - Sweetie** Social revenge as grubby, not triumphant. Parents loop drunk: touching her arm, sweetie, you're being crazy. Brad grabs her sore wrist. Jenna threatens to call cops on *her*, offers $60 to forget. Maya snaps — takes $340 cash from open safe (theft), forces Venmo transfer that shows "pending," makes Brad move Tesla barefoot in rain while kids listen through door. Makes Jenna stop touching her. No apology ritual — Jenna just loops. Lila asks through door if Uncle Kyle is bad now. Maya lies: everything's fine. End: red-blue lights wash windows, Jenna smiles: watch this, cops love us here. **Ch 8 - 5:15 AM - Aftermath** No absolution. Cops separate, believe house first. Footage ambiguous: dark, shaky, has Maya hitting and yelling. Maya gives calm chart-note report but leaves out extra hit and cash. EMTs: split lip reopening, sprained wrist taped. Kyle/Drez cuffed, Brad held about pills. Transfer still pending. Agency text: Jenna left 2-star "unstable." Noah gives her a drawing — not a cape, black scribble of what he *heard*. Lila: are you coming back tomorrow? Maya: no. Final image: dawn in Corolla that won't start at first, doors locked, Maya asleep for 20 minutes with blood on someone else's towel in her lap. No rule, just stain.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Maya Reyes **Background:** 32. El Paso raised, Fort Hood for four years as a medic — one deployment to Kuwait where mostly she treated dehydration, sprains, and guys who lied about drinking. Out two years. Now in a community-college nursing program she’s failing pharmacology by 3 points. Babysits through an app called Nest & Co because she can study after bedtime. Lives with a roommate in a one-bed where she sleeps in the living room for $650. This month she’s $162 short on rent because her roommate’s boyfriend ate the electric bill. **Personality, flaws, tics:** Resentful and proud in a way that costs her money. Won’t text twice about being shorted. Steals food from every house and then is furious at herself — cheese sticks, Goldfish by the handful. Does math constantly: *120 divided by 5 is 24. 24 minus gas.* Checks the microwave clock even when she knows the time. Narrates her own body like a chart to stay calm: *split lip, 1cm, bleeding controlled.* Freezes on stairs. Drops shit when hands are wet. Picks at her cuticles until they bleed. Muttering in Spanish when she’s actually mad — *no mames, pendejo* — English when she’s performing nice. Inappropriate nurse humor she only thinks: *sir, your pain is not 10/10 if you can yell this loud.* Mean in her head to kids she would die for. Thinks *shut UP* when Lila corrects her. Thinks something ugly when Noah kicks her shin. Considered walking out that night. Considered taking from the safe. Stays because if something happened after she left she’d never live with it, and because she needs the 5-star. **Physicality:** 5’4”, stocky, strong forearms, tired eyes. Hair up in a thinning scrunchie, baby hairs stuck with sweat. Thrift Eagles hoodie with a bleach spot, black leggings with a hole opening at the left knee, old Asics with the insoles sliding. Contacts gone dry by 10pm so she’s blinking hard. Starting her period with no pad — wadded toilet paper, checking the back of her pants in the hallway mirror. Tries to make herself small in rich houses. Shoulders up. When she’s in medic mode her voice drops and goes flat. **Motives / people:** Owes rent, owes her mom a lie that school is “going great.” Needs this family as repeat clients. Hates Jenna and Brad by 9:52pm and still needs them. Loyal to the kids in a feral, non-maternal way: *you’re mine till 2am, so nobody touches you.* Not loyal to the parents, not loyal to Kyle even if he cries. Loyal to herself last. **Voice:** > Internal: *120 promised. 80 sent. That’s my phone bill walking away. Smile, Maya.* > Out loud, too nice: “No worries, just send the rest tonight, yeah?” > Later, flat: “Don’t. Don’t grab my wrist. I’m telling you once.” # Lila Hartley **Background:** 9, third grade, anxious pleaser. Parents fight about “what really happened” a lot, so she films things on a cracked Samsung tablet. 9:47 PM - The Stiff They were already late when I got there, which I knew they would be. Rain on my windshield the whole way over, the Corolla wipers skipping. I pulled up to the Hartleys' at 9:47 and the Tesla was parked sideways across the end of the driveway, blocking me in. Not beside me. Across. So I had to park on the street and run up with my backpack getting wet. Jenna opened the door before I knocked. Smell of wine and vanilla hit me first. "Sweeeetie! Thank God," she said, and grabbed my forearm. She always grabbed. White jeans, bare feet, toenails chipped red. "We're so late, Brad's friend held the table—" I was wet in the doorway. My hoodie stuck to my arms. The house was hot, set to seventy-one and locked there with that little plastic box over the thermostat I’d seen before. "It's fine," I said. It's what you say. Brad came down the stairs pulling a jacket on, backwards cap, Tesla key spinning around his finger. He looked at me and then past me, like he was checking if I'd brought someone. "Maya, my man," he said. "Kids are half fed. Pizza's on the island. Lila knows bedtime." Lila was on the couch with her tablet, unicorn shirt gone gray from washing. Skinny legs tucked under her. She looked up. "Hi Maya," she said. "You say li-brary wrong last time." "What did I say?" "Lie-brary. It's lye-brary." "Shit. Noted." Jenna laughed too loud. "She's our little teacher." Noah ran in from the kitchen in dinosaur pants and no shirt, hot and sticky, blanket wadded up against his face so he could barely see. He ran straight into my leg and then kicked my shin hard with his bare foot. "Ow. Hey." "You're not my mom," he said. "I know. I'm worse, I make you brush teeth." He kicked me again, lighter, then grabbed my hand like we were fine now. My shin throbbed. I thought, *little shit,* and then hated thinking it. The island was sticky. Two slices of cold pizza in the box, crusts curled. I hadn't eaten since the vending machine at school at two. While Jenna went upstairs to get her purse I peeled a cheese stick from the Hartleys' fridge pack. It was for the kids' lunches. I ate it standing in front of the open fridge so the camera on the bookshelf wouldn't see. I told myself they'd never count cheese sticks. I counted the money instead. One twenty for tonight. That's what Jenna had texted Tuesday. Five hours, nine to two. Twenty-four an hour. Rent is six-fifty for the living room I sleep in, and I was one-sixty-two short because my roommate's boyfriend used our electric money for his truck. So I needed that one twenty like air. Jenna came down with her little purse. "Okay! Lila in bed by ten-thirty, Noah by ten, don't let them tell you different. Thermostat stays, okay? Pantry's off-limits, sorry, Brad's protein stuff is all measured. Back slider sticks, just slam it. Oh, and don't go in the basement, it's a mess lol." She said lol out loud. "Lol." "Got it," I said. My phone buzzed. Venmo from Jenna Hartley: $80.00. Memo: *tonight!! <3* I stared at it. "Hey," I said. "You sent eighty. We said one twenty." Jenna didn't even look. She was putting earrings in in the hallway mirror. "Did I? Ugh, I'll fix it later, okay? We're running, you’re the best, sweetie." Forearm grab again. Her fingers cold. Brad was already opening the front door. "Basically Venmo holds sometimes over a hundred, you know how it is." "It's eighty," I said. "We'll fix later," Jenna said, and kissed Lila's head and missed and kissed air. "Be good! Love you! Don't open for anyone!" "Wait, your car—" I said. "You're blocking me in. I parked on the street because—" Brad waved the Tesla key. "Oh yeah, sorry, just text when you're leaving, I'll move it. We're literally around the corner." They were gone. Door shut. Lock clicked. 120 promised. 80 sent. That's my phone bill walking away. I stood there with my wet backpack and did the math I always did. Eighty divided by five is sixteen. Sixteen an hour to get kicked and corrected. One sixty-two minus eighty is eighty-two still short. Plus gas to get home. Noah tugged my leggings. There was a hole opening at my left knee getting bigger every wash. "Pizza?" he said. "You had pizza," Lila said fast. "Mom said half fed means no more." "I'll cut you a tiny piece," I said. "Then teeth. Then bed." While I cut it with dull scissors because I couldn't find a clean knife, Lila followed me around with the tablet down. "Uncle Kyle came last week," she said. "He gives good hugs. He brought gummies but Mom threw them." "Yeah?" "Mom says don't open for him if he knocks," she said. "But he's funny. He knows dinosaur names." Noah, mouth full: "Stegosaurus." "Don't talk full," Lila said automatically. My pants felt wet. Not rain. I'd started spotting that afternoon in pharmacology and I had no pad, just toilet paper wadded up in the Hartleys' downstairs bathroom while the kids banged on the door asking what I was doing. I checked the back of my pants in the hallway mirror when they weren't looking. Nothing showed on black leggings. Small mercy. I got Noah to brush with the timer, spit everywhere, pajama shirt finally on backwards. Lila brushed for a full two minutes and showed me. "Perfect," I said. "Lyebrary girl." "Lye-brary," she corrected, but she smiled. Upstairs the house was a straight shot. I clocked it like I always do. Front stairs up to a landing, kids' rooms left, master with the attached bath right, office at the end of the hall with the door cracked and the safe light on green inside. Downstairs: kitchen island in the middle, sticky, living room with the dead Roomba in the corner, back slider to the patio, door to the garage by the laundry. Basement door under the stairs with a kid lock. Normal house. Rich-people rental normal. White towels I was afraid to bleed on. At 10:15 Noah was half asleep on my shoulder, hot hands on my neck, blanket in his face so I couldn't see where I was stepping. I carried him up and stepped on a Lego stegosaurus on the landing and almost went down. Pain shot up my foot. *Pendejo,* I muttered, not at him. At the Lego. "What?" Lila whispered behind me. "Nothing. Grown-up word for ouch." I got them down. Lila in her bed with tablet charging, Noah tucked with his sticky dinosaur. Baby monitor on the nightstand — the parent unit crackled when I picked it up. I brought it downstairs. I ate the second cold slice standing up. Ate another cheese stick. Hated myself for the second one more than the first. Checked my phone. 10:32. Checked the microwave. 10:32. Locked the front door, chained it. Went to the back slider and slammed it like she said. It stuck, then caught. I thought it locked. The little lock turned. I sat on their couch that smelled like other people's laundry and pulled out my pharm flashcards. Creatinine clearance. I kept reading the same card. Outside, headlights washed across the front windows, slow. A car went past. Then it came back and went past again, slower. I sat up.

Someone's teenager. I sat on the couch with my flashcards and my heart knocking too loud for nothing. *10:38. Heart rate up. Cause: being broke in someone else's house.* My phone was at 12% and going down fast. The screen had a fresh crack across the corner from that morning when I'd dropped it in the toilet at school. I'd been trying to pull my backpack onto the stall hook with my foot and it slid right out of my back pocket and into the bowl. I fished it out so fast I burned my wrist on the pipe. Dried it on paper towels while a girl waited outside pretending she didn't hear the splash. It worked after, but the battery bled out now if I just looked at it. I put it on the charger by the couch. The Hartleys only had those short cords that don't reach. So I had to leave it on the floor by the outlet, face down on their rug. It buzzed. Jenna: *btw if Kyle stops by don't let him in lol he's going thru stuff* Then, a minute later: *btw don't go in the basement it's flooded-ish lol* Then: *kids ok??* I stared at those three. Thru stuff. Flooded-ish. Lol. I typed back: *all good asleep*. I didn't say: your back slider sticks, your thermostat is locked, you shorted me forty bucks. I never say it twice. Once is asking. Twice is begging. Lila called down, thin through the hallway: "Maya? Noah's making noise." I took the parent monitor up. It crackled. Upstairs the hall light was on. Noah was sitting straight up in bed, eyes open, blanket over his face, breathing through his mouth. "Hey," I whispered. "You awake?" He didn't answer. He stood up and walked right past me toward the stairs. His feet slapping. Eyes half open. "Noah." I grabbed his shoulders gentle. "Hey, back to bed." Lila sat up in her doorway with her tablet dark in her lap. "He does that when he's tired. Mom yells and he cries." "I'm not gonna yell," I said. I walked Noah back. He was hot all over, sweaty neck. He let me tuck him again and rolled over with the stegosaurus stuck to his cheek. Asleep like someone flipped a switch. "He sleepwalks?" I asked Lila. "Only when it's loud," she said. She was chewing her sleeve. It was wet. "Are you staying downstairs?" "Yeah. Monitor's on. You yell, I hear." "Uncle Kyle knows dinosaur names," she said again, like she was trying it out. "I know a lady who knows drug names. Go to sleep." She almost smiled. "Lye-brary." "Goodnight, teacher." Downstairs I couldn't focus on the cards. Creatinine clearance swam. The house ticked. Rain on the patio. Fridge humming too loud. I noticed the little red blink on the bookshelf then. I'd thought it was a router. It wasn't. It was a camera, tucked between the cookbooks, lens right at the couch. At me. Nanny cam. They never said. My face got hot. I thought about the cheese sticks. I thought about picking at my pants in the hallway mirror. I thought about sitting here with my legs spread because my leggings were cutting in. *Hi Jenna,* I thought. *Hope the footage is good.* I stood up and turned my back to it to adjust the toilet paper wadded in my underwear. It was already damp and shifting. Spotting day is the worst because you can't trust anything. I checked the bathroom trash for a pad I could steal. Nothing but floss picks and a kid's Band-Aid. That's when I smelled the basement. I'd gone to throw the pizza box in the under-stair closet and opened the wrong door. The basement door. The kid lock was flipped up, unlocked. Warm, sour air came up — cat piss and old laundry and damp concrete. They don't even have a cat. I shut it fast. Flooded-ish, my ass. It smelled like something died down there and nobody wanted to pay to find it. I went to check the garage next because my brain wouldn't sit still. The door by the laundry. Brad had said don't touch the duffel? No, Jenna had texted that Tuesday when I asked where the extra blankets were: *in garage btw don't touch the black duffel lol Brad's work stuff.* It was still there. Big black duffel, half under a moving blanket, zipper straining. Next to it my Corolla would be if I could get to it, except I couldn't see my car from inside. Just the Tesla's ass blocking the driveway on the little window. Eighty divided by five is sixteen. Sixteen an hour to stare at a duffel I'm not supposed to touch while my phone dies. I heard the patter on the patio and went to the back slider. Rain harder now. I opened it a crack to listen for that car again, cold air on my face. Then Noah thumped upstairs — just rolled over loud — and Lila called "Maya?" and I grabbed the basket of clean kid laundry to bring up as an excuse, thinking *I'm coming, I'm coming,* and I pulled the slider shut behind me but I didn't turn the little lock. I thought I did. My hand did the motion. In my head I locked it. I know because later I kept replaying my hand. Upstairs I put folded shirts outside their doors. Noah was snoring wet through his mouth. Lila's light was off but her tablet glowed under the blanket. She wasn't filming. Just holding it lit, like a nightlight. "You good?" I whispered. "It's okay! It's fine!" she said too fast. "Okay. Sleep." Downstairs my phone was at 7%. The flashcards said *hold for renal dosing* and I couldn't remember what renal meant for a second, which scared me more than the car. I went to the kitchen for water and stood there with the drawer open looking at their knives. Big chef's knife in the block. I took it out. Heavy. I slipped it in my hoodie pocket and it pulled my hoodie down crooked. I stood there feeling stupid and dangerous. Then I thought about Jenna watching the footage later. *Unstable.* The agency drops you for less. I'd seen a girl get deactivated because a dad said she "went through drawers." I put the knife back in the block. Pushed the drawer shut soft. *Professional,* I told myself. *Be professional and get your eighty bucks and your star rating.* I sat back on the couch facing away from the blinking red light. Put the monitor on the coffee table. Turned it up. Breathing. Rain. Lila coughing once. My own contacts scraping every time I blinked. 10:58. 10:59. I checked the microwave even though I knew. Then from the kitchen — behind me — a beep. Keys. Numbers. The back door code being punched in, right.

[Analysis] This chapter executes its plan with considerable discipline and craft. The writing stays true to the established voice — plain, bodily, Anglo-Saxon, tired — and avoids the temptations of lyrical inflation that would undermine the pulp-grubby aesthetic the plan demands. The chapter's strongest quality is its physical specificity. The toilet paper bunched sideways, the wet on the back of her thigh she can't check, the blood bubbling on her lip when she speaks, the protein powder raining down from the pantry sign — these details are earned and precise. Nothing goes cleanly. The breaker-box failure is handled well — she kills the baby monitor instead of the lights, which is both a practical failure and an emotional one (she loses her ear on the kids). The plan specified this exact beat and the chapter executes it without underlining it. The reader feels the cost without being told to. Kyle's characterization is consistent with his profile: the "boss" and "my guy" verbal tics appear, he's simultaneously threatening and pathetic, he cries from bleach and lies on the concrete breathing dust. His line about Drez having a kid — "he's got a kid, man" — while he himself has a kid he owes support for is a nice ironic touch that isn't spelled out. The plan called for him to be "pathetic, not a function" and he is. The gun bluff is the chapter's centerpiece and it works because it's genuinely ambiguous and clumsy. Maya doesn't know if it's loaded. Her thumb fumbles the safety. Kyle sees it. He lunges. The click stops him anyway. This is exactly the kind of "bluff called" the chapter title promises — not a clever reversal but a near-disaster that happens to not fully collapse. The confession she extracts is messy and partial, which is consistent with the plan's note that the audio would be "garbled, half-usable." The ending — Jenna and Brad in the rain, drunk, staring — lands well. It's the chapter's promised beat and it arrives without fanfare. The image of Jenna's flat blowout and wet white jeans against the Tesla taillights is economical and character-consistent. Some weaknesses: The Lila monitor moment ("The loud stopped") is effective but the chapter could have used one more beat of her presence to deepen the cost. The extension cord knots being "bad, loose" is mentioned but not dramatized — it's a tell rather than a show, though it's brief enough not to seriously damage the chapter. The line "Mine till two. Mine till two." is the chapter's one moment of internal mantra that edges toward the kind of epigram the plan explicitly wanted to avoid, though it's restrained enough to survive. The dialogue is consistently good — Kyle's loops and self-justifications feel real, not villain-monologue. "Brad always —" cut off is a nice incomplete that implies more than it says. Jenna's scream ending the chapter is the right note: not a line, just a sound. The chapter follows its plan closely: breaker failure killing the monitor, cat-and-mouse in the garage, the gun bluff with garbled audio, both men tied, parents arriving drunk. The one deviation is that the "DIY spray + skillet, clumsy drop" sequence is somewhat compressed and the skillet drop happens earlier in the kitchen rather than the garage, but this is a structural adjustment that works better dramatically. Overall this is a strong chapter — disciplined, bodily, morally unresolved, consistent with character and plan. It doesn't reach for false triumph and it doesn't editorialize. The prose stays in its lane. [Analysis] This is a genuinely impressive piece of pulp revenge fiction that operates with considerable craft and restraint. Let me work through its strengths and weaknesses systematically. VOICE AND CHARACTER: Maya Reyes is one of the more convincingly rendered protagonists in this genre. Her interiority is built through accumulation of specific, grounded detail — the cheese sticks, the toilet paper wadded in her underwear, the pharmacology flashcards, the rent math that runs constantly in her head. The "medic voice" she uses to process trauma (the clinical self-assessments: "Split lip. Lower left. 1 cm. Bleeding a lot because mouths do.") is an excellent character device that reveals backstory economically while also serving as a coping mechanism. This is show-don't-tell working at a high level. The supporting characters are more mixed. Lila is genuinely well-drawn — her "It's okay! It's fine!" mantra is heartbreaking and consistent. Noah's sleepwalking and his crayon drawing of "the loud" are strong touches. Kyle has some dimension (his genuine affection for Lila, his grievance about the fifteen hundred dollars) but Drez is thin — essentially a guilt-ridden prop. Brad and Jenna are deliberately cartoonish, which works for pulp but limits their complexity. PLOT AND PACING: The story moves well through its chapters. The escalation from domestic irritation to genuine threat is handled with good timing. The detail about the back slider not being locked — Maya's hand doing the motion without completing it — is a smart piece of setup. The revelation that Brad is the actual criminal (the Oxy, the cash, the duffel) is satisfying and earned through earlier planted details. The action sequences are credible rather than cinematic, which is the right choice. Maya is not a superhero. She gets hurt badly, makes mistakes (dropping the knife, the failed breaker box gambit), and wins through improvisation and desperation rather than competence. The bleach spray, the little iron skillet, the bobby pin — these feel like real objects in a real house used by someone thinking under pressure. WEAKNESSES: The ending is the story's most significant problem. The arrival of the cops and the aftermath chapter (Chapter 8) is where the piece loses some of its grip. The two-star review from Jenna is a strong, bitter detail. But the resolution feels slightly rushed and the emotional payoff is muted in a way that reads as unresolved rather than deliberately ambiguous. Maya taking the cash is morally interesting but the story doesn't quite commit to examining it — she lies to the cop, she knows it's theft, and then the story ends with her sleeping in the car. This is tonally right for noir but the piece has been so precise elsewhere that this vagueness feels like avoidance rather than craft. The "pendeja/pendejo" interjections are used three times and feel slightly calculated — a way to signal Maya's background without doing the harder work of integrating it more fully. It's not egregious but it's noticeable. The pistol sequence is the weakest action beat. Kyle lunging when Maya can't fire, the click, him freezing anyway — this is a bit convenient. The story has been careful to avoid easy wins, so this moment of Kyle being stopped by an empty-chamber click feels slightly unearned. DIALOGUE: Generally strong. The Hartleys' speech patterns (Jenna's "lol" said aloud, Brad's "basically") are well-observed class markers. Kyle's dialogue is functional. The weakest dialogue is in Chapter 7 when Jenna loops "you're being crazy" — it's a real behavior but it's deployed a few too many times and starts to feel like a tic rather than a character trait. PROSE QUALITY: The prose is clean and controlled. The metaphors are mostly earned — "big red flower dried brown at the edges" for the blood on the towel is genuinely good. "Birds stupid loud" at dawn is excellent. The story avoids purple prose almost entirely. There are occasional moments where the clinical voice becomes slightly mannered, but these are minor. COHERENCE: The story is highly coherent. Details planted early (the camera, the duffel, the safe, the back slider, the Lego stegosaurus) pay off consistently. The timeline is tracked carefully. The physical injuries accumulate logically. PROMPT FAITHFULNESS: The story delivers on "they fucked with the wrong babysitter" in a way that subverts the genre expectation — Maya doesn't become an action hero, she survives through desperation and intelligence, and the victory is pyrrhic. This is a more interesting interpretation than a straightforward revenge fantasy. OVERALL: This is a strong, professional-quality piece of genre fiction with genuine literary ambition. Its weaknesses are real but minor relative to its considerable strengths. [Scores] Believable Character Actions: 17 Nuanced Characters: 15 Pacing: 16 World Building: 17 Compelling Plot: 16 Emotionally Engaging: 17 Coherent: 18 Weak Dialogue: 4 Tell-Don't-Show: 3 Unsurprising or Uncreative: 5 Amateurish: 3 Purple Prose: 2 Forced Poetry or Metaphor: 3 Unearned Transformations: 4 Well-earned Lightness or Darkness: 16 Faithful to Writing Prompt: 18

Initial Writing Prompt:
Queer Neo-Noir Romance Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.
+ Planning Phase (5 Steps)
Queer Neo-Noir Romance Write a short story over several chapters to this prompt: He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas. -- Your task is to create a writing plan for this prompt. The scope will be a short story, written over {n_chapters} chapters. Each chapter will be approximately 1000 words so plan accordingly for this scope. Your plan should be comprehensive and in this format: # Brainstorming <Brainstorm ideas for characters, plot, tone, story beats, pacing over the {n_chapters} chapters. The purpose of brainstorming is to cast a wide net of ideas, not to settle on any specific direction. Think about various ways you could take the prompt.> # Reflection <Reflect out loud on what works and doesn't work in these ideas. The purpose of this reflection is to narrow in on what you think will work best to make a piece that is a. compelling, and b. fits the prompt requirements. You are not making any decisons just yet, just reflecting.>
Model Output:
# Brainstorming **Purpose: Cast a wide net. No decisions yet, just possibilities for a Queer Neo-Noir Romance in 8 x ~1000 word chapters (~8000 words total).** **Core Prompt Line: "He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas."** * Ideas for how to use it: Chapter 1 first line voiceover; a repeated refrain that changes meaning each time; something the narrator says about the love interest, then later realizes is also true about himself; graffiti / police report / drag king stage name; ironic - he doesn't actually smoke anymore because of vaping ban, it's all performance. **Protagonists / Narrators (Who's telling this noir?):** * Jules, 34, lesbian ex-cop turned unlicensed PI in rain-drowned Portland, dry-witted voiceover, sober two years, takes photos of cheating spouses. * Theo / Thea? A nonbinary cab driver / night-shift EMT who sees the city at 3am and keeps everyone's secrets. * Marcus Bell, 42, Black gay true-crime podcaster who wanted a story and became one. * Elena + ??? - Butch insurance investigator in Neo-New Orleans after the levees went up and the rich went uptown. * Silas, 27, trans man, former runaway, now bartender at a queer noir bar called Femme, who cleans up other people's messes. * Two first-person narrators alternating? A detective and the suspect both telling lies. **The "He" - Cigarette Smoke and Bad Ideas:** * Variant A: Classic Homme Fatale - gorgeous, broke, lying through perfect teeth. Nico, 29, club kid / escort / aspiring actor who hires the PI to find his missing boyfriend, then vanishes himself. * Variant B: Older, ruined charm - Detective Ray Vidal, 50s, still wears a suit in heat, divorced three times (twice from women, once from a man), knows where bodies are buried because he helped. * Variant C: Soft-boy danger - Eli Park, grad student / hacker / arsonist for hire, doesn't look dangerous until he is. * Variant D: Not one he but a type - the narrator keeps falling for the same man in different bodies. * Variant E: Subversion - "He" is kind, stable, and the bad ideas are the narrator's projection. The smoke clears to reveal someone real. **Queer Angle Options (beyond just gay couple):** * Lesbian noir: take femme fatale trope and make it butch/femme, both women, with He/him lesbian lover for pronoun play. * Gay hardboiled: two men circling each other - client and detective, cop and criminal, journalist and source. * Trans / nonbinary noir: identity, passing, being unseen is a detective skill and a survival skill. The city misgenders and misreads clues the same way. * Bisexual love triangle as double-cross structure: who is playing whom? * Chosen family as stakes: it's not save-the-girl, it's save-the-bar / the youth shelter / the best friend who knows too much. * Queer community itself as the corrupt city: a Pride nonprofit, a gay real-estate developer gentrifying the gayborhood, a dating app selling data to cops. **Settings for Neo-Noir (Neon + Rain + Rot):** * Present-day Los Angeles: Silver Lake / WeHo at last call, wildfire smoke always on horizon, Influencers disappearing. * Near-future Seattle/Portland: constant rain, neon reflected in puddles, facial-recognition cameras everywhere, underground queer clubs off-grid. * Post-climate New Orleans: second-story bars, insurance fraud, saints and sinners. * Las Vegas / Reno: wedding chapels, blackmail videos, desert where you bury things. * A city that feels timeless: diners, motels with ice machines, payphones that still work for a reason. **Noir Engines / Cases (What pulls them together?):** * Missing person: He hires PI to find his lover, who may never have existed. * Blackmail: Photos / video / leaked texts. Someone is outed or will be. * Heist gone wrong: Steal back a hard drive from an ex. Burner phones, one motel room. * Murder: Body found in the club freezer. Everyone has a motive, everyone was dancing. * Inheritance / insurance: A dead drag queen leaves everything to a stranger named "him." * Surveillance romance: Narrator hired to follow Him, falls for him through long lens before they ever speak. **Tone Possibilities:** * Hardboiled + Tender: Cynical voiceover cracks to reveal sincere yearning. "I don't believe in love, I believe in alibis." * Lyrical Melancholy: James Baldwin meets Raymond Chandler - smoke, jazz, longing sentences. * Camp Noir: Over-the-top, self-aware, eyeliner and neon. Knows it's performing noir. * Slow-burn Erotic Thriller: Touch-starved, dangerous attraction, consent negotiated in the middle of lies. * Cozy-Noir? Rainy, sad, but ultimately hopeful - romance redeems noir, not the other way. **Story Beats & Images to Play With:** * First meeting in interrogation room / in back of taxi / over a body / bailing him out. * Cigarette as intimacy: lighting it for each other, sharing one in rain under awning, quitting as love language. * Mirrors, windows, surveillance footage - seeing double, not seeing clearly. * Bad ideas escalating: 1) take his case for cash 2) kiss him (don't kiss clients) 3) lie for him to cops 4) hide him 5) run with him 6) take a bullet / take the fall. * Queer noir motifs: last call lights, drag dressing room, Grindr messages as clues, chosen-name vs deadname on an ID as mystery, ketamine / poppers / hormones on nightstand, protest march as cover for meet. * Sex scene as truth scene: only time they stop lying. **Pacing Over 8 Chapters (~1000 words each):** * Model 1 - Classic 3-Act compressed: Ch1-2 Setup + Meet Cute-Noir, Ch3-4 Investigation + Seduction / First Kiss + First Lie, Ch5 Midpoint Reversal / Body or Betrayal, Ch6-7 Fall / Noir Night of Soul / Second Case Twist, Ch8 Choice: Run / Turn In / Stay. * Model 2 - Countdown: 8 nights, 8 cigarettes, 8 voicemails. Each chapter titled after a bad idea. * Model 3 - Case File Structure: Each chapter opens with police report / transcript / surveillance log, then messy human truth underneath. * Endings to consider: Tragic noir (one dies, one leaves town), Bittersweet romantic (solve case but lose each other, then find again), Hard-won hopeful (burn the money, keep each other, leave city), Open / ambiguous (lighter flicks, cut to black). # Reflection What I'm circling around here is tension: noir wants cynicism, everyone lies, the city is corrupt and love gets you killed. Romance wants vulnerability, someone tells the truth, connection redeems. A Queer Neo-Noir Romance has to hold both without one eating the other. The "cigarette smoke and bad ideas" line works best if it's attraction-as-warning. It's sexy because it's dangerous. So many of the He variants lean into the classic homme fatale - beautiful liar who will ruin you - because that gives instant plot fuel for 8000 words. That's strong for pacing: desire *is* the mystery. The narrator wants to know him and wants him, and those get confused. That confusion can power Chapters 1-4 easily. But I have to watch the trap: if He is *only* smoke and lies, he becomes a prop, not a love interest, and the queer romance feels hollow or stereotypical - the gay tragic hustler who dies to teach the detective a lesson. That would be compelling as noir but disappointing as romance, and it leans into tired queer tragedy tropes. The reflection here is: I need Him to have his own wound, agenda, and agency beyond seducing the narrator, or the last 3 chapters won't land emotionally. On the narrator side, the ex-cop / PI / bartender / driver ideas all work because they give a reason to be up at night, to ask questions, to be an outsider-insider in queer community. The ex-cop PI is the most plug-and-play for neo-noir voiceover, but also the most cliché. A non-PI narrator - like the bartender or EMT - could feel fresher and queerer, but then I need to manufacture why they keep investigating instead of calling cops (answer: they *can't* call cops - community distrust, immigration, sex work, past record). That distrust is actually very useful for neo-noir: the police aren't the solution, they're another threat. That fits queer history well. Setting-wise, rain + neon + wildfire smoke all do the same work: obscure vision, make lights bleed, give excuse for being inside close together. LA vs Portland vs New Orleans is less about geography and more about what kind of corruption I want. Real-estate gentrification of a gayborhood, a dating app selling data, a Pride org laundering money - those feel *neo* in a way a simple murder doesn't. They make the personal political without being preachy, and they raise stakes beyond just two people. For an 8-chapter scope, though, I can't build a huge conspiracy. I need one small, intimate crime that *implies* a bigger rot. Blackmail or a missing person is better than a city-wide conspiracy - keep it to ~5 characters max or 1000-word chapters will feel rushed. For tone, I'm thinking hardboiled voice cracking into tenderness is the sweet spot. If it's too campy, the danger won't feel real. If it's too lyrical, the 1000-word chapters could get flabby. The voiceover needs to be funny, tired, a little horny, a little heartbroken - that lets me do a lot of character work fast in Chapter 1. "He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas" as an opening line is almost too perfect not to use, but I need to earn it by complicating it by Chapter 8 - maybe narrator realizes *he* became the smoke and bad ideas for someone else. Structurally, 8 chapters means I have very little room to waste. Chapters 1-2 must establish voice, attraction, and case. Chapters 3-4 must deepen both investigation and intimacy - ideally the kiss and the lie happen in the same chapter. Chapter 5 has to be the gut-punch midpoint where we learn He lied about something core, or someone dies. If I wait until Chapter 6 for the twist, there won't be enough space for fallout and repair. Chapters 6-7 should be the noir low point - rain, betrayal, narrator alone - but with clues that recontextualize the lie as protection, not just manipulation. Chapter 8 can't just solve the crime; it has to answer: do damaged people get to choose each other anyway? What doesn't work: love triangle with too many players, sprawling cast, or an ending that's purely tragic *or* purely fluffy. Pure tragedy betrays the romance promise; pure fluff betrays noir. I'm leaning toward bittersweet-hopeful - they burn the evidence, lose the money, keep the bar / each other, leave town on a bus as sun comes up. Still noir lighting, but two silhouettes instead of one. So the strongest thread I'm seeing is: lonely queer investigator who doesn't believe in love takes a case from a beautiful liar, follows him, falls for him, discovers the lie was covering a more vulnerable truth about survival, has to decide whether to turn him in or run with him. Small cast, rainy neon city, one intimate crime, voiceover that starts cynical and ends sincere. That gives me both genres in every chapter, not just alternating between them.
