Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **What this story will be:** A Queer Neo-Noir Romance in 8 chapters (~1000 words each, ~8000 total). First-person hardboiled with a tender crack down the middle. Cynical voiceover that starts as performance and ends as confession. **My core choices, synthesized from brainstorming:** **Plot / Engine:** Small, intimate crime that implies big rot. Not a city-wide conspiracy — I don't have room for that in 8k. Nico Cassidy, 28, hires unlicensed PI Dev Menon, 37, to find his missing "boyfriend" Milo. The boyfriend is real, but the story is a cover: Milo stole a hard drive with blackmail videos / private data scraped from a queer dating app, owned by gay developer Hollis Crane who is buying up the gayborhood to build luxury condos under a Pride nonprofit front. Nico wants the drive back to protect Milo and blackmail Crane into leaving their bar alone. Only 5 characters total to keep 1000-word chapters tight. **Who's who:** * *Narrator:* Dev Menon, 37, gay Indian-American, ex-Portland cop pushed out for snitching on another cop, now unlicensed PI shooting cheating-spouse photos. Sober 2 years, lonely, up all night. Outsider-insider: distrusted by cops, not quite trusted by community. * *Him:* Nico Cassidy, 28, bartender/sometime escort at queer bar The Glass Femme. The line *“He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas”* is Dev's first read of him. Nico will earn agency: he's not just a beautiful liar, he's a protector lying to keep a runaway kid and a chosen-family bar alive. * *Supporting:* Mama Lou, 60s, Black lesbian owner of The Glass Femme; Milo Reyes, 22, queer runaway; Hollis Crane + his fixer (count as one threat). * *Why Dev can't just call cops:* Community history + Dev's own history. Cops are another danger, not the solution. This is what makes it queer noir, not just noir with gay people. **Setting:** Present-day Portland in endless November rain. Neon bleeding in puddles, wildfire haze in memory, diners, a motel with an ice machine, last-call lights. Timeless noir texture + neo surveillance: Grindr messages, doorbell cams, facial rec, burner phones. **Voice & Style:** * Past-tense first-person voiceover, dry, tired, horny, heartbroken. Chandler meets Baldwin. Opening line of Ch.1: *He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.* * Refrain that evolves: that line repeats in Ch.5 and Ch.8 with new meaning — first lust/warning, then accusation, then self-recognition. * Each chapter opens with 1-2 lines of fake case file: surveillance log / invoice / transcript. Then messy human truth undercuts it. * Cigarette as intimacy language: offering, lighting, sharing under an awning, quitting. Sex in Ch.4 is the only scene where they stop lying — the truth scene. * Lyrical but lean: 1-2 scenes per chapter max. No room for flabby description. **Romance + Noir structure:** Desire IS the mystery. Dev falls for Nico through a long lens before he touches him. Bad ideas escalate chapter by chapter: 1) take his cash case 2) follow him 3) kiss client 4) sleep with him 5) lie to cops for him 6) hide evidence 7) take the fall 8) run/stay with him. **What I aim for:** Bittersweet-hopeful, not tragic, not fluffy. Noir lighting, two silhouettes at the end. They burn the payout, save the bar/kid, don't fully beat the system but choose each other anyway. **What I will avoid:** * Homme fatale as disposable prop who dies to teach Dev a lesson. No bury-your-gays tragedy. * Love triangle, sprawling cast, exposition-heavy conspiracy. Keep it to one drive, one bar, one lie. * Camp that kills stakes, or lyricism that stalls plot. * Outing or deadnaming as twist/spectacle, cops as saviors, non-consensual or coercive sex. Consent will be explicit even inside lies. # Chapter Planning **Overall arc:** Act I (Ch1-2) Setup + Meet, Act IIa (Ch3-4) Seduction + Investigation, Midpoint (Ch5) Body/Betrayal, Act IIb (Ch6-7) Fallout + Recontextualization, Act III (Ch8) Choice. **Ch.1 - Bad Idea #1: Take Cash From a Beautiful Liar** Goal: Voice, world, want. Dev on a stakeout in rain, photographing a cheater. Nico walks into his office above the donut shop, smelling of rain and smoke, hires him to find missing boyfriend Milo. Dev's VO: *He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.* Establish rules: don't take missing-persons, don't kiss clients, don't smoke anymore. He breaks rule one. Ends on surveillance photo: Nico lying already about last time he saw Milo. Hook: Why pay cash for a boyfriend with no photos? **Ch.2 - Bad Idea #2: Follow Him Instead of Looking** Goal: Surveillance romance. Dev is supposed to look for Milo, instead follows Nico to The Glass Femme. Introduce Mama Lou and the bar as chosen-family stakes — eviction notice from Crane Revitalization on wall. See Nico tender with runaways, flirting with Dev, slipping out back with burner phone. Dev photographs him through window in rain — desire/confusion. Finds Milo's backpack stashed in bar freezer room, no Milo. Ends: Someone else is also looking — Crane's fixer asking questions. **Ch.3 - Bad Idea #3: Let Him In Your Car** Goal: First kiss + first lie in same night. Forced proximity: Dev gives Nico a ride after bar close to dodge fixer. Backseat interrogation becomes flirtation. Nico gives partial truth: Milo took something that could save the bar. Light-my-cigarette scene under awning in rain. Kiss — Dev breaks rule two. Immediately after, Dev lies to a night cop for Nico at a DUI checkpoint. Ends warm then cold: back at Dev's apartment, Nico pockets Dev's spare key / clones his phone when Dev sleeps. **Ch.4 - Bad Idea #4: Sleep With The Client** Goal: Deepen intimacy and case simultaneously. Morning-after case file: Grindr DMs, location pings point Milo to a motel by the highway. Dev + Nico go together, play couple to get room key. In room find Milo's hoodie, cam wiped, hard drive gone, poppers/hormones/test strips — lived-in kid, not a fiction. Only truthful conversation happens in bed/shower later — Nico admits he did sex work for Crane's circle, Milo was like a little brother. Sex as truth scene, no lies. Ends: Dev finds Nico's burner with text: *GET THE DRIVE BEFORE HE DOES.* **Ch.5 - Midpoint: Bad Idea #5: Believe Him** Goal: Gut-punch reversal. They find Milo — beaten in hospital, or body scare? Choose: Milo alive but in hiding after fixer beat him, now missing again. Dev realizes Nico never lost Milo, he lost the drive Milo stole. Confrontation in hospital parking garage: *You were all cigarette smoke and bad ideas* — now as accusation. Nico admits: drive has blackmail clips from Crane's app that outs closeted cops/developers, plus proof Crane is funding evictions. He planned to blackmail Crane to save Femme. Dev feels used professionally and romantically. Ends noir low: Dev calls Crane to trade information for money, betraying Nico. **Ch.6 - Bad Idea #6: Sell Him Out** Goal: Fallout, Dev alone. Dev meets Crane in daylight condo showroom — respectable gay villainy. Crane offers $20k + PI license help for drive location. Dev gives motel lead, hates himself. Goes home, sobriety wobbles, looks at surveillance photos of Nico — sees what he missed: Nico wasn't seducing him in photos, he was scared, checking for fixer. Mama Lou calls: fixer trashed Femme looking for drive, Milo ran. Dev realizes he sent danger to Milo. Throws away cigarette/whiskey. Decision: fix it. **Ch.7 - Bad Idea #7: Lie For Him For Real** Goal: Noir night of soul + recontextualization. Rainstorm night. Dev finds Nico + Milo hiding in closed Femme basement. Milo has drive. No time: fixer + off-duty cop coming. Dev finally gets full truth: Nico's blackmail plan wasn't greed, it was protection — tried legal routes, no one listened. Dev chooses: hides kids, gives false statement to cops, plants fake drive, risks arrest and license forever. Tight, tense hide-and-search scene. Intimate beat: Dev gives Nico his sobriety chip to hold, lights cigarette for him then throws it in puddle — quitting as love language. They decide to leak, not blackmail — burn the leverage to burn Crane. **Ch.8 - Bad Idea #8: Stay** Goal: Choice + hopeful-noir ending. Dawn after rain. From a bus / diner, they anonymously leak redacted proof of data scraping + eviction fraud to journalist/podcaster, mail cops' outing videos to no one — destroy them. No payout. Crane wounded but not dead — systemic rot remains. Femme saved for now via public pressure. Milo on bus out of town with Mama Lou's cash. Dev and Nico on rooftop, city steaming. Final refrain: *He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas. So was I. So we...* choose the next bad idea together: stay and fight for the block, sober, unlicensed, together. Last image: two silhouettes, one shared light flicking out. Cut to black.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
This is the right moment to get mean about the plan — not because it's bad, but because it's *too good*. Too clean. Too competent. That's the LLM tell. Let's break it down. ### 1. How a human would actually come at "He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas." A human doesn't start with a 5-person cast and an 8-act structure. A human starts with a *mouth-feel* and a memory. That line is voice-first. It's bitter and horny at the same time. It's something you say about an ex at 2am when you're still a little in love with him and you hate yourself for it. A human writer hears the rhythm — *all cigarette smoke and bad ideas* — sibilant, dismissive, affectionate — and thinks of a specific guy. Not "Nico Cassidy, 28, bartender/sometime escort, protector archetype." But: that guy with the chipped tooth who always bummed your lighter and never gave it back, who kissed like he was stealing something, who left ash in your car cupholder. A human would write *toward* embarrassment. They'd be a little ashamed how much they loved the smoke. They'd let the narrator be wrong, be creepy, be pathetic. They'd bring in stuff that has nothing to do with plot: what Dev's apartment smells like, what a stakeout actually feels like on your back at 37, a joke with Mama Lou that goes on too long, a fight about money that isn't noble. An LLM starts from trope and works down to character. A human starts from a splinter and works out — and often never fully explains it. For queer noir specifically, a human queer writer wouldn't treat "queer" as set-dressing + theme statement ("community distrust," "chosen family as stakes"). They'd treat it as *competence and illegibility*. Who knows how to read a bar at last call? Who knows when Grindr pings are lying? Who knows how to talk to a night cop without getting killed? Who knows what it feels like to want someone you shouldn't want and have to decide if that's desire or self-destruction? That knowledge is in the body, not in a Wikipedia paragraph about gentrification. ### 2. General LLM tells — and why they're poison for *this* piece **a) Safe-danger.** LLMs love to name danger without enacting it. "Escort," "sex work," "blackmail," "addiction" appear as backstory labels, but everyone behaves like a responsible adult in couples therapy. Sex is fade-to-black tender. Sobriety wobbles but never slips. Betrayal happens off-page and is instantly regretted. No one is truly predatory, gross, racist, transphobic, jealous, broke-desperate in a way that makes the reader flinch. Neo-noir romance *needs* unsafe heat. If there's no real power imbalance, no real possibility Dev will do something unforgivable, no real erotic risk, the smoke clears and there's nothing there. **b) The bow.** "Bittersweet-hopeful," "burn the payout, save the bar," "destroy the outing videos but leak the fraud." That's classic LLM moral accounting: let the characters touch sin, then prove they were good all along. Real noir doesn't let you off. Real romance doesn't either — love doesn't redeem you, it implicates you. An LLM wants Crane "wounded but not dead" so it can gesture at systemic critique *and* give you a cuddle. A human would let one of those threads fail. **c) Impressive at the expense of readable.** LLMs do Chandler cosplay: "neon bleeding in puddles," "city steaming," "cut to black," "two silhouettes." Every sentence tries to be a poster. It becomes exhausting and generic. You can swap Portland for Seattle for LA and nothing changes. The voiceover performs *hardboiled* instead of sounding like a tired 37-year-old who talks too much because he's lonely. Sentence tics to watch for: triple lyrical lists, "not X but Y" reversals ("not a savior, but a witness"), em-dash aphorisms, opening every chapter with a fake document that undercuts to "messy human truth underneath" — which is itself a very neat, MFA-workshop trick. Therapy-speak: "agency," "vulnerable truth," "chosen family," "quitting as love language," "sex as truth scene." Humans don't think in those phrases. LLMs do because they were trained to summarize themes. **d) Diversity as decoration + exoneration.** Dev is "gay Indian-American ex-cop pushed out for snitching." That's three clicks toward likable: queer (marginalized), Indian-American (representation), but good cop who snitched (morally clean). His ethnicity will likely never affect how he moves through a white Portland gay bar, how cops treat him, how Nico reads him, how his mother calls. Same with Mama Lou, 60s Black lesbian owner — high risk she becomes Magical Elder Who Calls To Deliver Theme. Milo becomes Innocent Runaway Prop, not an annoying 22-year-old who might be lying too. **e) Schematic escalation.** Bad Idea #1 through #8 in perfect staircase order. Kiss then lie then sleep then betray then redeem. It reads like Save The Cat. Human desire isn't linear. Sometimes you do the worst thing in Chapter 2 and then spend five chapters doing boring, decent things and hating yourself. ### 3. Deep dive: where OUR intention/plan is already falling into those traps Be honest about what we built: **The refrain is too neat.** "He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas" as lust in Ch1, accusation in Ch5, self-recognition in Ch8. That's satisfying on an outline. In prose it will feel stamped on. A human would forget to repeat it, or repeat it drunk and get it wrong, or have Nico throw it back and make it stupid. **The cigarettes are symbolic, not physical.** "Lighting as intimacy," "sharing under awning," "throws it in puddle — quitting as love language." That's an LLM metaphor chain. Real cigarettes are disgusting. They make your fingers stink, they make you cough in rain, they cost $11, you bum them when you're broke and sober and furious you're sober. We made smoking sexy-sad, never annoying. Dev is sober 2 years but still smokes? Or quit? We fudged it for poetry. A human would pick one gross reality and stick with it. **Nico is a hustler with a heart of gold.** We say he has "agency," but his whole plan is: lie to protect kid + bar, do sex work but for noble reasons, blackmail but for justice. He's never selfish, never cruel to Dev just because he can be, never enjoys manipulation. That protects the romance but kills the noir. If Nico never does anything Dev can't forgive, Dev's forgiveness means nothing. **Dev's betrayal is consequence-free.** He calls Crane and gives the motel lead in Ch5, then in Ch6 feels bad looking at photos and decides to fix it. No one dies because of it, he doesn't drink, he doesn't lose anything permanent. LLM remorse without cost. A human would make him live with the fact that his call got the Femme trashed or Milo hurt worse — and Nico doesn't just forgive him because he brought a sobriety chip. **The chip, the file headers, the drive.** These are all plot toys that signal depth. Sobriety chip to hold during a raid? Fake drive plant? Redacted leak that saves the bar via "public pressure"? That's heist-TV logic. How does a leak save a bar with an eviction notice in 24 hours? How do you destroy some videos but leak others without copies existing? We're hand-waving surveillance politics we don't understand to get a hopeful ending. **Crane is Respectable Gay Villainy in a showroom.** That's a strawman. Real gentrification villains are charming, queer-community fluent, probably *liked* Mama Lou once, probably use the same language we do ("revitalization," "safety," "chosen family"). Making him offer "$20k + PI license help" is video-game quest dialogue. A human would make Dev almost like him, which is scarier. **Sex as Truth Scene.** Ch4 note: "only truthful conversation happens in bed/shower later — no lies." That's LLM fantasy that bodies don't lie. Human experience: people lie *most* in bed. Aftercare, pillow talk, "I've never told anyone this" is often another performance. And the client/PI age-gap + cash dynamic is genuinely icky — we call it out as "rule-breaking" but never sit in the ick. We sanitize with explicit consent as a line of dialogue rather than an ongoing, awkward negotiation. **Portland in endless November rain.** Could be anywhere. Donut shop office, motel with ice machine, rooftop at dawn — all stock noir IKEA. No specific street, no specific regular, no specific Portland racism/class weirdness, no specific bar drink that costs too much, no specific song. LLM setting = weather + neon. ### 4. Brainstorm to make it human again — raw material, no decisions yet Not fixes, just provocations to steal from: **Make the voice embarrassing and specific, not hardboiled-generic.** - What if Dev's voiceover is bad at metaphors? Tries too hard, corrects himself. "He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas — Christ, that's the kind of line I'd write in a report to sound cool." - Give him a daytime register that leaks in: how he talks to his mum on the phone vs. to Nico. Code-switching, age showing. - Let him be funny in ways that don't advance plot: petty observations about cheating spouses, about Portland lesbians vs. gays, about his bad knee. - Plain sentences. One short ugly sentence after three pretty ones. Don't let every paragraph bleed neon. **Make bodies gross and inconvenient.** - Nico's smoke gets in Dev's eyes, makes him cough because he quit three years ago and now he's dizzy. Ash on Dev's clean sheets. Nico has smoker's cough in the morning that kills the mood. - Sex awkward: condom hunt, too cold motel room, Dev's back, Nico laughing at wrong moment, stopping to check phone for Milo. Desire that persists *through* annoyance is hotter and more human than seamless tenderness. - Sobriety not as chip prop but as boredom, sugar cravings, wanting to drink because Crane humiliated him, actually snapping at Milo. Maybe he *does* have a beer and lies about it. **Let people be unlikeable and unforgiven for a while.** - What if Nico *did* clone Dev's phone in Ch3 and doesn't apologize cleanly? What if he says, "Yeah, I did. You'd have done the same." - What if Milo is not grateful? Steals from Femme, lies about the beating, likes Crane's fixer a little, resents being anyone's cause. - What if Mama Lou is tired and a little bigoted herself — doesn't like Dev because he's a cop, doesn't like Nico's work, wants to sell the bar but won't admit it? Not wise, just exhausted. - What if Dev likes being needed a little too much? Follows Nico not for case but because watching through lens lets him want without being rejected. Name the creepiness. **Mess up the morals.** - What if they *keep* some money? What if leaking feels good for a night and then nothing changes and the eviction still stands? What if Dev *does* want to watch those outing videos? - What if blackmail would have worked and leaking doesn't? Forcing them to ask: are we good or just unwilling to get our hands dirty? - Let Crane have a point: bar *is* behind on rent, neighborhood *has* changed, he *did* come out late and is overcompensating. Let Dev see himself in him. **De-schematize structure.** - Drop the #1-#8 bad idea titles, or let Dev miscount. "Bad idea #4? Or #12? I stopped counting." - Let the midpoint betrayal come earlier and be pettier: Dev doesn't call Crane in a grand scene, he drunkenly texts a cop friend Milo's license plate because he's jealous Nico cares more about Milo. - Leave threads untied: we never find out who beat Milo for sure. The drive is corrupted. The fixer never gets a name. - End not on rooftop silhouettes but somewhere stupid: laundromat, DMV line, eating cold fries. Romance that isn't cinematic. **Specificity over symbolism.** - Replace "The Glass Femme" abstraction with one detail that only that bar has: a broken ice machine that everyone mentions, a specific $9 well drink, a bathroom stall with a memorial collage. - Replace "Portland rain" with one real corner: SE 11th and Division at 1:40am, bus 70 not coming, donut shop actually is Blue Star and the guy downstairs hates Dev. - Replace "hard drive with blackmail videos" with something smaller and weirder and more believable: one iPhone with 40 minutes of voice memo, a notebook with dates, a Grindr account still logged in. Something you could actually hide in a freezer. **Queerness as fluency, not lesson.** - No explaining chosen family, outing stakes, deadnames. Assume reader knows or will catch up. - Let queer community be corrupt too, not just victim: someone in the bar sells info to Crane. Someone thinks Milo is trouble and wants him gone. - Let straight world be mostly absent/indifferent, not actively hunting — which is lonelier and more neo-noir: no one cares enough to persecute you, they'll just let you disappear. The human version of this story wouldn't be about learning that He wasn't just smoke. It would be about inhaling anyway, knowing exactly what it will do to you, and being pissed off that you still want another drag.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **What this is:** An 8 x ~1000 word queer neo-noir romance. First-person, past tense. Not a puzzle to be solved cleanly, but a wanting that gets someone hurt. **Plot — kept small on purpose:** Dev Menon, 37, gay Indian-American, ex-Portland cop kicked out for reporting another cop, now unlicensed and shooting cheating-spouse photos for cash, is hired by Nico Cassidy, 28, barback and sometime escort at a dying queer bar, to find his "missing boyfriend" Milo, 22. There is no boyfriend. There is a kid who stole something: not a movie hard drive, but Milo's own cracked iPhone still logged into a shared hustle Grindr, plus a cheap notebook with dates, room numbers, and initials — enough to prove developer Hollis Crane scraped data from a queer dating app to out and pressure tenants to sell on the block where the bar sits. Nico wants it back to use it. Dev wants the $500 cash and then wants Nico. That's it. One phone, one notebook, one bar, five people. I can't afford a conspiracy in 8000 words, so the bigger rot stays off-page as implication. **Characters as people, not functions:** * *Dev:* Lonely, broke, sober 2 years and bored by it. Funny in a petty way, bad at metaphors and knows it. Creepy in the way surveillance work makes you creepy — he likes watching Nico through a long lens because it's wanting without risk of rejection. Brown in a very white gay bar scene and in traffic stops; that changes how cops talk to him and how room owners read him. Not noble. He will do a small jealous thing that has large consequences and he won't be fully forgiven. * *Nico — the "he":* Opens the book with Dev's line: *He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas.* Sexy, evasive, tender with runaways and shitty to Dev when he's scared. Did sex work for Crane's circle and doesn't moralize it. Clones Dev's phone and when caught says "yeah, I did" instead of crying. He likes being able to manipulate Dev and hates that he needs to. Smoker's cough in the morning, ash everywhere, steals lighters. * *Milo, 22:* Not grateful, not innocent. Lies about being jumped, steals from the bar till, resents being anyone's project. Annoying and vulnerable at once. * *Mama Lou, 60s, Black lesbian bar owner:* Not wise elder. Tired, behind on rent, half-wants to take Crane's buyout and retire, half-hates herself for considering it. Doesn't trust Dev because cop is cop. * *Hollis Crane:* Not a showroom villain. Late-out gay, charming, community-fluent, used to drink at the Femme. Actually likes Mama Lou. Almost sympathetic, which is scarier. He thinks he's saving the neighborhood. **Voice & style — against LLM polish:** Aim for a tired 37-year-old talking too much, not Chandler cosplay. Plain, specific sentences. One ugly short sentence after a pretty one. Dev tries a hardboiled line, then undercuts himself. No triple neon lists, no "not X but Y" aphorisms, no therapy words like agency / truth scene / love language. Cigarettes stay physical, not symbolic: $11 a pack, stink in car upholstery, Dev quit three years ago so one drag makes him dizzy and coughing under an awning while Nico laughs at him. Sex stays awkward: cold motel room, condom hunt, bad back, phone buzzing for Milo, stopping and starting. People lie in bed most of all. Queerness as fluency, no lessons. No explaining chosen family, Grindr, binders, deadnames. The straight world is mostly indifferent, not hunting — lonelier that way. **Structure — messy, not staircase:** No perfect Bad Idea #1-8 ladder. Dev stops counting. The worst betrayal comes early from jealousy, not as a midpoint set-piece, and it can't be undone. Threads left untied: we never learn for sure who hit Milo, the phone is half-corrupted, the fixer never gets a name. Endings: no bow. No "burn the payout, save the bar." They try leaking and it mostly fizzles. The eviction still stands. They keep a little of Crane's money and feel gross about it. **What I will aim for:** Embarrassment, specificity, cost. Desire that persists through annoyance. Love that implicates, doesn't redeem. **What I will avoid:** Safe-danger labels without behavior; instant remorse without cost; hustler-with-heart-of-gold; cameras and chips as plot toys; rooftop-silhouette romance; explaining queerness; making Portland anywhere-with-rain. # Chapter Planning **Ch.1 - Stakeout** One scene: Dev in his Corolla on SE 11th and Division at 1:40am, bus 70 not coming, shooting a cheater outside Blue Star where the kid downstairs hates him. Nico knocks on his office door next morning smelling of rain and smoke, pays $500 cash to find "boyfriend" Milo, no usable photo. Dev's VO tries the line: *He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas — Christ, that's the kind of line I'd put in a report to sound cool.* Takes the case because rent's due. Ends on a tell Dev notices but pockets: Nico says last saw Milo Tuesday, but Milo's backpack is already behind the bar in a photo on Nico's own phone. **Ch.2 - The Femme** One location: The Glass Femme. Specifics only this bar has: broken Hoshizaki ice machine everyone bitches about, $9 well called a Femme Burn, bathroom memorial collage. Mama Lou clocks Dev as cop in two seconds and is cold. Eviction notice from Crane Revitalization taped crooked by the till. Dev is supposed to look for Milo, instead watches Nico through window in rain. Sees tenderness (slipping cash to a kid, mopping puke) and slipperiness (back-door burner call). Finds Milo's backpack stashed in dry storage, notebook missing, a sock, T strips. Ends: Crane's fixer was there an hour earlier asking, and someone behind the bar gave him Milo's description. **Ch.3 - Ride** Forced proximity, one car ride after close to dodge a DUI checkpoint. Nico bums light, Dev coughs because he quit, Nico laughs. Kiss — clumsy, too much teeth, interrupted by checkpoint lights. Dev, who is brown and ex-cop and knows exactly how this goes, talks too friendly to the night cop and lies that Nico was with him all night. It works and it sickens him. Back at Dev's place with too-clean sheets, they almost go further, don't. Dev falls asleep. Wakes to find his spare key moved, his phone warm. He knows Nico cloned it. He doesn’t confront him because he liked being chosen. Worst thing early: half-asleep and jealous that Nico checks Milo's location more than him, Dev texts an old cop buddy Milo's plate to "just run it." **Ch.4 - Motel** Morning after, awkward and funny. They chase a Grindr ping to a Highway 99 motel, pose as bickering couple to get the maid to open Milo's room. Room is lived-in and gross: cold, hoodie, hormones, popped condom wrapper, cracked charger. No Milo. iPhone gone, but notebook page torn out under mattress with initials and $ amounts. Back at Dev's they shower because motel stink, then bed. Sex is interrupted, negotiated, decent and not transcendent. Pillow talk is where Nico lies best: says he did two dates for Crane's friends, leaves out that he kept notes. Tells a sweet Milo-as-little-brother story Dev half-believes because he wants to. Ends with burner buzzing on the sink: *did u get it yet.* **Ch.5 - Hospital** Consequence lands. Milo turns up at OHSU — beaten, lip split, says jumped for his phone, story shifting. In parking garage Nico explodes: you ran his plate. Dev admits it. That text sent a uniform to the motel lot, which sent the fixer to the right hallway. Nico: "You wanted to know where I was, so you put him on their screen?" Dev tries his line again and Nico throws it back stupid: "I'm smoke now? Fuck off with your novel." No grand Crane meeting. Dev, humiliated, goes to Crane's open house alone hoping to undo it, almost likes him — Crane remembers Lou's DJ nights, offers $3k for the notebook/phone and help with a license. Dev takes $800 "for time" and gives the torn page. Feels sick eating fries after. **Ch.6 - Trash** Fallout, Dev alone and unlikable. Sugar cravings, snaps at his mum on phone, looks at his long-lens photos of Nico and sees fear not seduction — Nico checking the street before locking up. Mama Lou calls: someone trashed the Femme dry storage that night looking, ice machine smashed further, till $140 short — Milo took it and ran again. The $800 sits on Dev's counter. He doesn't drink but buys a pack, smokes one, coughs, throws rest in wet trash where they sog out. Goes to return money to Lou, finds her with Crane's buyout papers on the bar. She’s considering signing. She won’t forgive him, tells him to leave. **Ch.7 - Basement** Rainstorm night, one tense hide. Dev finds Nico and Milo in Femme basement behind stacked kegs. Full truth comes ugly, not noble: legal aid ignored them, so Nico planned to blackmail Crane for a payoff and rent forgiveness, not justice. Milo doesn't want to be saved, wants his phone back to sell it himself. Cops + fixer knock upstairs. Dev hides them, gives a false statement that risks what’s left of his reputation, plants Milo’s dead Android as the "phone" to buy time. Intimate beat in whisper: Nico coughing, Dev holding his damp cigarette so it doesn’t stink up the hiding spot, then crushing it. No chip speech. They decide to leak what’s readable, not to be good, but because blackmail now gets Milo killed. Copy what they can to a reporter; the outing videos they delete without watching — Dev wanted to look, admits it, doesn’t. **Ch.8 - Laundromat** Dawn, no rooftop. Leak fizzles into a local blog post and a non-denial; Crane wounded, eviction delayed 60 days, not gone. Phone is half-water-damaged anyway. Lou takes a smaller payout to cover back rent and hates herself. Milo takes Lou’s bus money and the $140 and leaves mad, no hug. Dev and Nico do cold laundry at SpinCycle, eating cold fries, smelling of bleach. Dev doesn’t get the line right: *He was smoke and bad ideas. I was jealous and bored and...* trails off. Nico steals his fries. They still have $600 of Crane’s money in wet jeans, keep it for Milo’s ticket and feel gross. Last image: dryer buzzing, warm clothes between them, staying for the block for now because there’s nowhere else that knows their names. Not saved, but together in the stupid light.
Perfect. Now with the outline more crystallised, and bearing in mind the discussion on human writing vs LLM pitfalls, we will flesh out our characters. Lets go through each of our main characters: - Write about their background, personality, idiosyncracies, flaws. Be specific and come up with examples to anchor & ground the character's profile (both core and trivial) - Briefly describe their physicality: appearance, how they carry themselves, express, interact with the world. - Concisely detail their motives, allegiences and existing relationships. Think from the perspective of the character as a real breathing thinking feeling individual in this world. - Write a couple quotes of flavour dialogue / internal monologue from the character to experiment with their voice. Output like this: # Character 1 name <character exploration> # Character 2 name <character exploration> etc
Model Output:
# Dev Menon **Background:** 37, gay, second-gen Indian-American. Grew up in Beaverton, mum Vasanti still there and calls every Sunday to ask if he's eating and if he's met "a nice friend." Was Portland patrol for six years. Got pushed out at 33 after he reported his training officer for planting a pocket knife on a Black kid during a stop. The union hung him out, IA called him a rat, the kid's family never learned his name. Now unlicensed PI — mostly cheating spouses, $75 an hour plus mileage, photos shot from his 2012 Corolla with a busted heater. Two years sober after a DUI where he backed into his own mailbox. Goes to meetings on Tuesdays when he remembers, mostly for the coffee. **Personality, flaws, tics:** Lonely in a way that makes him chatty. Talks to clients too much, to cashiers, to himself on stakeouts. Petty-funny: keeps a Notes app ranking the excuses cheating husbands give ("working late at Nike" is #1). Cheap: reuses Ziplocs, steals sugar packets. Voyeuristic and he half-knows it — likes the long lens because wanting from far away is safer than being turned down up close. Jealous fast, then ashamed of it. When he's nervous he over-explains, especially to cops. Calls his mum back late and then snaps at her for worrying. Grounding examples: microwaves the same Trader Joe's palak paneer three nights in a row and eats it standing up; sleeps with his phone face-down but checks Grindr location at 2am with the brightness all the way down; bad right knee from a foot pursuit, takes the stairs sideways; carries cinnamon gum since quitting smoking three years ago, chews two at once until his jaw aches. **Physicality:** 5'10", soft around the middle now that he's not on foot patrol. Short black hair going grey at the temples — he dyes it once, hated it, never again. Brown skin that goes ashy when he's tired. Hands nicked from developing his own cheap doorbell-cam installs. Wears the same navy windbreaker until it smells. Moves like someone trying not to limp. In bars he sits with his back to the wall out of habit and then hates himself for doing cop shit. **Motives, allegiances, relationships:** Says he wants rent money and his license back. Actually wants someone to trust him without him having to audition for it. Owes loyalty to no institution anymore — not cops, not quite the bars either. Mama Lou clocks him instantly as cop and he's desperate for her to be wrong. Vasanti wants him to come home for Diwali; he keeps saying work is busy. Old buddy Danny Kehoe still on the force is his only cop lifeline — Dev uses him and resents needing him. With Nico, he wants to be the guy who stays, but he also likes being needed a little too much, which curdles into control. **Voice:** > Internal: *He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas — yeah, write that down, asshole. Very Raymond Chandler of you. Very divorced.* > Out loud, trying too hard at a checkpoint: "Evening, officer. Yeah, we were just at the Femme, you know how it is, ice machine's down again — he was with me all night, all night." # Nico Cassidy **Background:** 28, white, from Medford. Came out at 16, kicked around, moved to Portland at 19 for a boyfriend who was 34 and already married. Barback and closer at The Glass Femme for four years. Does dates sometimes — two regulars from Crane's circle, hotel bars, cash, no pimp, his own rules. Keeps a notebook not because he's a mastermind but because a friend got stiffed and he got scared. Has lived in the same studio above a laundromat for three years because Lou co-signed. **Personality, flaws, tics:** Charming when he's working the room, flat and mean when he's scared. Lies the way other people fidget — small, automatic, about stupid stuff (what time he got in, if he ate) so the big lies blend in. Doesn't apologize clean; says "yeah, I did" and stares at you until you drop it. Tender in practical ways: mops puke without making a face, slips a $20 to a kid and calls it "tip share," remembers who can't do shots because of meds. Selfish too: enjoys that Dev wants him, tests it. Steals lighters compulsively — has nine, none of them his, two don't work. Grounding examples: puts Cholula on everything including pizza; smoker's cough every morning that ruins any sexy morning-after; taps his cigarette three times before lighting even in wind; falls asleep with TV on at full volume — old *Law & Order* reruns because "I like knowing who did it." **Physicality:** 6'0" but slouches to 5'11". Lean from skipping meals, not gym. Dyed black hair growing out brown at roots, chipped front tooth from a fall he won't explain. Smells of rain, fryer oil, and Newports — it gets in everything. Hands long and red from bar sanitizer. Moves easy behind a bar, jittery outside it. That laugh — too loud — when Dev coughs on a drag: delighted, a little cruel, a little fond. **Motives, allegiances, relationships:** Says he'd do anything to save the Femme and Milo. More honestly: he can't stand being the person who watches and does nothing again, like he did when his Medford friend got evicted and OD'd. Loyal to Lou even when she annoys him, to Milo even when Milo steals from him, to no one who tries to own him. Sees Dev as mark, then ride, then risk — hates needing him because needing makes him stupid. Sex work isn't trauma or empowerment speech for him; it's rent and information and sometimes fun and sometimes gross. **Voice:** > "You don't get to do cop shit and then kiss me like that. Pick one." > "I'm not your boyfriend's boyfriend, okay? Milo's — he's just a kid I said I'd look out for. Don't make it Hallmark." # Milo Reyes **Background:** 22, queer, Mexican-American, from Gresham. Parents tried conversion counseling lite — not a camp, just a pastor and shame every Sunday. Left at 18, couch-surfed, worked door at the Femme, worked phones. Started hustling via a shared Grindr / Snapchat setup that passed phones around. Stole the cracked iPhone 11 and the notebook because he figured if everyone was using him for info, he should get paid. **Personality, flaws, tics:** Defensive, funny, exhausting. Changes his story mid-sentence if he feels pity coming — jumped vs. fell vs. "does it matter?" Watches TikToks at full volume in the ER to avoid talking. Steals small amounts ($140 from the till, Dev's charger, Nico's beanie) and then gets furious if you call him a thief. Craves being claimed and rejects it instantly. Smart about tech, dumb about people who are nice to him. Grounding examples: wears a too-big grey Nike hoodie with a bleach stain he pretends isn't there; keeps his nails bitten to stubs; knows every bus route by number but pretends he doesn't need help; allergic to cats but pets Lou's shop cat anyway and sneezes dramatically for attention. **Physicality:** 5'7", skinny-wiry, acne scars on jaw he covers with a mask even indoors sometimes. Lip split from the beating, swollen left eye that he keeps touching. Moves fast, takes up little space, sits on his feet. Looks 17 when he's asleep, which is part of why adults project all over him and he hates it. **Motives, allegiances, relationships:** Wants cash for a bus and to not owe anyone. Loyal to Nico only insofar as Nico doesn't lecture him. Thinks Lou is judgy, thinks Dev is a cop which is same as enemy, thinks Crane's fixer was almost nice to him once which confuses him. Doesn't want to be a cause. Would rather sell the phone himself for $2k than let Nico martyr it for the bar. **Voice:** > "Don't put me in your sad story. I'm not missing. I left." > To a nurse, grinning with a split lip: "Nah, I'm good. My boyfriends are fighting over who gets to pay. Let 'em." # Mama Lou — Louise Hart **Background:** 64, Black lesbian, Portland since '89. Owned The Glass Femme for 19 years — bought it with her late wife Denise's nursing money. Marched, tended bar through the AIDS quilt years, buried half her softball team. Denise died of cancer six years ago. Bar's been behind on rent 11 months. Knees shot, sleeps in the office sometimes. **Personality, flaws, tics:** No-nonsense that tips into tiredness. Loves the kids but is tired of bleeding for them. A little judgmental: doesn't love hustling in her bar, doesn't trust ex-cops even gay brown ones, thinks pronouns are fine but won't pretend she always remembers. Considering Crane's buyout and lying to herself that it's just "exploring options." Funny dry, not warm-grandma. Grounding examples: yells at everyone about the busted Hoshizaki ice machine like it's a person; drinks decaf out of a mug that says WORLD'S OKAYEST GRANDMA; does the till count with short unpolished nails and a pencil behind her ear; feeds a one-eyed shop cat tuna water; keeps Denise's photo taped to the register, turned slightly away from customers. **Physicality:** 5'6", big-shouldered, short grey twists, gold hoops. Wears orthopedic sneakers and an apron with keys that jangle. Moves slow, deliberate — every trip to the basement costs her. Voice low and carrying; can shut down a drunk with one look. **Motives, allegiances, relationships:** Wants to retire without feeling like a sellout and to not bury another kid. Loyal to Denise's memory, to the bar as a living thing, to Nico and Milo in that order when she's honest. Doesn't owe Dev anything. Knows Crane from back when he was a scared 40-year-old in a booth — part of her still likes him, which makes her angrier. **Voice:** > "Baby, I marched. I don't march no more. My feet hurt. You want a speech, go to the center." > To Dev: "Cop is cop, honey. You can be sweet and still be the reason they come." # Hollis Crane **Background:** 52, white gay man, came out at 44 after a straight marriage and two kids in Lake Oswego. Made money in logistics software, now "revitalization" — buying queer blocks cheap after COVID closures. Used to drink at the Femme, tipped big, cried once at a memorial. Funds a Pride nonprofit that is mostly a logo. **Personality, flaws, tics:** Charming, fluent, self-deluded. Really believes he's saving the neighborhood by making it "safe and sustainable." Collects queer history books he doesn't read. Remembers names, asks about your mum. Will ruin you politely and call it market forces. Not a screamer; a nodder. His cruelty is administrative. Grounding examples: wears a Patagonia vest even indoors; offers sparkling water in glass bottles; says "let's find a win-win" before offering you a third of what you're owed; texts with perfect punctuation and a rainbow emoji; keeps a photo of him and Lou from 2017 on his phone to show people he's one of us. **Physicality:** 6'1", fit in a golf way, salt-pepper hair cut every two weeks, very good teeth. Smells of expensive cedar soap. Handshake lingers. Smiles with his eyes in a way that almost convinces Dev until Dev remembers he's being played. **Motives, allegiances, relationships:** Wants legacy and absolution — to be the good gay elder after being the absent father and late husband. Loyal to his investors first, his kids second, his self-image third. Likes Lou genuinely, pities Nico, sees Milo as a liability, sees Dev as a useful hungry guy who might want to be respectable again. Doesn't think of himself as a villain at all. **Voice:** > "Lou played my coming-out party! Ask her. I'm not the enemy here, Dev. Blight is the enemy." > Sliding a paper across: "This is just for your time. Eight hundred for a torn page — let's find a win-win for the rest, yeah?"

The Corolla smelled like old paneer and wet floor mat. I had the heat off so the windows wouldn't fog and my knee was doing that sideways ache, so I was sitting twisted with my camera on the dash and two pieces of cinnamon gum going until my jaw hurt. 1:40 a.m. SE 11th and Division. Inside, the kid on nights — Jayden, twenty and already tired of me — was mopping and pretending I wasn't parked right out front again. I was shooting a guy named Craig. Craig told his wife he was working late at Nike. That's number one in my Notes app. Number one with a bullet. I'd been on Craig three nights. He wasn't interesting. One torso with no head. I closed it. That's the job. You sit far away and want things to happen so you can go home. The office is above the Blue Star. Single room, radiator that clanks, a desk I got off Craigslist and a second chair I tell clients is vintage. It isn't. It wobbles. He knocked at 9:12 the next morning while I was eating palak paneer standing up straight out of the Trader Joe's plastic. Microwaved. Third night in a row. I knew before I opened it. Cigarette smoke got under the door first. He was all cigarette smoke and bad ideas — yeah, write that down, asshole. Very Raymond Chandler of you. Very divorced. He was tall and trying not to be, black dye growing out brown, wet at the ends from rain. Lean like he forgot lunch. Chipped front tooth. He smiled with it anyway. "You the guy who finds people?" he said. "Sometimes cheating husbands. Depends if they want to be found." "Nico." He didn't offer a last name. He came in without being asked and looked around like he was casing it. "You got a license?" "Working on it." Which was true in the way most things I say before coffee are true. He sat in the wobble chair and put a folded envelope on the desk. Cash. Five hundreds, soft at the edges. He smelled like rain and Newports and fryer oil. It got in my windbreaker and stayed there. "I need you to find my boyfriend," he said. "Milo. Haven't seen him since Tuesday." "Got a photo?" He showed me his phone. Quick thumb. A grey Nike hoodie on a skinny kid with his face half-turned, jaw covered by a mask, giving the finger. Bleach stain on the sleeve. Bus window behind him. "That's it?" "He hates pictures." "Full name? Age?" "Milo Reyes. Twenty-two." Beat too long. "From Gresham." I wrote it down. Milo Reyes, 22, Gresham, last seen Tuesday. Boyfriend. "You call hospitals? Friends?" I used to be that reason they come. "Okay," I said. "Five hundred retainer covers about — you got somewhere he stays? Works?" "He doors sometimes at the Femme. The Glass Femme." Jayden downstairs dropped a tray and yelled fuck. Nico stood to smoke by the window because I pointed at the NO SMOKING sign I'd taped up when I quit three years ago. He opened the window two inches and blew it out into the rain. His hands were red and cracked from sanitizer. He did the tap-tap-tap again before he lit. Wind got it anyway and he had to cup it. "Rent's due," I said, which is why I said yes. Don't take missing persons. That was my rule. Missing persons means families and crying and cops. Cheaters pay better and nobody dies. But the envelope was there and my mailbox still had a dent in it from when I backed into it drunk two years ago. "Tuesday," I repeated. "Last Tuesday? He texted? Called?" "Yeah. Text. Said he needed space." "Can I see it?" Nico didn't blink. "Deleted. I delete stuff." "Sure." He paid in cash for a boyfriend with no photos who hated hospitals and whose texts were deleted. I took it. I told myself it was because I needed the money, which was true, and not because he'd stood close enough in my shitty office that I could smell him and I liked being looked at by someone who needed something. He was leaving when his phone lit up on the desk. Wallpaper photo. Same grey hoodie, same kid, asleep on a cracked vinyl booth. Behind him, out of focus, the Femme's dry storage door. And on top of a milk crate, a familiar black Jansport with a rainbow pin. I'd only been in the Femme twice, but I'd seen that backpack. It was there in his own photo. I didn't say anything. I pocketed the envelope. Let him get to the stairs. "Hey," I said. "Tuesday, you said?" "Yeah. Tuesday." I nodded. Outside, Jayden was taking out trash in the rain and glaring up at my open window and Nico's smoke. After Nico left I stood there chewing the gum to nothing and looking at my notes. Milo Reyes, 22. No DOB. One blurry finger. My mum called while I was rinsing the paneer plastic to reuse it. I let it go to voicemail. She'd ask if I was eating and if I'd met a nice friend. I was eating. The Femme is on Burnside where the rainbow crosswalk is already faded to gray. I got there at ten and sat in the Corolla across the street for twenty minutes like a creep, telling myself it was surveillance. Rain on the windshield. Inside was warm and loud in a way that made my knee feel better just looking at it. Low ceiling, Christmas lights that never came down, that sticky floor smell of beer and Pine-Sol. The ice machine behind the bar had an OUT OF ORDER sign taped on it with HOSHIZAKI printed across the front in big letters, and underneath somebody had written in Sharpie: ask ur mom if she’s out of order. It was a full collage, photos and flyers under thick packing tape. Denise & Lou 2004 Pride. A kid with blue hair holding a Narcan kit like a trophy. Candlelight vigil for somebody named Ray. A handwritten card: *If you saw Milo call Nico no cops.* No cops underlined three times. That stopped me stupid for a second. Mama Lou found me by the till. You just knew. Big shoulders, short grey twists, gold hoops, apron with keys that actually jangled when she moved. Late sixties but moved like her knees were keeping score. She had a decaf mug that said WORLD’S OKAYEST GRANDMA and a pencil behind her ear. Denise’s photo taped to the register, turned a little away from customers so the flash wouldn’t fade it. “You the detective?” she said. Not loud. “PI. Dev Menon. Nico—” “Cop is cop, honey.” She did the till count while she talked, short nails flicking bills. Didn’t look up. “You can be sweet and still be the reason they come.” I over-explained. I always do. “I’m not with — I got out. I’m just looking for Milo. Nico hired me.” At Milo her hands paused. One beat. Then she kept counting. “He doors sometimes. He ain’t here.” Tap crooked by the till was a white notice in a plastic sleeve: CRANE REVITALIZATION — NOTICE TO VACATE FOR RENOVATION. Thirty days already crossed out and initialed twice. Someone had drawn a dick on the letterhead. “He in trouble?” I said. “Baby, everybody in here in trouble. You want a speech, go to the center. My feet hurt.” Nico came out of the back with a mop bucket. Hair tied back, shirt sticking to him. He saw me and did this thing — half grin, half oh shit — and kept mopping where some bachelorette had puked glitter by the booth. He didn’t wave. He mouthed *give me ten* and went back to work like I was just some guy. So I was just some guy. I took my Burn to the little vestibule and then outside, because I told myself I needed to call my mum back. I didn’t. I stood under the overhang in the rain and watched through the front window. That’s the job, right? You tell yourself it’s work. Through the glass the whole bar went soft. Condensation at the edges. Nico wiping tables, laughing at something the shaved-head girl said. Then a kid — nineteen, twenty, track marks covered with sleeves pulled down — hovering by the bar, no money. Nico didn’t make a thing of it. Slipped him a twenty from his own pocket, called it tip share loud enough for Lou to hear and roll her eyes at. Then he was on his knees again with the mop, not making a face about the glitter puke. My chest did something dumb. Then he checked his phone, checked the door, and slipped out the back with his cigarettes. Not the front where I was. The back, into the alley where the dumpsters were. I went around. My windbreaker soaked through in thirty seconds. My sock got wet inside my shoe. He was in the yellow light by the kitchen vent, back to me, phone to his ear. Not his iPhone. A cheap burner, cracked screen. He was doing the tap-tap-tap on the cig before lighting. “—no, don’t come here,” he was saying, low. “I told you, I got a guy looking. Just stay where you — Milo, listen to me. Did you —” He stopped. Listened. Rubbed his face hard. “Where’s the notebook? Just tell me where the — fuck. Okay. Okay, don’t go to Lou’s. I’ll come to you.” He hung up and stood there in the rain getting wet and smoking too fast. Coughing. That morning smoker’s cough, wet and ugly. Then he crushed it half-finished and went back inside. I gave it five minutes and went in after him, nodded at Lou like I belonged. The dry storage door was propped with a milk crate — same crates from Nico’s photo. Inside: stacked cups, vodka boxes, mop heads. Hot and smelling of cardboard. The black Jansport with the rainbow pin was shoved behind theทน boxes. I knew it before I pulled it out. No phone. No notebook. One grey sock balled up. An empty T test strip wrapper. A bus transfer from three days ago, smeared. A sticker from the clinic on 12th. That was it. Somebody had already taken what mattered. When I came out Lou was watching me. “You find what you need, detective?” “Somebody else looking for him?” I said. “Besides Nico?” She sucked her teeth. “An hour ago. Clean shoes. Polo shirt. Asking nice about a boy in a grey hoodie. Said he was Milo’s uncle.” “You tell him anything?” “I told him we don’t get uncles in here.” She looked past me to the bar, to the shaved-head girl laughing too loud with a regular. “Somebody else told him Milo doors here Tuesdays. Close was 2:14 and raining sideways. I was still across the street with the heater blowing lukewarm and my right sock damp from the alley. Nico came out with the trash, tied-off bag in each hand, hair stuck to his forehead. He saw the Corolla and stopped. Then he just walked over and got in my passenger seat without asking, bags and all, dripping all over my floor mat. “Drive,” he said. “Before Lou makes me count the till again.” I drove. He smelled like mop water and smoke and that Femme Burn lime. He had his cigarettes out before we hit Morrison. “Gimme a light? Lost mine.” Of course he lost his. He had nine stolen ones at home, probably. I had a Bic in the cupholder from Craig nights. His hand was cold on my neck. My phone buzzed against my thigh and I ignored it. I put my hand on his thigh and he let it stay and then moved it up himself like I was taking too long. Headlights swept the back window. Red and blue. “Fuck,” he said into my mouth. DUI checkpoint on Burnside. Two cruisers, sawhorses, rain bouncing white under the work lights. A line of cars. My stomach dropped the way it used to when I was the one waving the flashlight. Except now I’m brown in a beater with a white guy half in my lap smelling like a bar, and I know exactly how that reads at 2:30 a.m. Nico sat back fast, wiped his mouth, tried to crush his cigarette in the overflowing ashtray. Smoke hung thick. “Windows down,” I said. “Let it air. Don’t talk unless — let me.” The cop was young, white, rain beading on his hat. Kehoe wasn’t on tonight. I didn’t know this one. “Evening. License and— have you been drinking tonight, sir?” I did the thing I hate. Too friendly. Too much smile. Ex-cop voice leaking out. “Evening, officer. Nah, DD tonight. The cop shined his light past me. Nico, hands visible on his knees like he’d been coached. Which he had been, by life. “You live at that address?” the cop asked him. Nico nodded. “Yeah.” Quiet. Good. The cop looked at me a second too long. I could feel him deciding what we were. Faggots, drunks, trouble, nothing. He waved us through. My hands shook all the way to 28th. Nico didn’t say anything until I parked and killed the engine and the rain got loud again. “You didn’t have to do that,” he said. “I know.” “I mean, thank you.” He was picking at the cigarette filter, shredded now. “Most guys just — yeah. Thank you.” Upstairs my place was too warm and too clean in the way of someone who lives alone and is ashamed about it. Dishes done. Bed made with actual tucked corners. Palak paneer plastic drying on the rack to reuse. My mum’s voicemail light blinking on the old landline I keep because I’m cheap and sentimental. Nico walked around like he did my office, touching stuff. My Notes app was open on my laptop: *Craig – Nike #1.* He laughed. “You rank them?” “Someone has to.” He used my bathroom, left the door half-open, pissed loud. Came out and sat on my bed and patted it. We didn’t — not really. Made out until my back cramped and his phone kept lighting up face-down on my nightstand and he kept flipping it over. Milo. *where u at.* *did u get it yet.* *don’t bring him.* That last one with no name. Nico turned the sound off but didn’t stop checking. Every buzz, his eyes cut over. I pretended not to notice because I wanted him to stay. That’s the truth. I wanted to be the guy he stayed with instead of answering. At some point he said Milo might be in his cousin’s beige Camry. Gave me the plate half under his breath while he was half-asleep against my shoulder, TV on loud — Law & Order, because he liked knowing who did it. Oregon plate, 7-something. I typed it into my phone like I was saving it for the case. He fell asleep with his mouth open, smoker’s breath sour-sweet. Chipped tooth showing. I watched him for a while like a creep. Then I got up to pee and stood there in my boxers with my knee aching, feeling 37 and stupid-happy. When I came back he was asleep on his side facing the wall. My spare key, which lives on the hook by the door turned inward, was turned outward. My phone, which I’d left on the counter at 18%, was at 41% and warm, plugged into my own cable but in the other outlet, the one behind the toaster I never use. He’d cloned it. Or put something on it. I knew how it worked. I’d watched vice do it. I stood there with my warm phone in my hand and listened to him breathe. I should have woken him up. At 4 a.m. he mumbled in his sleep and checked his phone again blind, thumb missing the screen. Location share. Little blue dot for Milo, blinking off Powell. Gone again. It started raining hard around nine, the kind that gets sideways under awnings and makes Burnside a river. I was in the Corolla outside the Femme with the engine off and the windows fogging because I didn't want to run the heat and waste gas. I'd been checking Nico's location share every twenty minutes like a psycho. Off, off, off. Then just after eight it blinked on for maybe thirty seconds — basement of the Femme, that blue dot wobbling — and then off again. Probably butt-dial. Probably nothing. I drove over anyway because I didn't have anywhere else to be and my sheets were still in a bag by the door. The bar was dark. CLOSED sign crooked. But Lou's office light was on upstairs and the back alley door by the dumpsters was cracked two inches, rain getting in. I know I shouldn't have gone in. Lou told me to leave before Nico did something he regrets. I went in. Inside smelled like mop water left too long and old beer. The dry storage was still trashed, cups kicked everywhere. Somebody had righted the mop bucket but brown water had dried in a tide mark halfway to the office. The Hoshizaki door hung open, wired shut crooked with that coat hanger now rusting. I heard it before I saw — a cough, wet, trying to be quiet. From the basement stairs behind the keg cooler. The basement is low and damp and smells like yeast and Denise's old cigarette smoke soaked into concrete. Stacked kegs, broken bar stools, a Christmas tub. Behind the kegs, in the gap where Lou keeps the extra well vodka because nobody steals that shit, were Nico and Milo on a flattened cardboard box sharing one blanket that said OHSU PROPERTY. Milo looked worse. Eye swollen almost shut, lip crusted. He had the grey hoodie pulled up and his knees up and he was eating Flamin' Hot Cheetos with his fingers stained red, crunching too loud on purpose. A cracked iPhone 11 with a spiderweb screen sat in his lap. My stomach dropped. "Oh, great," Milo said. "Cop." Nico's head snapped up. Hair wet, eyes rimmed red. He had an unlit Newport in his fingers, tapping it three times out of habit even though he couldn't light it down here — Lou would kill him, the smoke would go straight upstairs. "You need to go," he said. "I know." I stayed. My knee was already aching from the stairs. I crouched because there wasn't room to stand under the pipe. Rain hammered the sidewalk grate above us, dripping through in one steady line onto a keg. Plink. Plink. Milo held up the phone like a trophy. "Found the notebook, too. Under the ice bag. Dumbest hiding spot ever." "We had legal aid," Nico said fast, like he'd been waiting to say it to someone who wasn't Milo or Lou. "Last spring. I brought the notebook — not even the phone then, just dates. The lady said, 'Unless someone famous gets hurt, nobody cares if rent boys get recorded.' Her words." He laughed, short. "So yeah. I was gonna blackmail him. Not for justice. For us. Pay off Lou's back rent, get the eviction tossed, keep enough to get Milo out. Crane pays quiet money all the time. That's how he does it." "That's still—" I started, and then shut up because who was I to grade it. Milo snorted, Cheeto dust on his split lip. "I wasn't gonna let him martyr my phone for the bar. It's my phone. I was gonna sell it myself. Two grand. Guy on Sniffies offered." "You don't even know what's on it," Nico snapped. "I know there's videos. Old guys saying their names and room numbers like idiots. R.P. asking if I keep the phone in the bathroom." He looked at me, daring me to flinch. "You wanna see? Everybody wants to see." "I—" The ugly truth came up before I could sand it down. "Part of me did. When I gave Crane the page. Part of me wanted to know who—" I rubbed my face. My gum was gone, jaw aching empty. "I didn't. I won't. But yeah. I wanted to look." Silence except the drip. Nico stared at me. Not disgusted, which was worse. Just tired. Above us: three hard knocks on the front door. Then a pause. Then two more, heavier. My whole body knew that rhythm before my brain did. Nico mouthed *fixer*. Milo shoved the Cheetos under the blanket and went white around the blood. Footsteps. Lou's slow ones, then two other pairs. Muffled voices through the floorboards. "...confidential offer... just need to check the storage for our property..." "Cops?" Milo whispered. "Is that—" One voice had that cop boredom. Not Kehoe. Someone else. "Ma'am, if the boy's here we can help him—" I stood up too fast and cracked my head on the pipe. Stars. Fuck. I bit my lip so I wouldn't yell. Nico grabbed my wrist. Hard. Nails in. "Don't." But Lou was already stalling — "You got a warrant to come in my dry storage at ten p.m. in the rain? You got a warrant for my knees?" — and I knew we had maybe a minute. I took Milo's dead Android from the cardboard — the decoy he'd been playing TikToks on at OHSU — and shoved the cracked iPhone and the notebook deep behind the vodka boxes under a mildewed bar rag. Nico saw and nodded once. "Stay here. Don't cough if you can help it. If you have to—" I took his damp cigarette from his fingers. Held it pinched so the tobacco wouldn't stink up the air. "I'll be back." Upstairs Lou had the front door chained, arguing through six inches. The fixer: clean shoes now muddy, polo shirt, smiling. The uniform beside him young, white, rain on his hat. Same kid from the checkpoint? Maybe. They all look the same when you're brown and guilty. "Evening," I said, doing the voice before I could stop. Too friendly. Ex-cop smile cranked to ten. "Dev Menon. I was just — Lou called me about a break-in last night. I'm helping." The cop frowned. "You live here?" "Practically." Idiot. "No. I mean— I'm the PI. On the backpack thing. We found it. Kid's phone?" I held up the dead Android like I'd just found it on the bar. "This is it. Won't even turn on. Been dead two days. You're welcome to — there's nothing on it." The fixer held out his hand, still smiling. "We'll take it to be sure." "Be my guest. Needs a charger from like 2016." My hands were shaking. I put them in my windbreaker. "Kid's gone anyway. Bus out, I think. He took the till and ran. Ask Lou." Lou looked at me over her glasses. A long look. Cop is cop. Then she nodded once, barely. "Took one-forty. Little shit." They took the Android. They shone lights in dry storage, didn't go to the basement because the stairs were behind the cooler and the lights were off and Lou said the steps were rotted — which they are, one actually is. They left with wet shoes and nothing. When I got back down Nico was shaking, holding back a cough with his whole fist in his mouth. I gave him back his damp, crushed cigarette. He looked at it and laughed silently until his eyes watered, then crumbled it and dropped the wet tobacco on the concrete. "Blackmail's dead," he whispered. "They know his face now. If we try to squeeze Crane he'll just — he'll kill him." Milo picked Cheeto crumbs off the blanket, sullen. "So what? We just give it to you?" "No," I said. My head throbbed where I'd hit the pipe. "We copy what's readable — the dates, the Crane pressure stuff, not the — not the guys' faces. Send it to that blog girl who covered the Phase II thing. Redacted. The rest we delete. Tonight. In front of each other. No copies." Milo stared. "That's stupid. That's worth two grand." "It's worth you not getting killed for it," Nico said. He was looking at me, not him. "Okay. Okay, do it now before I chicken out." We did it on the basement floor with rain dripping on a keg and my laptop battery at 14%, Nico's lighter dead in his pocket and Milo breathing loud through his nose.

We deleted it on my laptop with 9% battery left, sitting on wet cardboard. Not fancy. No montage. Milo held the cracked iPhone with his thumb on the screen like it might bite him, Nico read the notebook out loud in a low voice so Lou upstairs wouldn't hear, and I typed what was readable into a burner email. Dates. Amounts. Initials. *J.K. asked for phone.* That text thread where Crane's guy says *save it, we save everything lol.* The screenshot of the data request that shows location pings from the app going to a Crane Revitalization spreadsheet. No names of the old guys. No videos. We watched the progress bar on the export and then Milo held the power button down on a factory reset until the Apple logo died. He cried a little when it went black and pretended it was his eye hurting. "Happy?" he said to both of us. "There goes my two grand." Nico didn't answer. He tore the notebook spiral out page by page and I lit the corner of the burn barrel behind the Femme in the rain with my Bic and we stood there getting soaked watching dates curl. The rain kept putting it out. We had to do it three times. We sent the email to a girl named Priya who runs a housing blog out of her kitchen. Not the Oregonian. Just *PDX Rent Watch.* Subject line: *from friends at the Femme.* Nico made me delete the sent folder twice. Then we went upstairs and told Lou nothing, which she knew was a lie and let pass because she was tired. The post went up Tuesday. Two hundred words. Blurry photo of the torn page I'd given Crane — because of course Crane had sent Priya the same photo to get ahead of it — plus our redacted dates. Headline: *Gay Developer Accused of Using Dating Data in Pearl Buyouts.* Crane's guy commented in under an hour: *We categorically deny any misuse. We support safe, sustainable queer spaces.* That was it. No FBI. No protest. One KUOW producer called Lou and then didn't call back. The eviction got pushed sixty days for "further review." Somebody from the city came and looked at the Hoshizaki and left a card. Lou took Crane's money anyway. Not the big number. A smaller one. Back rent plus the ice machine fix. She told Nico straight: "I can be righteous or I can keep the lights on. Denise's hospital bill's still on my card." She cried when she signed the interim thing. Then she yelled at the repair guy for tracking mud in. Milo left Thursday. Not a big goodbye. He signed himself out — again — stole Nico's beanie and my phone charger, and showed up at the Femme at noon with his eye almost open, lip scabbed, demanding bus money to his cousin in Fresno. Lou gave him $140 from an envelope marked TILL - DO NOT TOUCH in Sharpie, plus an extra sixty she said was tip share. He took it and said, "Don't Hallmark me," before either of them could start. Nico hugged him hard by the dry storage door and Milo went stiff and then hugged back for like half a second and then shoved him off. "Stop," he mumbled, eyes wet. "Fuck off." He nodded at me once. That was it. No thank you. The 70 came late and he got on with the grey hoodie up and his dead Android in his pocket and didn't look back through the window. I know because I watched the whole bus pull away like a creep. Some habits stick. Nico didn't cry until after. Just stood in the rain outside the Femme with his hands in his sleeves, coughing. "You wanna do laundry?" I said. It was the dumbest thing I could think of. His studio's machines were broken. Mine were downstairs and I still owed quarters. He said yeah. SpinCycle on 28th at like 7 a.m. Friday. Fluorescents too bright, smell of bleach and dryer sheets and somebody's old pizza. Our clothes mixed together in the big washer because neither of us had enough for two loads — my windbreaker, his bar shirts smelling of fryer oil, my sheets finally washed after sitting in a bag for a week, his jeans with the notebook paper lint in the pockets. We sat on the plastic chairs with our knees almost touching and shared cold Burgerville fries from yesterday. Salt and vinegar soggy. He stole the good crispy ones out of my hand and I let him. My phone buzzed. Mum. *Diwali Sunday. Are you coming? I made extra.* I texted back *will try, work busy* and then deleted it and typed *will come for an hour, save me food.* She sent back a heart emoji so fast I felt sick about Saturday. Nico was picking at his nails to nothing, tapping an unlit cigarette three times against his knuckle just to do it. Inside place, can't smoke. He put it behind his ear instead. "Crane's money," he said. I knew what he meant. The envelope. Lou had thrown it back at us — "I don't want your guilty money, take it" — minus two hundred she'd kept for the till Milo took. Six hundreds, damp now from going through the wash in Nico's jeans pocket because he's an idiot who doesn't check pockets. $600 on top of the dryer, curling in the heat. "We should give it back," I said. "Or — send it to Milo. He'll need—" "He'll spend it on stupid shit." "Yeah." I ate a limp fry. "Send it anyway." Nico nodded. Folded the bills, put them in his sock for safekeeping, which is where the notebook page was, which tells you everything about his system. The dryer buzzed. We didn't move right away. Warm air blowing out the vent, our stuff tumbling — grey hoodie (Milo left it, Nico kept it), my navy windbreaker, his black tee. I tried to think of something good to say. Something Chandler. All I had was: he was smoke and bad ideas. I was jealous and bored and — yeah. I trailed off because it sounded stupid out loud with bleach in the air and my knee aching from the plastic chair. Nico stole my last fry. Cold. Soggy end. "You still got that wobble chair?" he said. "In your office?" "Yeah." "Good. I need somewhere to sit while you follow me around and act like you're not." He leaned his head on my shoulder. Smelled like smoke even though he hadn't smoked since the basement because Lou would kill him. Ash in everything. My clean sheets ruined again already. We stayed until the clothes went cold. We had nowhere else that knew our names.
