Day 50 didn't write. Too tired to hold pencil. 51 now. Knuckle split open on the can lid yesterday. Right hand, fat part under thumb. Bled all over the dish shirt. This morning it's shut. Not scabbed, shut. Pink new skin, shiny. I keep opening and closing my hand staring at it. Ellis heard it first. The dog thing. We were out back trying to get the barrel going. Wood wet straight through. I was on my knees blowing till my chest hurt. He went still with his head tipped, mouth open. Like an idiot. "Wait," he whispered. Biscuit didn't hear nothing for a good ten seconds, then lifted up and growled low. It came out of the treeline by the Anders place, slow. Big dog shape, yellowish fur matted with white. Growths up its shoulders, thick clubs, and one big flat cap behind its left ear flopping when it walked. Limping. Breathing loud. Juno grabbed my coat from behind. Hard. Ellis said, "Don't — we need to observe —" and I already had the axe from the woodpile. It saw us and didn't run. Came straight, head low, making that chuffing sound. Biscuit went crazy barking, backing up at the same time, getting tangled in Juno's legs. I stepped out and hit it in the neck when it lunged. Missed clean, got shoulder. It yelped like a real dog and that turned my stomach. Hit again. Down. Twitching. I kept going till it stopped. My arms shaking after. Knees popped when I stood. Breath sawing through my nose. Juno crying into Biscuit's neck. Ellis white, glasses fogged, saying "good, good, okay" over and over. We dragged it to the tarp. Lighter than the man. I could see ribs. Dog ribs. My readers fogged the second I leaned in so I ripped them off and stuffed them in my pocket. Did it half-blind. Cut the clubs off first. Firm white inside, smell faint mushroom-butter. The big floppy one behind the ear bled that blue milk when I sliced. Salted a corner out of habit to see. Jumped. Still jumps. Juno looked away. Ellis hovered with his baggie book. "Gills are brown here so we should — I think if we parboil —" "You think a lot," I said. Meaner than I meant. Snapped the band on my wrist. Snap. Got maybe three pounds of white after I cut away the brown frill and burned it. Wasted a lot because I wouldn't cut close to the fur. Or to the ear. The stem went into the cheek and I just hacked high and threw the rest in the burn pile. Ellis said we were wasting calories. I said burn it. Boiled twice out back. First water came up gray and stank. Dumped in the weeds away from kale. Second boil I put in half onion left, hardtack broken up to thicken, pinch garlic rock, half broth packet. Couldn't help it. Smell got good fast. Porky. Fatty. Biscuit drooling strings, whining climbing higher and higher. Juno sitting on the steps counting. "That's mine, that's Ellis's, that's yours," she whispered, pointing at chunks with a stick. Keeping score already. Brought the pot in because the wind was killing the fire. Ellis said no spores in house, protocol, and I said it's boiled, it's soup, shut the door you're letting cold in. He shut it. Ate at the table standing too close to the stove. Real bowls. Not thimbles. Steam on all our faces. Nobody talked. That's the thing I keep thinking about. No grace, no "this is good," nothing. Just chewing. Too fast. Juno hunched with her arm around her bowl like always, shoveling. Gravy dripping off her chin. Ellis blowing and burning himself and eating anyway, counting forgotten. Me chewing and chewing, grit between my molars, fat slick on my lips I licked off quick. The browned bits off the bottom — I gave Juno one spoon, Ellis one, took two for me and said the pot needed scraping. Lie. I wanted them. Halfway through Juno laughed. Mouth full, snorted stew out her nose a little. We all looked up. She covered her mouth, eyes bright. "Biscuit farted," she mumbled. He had, loud under the table. I laughed so hard my eyes watered. Ellis laughed weird through his nose. Felt huge. Felt like before. Ellis held his hand up when I went to ladle again. "Go slow. Refeeding, we should wait twenty —" "It's stew, not hospital," I said, and gave Juno another half ladle and took one myself. He frowned but held his bowl out too. We all ate too much. Stomachs cramping happy-hurt. After, Juno drew on the pad margin. Pot with steam. Dog with too many legs. Ellis washed, quiet. I stood over the sink scraping and ate the spoon-scrape again and didn't even bother turning away all the way. He saw. Didn't say. Night sweats sweet. Woke up hot despite the cold room, blanket kicked off. Ellis snoring on the floor with two pairs of socks on, flushed pink. Juno sprawled across Biscuit, both panting. House 48 degrees and we were warm as bread. I woke humming. Low tune, nothing I know. Hmm-hmm-hmm while I pissed, while I fed Doughbi potato water. Stopped when I noticed. Started again without meaning to. Juno picked it up by breakfast, humming it back at the table. That chilled me more than the shit-cramps. Biscuit got into the trim bucket. Must not have latched it. Ate raw frill and skin bits while we slept. Found him bloated tight as a drum in the morning, groaning, trying to puke and couldn't. Juno screaming I killed him. Ellis panicking with the book. I walked him in circles in the snow in my slippers, feet going numb, massaging his belly, cursing him. "You stupid greedy bastard, spit it up." He shit watery yellow, then again by the back mat when we got in, huge stinking pile with white threads in it. Smell sweet-rot, wrong. I cleaned it on my knees. Knees screaming. Pop pop. Wanted to hit him again like with the broom last time and wanted to hold him. Did both — shoved his head away hard, then pulled him in and he licked my wrist where the knuckle sealed. Threw the rest of the trim in the fire. Watched it shrivel. My mouth watered anyway.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 3)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter is a remarkably disciplined piece of cozy-horror survival writing that executes its plan with unusual fidelity and craft. Let me work through it systematically. VOICE AND FORM: Mara's voice is consistent and earned throughout. The shorthand thinking ("Dog ribs. My readers fogged"), the cook's instincts bleeding into horror ("Salted a corner out of habit to see. Jumped. Still jumps."), the self-aware meanness ("Meaner than I meant. Snapped the band on my wrist. Snap.") — these feel like a real person writing in a real log, not a writer performing a character. The form breaks are organic: the missed day, the physical detail of the split knuckle, the way she records her own lies without quite admitting they're lies. HORROR MECHANICS: The chapter delivers its horror through accumulation of small wrongnesses rather than set-pieces. The sealed knuckle opening the chapter is quietly devastating — she keeps opening and closing her hand, staring. The humming is the best horror beat: she wakes humming a tune she doesn't know, stops when she notices, starts again, and then Juno picks it up at breakfast. The chapter earns the chill of that moment because it's been building through the warmth of the meal. The Biscuit sequence — white threads in the shit, the sweet-rot smell, her mouth watering at the burning trim — is genuinely disturbing and handled without underlining. CHARACTER WORK: All four characters are rendered with precision. Mara's lie about the browned bits ("said the pot needed scraping. Lie. I wanted them.") is exactly right — she records her own dishonesty in the log without self-pity. Ellis's "Go slow. Refeeding, we should wait twenty —" followed by holding his bowl out anyway is perfect character work: the rule-maker who breaks his own rules from hunger. Juno's laugh with stew coming out her nose, the arm around the bowl, the counting with a stick — all consistent with the profile. The "Felt huge. Felt like before" after the laugh is the chapter's emotional peak, and it's earned. THE MEAL ITSELF: The eating scene is the chapter's centerpiece and it's handled with real skill. "Nobody talked. That's the thing I keep thinking about." The specificity of the grit between molars, the fat slick on lips, the browned bits — this is food writing as labor and shame and pleasure simultaneously. The chapter avoids the trap of making the meal either purely disgusting or purely redemptive. WEAKNESSES: A few minor issues. "Felt huge. Felt like before" is slightly on-the-nose — the chapter has been showing this without needing to tell it. The Biscuit sequence, while effective, runs slightly long and the emotional beats (want to hit him, want to hold him, did both) are telegraphed a beat before they land. Ellis's dialogue is functional but occasionally feels like it's serving exposition ("Gills are brown here so we should — I think if we parboil —") rather than character. The chapter plan called for "Mara's split knuckle seals overnight" and this is delivered, but the chapter opens on it rather than discovering it mid-chapter, which slightly reduces the horror of the discovery. PLAN ADHERENCE: The chapter follows its plan closely — the dog-thing kill, the real stew with hardtack, the silence while eating, Juno's laugh, Mara pushing seconds, the overnight healing, the humming, Biscuit's bloat and the cleaning. The "best meal / worst manners" framing is delivered. The plan's note about "Mara wakes humming a tune she doesn't know" is executed precisely. PROSE QUALITY: The prose is clean and controlled. No purple passages, no forced metaphors. "Warm as bread" is the one slightly soft simile but it earns its place in context. The physical comedy of Biscuit farting is handled with exactly the right lightness — it doesn't undercut the horror, it makes the horror worse by showing what they've lost and briefly recovered. OVERALL: This is a high-quality chapter that executes a difficult tonal balance with skill. The cozy-horror blend works because the horror is inside the comfort, not adjacent to it. The sealed knuckle, the humming, the white threads in the dog's shit — these are genuinely unsettling precisely because they're embedded in a scene of warmth and laughter. Day 53. Skipped 52. Hands too cut up from wire. Ellis got it in his head we need to put up meat. Can't live hand to mouth, he said. He's right but I hated hearing it in his boss voice. We dragged the oil drum from behind the shed. Ray's old burn drum, rusted through at the bottom. Ellis packed mud around the holes while Juno fetched green sticks. I cut strips. Dog thing leftovers plus the man caps I kept cold in snow. Sliced thin as I could with my hands shaking. Some pieces firm and white, nice as pork loin. Some went slimy under the knife. Clear slime that stringed off the blade. I rinsed and rinsed, salted heavy. Still slimed. "You can't smoke slime," I told Ellis. "We have to try," he said. Thermometer with no batteries around his neck like a necklace. Built a little fire under, fed it damp alder. Smoke poured white and stung. Eyes watering all over again. Coughing into my elbow. Juno tended the flap with a stick, real serious, cheeks red. Biscuit sat too close like always, tail tipped singed again. Smelled it before — hair burning sweet. Hung strips on wire over the smoke. The good ones dried at the edges, turned tan, smelled like bacon and camp. The slimy ones just sweated. Hours and they stayed wet-shiny, dripping. Smell off-sweet, like fruit left in a hot car. Flies came. In December. Two big slow ones bumping the drum. I swatted and missed. "Till it looks right" never came. Ellis cleaned the cutting tarp while I watched the fire. Pulled his mask down because it kept fogging his glasses. "Just be quick," he said, scraping brown frill and wet gills into the burn pile with his bare hands. Dust puffed up. Seeds. He breathed right through it, coughed once. I said, "Mask up, idiot." He waved me off. Picking at his thumbs after, hiding them. By dark we had maybe a dozen decent sticks, leathery, salty. And a pile of slime that wouldn't take smoke. Ellis said discard, protocol. I looked at the pad. 3 tomato. 1 corn. That's it now. Peaches gone — Juno ate them cold yesterday while I was outside and lied about it with syrup on her shirt. I boiled the slime again. Third boil. Foam came gray. Dumped, boiled. Still slick between my teeth when I tested a corner. Like okra gone wrong. Chewed and swallowed anyway. We ate it for supper with watery oats. Forced it down. Juno gagged and I snapped, "Chew and swallow, don't waste." She cried quiet while chewing. I felt rotten but kept eating. Ellis ate fast, then got up to piss and came back coughing hard, rattling deep in his chest. That cough stayed all night. Wet rattle when he breathed in. This morning his breath smells sweet. Not like mint. Like soda poured out flat. He tried to hide it turning his head. Biscuit kept sniffing at his chest and whining. I made him sit by the window with a blanket. Steam pot with pine needles. He hated being fussed. Tried to tell me how to cut — "smaller strips, rotate every—" and I said, "Ellis, shut it. This is my kitchen." He shut it. Picked his cuticles till they bled. Doughbi's thin. Fed it potato water last night and it barely bubbled. Smells sharp, hungry. I know the feeling. Stirred it and talked to it stupid. "Hold on, you bastard." Juno heard and laughed with her mouth full of slime. Afternoon Biscuit got into the gill bucket again. Latch must've slipped. I came in from wood and he had his head in, gulping raw brown frill. Juno screaming his name. I grabbed the broom and hit him. Hard across the ribs. He yelped and dropped it, tail tucked, looking at me shocked. I hit the floor next to him again to scare him off. "Out! Out!" He ran to Juno, shaking. She wrapped around him, glaring at me. "You hurt him!" "He'll die," I yelled, breathing loud through my nose. "You want him bloated dead again? You want that?" She went silent. That worse silent. I sat on the floor after. Knees popping loud. Pulled Biscuit's head into my lap though he flinched first. Held his gray muzzle. His belly gurgling. My hands shaking. Cried a little into his dirty fur where Juno couldn't see. Smelled corn chips and sweet. "He's greedy like me," I whispered. Sorry, boy. Ellis coughed through the wall. Humming in his sleep earlier — that same tune. I didn't teach it to him. I know I didn't. Ate standing up again tonight. Two smoke sticks chewed slow, gritty, good. Licked grease off my thumb. Hid the best one under the dish towel for Juno's breakfast and then took it back out and ate half myself. Wrapped the other half back up. Stomach paid. Didn't care.

Day 60. Snow yesterday and stayed. No dog things for a week. Ellis says migrated. I say ate each other. Juno says nothing, picks at her lip till it bleeds and then sucks it. Cold's different now. Gets in the walls. Stove eats wood faster than we can haul. I sleep in my coat. Still I wake up sweating sweet under the arms. Pillow damp. Same with Ellis — shirt sticking to his back though the window frosts inside. Juno's hair smells like syrup when I braid it and my own mouth waters and I hate that. Dreams all the same shape. Damp dark and singing low, like a fridge hum. I wake humming that tune with my jaw aching. Yesterday Juno hummed it washing roots and Ellis joined from the couch before he caught himself. We all stopped and didn't look at each other. Found the mound Tuesday while looking for wood past Anders fence. Juno found it first, actually. Screamed for me, then stood there staring. Potato, if potatoes grew big as a rain barrel. Pale lumpy, split open on top with brown frill showing. Man's legs sticking out the bottom, boots gone, socks wet black. One hand out to the side, fingers curled. When the wind shifted it shuddered and made a noise — high thin through the slits, like air out a kettle. Eeeeee. Biscuit backed off whining. Juno stepped closer. "Don't touch," I said. "I've seen it before," she said. My stomach dropped. "When?" She shrugged. Picked at her lip. "Walking Biscuit." I wanted to yell. Knees hurt too bad to stand there long so I just grabbed her sleeve. "You don't come here alone." She pulled away. "It wasn't screaming that time. It was just breathing." Brought Ellis next day. He stood upwind with two masks on, cough rattling, and got excited in that annoying way. "Sessile fruiting! Caloric jackpot if the —" "It's a person with a growth," I said. "Stop rubbing your hands." We argued in the kitchen after. Ellis coughing into his elbow between words. Sweet breath filling the little room. Biscuit sniffing at him and licking his lips. "We fry fat," Ellis said. "Small pan upwind. Draw one walker in. We can't keep digging for roots and calling it supper." "You want to ring a dinner bell," I said. "It's already smelling us. You know it is." He tipped his head, listening without meaning to. Mouth open. "Something knocked last night at 2. You heard." I had. Three slow knocks on the shed wall. Told myself ice falling. Juno sat kicking the table leg. Thump. Thump. "I can do the pan. I'm fastest." "No," me and Ellis both said. In the end I did it. Of course I did. Took a spoon of saved grease — white hard stuff in the jar — and a cold smoke stick. Went back to the mound clearing with Ellis wheezing behind carrying the axe and Juno told to stay with Biscuit on the steps and following anyway at twenty feet with a rock. Kid never obeys. Set the little skillet on the twig fire. Grease melted. Hit hot and smoked up rich, pork and cheese and that sweet under. Smell punched through the cold. My mouth flooded instant. Swallowed thick. The mound woke screaming louder. Eeeee-eeeee. The slits pulsed. Sweet dust puffed off it in clouds. Ellis pulled his shirt up over his nose, coughing. Then movement in the trees. A walker, thin woman, caps up her neck like a collar, coming straight and fast, head tipped sniffing. Biscuit back at the house started barking his head off though he couldn't see. I froze with the spoon. Ellis whispered, "Now, Mara, now—" She came into the clearing reaching. I swung the axe and caught her in the knee first, bad hit, she went sideways screaming wet, not like the mound, like a person surprised. Second hit in the temple dropped her. Sound I feel in my teeth still. Quiet after except the mound screaming and my breath sawing and Juno saying "whoa" soft behind me. Hands shook the whole butcher. Readers fogged, I worked blind half the time. Cut high, wasted plenty, threw anything with purple threads in the fire though my glasses — when I could see — maybe missed some. Couldn't tell brown from shadow. The woman's nails were painted chipped red. I kept seeing that and cutting. Got enough white to fill the pot. Plus last carrots gone rubbery, last onion, snowmelt. Pot pie isn't pie. No flour to spare for crust, Doughbi's starving on potato water as it is. Thick stew with hardtack crumbled on top to soak. But the meat browned first in its own fat and smelled so good my hands shook holding the spoon. Gave Juno the spoon to lick while Ellis wasn't looking. She grinned with grease on her chin. I licked the spatula after. Ate inside with the door barred, stove roaring. Three bowls full, steam burning our faces. No one said grace. Ellis started to and Juno already had a mouthful and I was chewing. We just ate. Fast, hunched, arm around bowls. Gravy dripping. Grit in my teeth I sucked at and swallowed. The browned bits — I scraped them and kept them, told myself for Biscuit, ate them standing at the counter with my back turned. Heard Ellis's spoon stop and knew he'd seen. Best thing I've made since the Skillet closed. That's true and rotten both. Halfway through the knocking started. Shed wall. Slow. Thunk. Thunk. Thunk. Biscuit lifted his head, growled with his mouth full of scrap I'd snuck him. Juno froze, spoon halfway. Ellis tipped his head listening, then jerked straight when he realized he did it. "It's the smell," he whispered. Sweet breath hot. "They —" "Keep eating," I said loud. "Eat while it's hot." We did. Chewed faster. Didn't talk. The knocking kept time a while then stopped.

Day 64. Morning frost inside again. Ellis heard them before Biscuit did. That’s how I knew. We were at the table picking over roots. Juno kicking the leg. Thump. Thump. Biscuit asleep on my feet, farting soft. Ellis went still with his spoon halfway up, head tipped, mouth open. Listening. He hates when I catch him doing it but he does it now without knowing. “Movement,” he whispered. “Road side.” Biscuit lifted a second later and started barking his fool head off. Juno grabbed his collar. I got the axe from by the stove though my knees popped loud going up. Pop. Hands shaking before I even saw anything. Two men on the garden path. Thin in a way that scared me more than the walkers. Coats too big, tied with string. The taller one had a beard gone patchy, sores at his mouth. The younger limped, boots taped with white tape gone black. Both staring at our chimney where the smoke was coming out pork-smelling from last night’s pot still warming. My mouth went dry and then wet. Rubber band snap on my wrist. Snap snap snap. “Hello!” I yelled too loud through the door. “Stay where you are!” They stopped. Hands up quick. “Smelled cooking,” the tall one called. Voice cracked. “God. Please. We’re not — we’re not looking for trouble.” Ellis was behind me whispering, “Don’t open, protocol, Mara—” with that sweet cough-breath hot on my neck. Juno had gone quiet in the bad way, slipped off to the pantry corner where I keep the smoke sticks in the coffee can. I opened the door. Stupid. I did it with a big fake smile on like the Skillet lunch rush, performing. “Well come on in before you freeze, boys! Come on!” Too loud. Too friendly. My heart hammering in my ears. They crowded in bringing cold and a smell, piss and old smoke. Sat at the table where I pointed, eyes flicking everywhere. At the pot. At the pad with my counts. At Juno. At Biscuit growling low with his old teeth out. “I’m Mara. This is Ellis, that’s Juno. Soup’s hot.” I ladled big. Too big. Full bowls of the mound stew, the good thick stuff with hardtack soaked in. I knew as I was doing it we couldn’t afford it. Did it anyway so they’d see we had plenty and leave us alone. Pride and fear mixed stupid. “Eat, eat,” I said, hovering. “Plenty.” Lie. Maybe two suppers left after this if we stretch with water. They ate like we did that first real night. Fast, hunched, no talking, gravy on chins. The younger one burned his mouth and didn’t stop. The tall one kept closing his eyes while he chewed. That look — God forgive me — I liked being the one who gave it. Wanted them to say it was good. Ellis sat stiff, picking at his thumbs under the table till they bled. Coughing into his elbow every few breaths. The men noticed the sweet smell. Glanced at each other. “You sick?” the tall one asked Ellis, spoon paused. “Seeds in his lungs,” Juno said flat from the corner. “From cleaning.” “Juno,” I snapped. “Get more wood.” She went but not before I saw her shirt riding up and a grease spot on her pocket. My coffee can lid was crooked. After they slowed down the tall one talked. Said they were from Mill Creek, walked up after their place went. Said down valley by Harlan’s feed store people figured it out too. Only they weren’t hunting. “They’re feeding ‘em,” the younger muttered to his bowl. “Keeping a couple mounds behind wire. Giving—” He stopped. Looked at Juno. “Telling tales?” I laughed too loud again. “Come on now.” The tall one wiped his mouth with his hand. “Saw a man walk in there tied. Heard screaming after. Next week they had meat to trade. You do the math.” He wouldn’t meet my eyes. Coughing hard himself, wet. “Said it makes you hear things if you eat long. Said you run hot.” Quiet. Stove ticking. Ellis flushed pink, shirt damp at the neck though the room was cold enough to see breath. He tipped his head just a fraction toward the window, listening again, then jerked straight when he realized. I refilled their bowls though I wanted to snatch them back. “Well we just take what comes in the fence,” I said fast. “Boil twice. Cut away the brown. We’re careful.” Sounded like bragging. Sounded like begging them to think we knew what we were doing. The younger one nodded at my hands. “Your knuckle —” Healed shiny pink. I tucked it under. They wanted lamp oil. Saw the jug by the door. Asked nice and then not nice, standing. Tall one’s hand in his pocket where something heavy sat. My knees went watery. Breath loud through my nose. I gave it. Small jug, half full, our spare for dark nights. Handed it over smiling till my face hurt. “Take it, take it, we owe — neighbors—” Juno came back with two sticks, eyes on the men’s packs. The tall one ruffled Biscuit’s head on the way out though Biscuit snapped weak at him. They thanked me three times on the steps. Said they’d trade if they found antibiotics. Gone into the snow fast, looking back once at the chimney. I barred the door. Hands shaking so bad I missed the latch twice. Turned and yanked Juno’s pocket inside out. Half a smoke stick, crumbs. “I didn’t take it,” she said instantly, crumbs on her shirt, on her mouth. “Don’t you lie to me,” I yelled. My voice cracked. “We just gave away supper! You steal now?” She glared, tears coming but jaw set. “You gave them mine! You gave them big bowls to show off!” That hit true and made me meaner. “Go to your cot. Go on!” She went silent, kicked the table leg hard on the way, stormed off with Biscuit limping after her. Ellis started, “Mara, refeeding, stress—” “Shut it,” I said. Stood over the sink breathing hard, counting the pot. Half left. Half of half with water added. My stomach gnawed and I hated those men for eating and hated myself for wanting them to love it. Ellis whispered after a while, “They were coughing when they left. Before I saw them. I heard the wet in it from the road.” He picked at his cuticle, hid his thumbs. “I hate that I heard it first. I liked it.” I didn’t answer. Scraped their bowls into ours. Added water to stretch. Licked the ladle clean facing the wall so he wouldn’t see. Outside something knocked once on the shed. Soft. Stopped.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 6)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter is a strong execution of the plan's intentions, and it largely succeeds on its own terms. Let me work through it carefully. **Voice and Form:** Mara's voice is consistent and convincing throughout. The log-style narration feels genuinely inhabited — "Too loud. Too friendly. My heart hammering in my ears" reads like a person writing fast and honest, not a writer performing authenticity. The shorthand observations ("Lie. Maybe two suppers left after this if we stretch with water.") land cleanly. The rubber band snapping is used well as a physical tic without being overworked. The chapter maintains the planned form: handwritten log, plainspoken, tired, self-aware about her own failures. **Character Consistency:** All four characters behave exactly as their profiles dictate. Ellis's head-tilt listening, his sweet cough-breath, his admission at the end that he liked hearing the wet cough first — all consistent with his profile's note about hating his own useful mutation. Juno's flat lie with crumbs on her shirt, her counter-accusation ("You gave them mine! You gave them big bowls to show off!") — this is precisely the 11-year-old who keeps score and lies flat. Mara's performed generosity, her cruelty to Juno that she knows is displaced, licking the ladle facing the wall — all consistent. Biscuit's weak snap at the stranger is right. **Plot Execution:** The chapter plan called for: two gaunt men following the smell, Mara performing generosity too loudly and giving too much, Juno stealing jerky and lying badly, the men half-warning about the valley farm feeding people to mounds, Ellis admitting he can hear movement before it comes. All of these are delivered. The lamp oil detail (something Mara didn't want to give) is included. The warning about the valley is appropriately vague and distracted — the men are coughing, they don't press it, it lands as rumor rather than exposition. This is exactly right for the story's lore philosophy. **Horror and Cozy Balance:** The horror here is social and bodily, as planned. The men noticing Ellis's sweet smell, the healed knuckle Mara hides, Ellis running hot and damp — these are the body-horror elements embedded in a domestic scene. The cozy elements are present in the right register: the stove ticking, the soup ladled too generously, the argument over spoonfuls. The final knock on the shed is restrained and effective. **Dialogue:** The dialogue is mostly strong. "Seeds in his lungs. From cleaning." is a perfect Juno line — flat, tactical, slightly wrong in a way that reveals her. "You gave them mine! You gave them big bowls to show off!" is earned and true. The men's dialogue is appropriately thin and functional. The tall one's "You do the math" is a bit of a cliché but fits a tired, scared man. Ellis's "Mara, refeeding, stress—" cut off by "Shut it" is good — it shows his tendency to manage and her refusal. **Weaknesses:** A few moments approach the too-neat. "Pride and fear mixed stupid" is a tell-don't-show moment — the chapter has already shown this, so naming it is redundant. "That hit true and made me meaner" is similarly explanatory where the action already demonstrates it. The line "God forgive me — I liked being the one who gave it" is slightly on-the-nose for a story that otherwise trusts its readers. These are minor but real. The men's warning about the valley farm is handled well in terms of vagueness, but the younger man's hesitation ("Looked at Juno") before stopping is a slightly familiar beat — the "not in front of the child" pause. It works but it's not surprising. The ending — "Outside something knocked once on the shed. Soft. Stopped." — is effective but is the third or fourth chapter to end on an external knock or sound. Within this chapter it works, but as a pattern across the book it would be wearing thin by now. **Prose Quality:** The prose is controlled and largely avoids purple excess. "Piss and old smoke" for the men's smell is economical and right. "Gravy on chins" is good. The chapter doesn't overreach with metaphor, which is correct for this voice. One slightly strained moment: "My mouth went dry and then wet" — this is physiologically accurate (fear then salivation at the smell of food) but it's doing a lot of work quietly and might be too quiet to register as the horror beat it is. **Overall:** This is a well-crafted chapter that executes its plan faithfully, maintains voice and character consistency, and delivers its horror through domestic friction rather than spectacle. It's not a masterpiece — there are small tell-don't-show failures and a few predictable beats — but it's genuinely good work. Day 68. Sky yellow mean. Ellis heard the weather before the radio said. Stood at the window tipping his head at nothing. “Pressure drop,” he said, picking his thumbs till they bled. “We need one more run before it hits.” Pad says: tomato 1. Corn 1, seam bulging. Don’t trust it. Smoke sticks 9, and Juno swears she only took one. Oats gone. Oil finger gone. Grease jar half. Doughbi smells like nail polish, barely bubbles when I stir. I fed it the last potato water and talked stupid to it. “Hang on.” We got greedy. I got greedy. Said it out loud at the table like it was sense: fry a spoon of grease, draw one dog thing, fill the pot before snow locks us. Ellis nodded too fast, cough rattling. Juno lit up. “I can do the pan, I’m fastest,” she said again. I said no and then let her carry the skillet anyway because my knees screamed on the steps. Pop pop going down. Cold burned my nose from inside. Wind already picking up, throwing ice. We set up by the drum smoker out back because it was sheltered. Little twig fire under the skillet. I put in a big spoon of the white hard fat. It melted fast, started smoking rich. Pork and burnt cheese and that sweet under. Smell punched right through the cold and my mouth flooded. Swallowed thick. Biscuit whining high, pulling Juno’s arm. Ellis with his shirt yanked up over his nose, glasses fogging, coughing into it. “It’s a lot,” Ellis muttered. “Mara, that’s a lot of fat.” “One spoon,” I said. It was three. I wanted to be sure. The mound down past Anders — we could hear it start up faint. Eeeeee. Then closer, rustle in the treeline. Two dog things, not one, coming low and fast, shoulder clubs bouncing. Behind them a walker, woman with no shoes, caps up her legs like armor. “Shit,” Ellis breathed. “Okay. Okay—” Juno grabbed the axe before I could. “Juno, give me that—” I snapped, and she didn’t. Biscuit barking his fool head off, lunging, dragging her. I swung at the first dog thing as it hit the skillet, knocked it sideways yelping real-dog yelp. Second one went for Ellis, got his coat sleeve. He screamed thin, hit it with a stick. The walker came straight for Juno, arms out, breathing wet. It happened fast and stupid. I missed the walker’s head, got neck. She didn’t drop. Juno swung the little hatchet we split kindling with and caught her in the shin. Brave and dumb. The woman fell into Juno, knocked her flat in snow. Biscuit went in teeth bared — old hips, bad teeth — and got her wrist, shaking. She raked him down the side with her nails. He yelped. Then the smell turned. Rot-sweet, thick. Another one pushing out of the trees behind the shed, huge, overripe, belly split with brown jelly hanging. Every step it sloshed. Ellis yelled, “Don’t hit the belly! Don’t—” First dog thing I’d knocked got up and slammed into it from the side fighting over the grease smell. Claws in. The belly burst. Not pop. Splorch. Wet sheet of brown slime and dust blew out in a cloud. Seeds so thick you could see them. Smell like hot garbage and syrup. It coated the smoker drum, the woodpile, my coat sleeve. The dog thing rolled in it screaming. “Inside! Greenhouse!” Ellis coughed, choking, dragging Juno up by her hood. She was crying, holding Biscuit’s collar where blood spotted his yellow fur in a long slice along his ribs. Not deep but bleeding steady. We ran for the lean-to. Plastic walls Ray put up years ago for tomatoes, now holding three trays of pale sprouts we baby by the stove light. Wind tearing at it already. The walker woman followed, crawling now with her shin broke. The burst one staggered after, still coming, blind and dripping. The two dog things fought each other over the skillet, snarling. We got in and Ellis dropped the heavy tomato table against the door. Plastic bowing in. Cold and hot both. I grabbed the kerosene jug and the rags. Hands shaking so bad I spilled. “Burn her,” Ellis said, meaning the crawler at the door pushing fingers under the plastic. “Burn her now or she gets in.” We dragged the dead twig bundles and the spare chair broke up and piled on her arm where it came through. Lit it. Fire took fast in the little space, too fast. Smoke filled the lean-to, sweet and greasy. We tied shirts over our faces but it didn’t matter. Breathed it anyway. Hot lungfuls, pork and rot. She screamed going. Not words. High thin eeeeee through the slits in her neck, and under that a wet loneliness that punched me. Like a kid crying in another room and you can’t get to them. I felt pity so sharp it scared me — and at the same time I thought, clear as a ticket: back caps look firm, we can cut those after. I hated myself thinking it while she burned. Kept thinking it. Juno held Biscuit’s head in her lap, pressing my dish shirt to his side. Blood soaking through. She was humming that tune without knowing, hmm-hmm-hmm, tears cutting clean lines down her dirty face. “Shut up humming,” I snapped, mean with fear. She stopped, then started again. Outside the plastic the burst one pressed its face to the wall, smearing brown. The smoker drum was on its side, strips in the snow getting trampled. Wind ripped a long tear in the greenhouse roof and snow hissed in on the fire. We stayed till the crawler stopped moving and the fire burned low and the others lost interest or froze. I don’t know. Quiet except wind and Ellis’s rattle and Biscuit panting fast. Ellis sat too close to the coals on purpose. Scooted nearer till his pants steamed. Face flushed red, sweat running. “Need to stay hot,” he muttered, picking at his thumbs. “Keep seeds down. Stay hot.” I didn’t argue. My own chest felt lit from inside, fever-warm despite the snow on my shoulders. We cut in the smoke with my readers fogged blind. Took the firm white off her back high above the burn, wasted most. My knife found threads going down into red and I cut higher, hands numb. Juno watched and didn’t look away this time. Carried the meat and the bleeding dog back through blowing snow to the house. Left the drum on its side.

Day 72. Think. Lost one in the blow. Blizzard since night before last. Can't see the shed. Wind finds every crack. Frost inside thick on the nails. Stove eats and eats and the room stays cold enough to see breath, except right on top of it where Ellis sits. Pad: tomato 1. Corn 1, I won't open it, seam's domed hard. Sticks 6. Grease jar spoon left. Roots frozen dirt clods. Sprouts from the lean-to in a bowl, pale yellow, leggy. That's what we carried back before the plastic tore off. Doughbi flat gray water on top. He smells sweet under the rot smell. His piss in the snow by the door steams sweet and yesterday there was a fly on it. One slow winter fly. I killed it with my thumb. Ellis runs hot now. Shirt damp at the neck though the window's iced inside. Cheeks pink all the time. Sits too close till his knees steam. Says his chest feels tight if he moves away. Cough still down deep, rattles when he breathes in. Breath sweet enough I turn my head when he talks close. He eats and then is hungry an hour later. Counts chews to twelve and then forgets and shovels. Last night I heard him in his sleep doing that hmm-hmm-hmm with his mouth open. Didn't wake him. Juno took a bowl out last night without asking. Little tin one with thin soup and a piece of stick cut small. Set it on the step outside the back door in the snow. I saw from the window. "You feeding birds?" I said. She picked her lip. Bleeding. "If we don't they'll knock." "Who told you that?" She shrugged. Looked at Ellis. I wanted to yell waste. Didn't. Went out in my coat and boots unlaced and brought the bowl back in because we can't afford it and set it on the table and we ate it between us for breakfast added to the pot. Watery. She cried silent while she ate, mad. Kicked the table leg once. Thump. Biscuit put his head on her foot. Tonight the pipe knocked and then stopped. No water. I took the kettle rag and my hands and breathed on the elbow under the sink till my fingers went white and then burning. Juno held the candle though it kept going out. Ellis tipped his head at the wall listening to something that wasn't the pipe, mouth open, then caught me seeing and pretended to cough. Got a dribble. Brown. Boiled it anyway. Soup was sticks boiled long with snowmelt, salt, half the good fat to make it shine, sprouts thrown in last so they go limp. No thick. No browned bits to fight over because there weren't any. I scraped the pot anyway out of habit and there was nothing to scrape and my mouth still watered at the hot metal smell. Ate on the floor by the stove because the table's too cold. Four heartbeats close. No grace. Ellis started to say something and Juno already had her spoon up and I was blowing. Too fast, too quiet. Slurping loud. Juno hunched with her arm around it like always. I watched her spoon to make sure she didn't get more and hated myself watching and kept watching. She finished first and looked in my bowl. I turned a little away without meaning to. Biscuit got the wash water with fat eyes on top. Licked the bowl clean pushing it across the floor. Laid his head on my foot groaning old-man groan when he sat. I scratched his ear with my foot because my hands were around my bowl warming them. After, I tried to feed Doughbi. Nothing left. Chewed a corner of hardtack till it was paste and spit it in. Stirred. It smelled sharp, hungry. "Sorry, bastard," I whispered. Juno heard and didn't laugh this time. Mended Ellis's sleeve where the dog thing tore it. Thread too thick, needle too big, fingers too cold. Knots all over. He sat too close while I did it, heat coming off him like the stove. Sweat sweet. I had to breathe through my mouth. "Stay hot?" I said. He nodded, picking his thumb bloody. "Keep them down." I didn't ask what them meant. Knocking started around nine. Shed side, though the shed might be flat by now. Slow. Thunk. Thunk. Thunk. Biscuit lifted his head, growled low with his mouth full of nothing, then put it back down. Juno went still, spoon halfway. Ellis tipped toward it before he could stop himself. We didn't talk. Stove ticked as it cooled a notch. Wind gusted. The knocking stopped mid-pattern. Didn't start again. Juno got up and took the little tin bowl to the door. I didn't stop her. Can't afford it and I didn't stop her. She poured a spoon of our wash water in and set it outside quick and barred back fast, breathing hard. Stood with her back to the door listening. Nothing. Wind. Ellis's rattle. Biscuit farting soft in his sleep. I relit the lamp with the white fat because the oil's gone. It burns too fast and smokes and smells pork-sweet. Makes the whole room smell like supper when there isn't any. My stomach cramped smelling it and I swallowed and swallowed. No recipe tonight. Wasn't enough to call it a meal. Mouth waters at the wrong smells.

Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of post-apocalyptic survival horror that earns its "cozy-horror" designation through a distinctive narrative voice and careful accumulation of domestic detail against a backdrop of genuine dread. Let me assess it across the requested dimensions. VOICE AND CHARACTER: The first-person voice of Mara is one of the piece's greatest strengths. She speaks in a clipped, inventory-obsessed idiom that feels entirely authentic to someone rationing everything, including words. The list-making, the ticket-pad counts, the rubber band snapping — these are consistent behavioral tics that reveal character without announcement. Ellis's compulsive list-writing when scared, Juno's bowl-hugging and lip-picking, Biscuit's greedy nose — all three supporting characters are rendered with economy and specificity. The relationship dynamics (Mara's diner-boss authority, Ellis's anxious expertise, Juno's child-pragmatism) feel lived-in and consistent across all eight chapters. WORLD-BUILDING: The spore-mutant apocalypse is conveyed almost entirely through implication and sensory detail rather than exposition. We understand the mechanics — spores infect, walkers and dog-things are the result, the mounds are sessile fruiting bodies — without any info-dump. The detail of the humming tune spreading between characters is genuinely chilling and handled with restraint. The sweet smell, the running hot, Ellis hearing things before Biscuit — these are subtle transformation markers that accumulate dread without melodrama. THE HORROR-COZY BALANCE: This is where the piece truly excels. The horror is real and present (the woman's chipped red nails, the wet loneliness of her dying scream, Mara thinking about cutting the back caps while she burns), but it's embedded in the texture of domestic survival — the stove that won't draw, Doughbi the sourdough starter, Biscuit's embarrassed farts. The piece earns its darkness through this contrast rather than relying on shock. PACING: The chapter structure works well. Each chapter advances the situation while maintaining the grinding, day-by-day quality of survival. The blizzard chapter (8) effectively conveys stasis and desperation. The escalation from cautious first taste to greedy overreach in Chapter 7 feels earned. DIALOGUE: Dialogue is sparse and functional, which suits the voice. When it appears, it's sharp and characterful. "It's stew, not hospital" is perfect. The strangers' dialogue in Chapter 6 efficiently delivers exposition (the feeding operation down valley) without feeling like an info-dump. WEAKNESSES: The piece occasionally leans on its own stylistic tics to the point of slight repetition — the knee-popping, the rubber band snapping, the mouth-watering appear so frequently they begin to feel mechanical rather than organic by Chapter 6-7. The "snap snap snap" and "pop pop" constructions, while effective initially, are deployed so often they risk becoming self-parody. The transformation arc (the humming, running hot, hearing things) is handled with admirable restraint but the piece ends before any real reckoning with it, which is both a strength (ambiguity) and a weakness (the reader wants some payoff). The strangers in Chapter 6 feel slightly convenient as an exposition vehicle, though they're handled better than most such devices. FORCED POETRY: The piece largely avoids this trap. When it reaches for metaphor — "white lacing into red," "warm from the barrel, smelled like Sunday" — it lands. The "fruit, not person" self-deception is psychologically precise. There are occasional moments where the staccato style tips into affectation ("Lie. I wanted them.") but these are minor. UNEARNED TRANSFORMATIONS: The physical changes (healed knuckle, running hot, hearing things) are seeded carefully and never overstated. Mara's moral transformation — from reluctant survivor to someone who thinks about harvesting while watching someone burn — is the piece's central arc and is handled with genuine craft. It's earned. EMOTIONAL ENGAGEMENT: The piece is genuinely moving in places. The Biscuit scenes (hitting him, then holding him, crying into his fur) are the emotional heart. Juno setting out the bowl of wash water is quietly devastating. The laughter over Biscuit's fart — "felt huge, felt like before" — is perfectly placed. COHERENCE: The piece maintains internal consistency throughout. The inventory counts, the character behaviors, the escalating transformation symptoms all track logically. Overall this is a high-quality piece of genre fiction with a distinctive voice, genuine emotional intelligence, and effective horror. Its weaknesses are minor stylistic repetitions and an ending that, while appropriately ambiguous, leaves some threads unresolved. It's not quite a masterpiece — the repetitive tics and the slightly convenient Chapter 6 strangers hold it back — but it's well above average.
