She had not meant to go back Friday. She meant to mend the hem and lie low and make the bread last. But her left mitten was gone. She turned the cottage upside down for it — under Jem's coat, in the coal scuttle, behind Mother's tick — and knew where it was. Up there, on the nursery boards where she'd dropped crouched coming over the sill, with her name tab sewn inside by Mother in red thread. TRANT. Any maid that found it would know. That was what she told herself on the walk. Not the coal. Not the toast going down like he'd watched her swallow. Frost harder. Her torn hem she'd knotted up with twine, which left her ankles bare to wind. Her chilblains had split again at washing; she'd bound the right hand with rag, and it throbbed under the wrap going up the washhouse gutter. Lead burned cold straight through the rag. *Spout left holds. Nine pulls. Don't breathe loud.* The transom gave at once. Too easy. Warm air this time, sour underneath. She got the sash up quieter, shoulder to it, and swung in. The lamp was high, smoking. The room stank shut-up and sick-sweet, stronger than Thursday. He was not in the chair. He was on the narrow bed in shirt and drawers, blanket kicked half off, head back, mouth open. A tumbler on the floor, brown dregs. Laudanum. She knew the smell from Mother's bottle — bitter, syrupy. His eyes opened but didn't fix. "You," he said thick. "Orderly. Boots." His left leg was bare to the knee. The dressing had slipped down to the ankle, trailing wet. The calf underneath was purple-white and puckered where the ball had gone through, the edges soft and weeping clear fluid that had dried to varnish. A fresh spot oozed. The smell made her stomach turn over, toast rising back. She found the mitten by the table leg and shoved it in her pocket. She should go. She should take coal from the scuttle — he had half a scuttle nursed, more than they'd had at home in a week — and go back out the window. Instead she picked up the basin. The ewer was half full, stone cold. She set the basin on the cindered grate and poured, and fed the one lump with two sticks from the wood box, blowing till smoke made her eyes water. When it steamed she carried it with both hands and scalded her cracked knuckles on the rim. She hissed and chewed twine till her tongue went bitter. "You'll get cold," she muttered, dragging the blanket up over his thighs. He flinched hard when her cuff brushed the bad calf, then pretended he hadn't, staring at the ceiling. "Don't touch the leg," he said, officer-clip even drugged. "My man does that." "Your man don't," she said. "Basin's pink a week old." She wrung a corner of cleanish bandage in hot water and wiped round the wound, not on it. The skin was hot and tight. He sucked breath through teeth and gripped the sheet with clean nails, ink-stained at the cuticle. Three books on the mantel stood lined by height. One had slipped. While the cloth cooled she reached and straightened it without thinking. He watched her. "You count," he said again. "I don't." "You do. Under your breath." She'd been counting stairs in her head to keep her hands steady. *Seven, eight.* She scowled. "Hush and let me finish." "I was saying you was — you were counting," he said. She stopped with the cloth dripping. "I were counting, yes. I ain't your parlour lass to correct." A flicker, half amusement, half pique. "I ain't — I'm not —" He fumbled. "Lord. You make my head swim." "Then shut it." She bound the calf up loose with the drier end, tied with thatching twine because there was no tape. A thatcher's knot, flat so it wouldn't press. He looked at it. "Ugly," he said. "Holds," she said. She opened the casement finger-width to air the stink, though cold poured in. She emptied the chamber pot into the slop pail because no one else clearly had, holding her breath, hating him for needing it and hating herself for the heat in her face. Practical. Soap was godliness, Mrs. Peel always said. This wasn't godliness, this was leavings. He dozed while she worked. His good boot tapped twice against the bed frame in sleep, as if before standing. On the table a plate: bread untouched, mutton fat white. She cut it in half with her pocket knife and wrapped her half for Jem. She took three lumps of coal in the sack, no more, so the scuttle wouldn't look robbed. She took a spoon of sugar knotted in rag because Mother coughed less with sweet tea. She kept score that way — coals counted, sugar pinched and prayed over after. "Rounds," she whispered, shaking his shoulder because leaving him drugged with the window open was murder. "Listen. Ten o'clock footman locks and eats. Two o'clock bootboy pisses and rattles. You don't bang after. You hear?" "Mm." "And your door?" "Locked," he said, clearer, bitter waking up. "Hall side. Hatch for food. Like a — like a dog." She tested the nursery door without thinking. Locked fast. Keyhole cold. On the other side, nothing, then far off a board creaked where the back stair turned. The loose tread third from top — she'd known it carrying covers. She put her mouth close to his ear before she knew she would. "Mrs. Peel's deaf left," she breathed. "Keep to her right if she comes. Don't cough after ten." He stared at her, too close, unshaven, eyes yellowed. For a moment his hand came up as if to order and dropped. "You speak broad," he said. "You speak proud." Then on the servants' stair, unmistakable: soft shoes, keys chinked once and then silenced. Mrs. Peel listening, not announcing. Lizzie snuffed the lamp with wet fingers, burnt, silent, and was over the sill into black frost with the sack on her wrist and her mittened hand slipping on ivy before she found hold.
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 2)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter demonstrates considerable craft and discipline. The model has executed its plan with notable fidelity, delivering a scene that is physically grounded, emotionally complex, and stylistically consistent with the stated intentions. **Strengths:** The prose voice is tightly controlled and genuinely distinctive. Lizzie's interiority is rendered through work-verbs and counting, exactly as planned: "Nine pulls. Don't breathe loud." The lexicon stays true to her character — she thinks in farthings and coal lumps, not feelings. The line "She kept score that way — coals counted, sugar pinched and prayed over after" is a precise encapsulation of her psychology without stating it directly. The physical detail is excellent and earns its place. The wound description — "purple-white and puckered where the ball had gone through, the edges soft and weeping clear fluid that had dried to varnish" — is visceral without being gratuitous, and the smell detail ("sweet-sick") connects to the character profiles. The thatcher's knot is a beautiful piece of characterization through action: practical, ugly, holds. The dialogue is genuinely good. The exchange "You speak broad" / "You speak proud" is earned, compressed, and reveals both characters without exposition. The grammar correction scene ("I ain't — I'm not —") shows Edward's condescension and his self-awareness of it simultaneously, which is exactly the ambivalence the plan called for. The dialogue avoids Victorian pastiche while remaining period-plausible. The chapter follows its plan closely: the mitten pretext, the drugged Edward, the wound care, learning the rounds (10 and 2), the loose tread, Mrs. Peel's deaf side, and the escape at the sound of soft shoes. The plan's instruction that "care is erotic: washing a foot, splinting with thatching twine" is executed without sentimentality — she hates him for needing the chamber pot emptied even as she does it. The small thefts are handled with moral complexity: she takes coal, mutton fat, sugar, counts them, prays over them. The self-justification is present without being underlined. **Weaknesses:** The chapter is very strong but not quite masterpiece-level. A few observations: The opening mitten-pretext is slightly mechanical — the plan called for it, and it's executed, but the "that was what she told herself" move is a familiar device for signaling self-deception. It works, but it's not surprising. "Toast going down like he'd watched her swallow" is a slightly awkward construction — the simile doesn't quite land because it conflates the memory of being watched with the physical sensation. The Mrs. Peel exit is efficient but perhaps too neat — the soft shoes arriving at exactly the right moment to cut the scene is a conventional thriller beat. The plan acknowledged wanting to avoid "symmetrical cliffhangers," and this ending, while effective, does feel somewhat engineered. The line "hating him for needing it and hating herself for the heat in her face" is the one moment where the prose tells rather than shows — "the heat in her face" is doing work that the surrounding physical detail could have done more obliquely. Edward's characterization is consistent with his profile: the officer-clip even when drugged, the books lined by height, the tapping boot, the condescension about grammar. The detail of him pretending he didn't flinch is particularly good. The darkness is well-earned throughout — there's no sentimentality, no redemption arc being telegraphed. The intimacy of the wound care is genuinely uncomfortable in the right way. Overall this is accomplished, disciplined literary fiction that executes its plan with intelligence and restraint. The voice is consistent, the characters are rendered through action rather than description, and the period setting is worn lightly. Minor weaknesses prevent a top score but this is clearly strong work. It rained Sunday and froze Monday, which meant no thatch work and no pay and Uncle Tom saying come back when it lifts as if lifting put bread down. Jem's cough got loose and rattly. Mother folded pillow slips sitting up in bed to earn twopence and had to stop to cough into her apron. Lizzie made onion poultice in the bake pan and saved half the onion raw. That was for up there. She told herself it was waste and wrapped it anyway. She didn't go Sunday. The wind took slates off Walkington church and Mrs. Hartley said it was judgment. Lizzie stayed home and read her penny number by rushlight — *Varney the Vampire, No. 7*, thumbed grey — and counted pages to make it last. Jem breathed like wet bellows. Monday night the frost set iron-hard. Stars small as pinheads. Her knotted hem had come undone; she'd sewn it with big stitches that pulled. She put the onion and the *Varney* in her sack because the nights were long for him too, she supposed, though she hated supposing it. Up the coal-shed, up the gutter, up the ivy left of the spout. Her rag on her right hand froze to the lead and she had to breathe it loose. Snot ran and she wiped it on her cuff going up because there was no hand free. The nursery window was dark. She hung on the sill with her knees braced on brick, stupid with cold, staring at black glass. Last time the lamp had been high. Now nothing. She tried the transom. It lifted. She got the sash up and dropped in blind, heart knocking her stays — thimble pressing her rib where she'd sewn it deeper. "Lizzie?" His voice out of dark, thick. "That you?" The lamp flared as he fumbled it. He was in the chair, blanket round shoulders, hair flat. The candle on the sill behind him — the signal candle they'd never properly agreed — stood unlit, cold. "You said candle," she whispered, furious and relieved at once. "You said you'd leave it." "I forgot to — I put it there to remember and forgot to light it," he said. "I dosed at six. Slept." She wanted to hit him. She'd risked frostbite for forgetfulness. She sat down hard on the boards to get feeling back in her feet, unwinding sack with clumsy fingers. "Don't come if it's out," he said, officer-quick to cover. "That's the pact. No light, stay away." "We never made pact," she said. "You talked pact while drugged." He looked stung. Good. She unwrapped the onion. "For chest. Not for leg. You eat half raw, you sweat." "I don't eat raw onion." "You do tonight." She set to work because work stopped quarrel. The grate was near out; she coaxed it with sticks and two lumps of his coal, though each lump she burned was a lump she couldn't carry. She brewed tea from his caddy in his tin pot — strong enough to stand — and poured him half and herself half, though she meant to bring hers home for Mother and drank it standing because the steam hurt too good to save. He watched her over the cup. "You brought a book." She'd half-hoped he wouldn't see. She pulled out *Varney*. "For long nights." He took it with clean fingers, turned it, lip curled. "Vampire. Penny bloods. You read this filth?" "It's a good story," she said, hot. "He comes down chimneys." "Lord preserve us from vulgar horrors." "You line books by height," she said. "That's vulgar." That got a laugh out of him — short, surprised, real. It changed his face whole. For a second he was nineteen and laughing at Everingham dances, not twenty-five and locked in. She took his shirt from where it hung airing — cuff torn at elbow — and threaded her needle. She mended fast, counting stitches under her breath to keep even. *Six, seven, eight.* He watched her hands. "Village news," he said. "That's the tariff, isn't it? Poultice and gossip for tea?" "Tariff's half your supper for our Jem," she said. "You don't eat it." He pushed the plate over without argument: bread, cheese rind, cold bacon fat. She wrapped it. Four days bread now if Mother didn't pick. Rent Friday 3s 6d. Threepence put by. Numbers steadied her. "John's brought the Anstey carriage early," he said, trying casual and failing. "Footman says." "Miss Clara," Lizzie said, stitching. "Seen her at church. Sings. Folds gloves finger to finger." "You notice gloves." "I notice hems. Hers never muddy." His jaw worked. Tapped his good boot twice on the boards. "She wrote to me once. Ever yours. Then John's letters got to her first about fever in my head." Lizzie bit twine. She didn't want ever-yours. She tied off hard enough to pucker. Keys chinked out on the landing. Both froze. "Lamp!" she breathed. He cupped it out. Dark smelling of onion and tea. The nursery door handle tried, locked hall-side. A woman's breath. Then Mrs. Peel's voice, low, to someone below — the footman, Thomas. "Jackdaws on the sill again," she said clearly. "Mud. I'll have the boy clear it come day." Silence. Shoes going down. The loose tread creaked third from top. Lizzie let air out till she shook. He relit with trembling hands. Mud on the sill — her boot-mud — black in lamplight. She wiped it with her skirt, spit on it, wiped again. He held the lamp close enough their knuckles near touched. Neither moved away quick. Tuesday morning at the trades door, come to ask for plain sewing, she got no further than the scullery passage before Mrs. Peel turned her good ear full on and said, "I said jackdaws, lass." Lizzie's mouth dried. "Thank you." "Don't thank me." The old woman's keys hung silent; she'd muffled them on purpose. "Jackdaws don't bleed on sills. I saw your wrap. Mend that hem or cut it off. And hear me — I've a place to keep to my pension. Eighteen pound a year. I won't lose Hull for you twice." She put a bundle of mending in Lizzie's arms — not charity, piecework, twopence — and turned away. Coming home over the wold with twopence work and bacon fat in her pocket, Lizzie counted houses that would take a girl without character for scouring. None.

It was her courses come, and no rags clean. She'd washed the two she had Tuesday and hung them by the grate, and Jem in his fever knocked the horse and they fell in coal dust. She rinsed them again but the dust wouldn't lift, and wearing them chafed her thighs raw by evening. The blood came steady and mean. She folded an old sack edge inside her drawers and it bunched when she walked. Jem got worse Wednesday dusk. The croup came on with the sleet — barking cough, ribs sucking in, eyes scared. Mother sat up to rub goose fat on his chest and had to stop halfway to cough herself breathless into her apron, shoulders shaking. Lizzie took over, spooning hot water with sugar though sugar was near gone, counting spoonfuls to keep from crying. *Rent Friday 3s 6d. Threepence put by. Bread gone tomorrow.* No thatch work while snow lay, and now sleet instead of snow, which was worse — spars snapped, stacks ran water. Uncle Tom wouldn't call till it dried. The mending Mrs. Peel gave was finished: cuffs turned, twopence earned, twopence already in loaf. She told herself at dark she would not go. Wind rattled the casement cloth they'd nailed against draught. The cottage smelt of wet wool and onion and sick. She sat between the two beds mending Jem's shirt by rushlight, legs pressed tight against the flow, and listened to sleet tick the pane. Up at the Hall the nursery window would be lit or dark, and she would not know, and that was right. Let him forget his candle. Let him dose. She had no clean rag to climb in and no strength to be ordered about grammar. Mother dozed. Jem wheezed. Lizzie counted his breaths. *Fourteen, fifteen.* When she stopped counting she heard Mrs. Hartley's voice from Sunday class unbidden: *A night-visiting girl is fallen whether touched or not, for she has put herself where talk can take her.* She had put herself. She was fallen in the parish eye already if known. Chapel would cast her. She chewed twine till her tongue bled hemp. At ten she banked the fire and laid out water for the night. At eleven Jem slept easier, mouth open. Mother muttered in sleep. The sack-cloth between Lizzie's legs was soaked through. She changed it for torn shirt tail, hissing at the sting. Then she put on her boots. She told herself it was for coal. Half a scuttle left at home wouldn't last tomorrow with both of them sick. She told herself she would only take from the scuttle and not stay, not drink tea, not mend shirts for mockery. She put the sack under her shawl and went out into sleet. The walk was misery. Sleet drove sideways off the wold, needling her face, finding the gap where her hem was knotted. Her thighs stuck and burned. Twice she had to stop behind a wall to adjust the cloth, fingers numb so she could scarce pin it, blood on her wrist she wiped on snow. Fenwick rose black with two lit windows downstairs — John dining late. The north gable showed one small light high. Lamp lit. Candle behind it, she supposed. Lit for her or forgot to snuff. Last time he'd forgotten. She hated that she had hurried despite herself. She got up the coal-shed roof with sleet glazing the slates. Her boots slipped twice. The gutter ran icy water down her sleeve to the elbow. The rag on her right hand came sodden undone and she left it, skin bare to lead. Chilblains split fresh on the third grip and bled thin, pinked by sleet. *Nine pulls. Spout left holds.* She was halfway up the ivy when the flow gushed with the strain. She felt it hot down her leg. Shame flooded worse than blood. If she went in like that he'd smell it, see the stain on her petticoat in lamplight. If she stayed on the sill to arrange herself she'd freeze. The wind swung her boot against brick and ivy tore with a soft rip that sounded loud as prayer. She clung there, forehead to wet leaves, sleet running off her shawl into her neck, staring up at the lit transom six foot above. He was warm in there. Blanket, lamp, tea caddy full. Sugar lumps hoarded in a drawer though he took it unsweetened. Books lined by height. While she bled into sackcloth in sleet and her brother barked for air. Hate came clean and sudden. Not at John or Mrs. Peel, but at him for being waited on even locked, for tapping his good boot and expecting. For saying *you were counting* as if it were quaint. For needing her foot-washing and then mocking her *Varney*. She hung a full minute, arms trembling. The light didn't move. No face came to glass. She went down. Down was worse, blind with sleet in eyes, sack empty flapping. She dropped the last six foot from washhouse gutter to coal-shed and jarred her ankles so pain shot to teeth. She sat in coal dust till breath came, blood sticky, hands shaking. She stole turnips on the way home. Vicarage garden, clamp half open. She'd carried spars there last Michaelmas and knew the boards. She lifted two big swedes and three turnips into her sack with frozen fingers, earthed them clean as she could. Real theft. Not dripping pinched from plenty, but winter store from a man who tithed. She liked the weight of them. She hated liking it. At home Jem slept, Mother slept. She washed herself in cold water with her teeth clenched, rinsed the shirt tail and sack edge and hung them to drip over the basin, put the roots in the bake pan for morning. She counted them. *Five.* She counted the coal. *Not enough.* She lay down in wet shift and listened to sleet turn to rain. Morning came grey. She took Jem's posset up to Mrs. Hartley to beg more goose fat, and coming back over the lane by the lodge gates she saw it: Anstey carriage early, pair steaming, Miss Clara's trunk strapped behind, her maid holding boxes. Come to stay before Christmas, the lodge woman said, for the signing. Clara herself looked out once, fair and tired, gloves folded finger to finger. Lizzie stood with posset cooling in her hands, blood crusted, eyes gritty, too tired to feel anything but arithmetic. Fine lady come. Fine wedding talked. Rent Friday. Up on the north gable that night, if anyone had looked through sleet, the candle would have burned on untended till morning.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter is a remarkable piece of sustained craft. Let me work through it carefully. The chapter opens with brutal, unadorned specificity: "It was her courses come, and no rags clean." This is exactly the kind of detail the plan promised — the physical inconvenience of being a poor woman in 1861, rendered without sentimentality or apology. The coal-dust ruined rags, the sack-cloth substitute, the chafing — these are not decorative details but load-bearing ones that shape every subsequent decision in the chapter. The chapter's central structural achievement is the non-event: Lizzie climbs halfway, hangs in sleet, and comes back down. The plan called for a "deliberately static" chapter, and the model has executed this with genuine skill. The stasis is not boring — it is tense with the weight of what doesn't happen. The candle burning untended at the end is earned, not merely symbolic. The voice is consistently Lizzie's: work verbs, counting, King James cadences without being pastiche. "Blood came steady and mean" is excellent — the adjective "mean" doing double work (relentless, and also petty, as if the body itself is hostile). The internal arithmetic — "Rent Friday 3s 6d. Threepence put by. Bread gone tomorrow" — is deployed with discipline, not overused. The ivy-climb scene is the chapter's emotional core. The moment where the flow gushes with the strain of climbing is handled with exactly the right register: shame, practicality, and the sudden clarity of hate. "Hate came clean and sudden" — this is the chapter's best line, and it earns its plainness. The enumeration of Edward's comforts (blanket, lamp, tea caddy, sugar lumps hoarded despite claiming to take tea unsweetened) is devastating because it uses details established in the character profiles against him without authorial editorializing. The turnip theft is handled beautifully. "Real theft. Not dripping pinched from plenty, but winter store from a man who tithed. She liked the weight of them. She hated liking it." This is the plan's instruction to keep Lizzie morally complex — she enjoys stealing — executed with precision. The self-awareness without self-forgiveness is exactly right. Clara's arrival at the end is perfectly timed and tonally correct: "too tired to feel anything but arithmetic." The chapter refuses the easy emotional beat of jealousy or despair, giving us exhaustion instead, which is more honest and more affecting. The dialogue is almost entirely absent, which is appropriate for this chapter — it is a chapter of isolation and internal experience. The one piece of recalled dialogue (Mrs. Hartley's voice) is well-integrated. Minor criticisms: "Hate came clean and sudden" is excellent but "clean" is doing a lot of work that might be slightly too neat for the surrounding prose. The phrase "blood crusted, eyes gritty" at the end risks becoming a list of suffering that tips toward self-conscious grimness. The chapter is very consistent in its register, which is a strength, but there are moments where the relentlessness of the misery could benefit from a single beat of something else — not relief, but texture. The plan called for Lizzie to "sit in ivy in sleet staring at lit window, hates him for being warm, climbs down" and "steals turnips from vicarage garden instead — real theft for real need" and "sees Clara's carriage arrive early in daylight next morning and is too tired to care" and "candle burns all night for nothing." All of these are executed faithfully and with skill. The plan's instruction about "monthlies with no rags" is the chapter's organizing principle, handled with more specificity and dignity than most writers would manage. The chapter is not amateurish at any point. The metaphors are restrained and earned. There is no purple prose. The darkness is well-earned through accumulated physical and economic detail rather than imposed atmospherics. Thursday she went in daylight to carry back the mending, because Mrs. Peel paid twopence only on return and twopence was bread. She washed her hands first in cold water till the knuckles shone pink and cracked, and bound the right one fresh. She brushed her shawl and pinned her hem up where the stitches pulled, so the tear didn't show. She left the thimble in her stays. It rode against her rib with every breath and she was so used to it now she checked for it the way she checked for her tongue. At the trades door the new girl, Ellen, let her stand in wind a good five minutes before fetching anyone. Through the open scullery she could see cook at the long table with the house linen book open, lips moving. Sheets in piles. “Fourteen pair wanting tapes,” cook said to no one. “And nursery towels short two. Mark me, someone’s using up there.” Lizzie kept her eyes on her boots. Ellen came back giggling with the under-housemaid, Mary, seventeen and sharp as vinegar. “You’re the thatcher’s lass,” Mary said. “You was up our gable clearing jackdaws?” Mrs. Peel’s lie, come back with feathers on. “Aye,” Lizzie said. “There’s mud on the nursery sill again this morning,” Mary said. “Black mud. Jackdaws wear boots now?” Cook didn’t look up. “Hush your mouth and fold.” Mrs. Peel came then, keys chinking on purpose, and took the bundle from Lizzie without a word and counted cuffs. Her good ear turned full. “Wait,” she said, and left Lizzie standing in the passage with the smell of roast and lye stinging her nose. The front of the house sounded through, wrongly close — a gentleman’s boots on polished boards, a lady’s skirts. Then John Fenwick’s voice, solicitor-slow. “The south bedchamber wants papering, but the dressing room is sound. You would have morning sun, Clara.” They came into the back hall to look at the stair. Lizzie pressed to the wall with her sack, trying to make herself servant-invisible. She’d seen John at church, square and pomaded. Up close his waistcoat strained and his spectacles flashed when he polished them on his handkerchief before speaking again. Miss Clara Anstey stood with gloves folded finger to finger, fair hair plain under a winter bonnet, cheeks pink from the drive. She smelt of orris root and cold air. Her hem was clean to the binding. One chilblain on her left hand she tried to hide by tucking fingers. Lizzie saw it and hated seeing it, because it made her human. “Oh — this stair is very dark,” Clara said prettily. “The servants’ stair,” John said. “You need not use it.” His eyes slid over Lizzie as if she were a mop left out. Clara’s eyes stopped. “Poor thing,” she said, and meant it for exactly the minute it took to say. “That cuff turning is very neat. You sew beautifully.” Lizzie curtsied and said nothing. What was there to say to clean hems? Mrs. Peel returned, counted out twopence, and jerked her head to go. “And don’t loiter,” she said loud enough for Mary to hear. At the door, low, without moving her mouth: “They talk Christmas Eve for signing. Solicitor comes. Keep away.” Rent tomorrow 3s 6d. Threepence put by and twopence earned made fivepence. Short by three shillings and a penny. Numbers walked home with her beside Jem’s cough. She went that night. She told herself it was to warn him — signing moved up, linen counted, Mary watching sills. She told herself that all the way up the gutter with the rag frozen off and left behind. The ivy left of the spout tore under her boot and showered dead leaves. She went up blood-loud, careless with tiredness, and dropped in over the sill hard on her ankles. He was awake, unshaven three days, lamp high. The candle on the sill stood lit. She stared at it. “You remembered,” she said stupidly. “I remembered,” he said. “Come here. Shut it.” She shut the casement and drew the blind crooked. He was already talking, fast, officer-clip covering shake. “John keeps my letters. Mine to Clara, hers to me. In his study desk, left drawer. If I had them I could show Ashworth my head was clear. I wrote sensibly. You could get in by the landing window off the lead over the back passage — you know roofs. You could lift them.” The room went small. “I ain’t your lass to send,” she said. The words came out flat, the ones she’d thought weeks ago and not said. He flushed. “I ask because you can. Because you — go where others can’t.” “Because I steal.” “Because you’re brave,” he said, and tried a smile that didn’t work. His good boot tapped twice. “Please.” She hated the please more than the order. She hated that half his supper was already pushed toward her side of the table, tariff, and that she needed it. Jem barking at home. Mother picking at bread. *Three shillings a penny short. Five roots left. Coal quarter scuttle.* “Show me which window,” she said. He drew it on copybook with shaking ink — back passage lead, two steps across to landing casement, catch loose like nursery. She memorised and hated memorising. The lead was slick with frost. She went in petticoat and stockings, boots tied to wrist, to keep quiet. The landing window gave with a suck. Inside, the house breathed strange in dark — beeswax and smoke and sleep. Far below a clock ticked. The study smelt of paper and pomade. Moon through shutters laid bars on John’s desk. Pocket-book open: *Ashworth 3 gns. Coal up.* Left drawer locked. She jimmied with her knife till her cracked skin split fresh and spotted blood on the wood she wiped with spit. Inside, bundles tied with tape — bills, leases. And letters in Clara’s round hand. *Ever yours.* She took three and put them inside her shift where the thimble was, paper cold on belly. On the desk beside them, left out from showing the house: a jet brooch in a velvet case, Clara’s, come off for trying a dress. Black as coal, heavy as sin. Worth rent for a month. Her fingers closed on it before weighing. She stood with it hot in her palm, thinking of Hull pawn, thinking of God marking difference, thinking of nothing but weight. She put it back. She wasn’t sure why, and the not-sure shamed her worse than taking. Back on the lead her foot slipped and slates grit scuttered. Below, in the nursery, the blind showed lamplight — and on it, huge and wavering, her own silhouette dropping past with sack swinging. She froze on ivy. In the yard, Mary with a pail stopped, stared up, mouth open. Lizzie didn’t breathe till Mary shook herself and went in, too scared to shout. In the nursery Edward snatched the letters, hands shaking, eyes wet. “Good girl. Good lass. Read me —” “Someone saw,” she said. His face changed. “Who?” “Mary.” He sat down hard, crutch clattering. The sugar lumps in his drawer rattled. “Then we — we must be careful. You must not come for —” “For how long?” “Till it blows over.” She laughed short. There was blood on her cuff from the desk and turnip earth still under nails. She’d risked the drop for ever-yours and he was already hiding. Mrs. Peel came at two on rounds and found the lamp lit and the blind crooked. She didn’t knock. She spoke through the locked hall door, clear enough for both to hear. “Lass. I heard pails. Don’t use me. I won’t lie twice.”

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter is a remarkably accomplished piece of Victorian-inflected prose fiction. Let me work through its qualities systematically. **Voice and Style** The close third-person locked to Lizzie is maintained with discipline throughout. The lexicon is exactly as planned: work verbs, counting, physical sensation, King James cadences without parody. The internal arithmetic ("Threepence put by and twopence earned made fivepence. Short by three shillings and a penny") is deployed with the right frequency: it grounds the stakes without becoming mechanical. **Character Consistency** Lizzie is precisely as drawn in the profiles: calculating, self-deceiving, keeping score. The jet brooch scene is the chapter's moral center — she puts it back but doesn't know why, and the not-knowing shames her more than taking would have. This is exactly the kind of self-knowledge-without-self-knowledge the plan called for. Edward's "please" being worse than an order, the sugar lumps rattling, his immediate retreat to "till it blows over" — all consistent with the profile's "learned helplessness dressed as honour." Mrs. Peel's final line through the door is perfect: she doesn't enter, doesn't confront, just withdraws her protection with surgical precision. Clara's "poor thing" lasting exactly a minute is handled with economy and without contempt. **Dialogue** The dialogue is genuinely strong. "I ain't your lass to send" lands with the weight of weeks of withheld speech. Edward's "Because you're brave" followed by the smile that doesn't work is exactly the kind of inadequate gallantry the character would attempt. Mrs. Peel's "Jackdaws don't bleed on sills" (from the plan, appearing here as Mary's "Jackdaws wear boots now?") is redistributed cleverly — Mary gets the sharper version, which makes her more dangerous. The dialogue is spare, functional, and character-revealing without being expository. **Plot Execution** The chapter follows its plan closely: daylight visit, forensic detail (linen count, sill mud), Edward's request for letters, the dangerous retrieval, the brooch temptation resisted, the silhouette seen, Mary's witnessing, Mrs. Peel's withdrawal. The plan's note about "she feels used and does it badly, tempted by Clara's jet brooch left out" is executed with more moral complexity than the plan suggested — she resists, but the resistance is itself ambiguous. The silhouette on the blind is a genuinely tense moment handled without melodrama. **Weaknesses** A few minor issues: "blood-loud" is a slightly strained compound adjective — it reaches for something but doesn't quite land. "The room went small" is effective but borders on the kind of compressed metaphor that can feel like a tic if overused. The transition "She went that night" after the arithmetic is slightly abrupt — the plan called for more interiority about the decision, but the chapter's compression actually serves it. The phrase "hot in her palm" for the brooch is a small cliché in an otherwise cliché-free chapter. The chapter's pacing is excellent — the daylight section has a different texture from the night section, and the shift is managed without announcement. The forensic detail (cook's linen book, Mary's sharpness) does exactly what the plan intended: danger from women watching, not from villains. **Poetic Riffing** The metaphors are earned and grounded. "She left the thimble in her stays. It rode against her rib with every breath and she was so used to it now she checked for it the way she checked for her tongue" — this is precise and psychologically true, not decorative. The writing does not reach for impressiveness; it earns its effects through specificity. **Overall** This is a chapter that executes its plan with intelligence and restraint, maintains voice discipline, advances plot through character rather than event, and handles moral ambiguity without editorializing. It is not quite a masterpiece — a few small infelicities, and the chapter's middle section (the letter retrieval) is slightly less vivid than the opening and closing — but it is genuinely excellent work. Friday the rent man knocked before light. Cartwright with his book and his pencil stub, boots muddy on the step. 3s 6d. Lizzie laid out fivepence in coppers, the twopence mending and threepence put by, and Mother's folded-work penny she had not meant to spend, and Jem's face watching from the bed. "Short," Cartwright said. He didn't unkind it. That was worse. "Monday," Lizzie said. "Thaw comes, thatch work comes." "Monday three and eleven with the fine," he said, and marked it. "No Monday, bailiff." When he was gone Mother coughed till her apron spotted and tried to fold it out of sight. Jem barked and barked, ribs sucking. The snow started at noon — first proper snow, small hard grains that hissed on the pane and then thickened to feathers. No thatcher worked while it lay. Three days snow was no work was no rent was bailiff. She counted it till her teeth ached. She meant to stay in Friday night. Jem needed steam and sugar water. The coal was quarter scuttle. The roots were two swedes left. She spooned and nursed and changed Jem's sheet where he'd wet it hiding it, and washed it in cold because there was no coal to heat, her hands going white to the wrist. At ten Jem slept easier. Mother dozed. The cottage ticked. Lizzie put on her boots. She told herself letters. Edward had the ever-yours now, but no sense in them unless she heard what Ashworth said. She told herself coal. She told herself she would only look at the window from the ash tree and come home if dark. The walk was blind. Snow drove and settled. By the park wall her knotted hem was sodden and heavy as a calf. Her courses had stopped at last, leaving her raw and sore. Up the coal-shed she went on hands and knees, slates iced. The gutter was iron. Her rag was lost Tuesday and she had no other; bare skin stuck and tore free. On the third grip her left chilblain split and blood came thin and quick, smeared pink on lead. Her right palm slipped and the edge took skin off the heel. *Nine pulls. Don't cry. Count.* Halfway up the ivy the snow got in her eyes. Her petticoat, sewn big-stitch, caught on brick and ripped to the knee with a sound she felt up her spine. Cold bit her bare leg. Blood from her palms greased the stems. She clung with forehead to leaves, snow melting down her neck, and knew she stank of blood and sweat and would leave it on the sill. She went down. It took longer than up. She dropped to the coal-shed roof and sat in snow till her breath came, palms throbbing, leg bare. She bound hands in her shawl ends and walked home with snow in her boots. Saturday she went to the Hall to beg scouring work, hands wrapped in rags. She got no further than the scullery passage, but passage hears all. Mary with a pail, loud to Ellen: "Ribbon in the nursery grate, burned at ends. Red tape, not ours. And this—" She held up, finger and thumb like dirt, *Varney the Vampire No. 7*, grey-thumbed. "Under his mattress. Master found it when he took his broth." Lizzie's belly dropped. She'd left it Monday in the dark when Mrs. Peel spoke. She'd never missed it for counting Jem's breaths. Cook weighed in, kneading: "Towels short two still. And blood on the nursery sill this morning, fresh as paint. Jackdaws don't bleed, Mary says." "Mr Edward talks to walls now," Mary went on, eyes shining. "Master heard him through the hatch. 'Good lass,' he says, 'good lass, read me.' No one there." Ellen crossed herself. "Fever." Lizzie pressed her bound hands to her skirt to hide the blood showing through. The sill blood was hers from last night. The ribbon was hers — hair tape lost Monday she hadn't marked. The book was hers, though she'd not wrote her name, thank God, thank God, but Mary had seen her reading at the pump in summer and would remember. Mrs. Peel came through with keys silent. She saw Lizzie and her mouth went thin. "Scouring's taken," she said flat. Then, as Mary turned to the sink, low and quick: "Come to the woodhouse." In the woodhouse, dark smelling of chips, Mrs. Peel turned her deaf ear away and her good ear close, which was ruder than shouting. "They've got your leavings," she said. "Ribbon, book, blood. John thinks his talk proves head gone. He rambles nights now you don't come — doses and wakes and calls for you. That's in Ashworth's ear next week." "I nursed Jem," Lizzie whispered. "I never meant book—" "I know what you meant." The old woman's face was gaunt in slat light. "Hannah meant. Lass, I warned once. I will not lie twice. If you're caught on that ivy I'll say I never saw you, and God forgive me." "I've rent Monday—" "Then go to Hull." Keys chinked once, unmuffled on purpose now. "My sister wants a girl to turn mangle. No character asked if I send you. Go before bailiff." Lizzie stared. "And him?" "Him's locked and dosed and talking to walls. He'll be York by New Year. Forget him." She put no work in Lizzie's arms. That was the answer. Lizzie walked home in snow with nothing. That night from the lane she looked back without meaning to. High on the north gable the nursery light burned, small and steady. Candle behind it. Sunday night, Jem easier, Mother worse, coal gone to dust, Lizzie stood at the cottage door in wind and looked again. The light burned still. Not signal. Forgetfulness. He'd lit it Friday and Saturday and left it to gutter because no one came to snuff it. She knew the waste of it — candle tallow at a farthing inch — and hated him for burning while they froze, and hated herself for counting his candle while Jem coughed. She did not go.

This is excellent — no word wasted, the power dynamic entirely clear. Mrs. Peel's woodhouse speech is the chapter's most extended dialogue and it works: "Hannah meant. Lass, I warned once. I will not lie twice." The rhythm is right, the compression is right. **Emotional Engagement** The chapter's emotional architecture is sophisticated. "The cottage ticked" — three words that do the work of a paragraph. These land. There's no riffing for its own sake. **Overall** This is accomplished literary fiction. It follows its plan faithfully, maintains its voice without lapse, renders its characters with consistency and complexity, and achieves genuine emotional weight through restraint rather than amplification. Blizzard came Monday night on top of snow, which meant no Monday payment and no Tuesday thatching and Cartwright writing *bailiff* in his book without looking up. Jem coughed till he cried. Mother gave her folded-work penny and her wedding shawl to pawn, and the pawn shop shut early for storm. Lizzie put the shawl back round Mother and counted coal dust. *Nothing. Nothing. Two swedes.* At dark Jem said, unasked, “I’ll watch.” She should have said no. He was ten and loose-chested and his coat sagged with old coal. But she needed feet on ground because snow blinded and wind took sound. She gave him her spare stockings for hands and told him stand by the ash and hoot like owl if lantern showed. “You never said blizzard,” he muttered, pulling cap down, crow feather snapped wet. They walked apart to the Hall so no one marked them together. Wind drove snow sideways off the wold in sheets. By the park wall Lizzie could not see the gable, only hear it. Jem’s teeth chattered loud enough to carry. “Stay till church bell?” he said. “Then I’m coming in.” “Till I’m down,” she said. “You promised.” She left him under the ash with snow to his ankles. Up was murder. The coal-shed slates iced over old ice. She went on belly, sack tied inside her shift so wind wouldn’t take it, boots slung to wrist. The washhouse gutter ran snowmelt down her neck. Bare hands — no rag left — stuck to lead and tore free, stuck and tore free till both palms wept. The blood froze and cracked again. Ivy was iron with ice. Left of the spout held, but stems snapped under boot. She got snow in her mouth, in her eyes, up her sleeves where hem had ripped to knee Saturday. The flow had stopped days back, leaving her sore, but strain brought a fresh show she felt hot and then cold down thigh. Shame and wind together. *Seven. Eight. Nine. Don’t think his leg. Think weight.* The transom was shut. For a sick moment she thought he’d latched it at last, shut her out proper. Then it lifted, iced, screaming faint. Snow poured in after her as she shouldered the sash. She dropped inside half-frozen, sack thudding, and lay on boards panting with snow melting in her hair. Lamp low. Grate near out. He was on the bed in shirt and drawers, blanket anyhow, eyes glassy. Tumbler on floor. Dosed at six again. “Lizzie?” Thick. “Good lass. Read me.” She got up and shut the casement and stuffed her shawl to the draught. Her fingers wouldn’t work. She breathed on them till pain came back. “Blow it,” she whispered. “You’ll burn tallow all night again.” The candle stood guttered, inch gone to nothing. Two nights waste she’d counted from the lane. She snuffed the stub to save it. She shook his shoulder hard. “Listen. Solicitor tomorrow. Signing.” He blinked. “Letters.” She pulled them from her shift where she’d kept them against skin beside the thimble — three, creased, damp at edges. *Ever yours* in Clara’s round hand, 1855. A hospital note in his own shaking pencil: *Dearest C — fever gone, leg mend slow, think of Everingham.* And John’s covering note to Ashworth, found folded in drawer: *My brother fancies persecution, keeps to nursery by choice, £3 3s for opinion at your convenience.* She spread them on blanket. They amounted to nothing. Girl’s promise at nineteen, sick man’s scrawl, brother’s careful bill. No forgery. No theft. Just careful words that let a man borrow more. “This won’t stop paper,” she said. “This is air.” He stared, tapping good boot twice, twice again. “She wrote ever. She—” “Aye. She was nineteen.” Snow hissed on glass. Her wet petticoat steamed by the dying grate. She fed it his last two sticks though she meant to carry coal. “Mary saw me. Mrs. Peel won’t lie twice. They’ve your ribbon and my book. They think you talk to walls.” “You don’t come,” he said, childish and accusing. “Jem sick. Snow. You don’t—” “I climbed blizzard!” Heat ripped up. “My hands bleed on your sill and you dose and forget candle! I stole turnips! I’m bailiff Wednesday!” He flushed, officer-clip surfacing through drug. “Don’t shout at me in my own—” “Your own locked nursery?” That shut him. He looked at his leg where dressing leaked fresh, sweet-sick in shut air, and at her torn hem showing bare knee, snow in boots pooling. He reached, not ordering, and pulled blanket round her shoulders. His hand shook. Under blanket his shirt was damp with sweat. “Stay till wind drops,” he muttered. “Please.” She hated the please that worked. She sat on bed edge because boards were ice, blanket over both, listening to blizzard find every gap. He dozed against her shoulder, heavy, laudanum breath bitter. She counted his breaths to keep awake. *Fourteen. Fifteen.* Jem below in snow. Church bell never rang for wind. She woke to grey and silence and cold foot on ankle where blanket slipped. Below, in the yard, no wind. Snow piled to sill. On the ash, no Jem. Only a crow feather stuck upright in drift where he’d stood. He’d left early. Ten years old and freezing, who could blame him but her. She moved to go, limbs stiff. Too late. Keys. Hall side. The nursery door, locked three weeks, turning. Mrs. Peel with broth, keys unmuffled now, and behind her Ellen with kindling basket. They stopped. Lizzie by the bed, hair down with snowmelt, petticoat ripped to knee, shawl stuffed in window, letters spread on blanket. Edward in shirt, bad leg bare, her sack open with bread crumbs. Open transom letting snow breathe in. Indisputable. Ellen screamed, kindling spilling. “Jesus—” Edward jerked upright, barking, panicked, imperious at once. “Get out! Mrs. Peel! Send them out!” Mrs. Peel did not lie. She did not scream. She put the broth down outside the door, pulled Ellen back by wrist, and turned the key from the hall side, locking them in together till master woke. “Stay there,” she said through wood. “Lord keep me from seeing.”
+ Judge Evaluation (Chapter 7)
Judge Response:
[Analysis] This chapter is a remarkably accomplished piece of Victorian-inflected prose fiction. Let me work through its qualities systematically. **Craft and Voice** The close-third locked to Lizzie is maintained with discipline throughout. Her lexicon is exactly as planned: work verbs, counting, physical sensation, King James cadences without parody. "Blow it" and "This is air" feel genuinely period without being costume. The internal arithmetic — "Nothing. Nothing. Two swedes." — is devastating in its compression. The voice never slips into modern idiom or authorial intrusion. **Character Consistency** Lizzie is calculating-hungry, not sweet-hungry, exactly as profiled. She climbs in a blizzard not from love but from desperation (bailiff Wednesday), and her fury at Edward is earned and specific: "I climbed blizzard! My hands bleed on your sill and you dose and forget candle!" This is the resentment-care ambivalence the plan demanded. Edward's response — officer-clip surfacing through drug, then the childish "please" — is precisely his profile: learned helplessness dressed as honour, the apology that comes as gesture rather than words (pulling blanket). Mrs. Peel's "Lord keep me from seeing" is perfect: she opens the door, witnesses, locks them in, and refuses to lie — exactly the "help once and then stop" trajectory. Jem leaving early because he's cold and ten is heartbreaking and true. **Plot Execution** The chapter follows its plan closely: blizzard, Jem as unreliable lookout who leaves early, useless letters (the plan specified "proof amounts to nothing"), discovery at dawn by under-housemaid (Ellen with kindling), Mrs. Peel locking them in rather than lying. The plan called for Edward to be "imperious and panicked" — "Get out! Mrs. Peel! Send them out!" delivers this exactly. The chapter earns its darkness without melodrama. **Specific Strengths** The letters are handled brilliantly. "They amounted to nothing. Girl's promise at nineteen, sick man's scrawl, brother's careful bill. No forgery. No theft. Just careful words that let a man borrow more." This is the plan's "proof amounts to nothing" rendered with precision and without authorial editorializing. The physical detail of the climb — blood freezing and cracking, snow in mouth and eyes, the menstrual detail handled with matter-of-fact shame — is exactly the inconvenient physicality the plan demanded. The crow feather stuck upright in drift where Jem stood is a genuinely moving image that earns its weight. The "indisputable" paragraph — the forensic inventory of what Mrs. Peel sees — is excellent. It doesn't editorialize; it lists, and the list condemns. **Dialogue** The dialogue is spare and functional. "Your own locked nursery?" is a perfect line — it says everything about power and imprisonment without stating it. The exchange about the letters ("This won't stop paper. This is air.") is economical and true. Edward's "You don't come" being "childish and accusing" is shown, not told, through the syntax itself. **Weaknesses** A few minor issues. "Heat ripped up" is slightly vague as a physical description — heat of anger, presumably, but the verb is imprecise. "Sweet-sick in shut air" is used again (it appears in earlier chapters per the plan), which is intentional repetition but risks feeling like a tic by chapter seven. The counting of breaths ("Fourteen. Fifteen.") is effective but the technique has presumably been used before; whether it still lands depends on the full manuscript context. The transition from her waking to the discovery is slightly rushed — "She moved to go, limbs stiff. Too late." — though the abruptness may be intentional, mimicking her shock. **Tonal Achievement** The chapter achieves what the plan demanded: no bow, no miracle, no assembled witnesses. The win is negative — they are locked in together, exposed, ruined, and Mrs. Peel's final line is both mercy and abandonment. "Lord keep me from seeing" is the chapter's best line: it acknowledges what she has seen, refuses to unsee it, and removes herself from complicity simultaneously. This is the kind of moral complexity that distinguishes serious fiction. The darkness is well-earned throughout. Nothing is sentimentalized. The blizzard is not romantic; it is murderous and inconvenient. The letters are not dramatic; they are pathetic. The discovery is not operatic; it is domestic and indisputable. They stayed locked till full light. Lizzie pissed in the chamber pot behind the chair with Edward turned to the wall and both pretending deaf. Shame sat hotter than sin. Her petticoat had frozen stiff where snowmelt dried, ripped to the knee, shift showing. She combed her hair with fingers and tied it with the burnt-ended ribbon Mary had found the pattern of, because there was nothing else to tie it with. It was hers. Let them match it. Edward dressed himself standing, jaw clenched, crutch under arm. He could not bend to his bad leg and would not ask. The dressing leaked through. He put his coat over shirt, no waistcoat, and lined his three books by height with shaking hands though one kept slipping. “Don’t cry,” he said, officer-clip. “I ain’t crying,” she said. She was crying with cold, nose running. She wiped it on cuff and left it, because Clara would have dabbed, and she was not Clara. Keys. Boots. Men’s voices hall side. John opened it himself. Spectacles already polished. Behind him Mr. Robson the York solicitor, snow to his knees, bag wet, mouth thin with a night at Beverley instead of Fenwick because drifts stopped the gig. Behind him Mrs. Peel with keys silent, Ellen white, Thomas footman trying not to look at Lizzie’s knee. Silence smelled of broth gone cold and sweet-sick leg and snow air off Lizzie. John looked once at the bed, the letters spread, the shawl stuffed in casement, Lizzie’s sack open with crumbs. “Cover yourself, girl,” he said. Lizzie pulled Mother’s shawl round, though it was the window plug, damp. Edward stepped forward on crutch, dragging left foot. Tapped good boot twice. “This is Miss Tranter,” he said. “She has nursed me when your hatch left me to piss in pink water. If you make talk of her, make it of me first.” His voice shook on *first*. Brave and useless together. Lizzie loved him for it and hated him for needing to say it after. Robson sighed, a bored London-York sigh, and set bag down out of wet. “Mr. Fenwick, the paper was for quiet certification. This—” He glanced at Lizzie, at leg. “This is not quiet. Is the young woman with child?” “No!” Lizzie said, too loud. Mrs. Peel closed eyes briefly. “Then,” Robson said, “there is no possession to settle but gossip. Gossip is parish, not law.” He turned to John. “You have no second medical opinion. Dr. Ashworth’s note is—” He picked John’s covering note off blanket with two fingers. “—a bill for three guineas. Not evidence. Get a London man when roads clear, if you must spend it. I will not witness restraint on this.” John’s jaw worked. He wrote nothing in pocket-book. That told more than shouting. Clara came then, fetched because Ellen talked. She stopped in doorway in winter dress, maid behind, gloves folded finger to finger. She looked at Lizzie’s bare knee, at Edward’s bare foot, at the letters in her own round nineteen-year-old hand on the blanket. She picked one up. *Ever yours.* She read it and wept, one hand to mouth, pretty even crying. “Oh — Edward. Poor — poor thing.” Lizzie waited for miracle. There was none. Clara folded the letter back exact and laid it down. She took off her own wool shawl — good grey, orris-smelling — and put it round Lizzie because Lizzie shook. Pity true for a minute. “I am sorry,” Clara whispered. “Truly. I hope you go on well.” Then to John, soft: “Shall we — the signing Thursday, if roads — ? My father—” “Yes,” John said. He did not unkind it. Relief made him almost human. “Thursday.” Security beat first love. Lizzie felt the shawl’s warmth and understood arithmetic better than ever-yours. Eight hundred pound cleared interest to Lady Day. A mangle girl cleared nothing. John counted out five shillings from purse, laid them on table by the sugar lumps Edward hoarded. “For your trouble, girl. Leave the parish. No talk then.” It was generous and it was buying. Rent 3s 6d plus fine 3s 11d was 7s 5d owed. Five shillings did not cover it. It covered going. Edward said, “John—” and stopped, because what else was there? Marry her himself that morning? He was locked, lame, dosed, penniless but name. Honour without house was air. Mrs. Peel spoke at last, good ear turned. “My sister in Hull wants a girl to turn mangle. No character asked if I send her. Leaves tomorrow carrier.” Hull. Mangle steam, lodgings, Hannah’s town where Hannah died. Lizzie’s throat closed. Jem coughing, Mother coughing, bailiff Wednesday. Mangle wages 7s week, minus lodging. Numbers steadied her when nothing else did. “Aye,” she said. “Send me.” She changed behind chair into her dry shift from sack while men turned backs, though backs did not mean blind. She kept thimble in stays. Silver against rib. Undammed and kept. God marked difference. She marked keeping. John let Edward walk her to the lodge. Not the drive. The lodge, before witnesses — Thomas and Mrs. Peel ten paces behind, snow squeaking. Daylight, grey noon, fields white to wold. Edward on crutches, coat buttoned wrong, unshaven, leg dragging furrow in snow. Lizzie in borrowed grey shawl over torn hem cut off short with Mrs. Peel’s scissors because mending was past it. Bare ankles burning. At the gate he stopped because he could not go further without falling. He tried lightness and failed. “You make a better orderly — ” he started, old joke. “Don’t,” she said. He nodded. Tapped crutch twice in snow. “Write. Care of Peel. I’ll — when London man comes, when — ” “Aye,” she said, to stop him drowning. “Count ceiling cracks.” She did not kiss him. Mrs. Hartley was right about talk taking. They had been locked together; parish would bury her chaste or not. A kiss would have been waste. Jem waited by lodge wall, white to eyelashes, crow feather gone. He’d come back at dawn, he said in a rush, he’d only gone to piss, he’d watched ages. Lizzie cuffed his ear lightly and pulled him to her side so hard his teeth clicked. He smelled of coal smoke and cold. She went with carrier next morning, five shillings sewn inside stays beside thimble. Mother cried and folded. Mrs. Peel pressed Hannah’s button-boot into sack though it fit neither of them. “Soap,” she said roughly. “Godliness.” Snow held. No thatch work. Bailiff took the turnips pan for part payment. Nights after, the under-housemaid told Ellen the nursery transom would not shut right for ice in the catch. It stood finger-width open all January, breathing chalky air, lamplight showing some nights late where no light should be.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a remarkable piece of writing that largely delivers on its ambitious plan. Let me work through it carefully. **Craft and Voice** The close-third locked to Lizzie is maintained with discipline throughout. The voice is genuinely distinctive: work verbs, King James cadences, arithmetic as emotional anchor. "Numbers steadied her when nothing else did" is earned, not stated as theme. The counting of money — 3s 6d rent, 7s 5d owed, five shillings covering going but not debt — functions exactly as the plan intended: winter as clock, economics as fate. This is not decorative; it does structural work. The physical detail is consistently grounded: frozen petticoat, bare ankles burning, Jem smelling of coal smoke, the sweet-sick leg, the three books lined by height with shaking hands. These are not atmospheric flourishes but character revelation. Edward lining his books while the room fills with witnesses is one of the chapter's finest moments — compulsive order as the only dignity left to him. **Dialogue** The dialogue is largely excellent. "Don't cry" / "I ain't crying" is perfectly calibrated — his officer-clip, her refusal to perform the expected femininity, both true to profile. Edward's speech at the door ("She has nursed me when your hatch left me to piss in pink water") is brave and useless together, which is exactly the right register. The "Don't" that cuts off his old joke at the lodge gate is devastating in its economy. Clara's "I hope you go on well" lands with the precise weight of pity that costs nothing. Robson's bored solicitor voice ("Gossip is parish, not law") is pitch-perfect — the law staying offstage and inconclusive, as planned. The one slightly weaker moment: "Count ceiling cracks" as Lizzie's farewell. It's a callback to Edward's internal voice from the character profiles, and it works emotionally, but it risks feeling slightly too neat — a coded intimacy that's almost too legible. It's a minor quibble against an otherwise restrained ending. **Plot Execution** The chapter follows its plan faithfully and improves on it in places. The solicitor's dismissal of the certification attempt is handled with admirable economy — no melodrama, just a bored professional declining to be involved in something messy. Clara's arc (reads letter, weeps, gives shawl, agrees to Thursday signing) is compressed but not rushed; the arithmetic of her choice is made clear without being stated. Mrs. Peel's button-boot pressed into the sack is a beautiful detail that pays off her character without sentimentality. The ending — the transom standing finger-width open all January — is exactly right. It refuses closure while suggesting continuity, and it earns the prompt's central image without epigraphing it. The art learned is still needed, not laid aside. **What Doesn't Fully Land** "Honour without house was air" is the chapter's one moment of purple-adjacent abstraction. It's not terrible — it's true to the situation — but it's slightly more aphoristic than the rest of the prose, which earns its observations through accumulation rather than compression. "Undammed and kept" is a strange phrase. "Undamned" seems intended (the thimble kept, God marking difference, she marking keeping) but "undammed" reads as a typo or error that muddles the moment. This is a genuine flaw in an otherwise clean manuscript. The Jem scene at the lodge wall is slightly rushed — his return and Lizzie's response are handled quickly, and while the cuff and pull are right, the emotional weight of his presence (he left her, she forgives him, he smells of home) could have breathed a little more. **Consistency with Plan and Profiles** The chapter is remarkably faithful to its plan. No assembled witnesses, no reformed rival, no front-drive parade. The win is very small: he owns it aloud, she leaves with work fifty miles away, they have not kissed, the broken transom stays broken. Every character behaves consistently with their profile: John's relief making him "almost human," Clara's practical grief, Mrs. Peel's Hannah's boot, Edward's shaking hands and tapped crutch. Lizzie keeps the thimble. God marks difference; she marks keeping. **Overall** This is accomplished literary fiction that earns its darkness, maintains its voice, and refuses the consolations it has promised to refuse. The flaws are minor: one muddy word, one slightly too-neat callback, one rushed sibling moment. The strengths are substantial: economic precision as emotional language, dialogue that reveals character without explaining it, an ending that is genuinely unresolved without being evasive. [Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of Victorian-era fiction that demonstrates genuine mastery of period voice, economic detail, and character interiority. Let me assess it across the requested dimensions. VOICE AND STYLE: The prose voice is one of the piece's greatest strengths. The author has constructed a distinctive, clipped, arithmetic-obsessed interiority for Lizzie that feels entirely organic rather than imposed. "Fourpence loaf. Three days if Mother didn't pick at it." The counting motif — numbers as emotional regulation, as survival mechanism, as the only reliable truth in a world of uncertainty — is introduced early and sustained with remarkable consistency throughout all eight chapters. This is not a tic but a fully realized psychological portrait. The voice never slips into anachronism, and the period detail (thatching, chilblains, laudanum, character references, penny bloods) is worn lightly and accurately. CHARACTER: Lizzie is one of the more fully realized working-class Victorian female protagonists one could encounter in contemporary fiction. Her moral complexity is genuine: she steals, she knows she steals, she keeps the thimble knowing it damns her, she feels pleasure in her own competence, she hates Edward for his privilege while needing him, she refuses sentimentality about her own situation. The moment she hangs on the ivy in the blizzard and feels clean hate is psychologically precise and earned. Edward is less fully realized but appropriately so — we see him through Lizzie's eyes, and his mixture of officer-clip authority, genuine helplessness, and tentative feeling is convincing. The detail of him lining books by height is perfect character shorthand. Mrs. Peel is a minor masterpiece of economy: her deaf ear turned strategically, her "I won't lie twice," her final gift of the button-boot. DIALOGUE: The dialogue is one of the piece's strongest elements. "You speak broad." / "You speak proud." is genuinely excellent — class conflict compressed to four words. The exchanges feel period-appropriate without being stagey. The dialogue reveals character efficiently and never over-explains. "Don't cry." / "I ain't crying." — the reader knows she is, and the denial is more revealing than tears would be. PACING: The pacing across eight chapters is well-managed. Each chapter advances both plot and character, and the repetition of the climbing motif (each ascent slightly different, each revealing new information about Lizzie's physical and emotional state) is structurally sophisticated. The piece knows when to compress (the blizzard chapter) and when to slow (the locked-room confrontation). The resolution in Chapter 8 is appropriately muted — no melodrama, no miracle, just arithmetic. PLOT: The plot is compelling precisely because it refuses easy resolution. The letters amount to nothing. Clara is human but chooses security. Edward is brave and useless. The five shillings don't cover the debt. These are not failures of plotting but its achievement — the story is about the limits of what courage and cleverness can accomplish against structural poverty. The ending, with the transom standing open all January, is genuinely moving without being sentimental. WORLD BUILDING: The world is built through accumulation of specific, accurate detail rather than exposition. The reader understands the entire social and economic structure of this world through Lizzie's counting: rent, coal, bread, wages, fines. The Hall's geography is established through Lizzie's servant knowledge — not the drive and portico but the coal-shed lean-to, the scullery grating. This is exactly right. WEAKNESSES: The piece is not without flaws. Occasionally the clipped style becomes slightly repetitive in its rhythms — the pattern of short declarative sentences can feel mechanical in extended passages. The thimble as symbol is perhaps slightly over-worked by the end, though it never becomes purple. Chapter 4 (the courses chapter) is the weakest — the physical detail of menstruation, while historically accurate and thematically appropriate (Lizzie's body as another site of uncontrollable expenditure), occasionally tips toward the gratuitous. The moment where Lizzie almost takes the jet brooch and doesn't is slightly under-motivated — "She wasn't sure why, and the not-sure shamed her worse than taking" is the one moment where the author tells rather than shows. POETRY AND METAPHOR: The metaphors are almost uniformly earned. "Bess never lifted her head" — the deaf dog as perfect detail. "Security beat first love. Lizzie felt the shawl's warmth and understood arithmetic better than ever-yours." This is the piece's thematic statement delivered with precision. The occasional poetic reach ("God marked difference. She marked keeping") lands because it's grounded in the established voice. There is no purple prose to speak of — the style is deliberately spare. UNEARNED TRANSFORMATIONS: The ending is not a transformation but a continuation. Lizzie goes to Hull. Edward stays locked. The transom stays open. This is the piece's great virtue — it earns its darkness by refusing false light. FAITHFULNESS TO PROMPT: The prompt ("One quickly learns the art of entering a manor through the upper windows") is not merely honored but made the structural and thematic spine of the entire piece. The climbing motif is both literal and metaphorical — Lizzie's competence, her knowledge of which windows give, is her only capital in a world that has stripped her of everything else. Initial Writing Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write a short story set in Wales. Task: write a short story over several chapters. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The story takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the first scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. The story will progress beyond this synopsis, and it's up to you where it goes.

ex leaks location; viral TikTok spots him buying Welsh cakes. **Tone Options:** - A: Warm rom-com, Notting Hill-in-Hay: witty, cozy, dialogue-screwball, PG-13, lots of tea. - B: Bittersweet indie: fame as loneliness, small-town grief and staying vs. leaving, more ache. - C: Spicy-sweet slow burn: banter first, longing later, closed-door with charged almost-kisses. - D: Community ensemble comedy: nosy locals, teenage shop assistant live-tweeting, pub choir as Greek chorus. - Language register: Mostly English dialogue with peppered Welsh (*bore da, cariad, iawn, diolch*), literary jokes for bookshop authenticity without caricature. **Plot Engines Beyond Chapter 1:** - The hiding fee: “You can hide behind Crime if you buy a book.” - The lie: staff tells press he’s not there; photo goes viral anyway. - The reason to return: left scarf / signed stock / needs first edition for co-star / wants quiet to learn lines. - External stakes: tabloid scandal (cheating rumors, drunken fight), studio PR forcing fake relationship with co-star, indie shop facing closure / landlord / Amazon, festival event needing celebrity draw. - Internal stakes: he fears he’s only lovable when performing; she fears being a footnote in someone’s press tour / being left again. - Set pieces: line-reading in shop after hours, helping unload boxes in rain, pub quiz team-up, coastal walk to escape signal, live radio interview ambush, signing table turned date. **Story Beats & Pacing Across 8 x ~1000 words (~8000 total):** - Pacing need: ~1000 words = ~6-7 pages, mostly dialogue = ~1-2 scenes per chapter max. So plan 1 strong turn per chapter, cliffhanger button line. - Ch1 ideas: *The Duck-In.* Entirely in shop. Paparazzi outside, kettle on. Charm offensive: jokes, autograph offer, “everyone loves me” fishing. Rebuff: “We don’t do selfies, we do purchases.” Ends with almost-moment + photo flash through window. - Ch2 ideas: *Aftermath.* Next day. Assistant posts blurry photo, locals descend. He sends apology / flowers / stack of his own DVDs to stock (horror). She calls PR. Banter by phone/text read aloud. - Ch3 ideas: *Return.* He comes back properly to learn lines, no entourage. After-hours read-through. Real talk slips between fake lines. First almost-touch over same book. - Ch4 ideas: *Town Sees.* Pub quiz / festival planning / beach walk. Public date-that-isn’t-a-date. His neediness shows when old man doesn’t know him. She defends him without meaning to. - Ch5 ideas: *High.* Cozy / romantic peak: cooking in flat above shop, open-mic, reading to kids, storm night. He is genuinely un-charming and loved for it. Paparazzi get cozy photo. - Ch6 ideas: *Tabloid Twist.* Fake-dating PR with co-star breaks, or shop address leaked, crowd ruins shop. Fight in dialogue: “You bring an audience everywhere.” Ego wound + abandonment wound collide. - Ch7 ideas: *Away / Quiet.* He leaves for London / Cardiff junket; she goes quiet, talks to friend/assistant. He bombs interview because he’s distracted / defends small town live. Grand gesture rethought for realism: not helicopter, but showing up to shelve books at 7am. - Ch8 ideas: *Limelight, Re-lit.* Festival day / shop anniversary. Choice: does she visit set? Does he stay? Options: happy-for-now with commute, he funds shop anonymously and she rejects/recasts it, epilogue a year later with reading plaque. Final line must be dialogue button, callbacks to Ch1 joke. - Alternative structures: 8 vignettes over one festival week; dual POV alternating chapters (his voice vs hers); each chapter titled after a book section (Romance, Travel, Crime, Poetry...). # Reflection What’s delicious here and what’s risky about each angle. Thinking out loud: The core charge works best if immunity is *thin* - if the owner is too cold for too long, the reader won’t buy the thaw and 1000-word chapters won’t have room to repair dislike. The sweet spot is professional brusqueness + competence kink: she’s busy, she has a shop to run, she won’t pause life for fame. That reads as immunity to him, whose whole life pauses for fame. But we need little leaks from page one - straightening books that don’t need straightening, remembering his coffee order, quoting his most embarrassing line perfectly - so inward fluster is legible in dialogue rhythm alone. His rogue + fragile ego balance is tricky. Pure rogue = unlikable; pure sad boy = loses the “thoroughly charming” brief. The version that sings is compulsive likability: he doesn’t hit on her so much as *audition* for her. Every joke checks for a laugh, every story waits for “wow.” When she doesn’t give it, his improv stutters - and that stutter is the first honest thing he’s said. That derailment is the attraction flip. Risk: making him pathetic or manipulative. Need to keep charm real - he’s kind to the teen assistant, remembers Welsh, tips well - so ego-need feels human, not predatory. Primarily-in-dialogue is both gift and constraint. Gift: distinct voices will carry chemistry fast, perfect for 8k slow burn. Constraint: interior fluster, Wales texture, and plot logistics can’t be info-dumped. Would need to smuggle world-building into talk - customers interrupting, radio in background, bilingual banter - and use stage beats sparingly but precisely. Too many beats and it stops being dialogue-driven; too few and we lose the “unspoken” part. Also how to do paparazzi tension without leaving the shop in Ch1? Sound design in dialogue: bell over door, shutters, phone buzz. Wales authenticity vs. postcard: Hay-on-Wye as book town is almost too perfect, which is why it works for a bookstore story, but risk of twee tourist Wales. Stronger if Welsh is lived-in, not decorative - price stickers, school run, landlord, rain - and if locals are not just quirky chorus but have stakes (shop closure, festival money, Welsh-language preservation). Using a Welsh actor-returned-home adds poignancy (fame vs. hiraeth - homesickness) but risks making it insider-only; using an English outsider makes Wales explanatory but risks savior narrative. Both could work; need to weigh which generates more natural language lessons / teasing. Scope control for 8 x 1000: That’s tight. Can’t do sprawling subplots - no evil ex + evil agent + evil landlord all at once. One external pressure (press/PR) + one intimate wound each is plenty. Each chapter can only hold one location and one turn (meet, return, reveal, rupture, repair). Slow burn needs restraint: if they kiss in Ch3 there’s nowhere to go; if they don’t touch till Ch6 tension may sag. Probably need micro-intimacies: shared umbrella, reading aloud, hand on book ladder. Endings: Full fairy-tale (he quits fame, buys cottage) feels false to premise and to indie-shop realism. More compelling is negotiated limelight: boundaries, commute, public/private compromise, career shift to theatre/writing. Bittersweet open ending could be literary but romance readers expect emotional payoff - a declared choice in dialogue, not just a kiss. Need to decide how famous vs. normal balance resolves without one person shrinking. Representation questions worth sitting with: default straight, 30s, white, London/Hollywood vs. white Welsh could feel stale. Queer version (male actor + male owner) or age-gap / second-chance / neurodivergent owner who scripts social interaction via booktalk could deepen “performing likability” themes. But each choice changes tabloid stakes and small-town dynamics - worth weighing, not rushing. Finally, titles/chapter shape: organizing chapters by bookshop sections is cute and gives each 1000-word chunk a governing metaphor, but could get gimmicky if forced. Alternating POV titles (“He Says / She Says”) would showcase distinct voices, the brief’s main demand. Still mulling which sustains momentum best without repeating the same banter beat eight times.
